findings.finding_value: T3 reveals forgiveness as uniquely faculty-comprehensive — it engages more named faculties with greater specificity than any other characteristic reviewed in this revision series. Memory is explicitly named (Jer 31:34 — divine memory as the content of forgiveness) and distinctively: forgiveness transforms memory in both directions — God's memory of sin is set aside permanently; the human forgiver releases the active use of memory against the offender. Affect is bidirectionally engaged: as prerequisite (somatic compassion, Mat 18:27) and as product (love, Luk 7:47; reverence, Psa 130:4). Conscience is addressed and purified by forgiveness (Heb 9:14). Volition is constitutive (the heart-level release is chosen). Cognition is enabled (Jer 31:34 — forgiveness → knowing God). The single silence is creativity (T3.5). T3's synthesis: forgiveness is the most faculty-comprehensive characteristic in the current review set — it reaches every major faculty with specific evidenced content, most strikingly in the memory domain.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-009: T1's four modes explain T3's faculty engagement pattern. The covenantal-objective mode (no inner-being prerequisite) corresponds to T3's absence of any faculty requirement for that mode. The divine re…
findings.finding_value: T1's four modes explain T3's faculty engagement pattern. The covenantal-objective mode (no inner-being prerequisite) corresponds to T3's absence of any faculty requirement for that mode. The divine relational-personal mode (faith, repentance, confession as access-postures) engages volition, conscience, and cognition. The human horizontal mode ("from your heart") requires volition, conscience, and moral evaluation. The intercessory mode requires the dependence-posture that engages cognition (accurate assessment of the grounds of the plea — God's character, not human merit) and volition. T1's definition of forgiveness as transitional (not terminal) is confirmed by T3's finding that every faculty engaged by forgiveness is deepened toward further engagement — not closed by the act but opened by it.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-014: T2's constitutional locations map onto T3's faculty engagements. The heart-locus (T2.3 — Mat 18:35) corresponds to T3's volition, moral evaluation, and conscience faculties — all heart-level. The cogn…

The cognition-locus (T2.4 — Jer 31:34) corresponds to T3's cognition and memory faculty engagements. The somatic-compassion locus (T2.5 — splagchnizomai) corresponds to T3's affect faculty at its somatic depth. The constitutional movement (T2.10 — guilt-bearing → forgiveness → love) is the sequence in which T3's faculties are engaged: conscience identifies the guilt → volition releases the claim → affect produces the love-response. Constitutional location determines faculty engagement sequence.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-020: T3's faculty deepenings (cognition enabled — Jer 31:34; love produced — Luk 7:47; conscience purified — Heb 9:14; volition redirected) are T5's formation products described at the faculty level. The f…
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty deepenings (cognition enabled — Jer 31:34; love produced — Luk 7:47; conscience purified — Heb 9:14; volition redirected) are T5's formation products described at the faculty level. The formation sequence (T5) is the longitudinal account of which T3's faculty engagements are the synchronic snapshots. The commanded forgiveness as sanctification discipline (T5.5 — Eph 4:32) is the formation vehicle through which the volitional faculty (T3.6) is habituated and the moral evaluation faculty (T3.8) is deepened. T3 and T5 together reveal the full formation arc: T3 shows what happens to each faculty in the moment of forgiveness; T5 shows what sustained habitual forgiveness does to the person over time.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-021: T3's memory faculty finding (Jer 31:34 — divine "remember no more") explains the R160 thought/knowledge co-occurrence at that verse: the divine cognitive act of non-remembering and the human cognitive…
findings.finding_value: T3's memory faculty finding (Jer 31:34 — divine "remember no more") explains the R160 thought/knowledge co-occurrence at that verse: the divine cognitive act of non-remembering and the human cognitive outcome of knowing God meet in the same verse because they are structurally connected — the guilt-barrier's removal (forgiveness) enables the cognitive-relational access (knowing God). T3's affect-faculty finding (love produced — Luk 7:47) explains the R103 love co-occurrence (8 shared verses) — love is the affective downstream product of forgiveness. T3's conscience faculty finding confirms the R073 guilt structural partnership — guilt is what conscience identifies as the prior condition that forgiveness addresses. Faculty engagements (T3) and structural co-occurrences (T6) are mutually explanatory.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-022: T7's literary forms explain why T3 finds different faculty engagements in different evidential contexts. The cultic-legal corpus (Lev 4:20) — covenantal-objective mode — requires no named faculty enga…
findings.finding_value: T7's literary forms explain why T3 finds different faculty engagements in different evidential contexts. The cultic-legal corpus (Lev 4:20) — covenantal-objective mode — requires no named faculty engagement (T3 finds no faculty requirement for this mode). The prophetic corpus (Jer 31:34) primarily engages cognition and memory (T3.2, T3.3). The Synoptic narrative corpus (Luk 7:47, Mat 18:27, Mat 18:35) engages affect, volition, and conscience most richly. The apostolic letter corpus (Eph 1:7, Eph 4:32) grounds the formation dimension (T3.10 conscientiousness, T5.5 sanctification). Each literary form carries specific faculty registers — T7's literary analysis explains T3's faculty engagement distribution.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-003: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion re…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion responds, it does not originate or create. It is the most responsive of the faculties-engaging characteristics. Second, affect and moral action are structurally unified in compassion — not sequentially related but simultaneous. Affect is the mechanism of movement (splanchnizō is both the felt inner event and the cause of the action), not a precursor or accompaniment. This is unique among the characteristics reviewed: in most other registries, affect and volition are distinguishable stages; in compassion, the felt movement is already the morally motivated action beginning. A third distinctive finding: compassion converts moral knowledge into motivated action — it is the motivational ground of conscientiousness, not a product of it. The conscience faculty engagement reveals compassion as conscience-healing: it addresses the pitiable condition that conscience perceives as a moral claim, resolving the tension between moral knowledge and moral incapacity. The three relational modes (building/sustaining — chesed; restoring/repairing — splanchnizō; extending across difference — Good Samaritan) are a new finding not in the instruction typology.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-003: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked …
findings.finding_value: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I but the grace of God that is with me." Agency is not displaced but constituted by grace. This relationship holds in paradox that the T3.6 prompt options (enable/deepen/bypass/impair) cannot accommodate — a prompt design limitation noted for catalogue revision. Second, grace produces moral clarity (T3.8 — sharpens moral evaluation rather than bypassing it): the person who recognises grace has made a precise moral evaluation (they know they received what they did not deserve). Third, grace and conscience are mutually necessary: grace is the condition within which conscience can operate fully without destroying the person; conscience without grace produces condemnation; grace without conscience produces presumption (T3.9). Fourth, grace is the primary relational faculty developer in the registry's evidence — it reaches every relational register (vertical access, horizontal forgiving, speech-grace) and enables each one. Creativity (T3.5) is the one genuinely silent faculty — not an impairment but a non-engagement: grace receives and constitutes, it does not create.

The covenant's primary sustained effect is a knowing of God — a cognitive-relational act of recognition and knowledge at the deepest personal level. (4) 2 Cor 3:6 — "not of the letter but of the Spirit" — spiritual cognition (Spirit-enabled understanding) is contrasted with mere cognitive processing of the letter. Covenant engages cognition profoundly: it both produces and depends on a particular quality of knowing.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-099-003: T3 reveals that kindness engages a remarkably wide range of inner faculties — nine of eleven are evidenced with at least partial engagement. The two genuine absences (imagination and creativity) are s…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals that kindness engages a remarkably wide range of inner faculties — nine of eleven are evidenced with at least partial engagement. The two genuine absences (imagination and creativity) are structurally coherent: kindness is relational and loyally directed, not generative. The most significant faculty engagements are: (a) volition — kindness is chosen, not merely felt; the "put on" and "love kindness" language makes this constitutive; (b) agency — chrēsteuomai names love actively exercising kindness — kindness is enacted, not passive; (c) relational capacity — kindness constitutes relationships in their quality, not merely accompanies them; (d) conscientiousness — the chasid represents the full integration of moral awareness, will, and action in consistent reliable pattern; (e) taste as the primary perceptive mode — "tasted that the Lord is good" establishes that kindness is encountered experientially before it is understood conceptually. The pattern across all engaged faculties: kindness integrates the whole inner person — it does not operate as a single-faculty characteristic but as a whole-person orientation. T3's most significant intra-tier finding: kindness is a multi-faculty characteristic whose breadth of engagement reflects its status as a constitutive relational orientation rather than a single affective or volitional act.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-099-022: T3's finding that taste is the primary perceptive faculty for kindness (1Pet 2:3 — "tasted that the Lord is good / chrēstos") is grounded in T7's lexical finding that chrēstos itself carries the quali…
findings.finding_value: T3's finding that taste is the primary perceptive faculty for kindness (1Pet 2:3 — "tasted that the Lord is good / chrēstos") is grounded in T7's lexical finding that chrēstos itself carries the quality of agreeable goodness — something that can be tasted and found to be of a certain quality. The word chrēstos, which names the characteristic, contains an implicit sensory metaphor: it is the kind of characteristic that one encounters through experience (taste) before grasping conceptually. T7's lexical finding that chesed's semantic range includes goodness/faithfulness — not merely kindness — maps onto T3's cognition finding (T3.2 — Hos 6:6 pairing chesed with knowledge of God): genuine chesed requires a cognitive grasp of who God is, which is consistent with chesed carrying a knowledge-dimension in its semantic range. T7's most useful human science framework (developmental psychology/attachment theory) connects with T3's relational capacity finding: attachment theory explains the faculty-level mechanism by which the "secure base" of divine chesed enables the human person to exercise relational capacity toward others.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-060-003: T3 as a whole reveals that this characteristic engages virtually every inner faculty in the programme's 11-faculty model — the only consistent gap is creativity (T3.5, S across three prompts). The pat…
findings.finding_value: T3 as a whole reveals that this characteristic engages virtually every inner faculty in the programme's 11-faculty model — the only consistent gap is creativity (T3.5, S across three prompts). The pattern of engagement is not uniform: perception is engaged as precondition (God hears before giving); cognition is constituted (wisdom is given, not generated); memory is deepened (the narrative-temporal dimension of covenantal giving); affect is the source of giving (compassion, anger) and the target of transformation (mourning→gladness); volition is called forth and elevated (genuine giving cannot be coerced); agency is the bridge between disposition and act; moral evaluation both produces and is produced by the characteristic; conscience is engaged indirectly through Spirit-forming and prophetic warning; conscientiousness at the human apex is the full integration of all three (moral awareness, will, act). Relational capacity is intrinsic — every mode is two-party. What T3 reveals as a whole: faithfulness-as-giving is not a faculty-specific characteristic but a whole-person characteristic — it recruits and integrates all active faculties into a unified inner-being act. The creativity silence is the only dimension where the data cannot confirm engagement.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-013: The faculty engagement pattern (T3) and the formation arc (T5) are directly linked: the faculties engaged by the characteristic are precisely the faculties that are formed through it. Cognition is bot…
findings.finding_value: The faculty engagement pattern (T3) and the formation arc (T5) are directly linked: the faculties engaged by the characteristic are precisely the faculties that are formed through it. Cognition is both constituted by endowing giving (T3.2 — wisdom deposited) and is the target of formation (T5.5 — Spirit given to instruct shapes over time). Memory is engaged by the covenantal mode (T3.3 — narrative-temporal dimension) and is the sustained environment of covenantal formation (T5.5 — the history of received giving shapes identity). Agency is both the bridge between disposition and act (T3.7) and is restored/enabled by eschatological giving (T3.7 Q&A-087 — depressed agency is renewed). Suffering reveals (T5.4 — tests the characteristic) and tests affect, volition, and conscientiousness (T3.4, T3.6, T3.10). What this pair reveals: the characteristic forms the person by engaging and developing the same faculties it requires for its own expression. Formation is circular in this characteristic: it needs faculties to be enacted, and its enactment develops those faculties further.

In the righteous register: Psa 119:104 — "through your precepts I get understanding; therefore I hate every false way" — cognition (understanding through the precepts) produces directed hatred. The cognitive sequence runs: learning → understanding → hatred of the false. In the disordered register: Pro 26:24 — "whoever hates disguises himself with his lips and harbours deceit in his heart" — cognition is recruited into the service of the hidden hatred, managing the concealment.

The cognitive faculty is both the origin and the instrument of contempt. Psa 10:13: the cognitive conviction ("you will not call to account") is what generates the contemptuous inner speech. The mind renders a verdict that then operates as the ground of the dismissal. Sustained contempt also impairs cognition: Jer 23:17 — the community that despises God's word becomes receptive to false prophets. The contempt has corrupted the cognitive capacity to distinguish true from false prophetic address.

Rom 2:22 (bdelussomai) shows the cognitive dimension: the person claims to abhor idols — a cognitive position they hold. But the apostle's challenge ("do you rob temples?") exposes that the cognitive claim does not correspond to an actual inner state. The cognitive faculty can assert abhorrence without the genuine visceral recoil being present. This is the gap between claimed abhorrence and genuine abhorrence.

The cognitive element is present in Psa 54:3's "they do not set God before themselves" — a cognitive-dispositional failure. The mind's governance framework has excluded God. The ruthlessness is downstream of a cognitive framework that operates without the governing premise of divine accountability.

Job 19:5: "if indeed you magnify yourselves against me and make my disgrace an argument against me" — reproach is being deployed cognitively as an argument against the person. The cognitive dimension of reproach is its use as evidence — others use the condition of being reproached as proof of unworthiness. The reproached person must cognitively resist that argument from inside the condition.

1Pe 5:8: "be sober-minded" — the adversary relationship demands disciplined cognitive engagement. Clear-headed, accurate cognitive assessment of the threat is the prescribed response to the cosmic adversary.

The moral evaluation faculty (cognitively expressed) has been so thoroughly inverted in malice that destruction is evaluated as good and the other's loss is evaluated as gain. Eze 36:5: "gave my land to themselves as a possession" — the malice is combined with acquisitive cognitive re-categorisation of the other's property as one's own legitimate prize.

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** Yes — "knowing that God's righteous judgment" (Rom 2:5, VSG 3207-001); the proclamation of God's righteousness produces knowledge in those who hear it. Felix's encounter (Act 24:25) was a cognitive engagement with the standard of righteousness through Paul's reasoning.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Yes — "the thoughts of the righteous are just" (Pro 12:5, VSG M26-A2-011). The cognitive content of the righteous person — their inner reasoning and deliberation — is characterised as just and right. Righteousness shapes cognition: what the righteous person thinks is shaped by righteousness.

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** Yes — "then you will understand righteousness and justice and equity, every good path" (Pro 2:9, VSG 1212-002). Understanding is a cognitive function; uprightness produces understanding. B engages the cognitive faculty in its discernment mode.

**[C — Justification]** Yes — "for we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law" (Rom 3:28, VSG 3410-001, in the F-group but directly relevant to C's cognitive dimension). The cognitive act of understanding and believing the grounds of justification is integral to receiving it.
**[D — Avenging Justice]** The cry for justice is primarily volitional and affective rather than cognitive. Silence on primary cognitive engagement.

**[E — Condemnation]** Yes — "by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned" (Mat 12:37) — the cognitive content of speech becomes the grounds of verdict. Self-condemnation (autokatakritos) involves cognitive self-assessment.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** Yes — this is the sub-group most explicitly engaging cognition. Logizomai is a cognitive-deliberative act: reasoning, counting, reckoning, considering. The entire F-sub-group is a study in how the cognitive faculty is applied to moral reality.

**[G — Structural Opposites]** Yes — but impaired. "They do not know how to do right" (Amo 3:10); "none of the wicked shall understand" (Dan 12:10). Wickedness distorts and disables the cognitive faculty's application to moral truth.

**[CLUSTER — T3.2]** E. Cognition is engaged across A2 (righteous thoughts), B (understanding), C (belief in the grounds of justification), E (self-assessment), and F (the deliberative reckoning act). It is impaired in G. The reckoning faculty (F) is the most explicitly cognitive sub-group. The cluster reveals that righteousness and cognition are deeply connected: what the person thinks and how they reason is shaped by their moral state.

findings.finding_value: M01-A is the most cognitively engaged sub-group in the cluster. Reverential fear is the **root of knowing**: Pro 1:7 (anchor A-VCG-02: "the foundational inner disposition from which all knowledge begins"); Psa 111:10 ("fear of the Lord is the foundational inner disposition from which wisdom begins — constitutive of understanding"); Job 28:28 ("fear of the Lord is identified as wisdom itself"). Fear of God is not merely a precondition for knowledge but is identified as the inner posture that constitutes genuine understanding. It is epistemologically foundational.

M01-B's acute fear engages cognition in a disruptive mode: 1Sa 17:11 (Saul and all Israel "dismayed and deeply afraid — Goliath's words produce a two-layered inner impact: shock that **disorganises thought** and fear that disables action"); Mar 9:6 ("Peter's inability to know what to say at the transfiguration is explained by the terror gripping the disciples — the fear so overwhelms their inner faculties that thought and speech are disabled").

M01-D dismay is a cognitive-shutdown characteristic: Isa 21:3 (cannot see — cognitive-perceptive shutdown); Job 32:15 (friends "dismayed into complete speechlessness — the rational and verbal faculties entirely shut down"); Dan 7:28 (dismay "works through Daniel's thoughts" but Daniel resolves to keep the matter inward — a last cognitive act before the colour changes).

M01-F anticipatory dread is the cognitively richest disordered sub-group. De.a.gah (H1674) as anxiety carries a cognitive-ruminating quality (Borkovec's verbal-linguistic worry model is directly applicable — see T7.3). 2Cor 12:20 (anchor F-VCG-05: "Paul's fear is an anticipatory dread rooted in **thought** about what he may find — engaging the mind with anxious expectation"). The cognitive engagement is anticipatory and future-oriented.

The cognitive faculty is engaged across M01 in two opposed directions: M01-A **enables** cognition (fear-of-God as the root of knowledge), while M01-B, D, and F (in different degrees) **disrupt or distort** cognition. This is a structural finding: ordered fear (M01-A) is epistemologically constitutive; disordered fear (M01-D, M01-B's paralysing dimension) is epistemologically destructive.

Yes. Gen 4:6 (M02-B-VCG-02): God questions Cain directly about his incensed state — "the emotion is subject to moral examination and is not beyond the person's control." The cognitive faculty of self-examination is engaged by the anger. Job 32:2–5 (M02-B-VCG-04): Elihu's anger arises from theological reasoning — he perceives a logical failure (Job's self-justification before God) and the anger is the response to that cognitive assessment. The anger is cognitively grounded.

Yes. Gen 4:6 (M02-B-VCG-02): God questions Cain directly about his incensed state — "the emotion is subject to moral examination and is not beyond the person's control." The cognitive faculty of self-examination is engaged by the anger. Job 32:2–5 (M02-B-VCG-04): Elihu's anger arises from theological reasoning — he perceives a logical failure (Job's self-justification before God) and the anger is the response to that cognitive assessment. The anger is cognitively grounded.

Rom 2:5 (M02-A-VCG-03): a hard and impenitent heart "actively accumulates wrath as a mounting store of divine judgment" — the cognitive orientation of stubborn unbelief is the mechanism that accumulates the wrath-consequence. The cognitive faculty of assessment (of one's own moral state before God) is the faculty engaged.

Grief engages cognition in two ways. First, cognitive recognition produces grief: the disciples' grief at Jesus's betrayal announcement (Mat 26:22 — M03-C-VCG-02) is triggered by understanding the implication of the announcement; Peter's grief at the third question (Joh 21:17 — M03-C-VCG-01) arises from cognitive recognition of his own past failure. Second, grief impairs cognition: the prophet's grief so total that the prophetic perception precedes cognitive processing (Elisha weeping before Hazael asks why — 2Ki 8:11-12 — M03-A-VCG-04); pain fills all days and prevents the heart from finding rest (Ecc 2:23 — M03-F-VCG-01), interrupting normal cognitive function.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, as a precondition. Isa 25:9 shows the cognitive recognition ("behold, this is our God; we have waited for him") preceding and grounding the exultation ("let us be glad and rejoice in his salvation"). Exo 18:9 shows Jethro's exultation arising from hearing (cognitive reception) of God's acts. The commanded exultations (Psa 32:11; Isa 65:18) presuppose knowledge of who God is as the ground for the commanded inner state.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, as a consistent enabling precondition. Neh 8:12 — joy arising "because they had understood the words declared to them" — the most direct evidence that cognitive comprehension produces Joy. Isa 25:9 — "we have waited for him… behold, this is our God" (recognitive cognition → exultant rejoicing). Act 13:48 — "when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing" — hearing and cognitively receiving the word produces joy. 1Cor 13:6 — love "rejoices with the truth" — the cognitive-evaluative act of recognising truth is the object of Joy. Mat 25:21 ("enter into the joy of your master") — the cognitive understanding of what the master's joy is shapes the servant's aspiration.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Yes, through specific cognitive acts: Jas 1:2 ("count it all joy") — counting/reckoning is an arithmetic-like cognitive act; Heb 12:2 ("for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame") — Christ's cognitive holding of the eschatological joy as more real than the present shame is a sustained cognitive orientation; Mat 5:12 ("for your reward is great in heaven") gives the cognitive ground for commanded rejoicing — a propositional truth that orients the cognitive frame.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes — this is the primary faculty for Gladness, as established at T1.8. The entire M04-L-VCG-02 corpus (45 verses of moral appraisal) is an exercise of the cognitive faculty: weighing conduct against standards of goodness (Exo 18:17; Neh 5:9; Pro 17:26; 18:5; Mic 6:8); comparing relational worth (Rut 4:15; 2Sa 18:3); assessing comparative value of wisdom over wealth (Pro 8:11; 16:16; 16:8). Job 34:4 ("let us know among ourselves what is good") explicitly names cognition as the faculty being exercised.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes, in the study-and-meditation register: (1) **Psa 1:2** — delight in the law → meditation day and night — Delight producing sustained cognitive engagement; (2) **Psa 111:2** — delight in God's works driving their study; (3) **Psa 119:24** — "your testimonies are my delight; they are my counselors" — Delight in testimonies producing the cognitive guidance that the testimonies provide; (4) **Ecc 12:10** — the Preacher seeking words of delight — cognitive-aesthetic search; (5) **1Ch 28:9** — "a willing mind" (cha.phets adj) — cognitive-volitional orientation; (6) **Pro 8:11** — nothing desired (che.phets) can compare with wisdom — the cognitive act of comparing wisdom against all other desired objects.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Partially, in the wisdom-comparative register: M04-K-VCG-03 (the better-than comparatives) require cognitive evaluation to assess which option is genuinely more pleasant — Psa 37:16 (little of the righteous better than abundance of wicked); Pro 15:16, 17; 16:32; 17:1 (various integrity-vs-abundance comparatives). This is a cognitive-evaluative engagement, albeit secondary to the primary affective-receptive dimension. Psa 34:8's "taste and see" also involves a cognitive element: the imperative to see (perceive and assess) alongside taste.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes — this is Wonder's primary faculty, as established at T1.8: (1) **"Things we cannot comprehend"** (Job 37:5) — comprehension as the cognitive faculty Wonder presses against; (2) **"Things too wonderful for me, which I did not know"** (Job 42:3) — knowledge as the measure of Wonder; (3) **"Make me understand… I will meditate on your wondrous works"** (Psa 119:27) — understanding enabling meditative engagement with Wonder; (4) **"The wisdom of their wise men shall perish"** (Isa 29:14) — human cognitive accumulation eclipsed by God's wonders; (5) **"Do you know the balancings of the clouds?"** (Job 37:16) — rhetorical challenge to human knowledge producing Wonder-recognition.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Cognitive faculty engagement varies significantly across the seven: (1) **Cognitively-primary**: Gladness (Char 3) and Wonder (Char 6) — the two most cognitively-primary characteristics; (2) **Cognitive as enabling condition**: Joy (Char 2) — Neh 8:12 (comprehension → Joy); Exultation (Char 1) — knowing God's acts (Exo 18:9; Isa 25:9) as the cognitive ground for exultation; (3) **Cognitive as sustained-engagement driver**: Delight (Char 4) — the most powerful cognitive-driver in the cluster; Delight in God's word produces sustained meditation, study, and wisdom (Psa 1:2; 111:2); (4) **Cognitive as eschatological-reframing**: Suffering-Joy (Char 7) — Jas 1:2's "count it all joy" and Heb 12:2's "for the joy set before him" are the cluster's most explicit cognitive-reframing acts; (5) **Cognitively secondary**: Pleasure (Char 5) — engages cognition only in the wisdom-comparative register (M04-K-VCG-03); primarily affective-receptive without cognitive mediation; Exultation (Char 1) — cognitive knowledge provides the ground but the characteristic itself is primarily affective-volitional.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. The idolatry-shame passages (M07-B-VCG-02) show shame as the product of cognitive collapse — when the mind's confident belief in the idol is exposed as false, the cognitive disorientation (confusion, bewilderment — Isa 45:16: "go in confusion together") is itself the shame experience. Jer 31:19 (vc=38509) — "after I was *instructed*, I struck my thigh; I was ashamed" — instruction (cognitive engagement) produces the shame recognition. The wisdom literature pattern (Pro 18:13 — answering before listening is folly and shame) shows shame as the consequence of cognitive failure (listening bypassed). Shame is cognitively engaged throughout: it requires self-assessment, comparison with a standard, and recognition of the gap.

**[CHAR-2]** E — CHAR-2 collapses confident cognition: the defeated "go in confusion" — their ability to think through their situation and act effectively is destroyed. Cognitive paralysis accompanies military defeat (Jer 49:23 — "melting in fear, troubled like the sea"). In VCG-03, God's abasement targets the cognitive self-assessment of the proud.

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — The cognitive worth-assessment process is engaged and distorted in CHAR-3: the dishonorer makes a wrong cognitive judgment about worth. The structural-dishonour mode (VCG-02) is more cognitively neutral — it is the result of sovereign assignment rather than a cognitive failure.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4 is a cognitive operation — the conscience assesses against a standard (God's sight, created order, community norms) and produces a judgment. The cognitive faculty is CHAR-4's primary operating mode. VCG-03 shows cognitive corruption: the evaluative judgment is produced but by a wrong standard.

---

**[CHAR-5]** E — The contempt-er's cognitive faculty is engaged: the worth-assessment judgment ("this person is of no account") is a cognitive act. 1Cor 6:4's cognitive assessment about standing; Rom 14:3/10's cognitive-evaluative judgment about a brother's worth before God — these show the cognitive faculty producing CHAR-5. For the recipient, the cognitive dimension is engaged in the ongoing self-assessment that contempt-shame distorts.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — Cognition is engaged in CHAR-6 through the moral self-assessment that innocence requires. Abimelech's appeal to his innocence (Gen 20:5) involves cognitive self-assessment: he knows he acted in ignorance and moral intention. Psa 73:13's lament involves cognitive evaluation: the psalmist has cognitively assessed his own moral maintenance and found it, in his experience, to have been in vain. The cognitive faculty is engaged in CHAR-6's self-assessment and moral accounting.

---

**[CLUSTER]** E — Cognition is engaged across all six with varying prominence. Char 4 is primarily cognitive (the evaluative judgment is a cognitive act). Chars 1, 3, 5 engage cognition in self-assessment and worth-assessment functions. Char 2 engages it in the cognitive collapse of the humiliated (confusion, dismay). Char 6 engages it in the cognitive self-assessment that constitutes the innocence-claim. Cluster-level cognitive theme: the shame-field is irreducibly cognitive — it involves ongoing assessment of standing, worth, and moral quality across all six characteristics. The cognitive faculty is the site where worth-assessments originate and where the shame-field's distortions begin. The correction of the shame-field therefore requires cognitive correction as one of its components.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. CHAR-1 engages the cognitive faculty primarily through distorting the faculties of understanding, discernment, and self-assessment. Eze 28:17 (vc=34047, M08-A1-VCG-02): "your heart was proud because of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom for the sake of your splendour" — wisdom (the highest cognitive faculty in the Hebrew tradition) is directly corrupted by CHAR-1. Luk 1:51 (vc=33930, M08-A1-VCG-03): arrogance is located "in the thoughts of their hearts" — the cognitive-mental faculty (dianoiai) named as the seat. 1Sa 16:7 (vc=12091, M08-A1-VCG-03; vc=54394, M08-A4-VCG-05): the human cognitive standard prizes outward height, while God's knowing looks at the heart — CHAR-1 in the cognitive register produces wrong standards of assessment. Rom 12:16 (vc=60877, M08-A4-VCG-01): "never be wise in your own sight" — the cognitive self-assessment is the specific pride-form being addressed here, naming a distorted self-knowing as the danger.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes. CHAR-2 engages the cognitive faculty through self-deceptive miscalculation of the self's actual position and vulnerability. Obd 3 (vc=34108, M08-B-VCG-02): "arrogance located in the heart as self-deceptive confidence in physical inaccessibility" — the cognitive assessment is distorted into false security. Jer 49:16 (vc=34115, M08-B-VCG-02): "the arrogance of your heart has deceived you" — CHAR-2 as a cognitive distortion that produces confident miscalculation.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, centrally. 1Cor 4:7 (vc=33871, M08-C-VCG-01): "what do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" — the cognitive attribution process is the specific locus of CHAR-3's error; the boaster cognitively misattributes received goods as self-generated. 2Cor 10:12 (context of M08-C-VCG-02): "when they measure themselves by one another and compare themselves with one another, they are without understanding" — false self-comparison as a cognitive process named as "without understanding" (asunetos).

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes — as its primary faculty. CHAR-4 is constitutively a cognitive phenomenon. Col 2:18 (vc=33941, M08-D-VCG-01): "inflated by his sensuous mind [nous]" — the mind is both the seat and the vehicle of CHAR-4. Rom 12:3 (vc=60866, M08-D-VCG-02): the froneō (thinking/mind-setting) faculty is directly addressed — "do not think [huperfroneō] more highly than you ought." 1Cor 8:1 (vc=33935, M08-D-VCG-01): knowledge (gnōsis — a cognitive content) generates the inflation. CHAR-4 is the cognitive faculty malfunctioning as a self-assessment mechanism.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes. Isa 47:8 (vc=9563, M08-E-VCG-02): "you who say in your heart, 'I am, and there is no one besides me; I shall not sit as a widow or know the loss of children'" — the cognitive faculty generates an explicit self-ontological claim: CHAR-5 has produced a cognitive picture of the self as ontologically complete and self-sustaining. Obd 3 (vc=65674, M08-E-VCG-02): "who will bring me down?" — a cognitive assessment of invulnerability. These are cognitive self-assessments of the highest order — not merely social standing but ontological self-completeness.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All five characteristics engage the cognitive faculty. The cluster comparison reveals that cognitive engagement in M08 consistently involves a specific type of cognitive error: misattribution of self-generated versus received. CHAR-1: cognitive displacement of God from the inner awareness. CHAR-2: cognitive self-deception about vulnerability (Obd 3, M08-B-VCG-02) and self-authorisation beyond one's standing. CHAR-3: misattribution of received goods as self-generated (1Cor 4:7, M08-C-VCG-01). CHAR-4: inflated cognitive self-assessment beyond warranted measure (Rom 12:3, M08-D-VCG-02). CHAR-5: cognitive self-sufficiency claim — the most extreme misattribution, declaring "I am" (Isa 47:8, M08-E-VCG-02). The cluster-synthesis: M08's cognitive engagement is dominated by misattribution — the creature misattributes to itself what comes from God. CHAR-4 names this at the cognitive faculty level most precisely (inflated self-picture), but the same misattribution dynamic runs through all five.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, directly and explicitly. 2Cor10:5 — "take every thought captive to obey Christ" — the cognitive faculty (every thought, noēma) is the battleground. The "arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God" are cognitive constructs that submission must overcome. The cognitive faculty is engaged as both the site of resistance (proud reasoning) and the domain where submission must be established (cognitive allegiance to Christ). Additionally, the discernment required to distinguish legitimate from illegitimate authority (Gal2:5 — Paul deliberately withholding submission) is a cognitive-evaluative function that submission requires.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, indirectly. Genuine contrition requires genuine cognitive self-assessment — the accurate knowledge of one's failure or limitation before God. Without a cognitive grasp of the moral reality (what has occurred, why it matters before God's holiness), the characteristic cannot be genuine. However, the two-verse corpus does not name the mind or cognitive faculty explicitly; the cognitive engagement is implied by the nature of the characteristic rather than directly evidenced in the text of these two verses.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes. The self-assessment of shared weakness (Heb5:2 — "he himself is beset with weakness") requires a genuine cognitive recognition of one's own creaturely limitation — not merely an emotional sense of weakness but a clear cognitive understanding of one's shared condition with those who err. Metriopatheō's "measured" quality (metrios) also implies cognitive calibration: the person must cognitively assess what measure of engagement is appropriate to the erring person's condition, neither excessive nor insufficient.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Semnotēs engages the cognitive faculty in the self-assessment dimension: genuine possession of the characteristic requires accurately assessing what is appropriate gravity for one's role and context (the comprehensiveness of "in every way" in 1Ti2:2 and "all dignity" in 1Ti3:4 implies an ongoing cognitive calibration). Tit2:7 — dignity alongside integrity authenticating teaching — implies that the teacher must cognitively maintain the connection between inner character and outward instruction, ensuring consistency.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The cognitive faculty is engaged in the assessment of what to give and how to serve: 1Ch28:21 — "every willing man who has skill for any kind of service" — the willingness operates alongside skill (cognitive-technical competence) rather than replacing it. The willing person brings their cognitive skill to the service rather than operating without cognitive engagement. The characteristic does not bypass the cognitive faculty but enables its wholehearted engagement rather than its reluctant or partial participation.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, and extensively. Pro11:2 directly links humility to wisdom as its cognitive companion: "with the humble is wisdom." Phili2:3 defines humility as a cognitive act — "count others more significant than yourselves" — using hēgeomai (to reckon, consider, evaluate). This cognitive dimension is not peripheral but central to the definition: genuine humility requires an accurate cognitive assessment of relative worth that re-orders the self's self-assessment. Col2:18 evidences the distorted cognitive state that false humility produces: the "sensuous mind" that is puffed up, revealing that genuine humility requires cognitive realism rather than self-inflated assessment. Mat11:29 ("learn from me") frames humility as itself an educational-cognitive process.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All six engage the cognitive faculty; the engagement is most constitutive for CHAR-1 and CHAR-2, most presuppositional for the others. CHAR-1: Phili2:3 names a cognitive act (counting others more significant — hēgeomai) as the definition of humility; Pro11:2 directly links humility to wisdom as its cognitive companion. CHAR-2: 2Cor10:5 makes the cognitive faculty (taking every thought captive to Christ) the explicit battleground of submission. CHAR-3: requires genuine cognitive moral self-assessment as precondition for the characteristic. CHAR-4: requires cognitive self-assessment of shared weakness as its enabling ground. CHAR-5: requires ongoing cognitive calibration of appropriate gravity for each context. CHAR-6: cognitive skill must be deployed alongside willing-heartedness (1Ch28:21 — skill plus willingness); the characteristic enables wholehearted cognitive engagement. Cluster-level: CHAR-1 and CHAR-2 are the most distinctively cognitive among M09's characteristics — both explicitly name cognitive reordering as part of their constitutional identity. This distinguishes them from CHAR-3 through CHAR-6, where cognition is enabling rather than constitutive. The implication: M09's foundational characteristics (CHAR-1, CHAR-2) are cognitively demanding in a way the supplementary characteristics are not.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. The "wilful" (knowing) element of the characteristic name directly implicates cognition. The definitional marker is that the person knows what they are doing. Gen 39:9 — Joseph's cognitive evaluation ("how then can I do this great wickedness?") is the evidence of active knowing. Lev 4:23 and 4:28 ("the sin which he has committed is made known to him") show that realisation (cognitive awareness arriving) triggers obligation — the cultic system is activated precisely when cognition registers the sin. Deu 19:15 ("only on the evidence of two witnesses shall a charge be established") grounds sinning in legally verifiable cognitive fact. The cognitive faculty is engaged as the basis for the "wilful" quality: knowing the wrong before doing it.

**[CHAR-10]** E — The cognitive faculty is engaged through Act 21:21's apostasy mechanism. "Teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or walk according to our customs" — the accusation names a cognitive-instructional transmission: teaching is the cognitive mode through which apostasy is allegedly spread. The cognitive faculty is the target: what the Jews are taught shapes what they believe about their covenantal obligations. For enticement, the cognitive faculty is bypassed rather than directly engaged (desire operates below deliberate cognition); for hypocrisy, the cognitive faculty assesses the social situation and chooses the performed identity.

**[CHAR-11]** E — The cognitive faculty is engaged centrally through the law's function. Rom 3:20 — "through the law comes knowledge of sin" — the law's primary cognitive function is to produce knowledge of the sin-condition in the person's mind; without the law, the condition lacks cognitive recognition. Rom 7:7 — "if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. For I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, 'You shall not covet'" — the cognitive content of the condition becomes known through the commandment's prohibition. The cognitive faculty receives the law's content and thereby recognises what the condition involves.

**[CHAR-12]** S — The 9-verse corpus does not explicitly engage the cognitive faculty in connection with sin's enslaving power. The characteristic operates through will-captivity, identity-allegiance, and structural imprisonment rather than through explicit cognitive processes in the corpus.

**[CHAR-13]** E — The cognitive faculty is engaged through the law's disclosure function and through accusation. Rom 3:20 (CHAR-11 corpus, but relevant principle) — the law provides the cognitive framework for recognising the record. Directly in CHAR-13: Pro 24:9 — "the devising of folly is sin" — the cognitive act of deliberate scheming creates a record entry; the mind's devising is itself sinful. Job 13:23 — "how many are my iniquities and my sins? Make me know my transgression and my sin" — Job's cognitive faculty cannot self-enumerate the record; he requires divine cognitive disclosure to know what the record contains.

**[CHAR-14]** E — Yes — centrally through the recognition and repentance dimensions. Lev 4:14 — "when the sin which they have committed becomes known" — cognitive recognition is the prerequisite. Act 2:38 — "repent" (metanoeō — change of mind) — the cognitive reorientation is explicitly named as the seeking-act in the NT. Act 10:43 — "to him all the prophets bear witness" — the prophetic cognitive testimony provides the intellectual content that faith engages; the cognitive knowledge of who Jesus is and what the prophets said is what enables the believing-for-forgiveness.

**[CHAR-15]** E — Yes — through the unbelief dimension. Psa 78:32 — "they did not believe" — belief is a cognitive-trust act; the failure to believe despite wonders is a cognitive failure to integrate evidence correctly. Isa 43:27 — "your first father sinned" — the prophetic speech engages the cognitive faculty of the present generation as it hears its ancestral history named; the cognitive reception of this naming is required for the generational pattern to be addressed.

**[CHAR-16]** E — Yes — through the self-assessment and category-application dimensions. Joh 9:24/25 — "we know that this man is a sinner" / "whether he is a sinner I do not know" — the cognitive act of determining who qualifies as a sinner is explicitly contested; Gal 2:15 — "Gentile sinners" is a cognitive-ethnic categorisation; Rom 7:13 — "that sin might be shown to be sin, and through the commandment might become sinful beyond measure" — the commandment's function is cognitive: it reveals and magnifies sin's character so that the mind can know it accurately.

**[CHAR-17]** E — Yes — through the knowledge-triggers and the retrospective-causal reasoning. Lev 5:17 — "though he did not know it, then realizes his guilt, he shall bear his iniquity" — the cognitive knowledge of the violation is what activates the guilt-state; knowledge is the guilt-trigger. Gen 42:21 — "that is why this distress has come upon us" — the brothers' cognitive causal reasoning (past guilt → present suffering) is a mind-level attribution of moral causation.

**[CHAR-18]** E — Yes — through the self-assessment, concealment, and acknowledgment dimensions. Psa 36:2 — "he flatters himself in his own eyes" — the cognitive self-assessment is the faculty being distorted by pride-generated false evaluation; Job 31:33 — "hiding my iniquity in my heart" — the cognitive choice to conceal; Job 13:23 — "how many are my iniquities?" — the cognitive desire to enumerate and know one's moral-crime account; Jer 14:7 — "though our iniquities testify against us" — the cognitive recognition of iniquity as self-accusing witness.

**[CHAR-19]** E — Yes — the cognitive faculty is the knowledge-prerequisite of transgression. Rom 4:15 — "where there is no law there is no transgression" — cognition of the law must precede transgression; the crossing is only transgression when the boundary is cognitively known. Isa 46:8 — "remember this and stand firm, recall it to mind, you transgressors" — the cognitive act of recall is addressed to transgressors; their problem is cognitive failure to retain what they know. Dan 8:23 — "when transgressors have reached their limit" — the accumulation has a cognitive measure.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The cognitive faculty is engaged through its *absence* at the moment of sinning and its *activation* at the moment of realisation. Lev 4:2 ("sins unintentionally") — the cognitive faculty did not process the act as a violation of a known prohibition. Lev 5:5 ("when he realizes his guilt") — the cognitive faculty activates upon realisation: "realizes" (yada/yadah — to know, to come to know) is a cognitive event. Num 22:34 ("I did not know") — explicit cognitive-absence statement at the moment of sinning; the knowing arrives post-fact when the angel is disclosed.

**[CHAR-20]** E — Yes — through the deliberation and the self-justification dimensions. Psa 73:15 — "if I had said, 'I will speak thus,' I would have betrayed the generation of your children" — the psalmist's cognitive deliberation about whether to voice his doubts recognises that the spoken thought could constitute betrayal; the cognitive evaluation of speech determines whether an act is faithless or faithful; Psa 59:5 — "those who treacherously plot evil" — deliberate cognitive planning constitutes the treachery.

**[CHAR-21]** E — Yes — the cognitive faculty is perversion's primary target in the NT. 1Ti 6:5 — "depraved in mind (*nous*)" — the mind is the specifically named faculty; the depravity is at the seat of understanding; 2Cor 11:3 — "your thoughts (*noēmata*) will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ" — the thoughts are the target; Isa 29:16 — "you turn things upside down! Shall the potter be regarded as the clay?" — the cognitive assessment of the creator-creature relationship is inverted.

**[CHAR-22]** E — Yes — through deliberation and God-knowledge. Psa 58:2 — "in your hearts you devise wrongs" — the cognitive devising faculty; Psa 64:6 — "they search out injustice, saying, 'We have accomplished a diligent search.' For the inward mind and heart of a man are deep" — cognitive deliberation toward injustice; Job 18:21 — "him who knows not God" — the God-knowledge deficit as cognitive failure; Psa 53:1 — the cognitive proposition "there is no God" asserted in the heart.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. Cognition is engaged through the *knowing* that grounds confession: 2Sa 19:20 — "your servant knows that I have sinned" — explicit cognitive knowledge as the basis. Dan 9:5/11 — the confession names specific theological and historical facts ("All Israel has transgressed your law and turned aside, refusing to obey your voice. And the curse and oath that are written in the Law of Moses... have been poured out upon us, because we have sinned against him") — the confession requires knowing the Law's content, knowing that Israel violated it, knowing the covenantal consequences. Confession in this mode is cognitively dense — it requires knowing what the standard was and knowing how the act deviated from it.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes — cognitive failure is the evidenced mode of conscience suppression in the perceptual-blindness instances. Jer 16:10 — the people's "what sin?" is a *cognitive failure*: they do not know. 1Cor 15:34 — "some have no knowledge (*gnōsis*) of God" — knowledge is the explicit cognitive category; its absence produces the stupor. The cognitive faculty fails to apply the moral standard (God's law, God's character) to the person's own conduct — resulting in the conclusion that nothing wrong was done.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The cognitive faculty is centrally engaged in Heb 10:26 — "sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth" — the person has the relevant knowledge cognitively (the truth has been received) and the will acts against it. The cognitive faculty holds the truth but the will refuses to act in accordance with it. 1Ki 16:31 — the minimisation of Jeroboam's sins ("a light thing") is a cognitive assessment. The cognitive faculty is engaged in both the knowing-the-truth mode (Heb 10:26) and the false-evaluation mode (1Ki 16:31).

**[CHAR-6]** E — The cognitive faculty is engaged through the epistemic statement of 1Jo 3:6: "no one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or *known* him" — *known* (*egnōken* — perfect: has known) names the cognitive-relational knowing as the second dimension of the habitual sinner's deficit alongside seeing. 1Sa 2:25 — "they would not listen" — the refusal to listen is a cognitive-receptive failure: the corrective word (father's voice) reaches them but the cognitive faculty refuses to process and integrate it. The habitual sinning pattern is thus associated with a failure of both the deepest cognitive knowing (1Jo 3:6) and the receptive-cognitive processing of correction (1Sa 2:25).

**[CHAR-7]** E — The cognitive faculty is engaged through the teaching mode. Deu 20:18 — "that they may not *teach* you to do according to all their abominable practices" — the cognitive faculty is the target of the teaching: the community's understanding of what to do in worship and life is shaped by what they are taught. If the teaching is of abominable practices, the cognitive framework for moral action is corrupted. The cognitive faculty receives content (what to do, how to worship) that is directed toward sinning rather than toward God.

**[CHAR-8]** E — The cognitive faculty is engaged through the strategic assessment that revolt requires. 2Ki 3:7 — Jehoram's sending word to Jehoshaphat to form a military alliance against Moab — reveals that the response to revolt requires political-cognitive assessment: who are the allies, what is the military strategy, how is the revolt to be addressed. The cognitive engagement is at the political-strategic rather than the moral-theological level in the corpus.

**[CHAR-9]** E — The cognitive faculty is engaged through both its absence and its distortion. 1Ti 6:4 — "understands nothing" — cognitive failure as the enabling condition for slanderous speech; the mind does not process moral reality accurately. 1Ti 1:13 — Paul's former blasphemy from "ignorant unbelief" — cognitive-epistemic ignorance (not knowing the truth about Jesus) as the ground of the blasphemy. VCG-02 — the scribes deploy their knowledge of divine prerogatives ("who can forgive sins but God alone?" — Mar 2:7) in a cognitively correct theological premise but reach a false conclusion (Jesus blasphemes) through failure to recognise his identity.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. Cognition is significantly engaged and corrupted. Pro 12:5 (VCG-08): "the counsels of the wicked are deceitful" — the deliberative cognitive function is oriented toward deceptive output. Job 21:16 (VCG-10): "the counsel of the wicked is far from me" — wickedness generates a morally alien cognitive framework. Psa 10:4 (VCG-02): "all his thoughts are 'There is no God'" — the cognitive contents of the wicked person are systematically God-excluding. Pro 4:19 (VCG-07): the wicked "do not know over what they stumble" — cognitive self-knowledge is impaired. Isa 5:23 (VCG-05): the corrupt judicial will "acquitting the guilty for a bribe" — the judicial cognitive faculty (discernment of right from wrong) is deliberately perverted. Dan 12:10 (VCG-05): "none of the wicked shall understand" — cognitive capacity for understanding is closed at the eschatological level.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes. Cognition is significantly engaged. Mat 9:4 (vc=14418 — VCG-03): "Why do you think evil in your hearts?" — evil cognition is directly named; the heart as the site of morally corrupt thought. Mat 12:35 (vc=14420 — VCG-03): the evil person draws from an inner treasury — this is an active cognitive act of retrieval. Col 1:21 (vc=14424 — VCG-06): "hostile in mind, doing evil deeds" — the mind as the cognitive-evaluative faculty is the seat of the constitutionally hostile orientation that produces evil deeds. 1Ti 6:4 (vc=14470 — VCG-06): evil suspicions arising from a mind inflated with conceit and devoid of understanding — cognitive corruption producing relational damage.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. Cognition is directly engaged. Pro 15:26 (vc=1679 — VCG-02): "the thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to the Lord" — deliberate inner thought is named as the site of abomination; the cognitive faculty generates abominable content. Pro 17:15 (vc=1690 — VCG-01): perverted judgment — the cognitive faculty of moral assessment has been inverted. Isa 44:19 (vc=65961 — VCG-05): the absence of "consideration" (a reflective cognitive act) enables abomination; cognitive reflection would prevent the abominable act by naming it for what it is. Luk 16:15 (vc=21 — VCG-02): "God knows your hearts" — divine cognition penetrates the human heart's self-justifying cognitive constructions.

Eze 20:4 (vc=65994 — VCG-05): "let them know the abominations of their fathers" — the command to know implies they don't currently understand the weight of what they inherited. Eze 11:2 (vc=38193 — VCG-02): "men who devise iniquity and give wicked counsel" — devising is a deliberate cognitive act of planning. Mic 2:1 (vc=38217 — VCG-02): "those who devise wickedness… on their beds" — nocturnal deliberate planning. Isa 32:6 (vc=38181 — VCG-02): "his heart is busy with iniquity" — cognitive busyness as the mode. Isa 59:7 (vc=38203 — VCG-02): "their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity" — the entire thought-content is colonised by iniquitous cognitive material. Psa 64:2 (vc=38244 — VCG-03): "secret plots of the wicked" — plotting as a cognitive-scheming act.

The cognitive failure is comprehensive: everything not understood is blasphemed. Char 5 shows cognitive co-optation most directly: the deliberative-planning faculty (devising, plotting — Mic 2:1; Eze 11:2) is fully operational but producing evil schemes. Char 6 shows cognitive bypass (Jude 10 — contempt substituting for understanding). Char 3 shows cognitive-evaluative inversion (Pro 17:15 — justifying the wicked and condemning the righteous). Char 4 shows cognitive assessment failure (Eze 8:17 — abomination treated as trivial). Char 2 shows the mind's futility (Eph 4:17-18 — futility of mind; darkened understanding). Char 1 shows cognitive-practical atheism (Psa 10:4 — "all his thoughts are 'There is no God'"). The cluster's cognitive pattern: M10b characteristics engage cognition in four modes — co-optation (Char 5), bypass (Char 6), inversion (Char 3), and suppression (Chars 1, 2, 4).

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. The most explicit cognitive engagement is the discernment imperative of M10c-B-VCG-01: Lev 10:10 ("to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean"), Lev 11:47 ("to make a distinction between the unclean and the clean"), Lev 14:57 ("to show when it is unclean and when it is clean"), Lev 20:25 (commanding Israel to "separate the clean beast from the unclean"). The cognitive faculty is engaged in learning, applying, and transmitting the categorical system. Lev 10:10 frames the priestly vocation as inherently cognitive: the priest must know the distinctions and teach them. Act 10:14/28 (M10c-B-VCG-05) shows the same categorical knowledge in NT conscience — Peter's cognitive framework of clean/unclean is fully internalized and requires divine speech to revise.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes. The defiled-mind reference in VCG-03 (Tit 1:15: "both their minds and their consciences are defiled") most directly names the cognitive faculty. Within §3: 2Pe 2:10 (VCG-03) — "bold and willful" — names a specific cognitive-volitional posture (bold defiance) that accompanies the defilement. Mat 23:27 (VCG-04) — the hypocrites' outer appearance and inner reality being in contradiction — reveals that cognitive-self-assessment (they present themselves as righteous) is distorted by the defilement: they cannot correctly cognise their own condition.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. Eze 22:26 (VCG-05): the priestly failure to "make distinction between the holy and the common" is a failure of the cognitive-categorical faculty — the structured knowledge of clean/unclean that the characteristic requires is collapsed by priestly dereliction. Jer 2:23 (VCG-02): self-deceived cognition — the community asserts claims about its own condition that are not accurate.

**[CHAR-4]** S — The 21-verse corpus does not explicitly evidence engagement with the cognitive faculty (knowing, understanding, discerning) in the inhabited person. The spirits themselves demonstrate cognitive self-awareness (Mar 3:11 — recognising divine identity), but this is the spirits' cognition, not the person's.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All four characteristics engage the cognitive faculty, with Characteristic 4 the most minimal. Characteristics 1, 2, and 3 each engage the cognitive faculty substantially: Characteristic 1 through the categorical discernment system (Lev 10:10/11:47 — the clean/unclean distinction as a cognitive curriculum); Characteristic 2 through the defiled mind's distorted moral cognition (Tit 1:15 reference — "both their minds and their consciences are defiled"; Mat 23:27 — self-deceptive cognition); Characteristic 3 through institutional cognitive failure (Eze 22:26 — priests failing to maintain the categorical distinction) and community self-deception (Jer 2:23). Characteristic 4 engages cognition only through the spirits' own cognitive self-awareness (Mar 3:11 — recognising divine identity) — the person's cognitive faculty is not explicitly targeted.

findings.session_b_note:
The data supports both enabling and a form of cognitive termination:

**Enables cognition:** Jer 31:34 — "they shall all know me" follows from "I will forgive their iniquity." The new covenant forgiveness enables a new quality of direct cognitive access to God — universal, unmediated, not requiring instruction. Forgiveness removes the barrier (guilt, relational breach) that blocked direct knowing. In this sense, forgiveness **enables deeper cognition** of God.

**Terminates cognitive operation (in God):** Jer 31:34 — "remember no more." Divine forgiveness involves the active cessation of a cognitive operation — the remembering of sin against the person. This is not impairment but a deliberate cognitive termination in the service of relational restoration.

**Human analogue — cognitive release:** By extension (not explicitly stated in the data), the human act of forgiving from the heart (Mat 18:35) likely involves a cognitive component — releasing the mental record-keeping of the wrong. The "poisoning of the inner life of the withholder" (OBS-064-001) may include the cognitive dimension of rumination and retained grievance. But this is implied rather than evidenced directly.

findings.session_b_note:
**Compassion deepens cognition in the Good Samaritan pattern:** As noted at T3.1, the Samaritan's compassion deepens his perception and by extension his understanding of the wounded man's full humanity. Compassion-generated sight produces a form of moral knowledge — the knowledge of what the other truly is, beyond category and boundary.

**Compassion can operate before cognition (pre-cognitive somatic movement):** The splanchnizō gut-stirring is pre-volitional and, by implication, pre-reflective. The somatic arousal precedes deliberation. In this sense, compassion does not bypass cognition but precedes it — the inner body moves before the cognitive faculty has evaluated the situation. Cognition follows the gut-stirring and gives it direction and form.

**What is missing (P):** The data does not address whether sustained compassion deepens the cognitive faculty over time — whether the compassionate person becomes a more discerning perceiver of need, or whether compassion and cognition are structurally linked in a developmental relationship. This is a gap; no SD pointer addresses it.

findings.session_b_note:
Contrition **enables and clears** cognition — specifically, it removes the cognitive distortions produced by pride and self-justification. The person who is contrite has arrived at honest cognitive self-assessment; their understanding of their own moral condition is not filtered through self-protective defences. Psa 51's cognitive clarity ("I know my transgressions") is the product of a contrite condition. The prior hardened state (before Nathan's confrontation) was a state of cognitive self-deception or avoidance. Contrition, when it arrives, clears this — it enables the person to think truthfully about themselves before God.

The contrasting data from Jer 44:10 — failure to walk in God's law, failure to fear — implies a state of cognitive closure: the people cannot or will not cognise their condition accurately. The absence of contrition correlates with impaired honest self-cognition.

*New finding: contrition functions as a cognitive clarifier — it enables honest self-knowledge by removing the distortions that pride and self-protection produce. This is not primarily an emotional phenomenon but a cognitive one in its foundational operation, though the two are integrated.*

findings.session_b_note:
**Deepening cognition:** Divine nature fellowship (2Pe 1:4) and knowing-Christ fellowship (Phili 3:10) both represent modes in which fellowship deepens cognitive access — the person comes to *know* something (God, Christ) more fully through participatory fellowship than through propositional knowledge alone. Fellowship augments the cognitive faculty by giving it relational-participatory access.

**Bypassing cognition (partially):** The wound-fellowship groups (Pro 20:30 — disciplinary wounding reaching innermost parts; Isa 53:5 — redemptive wounding producing healing) appear to operate below the level of deliberate cognition. The purification from disciplinary wounding is not primarily a cognitive event — it reaches the innermost parts through the somatic rather than through mental reasoning.

**Gap:** The extent to which fellowship bypasses cognition in the wound-fellowship and idolatrous-joining modes is not directly analysed in the data.

findings.session_b_note: Goodness enables and deepens cognition. The comparative wisdom mode actively trains the evaluative intellect — the better-than sayings of 884-004 require and cultivate discerning moral cognition. Rom 15:14 pairs goodness with knowledge in a single characterological portrait: "full of goodness, filled with all knowledge" — suggesting a natural coherence between goodness and cognitive fullness. The absence of goodness impairs cognition: the moral inversion of Mal 2:17 / Jer 44:17 (calling evil good) is a cognitive failure — the evaluative faculty is corrupted. The direction is clear: goodness present deepens moral cognition; goodness absent or distorted impairs it. (OBS-067-OBS-012, OBS-067-OBS-021, OBS-067-OBS-025)

findings.session_b_note: Love **enables and deepens** cognition in its righteous form. Joh 15:15 (OBS-103-052): love opens access to knowledge the beloved has — the cognitive gift is inseparable from the love-relationship. Hos 6:6 (OBS-103-091): God prioritises 'knowledge of God' alongside chesed — love and knowledge advance together. Jer 31:34 (OBS-103-072): the eschatological love-community is one of direct knowledge — love's fullness produces cognitive fullness. Disordered love **impairs** cognition: love-of-money produces departure from faith and consequent cognitive loss (1Ti 6:10, OBS-103-132); love-of-darkness refuses the cognitive reorientation that light would require (Joh 3:19, OBS-103-147). Love enables the kind of knowledge (da'at — relational knowing) that is inaccessible without the love-relationship; it does not bypass discursive reason but opens the relational dimension of knowledge that reason alone cannot reach.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-111-003: Reading T3 as a whole reveals mercy as a faculty-activating characteristic — it does not primarily engage one or two faculties but activates the inner-being faculty system comprehensively. The pattern…
findings.finding_value: Reading T3 as a whole reveals mercy as a faculty-activating characteristic — it does not primarily engage one or two faculties but activates the inner-being faculty system comprehensively. The pattern: mercy enables perception (face-access), opens cognition in both directions (upward to divine knowledge; downward to self-knowledge), creates an asymmetric memory structure (divine forgetting / human remembering), engages affect as its native register, expands volition (received mercy increases mercy-capacity), demands agency, reframes moral evaluation (mercy as higher-order moral evaluation), presupposes and deepens conscience, enables conscientiousness, and constitutes relational capacity. The single faculty not evidenced is creativity (T3.5.2 — S status). Reading T3 together: mercy is characterised by faculty-comprehensiveness; its absence (mercilessness in Rom 1:31) appears alongside affective incapacity (*astorgos*) and other faculty-failures — confirming that mercy's presence is correlated with full faculty activation and its absence with faculty contraction.

findings.finding_value: T7's primary anchor verse identification (Psa 78:38) and its confirmation of mercy's cross-genre literary evidence maps to T3's faculty engagement profile. Psa 78:38 (T7, Q&A-185) contains within it a four-stage inner sequence (compassion → atoning act → anger restraint → wrath modulation) that traverses multiple faculties: affect (compassion), agency (atoning act), moral evaluation (anger restraint as moral-evaluative act), and volition (not stirring up wrath). The verse T7 identifies as primary anchor encodes the T3 faculty engagement in concentrated form. T7's human-science divergence finding (Q&A-189 — mercy grounded in prior reception, not autonomous moral development) is the methodological form of T3's receiving-before-generating faculty activation pattern.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-003: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion re…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion responds, it does not originate or create. It is the most responsive of the faculties-engaging characteristics. Second, affect and moral action are structurally unified in compassion — not sequentially related but simultaneous. Affect is the mechanism of movement (splanchnizō is both the felt inner event and the cause of the action), not a precursor or accompaniment. This is unique among the characteristics reviewed: in most other registries, affect and volition are distinguishable stages; in compassion, the felt movement is already the morally motivated action beginning. A third distinctive finding: compassion converts moral knowledge into motivated action — it is the motivational ground of conscientiousness, not a product of it. The conscience faculty engagement reveals compassion as conscience-healing: it addresses the pitiable condition that conscience perceives as a moral claim, resolving the tension between moral knowledge and moral incapacity. The three relational modes (building/sustaining — chesed; restoring/repairing — splanchnizō; extending across difference — Good Samaritan) are a new finding not in the instruction typology.

findings.finding_value: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I but the grace of God that is with me." Agency is not displaced but constituted by grace. This relationship holds in paradox that the T3.6 prompt options (enable/deepen/bypass/impair) cannot accommodate — a prompt design limitation noted for catalogue revision. Second, grace produces moral clarity (T3.8 — sharpens moral evaluation rather than bypassing it): the person who recognises grace has made a precise moral evaluation (they know they received what they did not deserve). Third, grace and conscience are mutually necessary: grace is the condition within which conscience can operate fully without destroying the person; conscience without grace produces condemnation; grace without conscience produces presumption (T3.9). Fourth, grace is the primary relational faculty developer in the registry's evidence — it reaches every relational register (vertical access, horizontal forgiving, speech-grace) and enables each one. Creativity (T3.5) is the one genuinely silent faculty — not an impairment but a non-engagement: grace receives and constitutes, it does not create.

findings.session_b_note: Both enabling/deepening and impairing are evidenced. Enabling/deepening: the new covenant produces the deepest form of knowing — "they shall all know me" (Jer 31:34). This knowing is not mere cognitive information but intimate personal knowledge, generated by God's own interior action (writing on the heart, Spirit-administration). The new covenant enables a quality of cognition that was not available under the old: unmediated knowing of God across all persons, "from the least to the greatest." Impairing: 2 Cor 3:14 — cognitive hardening under the old covenant. When read without Christ, the old covenant produces a veil that impairs the very cognition it should inform. This is a structural impairment — not failure of effort but a covenantal condition that blocks cognitive access. The same covenant (old) that was designed to enable knowing God becomes, through hardening, an obstacle to that knowing.

findings.finding_value: M01-A **enables and deepens** cognition. Pro 2:5 (fear as "an inner understanding arrived at through diligent pursuit — not merely an emotion but a formed insight"); Pro 1:29 (rejecting fear is "an act of the will — the inner choice to hate knowledge and refuse reverence" — absence of fear closes cognition). Fear-of-God is presented as cognitively constitutive: the person who fears God genuinely understands; the person who does not lacks foundational knowing.

M01-B and M01-D **impair** cognition. Mar 9:6 (M01-B: fear disabling thought and speech at the Transfiguration); Isa 21:3 (M01-D: dismay shutting down perception and sight). M01-D's D-VCG-03 (Dan 5:6; 5:10) shows the cognitive origin of dismay (thoughts alarmed) and its cognitive consequence (the system shut down).

M01-B and M01-D **impair** cognition. Mar 9:6 (M01-B: fear disabling thought and speech at the Transfiguration); Isa 21:3 (M01-D: dismay shutting down perception and sight). M01-D's D-VCG-03 (Dan 5:6; 5:10) shows the cognitive origin of dismay (thoughts alarmed) and its cognitive consequence (the system shut down).

M01-F **distorts** cognition by fixating it on anticipated negative futures. De.a.gah (H1674) is a worry-based cognitive engagement that prevents the mind from resting on present reality. It "bypasses" present truth by substituting anticipated threat.
M01-G timidity **impairs** cognitive action: Mat 25:25 (servant's failure to think productively about how to use the talent — fear suppresses the cognition that would enable faithful investment).

The pattern: M01-A enables/deepens cognition; M01-D impairs it most severely; M01-F distorts it toward anxious anticipation; M01-B impairs it acutely in moments of overwhelming encounter; M01-G suppresses it volitionally. The ordered fear (M01-A) and the disordered fears (B-severe, D, F, G) are cognitively opposed.

Possessing rage bypasses cognition. Dan 3:13 (M02-B-VCG-03): Nebuchadnezzar's furious rage "bypasses deliberation and demands instant compliance." Est 3:5 (M02-B-VCG-03): rage filling Haman "takes possession of him and will drive all subsequent planning against Mordecai" — the planning is driven by rage rather than by free deliberation. The possessing form bypasses the normal deliberative function of cognition.

Righteous anger deepens cognition toward its moral target: Elihu's anger at theological error (Job 32:2–5) drives him to articulate a careful theological case (Job 33 onwards). The anger intensifies cognitive engagement with the problem.

Godly grief deepens cognition: the Corinthians' grief produces a change of mind (metanoia — 2Cor 7:9, 7:11 — M03-C-VCG-02), showing grief enabling cognitive reformation. The cost of wisdom producing pain (Ecc 1:18 — M03-F-VCG-01) suggests that deeper cognitive engagement with reality produces grief — a bidirectional relationship. Sustained grief can impair cognition: pain preventing rest (Ecc 2:23 — M03-F-VCG-01), grief draining all vitality (Psa 31:10 — M03-C-VCG-01).
