findings.finding_value: The pattern reveals that fear has a fundamental cognitive dimension: it either opens or closes the person's capacity for genuine knowing. Ordered fear of God opens — it is the epistemological root. Disordered fear closes — it either shuts down (M01-D), distorts (M01-F), or suppresses (M01-G) the cognitive faculty. This confirms that fear is not merely an affective experience but a cognitive-orienting characteristic: what the person fears determines what they can genuinely know and what they will fail to see.

**Contrast: B-VCG-02 vs B-VCG-03:** The pattern reveals that the characteristic's relationship to cognition depends entirely on its form. When anger arises from accurate cognitive-moral assessment, it can deepen and sharpen that assessment (righteous anger, M02-B-VCG-04). When it arises from wounded pride and takes a possessing form, it bypasses cognition and drives from its own momentum (M02-B-VCG-03). The characteristic is not inherently cognitive or anti-cognitive — its relationship to cognition depends on its moral grounding.

Grief is not primarily a cognitive characteristic but it has cognitive consequences in both directions: accurate cognitive perception of reality (especially moral and relational reality) tends to produce grief; and grief tends to produce cognitive reformation (repentance as cognitive-moral revision). The relationship is bidirectional and significant, but the primary seat of grief remains affective, not cognitive.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Exultation is cognitively grounded but not cognitively produced — knowing provides the ground; the affective-volitional surge of exultation is the response. The characteristic bridges cognition and affect: the mind provides the true object; the soul rises in response.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Cognition and Joy are mutually reinforcing in the normal pattern: comprehension produces Joy; Joy sustains and reinforces the engagement with what is understood. The occasional instances of Joy temporarily exceeding cognitive function (Luk 24:41; Act 12:14) reveal Joy as a characteristic that in its most intense forms temporarily subordinates cognition to affect — the inner being is so flooded with gladness that ordinary reasoning is suspended. This is exceptional rather than normative.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Suffering-Joy's cognitive engagement is specifically eschatological — its cognitive dimension is the holding of future-reality as present-real. This distinguishes it from Gladness (whose cognitive primary is moral evaluation) and from Joy (whose cognitive ground is comprehension of God's acts). Suffering-Joy's distinctive cognitive mode is eschatological reframing: the present suffering is real but is contextualised by a greater real — the glory to come.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Gladness is the most cognitively-constituted characteristic in M04. Its health is directly dependent on the quality of cognition: accurate cognitive evaluation of moral reality produces genuine Gladness; distorted cognition produces distorted Gladness. This makes Gladness uniquely susceptible to formation through instruction — the wisdom literature's training of the evaluative faculty is the primary formative vehicle.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Delight is uniquely positioned as a cognitive-driver: unlike the other M04 characteristics, Delight consistently produces sustained cognitive engagement with its object (study, meditation, inquiry). The pattern reveals that the person's deepest Delight determines what they most consistently think about and explore. Properly directed Delight in God and his word is therefore the most powerful driver of theological and spiritual cognition — it produces a mind that returns repeatedly to its object.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Pleasure and cognition are indirectly related: Pleasure in wisdom sustains cognitive engagement; Pleasure-seeking without wisdom distorts and bypasses accurate cognition. The relationship is not direct (Pleasure is not a cognitive characteristic) but instrumental: right Pleasure reinforces right knowing; wrong Pleasure corrupts knowing.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Wonder is the most cognitively-rich M04 characteristic in the perceptive-contemplative mode. Unlike Delight (which is cognitively engaged in wisdom evaluation) or Gladness (which is cognitively evaluative of moral goodness), Wonder's cognitive engagement is specifically at the boundary of comprehension — it is the response when cognition reaches its limit. The pattern reveals Wonder as the characteristic most directly involving the mind in a posture of humble but active engagement with what exceeds it.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster reveals a nuanced account of the relationship between positive inner states and cognition: they are mutually reinforcing in healthy operation and mutually distorting in misdirected operation. The most distinctive cluster-level finding: Delight (Char 4) is positioned as the inner-being characteristic that most reliably produces sustained cognitive engagement with its object — making it the key formation characteristic for intellectual and spiritual formation. The person whose Delight is in God's word (Psa 1:2) is the person who meditates day and night; the person whose Delight is in God's works (Psa 111:2) is the person who studies them. This positions Delight as the motivational foundation for the entire intellectual formation tradition of the wisdom literature.

**[CHAR-1]** E — That shame is cognitively engaged at both ends: it is produced by cognitive failure (misplaced trust, idolatry, folly) and it produces cognitive response (either collapse-confusion or clarity-through-correction). The cognitive dimension confirms that CHAR-1 is not a purely emotional phenomenon — it has deep cognitive roots and cognitive consequences.

**[CHAR-2]** E — CHAR-2 collapses confident cognition: the defeated "go in confusion" — their ability to think through their situation and act effectively is destroyed. Cognitive paralysis accompanies military defeat (Jer 49:23 — "melting in fear, troubled like the sea"). In VCG-03, God's abasement targets the cognitive self-assessment of the proud.

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — The cognitive worth-assessment process is engaged and distorted in CHAR-3: the dishonorer makes a wrong cognitive judgment about worth. The structural-dishonour mode (VCG-02) is more cognitively neutral — it is the result of sovereign assignment rather than a cognitive failure.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4 is a cognitive operation — the conscience assesses against a standard (God's sight, created order, community norms) and produces a judgment. The cognitive faculty is CHAR-4's primary operating mode. VCG-03 shows cognitive corruption: the evaluative judgment is produced but by a wrong standard.

---

**[CHAR-5]** E — The contempt-er's cognitive faculty is engaged: the worth-assessment judgment ("this person is of no account") is a cognitive act. 1Cor 6:4's cognitive assessment about standing; Rom 14:3/10's cognitive-evaluative judgment about a brother's worth before God — these show the cognitive faculty producing CHAR-5. For the recipient, the cognitive dimension is engaged in the ongoing self-assessment that contempt-shame distorts.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — Cognition is engaged in CHAR-6 through the moral self-assessment that innocence requires. Abimelech's appeal to his innocence (Gen 20:5) involves cognitive self-assessment: he knows he acted in ignorance and moral intention. Psa 73:13's lament involves cognitive evaluation: the psalmist has cognitively assessed his own moral maintenance and found it, in his experience, to have been in vain. The cognitive faculty is engaged in CHAR-6's self-assessment and moral accounting.

---

**[CLUSTER]** E — Cognition is engaged across all six with varying prominence. Char 4 is primarily cognitive (the evaluative judgment is a cognitive act). Chars 1, 3, 5 engage cognition in self-assessment and worth-assessment functions. Char 2 engages it in the cognitive collapse of the humiliated (confusion, dismay). Char 6 engages it in the cognitive self-assessment that constitutes the innocence-claim. Cluster-level cognitive theme: the shame-field is irreducibly cognitive — it involves ongoing assessment of standing, worth, and moral quality across all six characteristics. The cognitive faculty is the site where worth-assessments originate and where the shame-field's distortions begin. The correction of the shame-field therefore requires cognitive correction as one of its components.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — The pattern confirms that CHAR-1 is a cognitively distorting characteristic — it does not merely feel wrong or orient wrong, it thinks wrong. The proud person constructs a cognitive picture of themselves (above God, above others) that is systematically at variance with reality as God assesses it. Luk 1:51 (vc=33930, M08-A1-VCG-03) — arrogance as the structured pattern of thought "in the thoughts of their hearts" — confirms that CHAR-1 is not an impulse but a cognitive framework through which the proud person processes reality. Eze 28:17 (vc=34047) shows the consequence of this cognitive distortion: wisdom is corrupted, leading to decisions that are objectively destructive. This cognitive self-distortion is what makes CHAR-1 systemically self-defeating: the proud person cannot accurately predict their own consequences because their cognitive framework is built around a false self-elevation.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The pattern reveals that CHAR-2's cognitive distortion is specifically self-protective: it produces the false confidence (Obd 3; Jer 49:16) that enables the will to act presumptuously without internal resistance. The cognitive miscalculation is functional for CHAR-2 — it allows the will to proceed without the corrective brake that accurate self-assessment would provide. CHAR-2 weaponises self-deception in service of transgression.

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3's cognitive pattern reveals that the characteristic is constitutively about self-assessment: what one believes about oneself generates what one boasts about. CHAR-3's condemned form requires cognitive misattribution (self-generated rather than received); its examined form requires cognitive accuracy (conscience-grounded assessment); its God-directed form requires cognitive redirection (knowing God, not self, as the object of glory — Jer 9:23, vc=33342, M08-C-VCG-01 negative; Jer 9:24 positive implied).

**[CHAR-4]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that CHAR-4 is a uniquely cognitive form of self-corruption: it uses the mind's self-assessment faculty to generate a false picture, and then that false picture corrupts all subsequent cognitive function. 1Ti 6:4 (vc=33925): the terminal state of sustained CHAR-4 is comprehensive epistemic blindness ("understanding nothing") — confirming that the cognitive self-corruption is progressive and comprehensive.

**[CHAR-5]** E — CHAR-5's cognitive pattern reveals that structural power generates the most extreme form of cognitive self-deception: not merely self-inflation (CHAR-4's fusioō) but ontological self-declaration ("I am, and there is no one besides me" — Isa 47:8, vc=9563). The structural goods (wealth, power, fortification) provide the material basis for the cognitive self-assessment, making it feel more evidenced than CHAR-4's ungrounded inflation — but the evidence is ultimately false, as God's judgment consistently demonstrates.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster-level cognitive pattern reveals that M08 characteristics are epistemologically self-reinforcing — each generates a cognitive picture of the self that then resists the evidence that would revise it. CHAR-4's comprehensive "understanding nothing" is the terminal form of what CHAR-1's God-displacement, CHAR-2's self-deception, CHAR-3's misattribution, and CHAR-5's invulnerability-claim each begin. The cluster-synthesis: M08 is a progressive cognitive-corruption cluster — each characteristic begins with a specific cognitive distortion and tends toward the comprehensive epistemic blindness that CHAR-4 names.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The pattern reveals that submission and cognition have a genuine reciprocal relationship: genuine submission enables more accurate cognition (by reorienting it under Christ's authority and producing wisdom, Rom16:19); and accurate cognition is required for submission (discerning legitimate authority, Gal2:5; taking thoughts captive as a deliberate cognitive act, 2Cor10:5). The characteristic is not anti-cognitive but rather requires and enables the cognitive faculty to function at its best — under legitimate authority rather than in self-generated autonomy.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that contrition is grounded in a cognitive act of moral self-knowledge even while it is primarily an affective-existential state. The characteristic requires cognitive honesty as a precondition — without it, the crushing cannot be genuine (mere emotional breakdown without cognitive moral self-knowledge is not contrition in the biblical sense). This makes cognition a secondary but necessary faculty: the characteristic is primarily affective-existential (T1.8.1) but requires and validates accurate moral cognition as its ground.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that metriopatheō (Heb5:2) is an *epistemically enabling* characteristic — it grounds more accurate cognition of others' conditions by requiring prior accurate cognition of one's own. The calibrated quality of the engagement (measured/metrios) requires cognitive assessment of what is proportionate; the shared-weakness ground requires cognitive honest self-assessment. The characteristic thus requires and enables genuine cognitive functioning rather than bypassing it.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The pattern reveals that semnotēs enables the cognitive reception of authority and teaching by providing the character-ground that authenticates content. Where the characteristic is absent (in teaching or leadership), the cognitive content may be rejected not on its merits but because the character-ground that would make it credible is lacking (Tit2:7 implies this — dignity as authenticating quality).

**[CHAR-6]** E — The pattern reveals that willing-heartedness enables genuine cognitive investment rather than mere presence — the 1Ch28:21 pairing of willingness with skill implies that genuine skilled service requires willing-heartedness as its motivational ground. Without the inner willing disposition, the cognitive skill is present but not fully engaged; with it, the cognitive faculty operates in wholehearted integrated service.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The cognitive engagement reveals that humility is, in part, an *epistemic virtue*: the character-disposition that enables accurate knowing. Pro11:2 is the summary statement; the broader corpus confirms it — Ahab's humbling (1Ki21:29) involves genuine acknowledgment of his situation before God; Josiah's humbling (2Ch34:27) involves receiving God's word as accurate address to his situation; the tax collector's humbling (Luk18:14) involves accurate self-knowledge before God ("be merciful to me, a sinner" — outside this corpus but the same register). Humility enables the person to know what is genuinely true about themselves and their situation, which is the prerequisite for genuine wisdom.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cognition pattern reveals that M09 characteristics are epistemic virtues as well as moral virtues — they enable the person to know more accurately, not merely to behave better. The clearest statement is Humility (CHAR-1): Pro11:2 (humility → wisdom) positions the characteristic as a condition for genuine understanding. The Colossian critique of false humility (Col2:18 — the puffed-up sensuous mind beneath performed asceticism) confirms the converse: where M09 characteristics are performed without genuine inner reality, cognition is distorted rather than deepened. Submission (CHAR-2) is the characteristic that most directly names cognitive reordering as constitutive — 2Cor10:5 makes the mind's reasoning capacity the specific territory that submission must take. The cognition pattern is universally enabling across all six characteristics: no M09 characteristic suppresses or bypasses the cognitive faculty, which confirms the cluster's character as a cluster of genuine virtues (genuine virtues enable all the faculties) rather than as a cluster of cognitive-bypassing pietistic postures.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — The pattern reveals a fundamental tension: wilful sinning is constitutively known (the "wilful" qualifier) yet the will commits it anyway — making the relationship between cognition and volition in sinning one of *knowing-and-nonetheless*. Joseph (Gen 39:9) shows the knowing producing refusal; Saul (1Sa 15:24) shows the knowing overridden by fear. Achan (Jos 7:20) shows the knowing fully present yet insufficient to prevent. This knowing-and-nonetheless dynamic is what distinguishes wilful sinning from CHAR-2 (Unintentional sinning) — the cognitive element is present in CHAR-1 precisely because the will acts against available knowledge.

**[CHAR-10]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that the three mechanisms engage cognition differently: enticement primarily bypasses it (desire precedes deliberation — Jam 1:14), hypocrisy distorts it (social cognition produces wrong moral output — Gal 2:13), and apostasy targets it through instruction (Act 21:21 — teaching reshapes what is believed about covenantal identity). This diversity confirms the characteristic's composite nature: the mechanisms operate at different cognitive levels and through different cognitive engagements.

**[CHAR-11]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that the condition's relationship to cognition is complex and bidirectional: (1) the law as a cognitive framework reveals the condition (Rom 3:20 — knowledge of sin comes through law); (2) but the condition exploits the same cognitive framework for its own activation (Rom 7:8 — sin seizes the commandment). This is why Paul argues in Romans 7 that the law is not sin (Rom 7:7) — the law is good; the condition is what uses the good cognitive framework perversely. The cognitive faculty's recognition of the condition (through the law) does not by itself produce liberation from the condition (Rom 7:23 — the mind's law is overridden by the law of sin in the members).

**[CHAR-12]** S — The silence on the cognitive faculty is consistent with the corpus's focus on the will's captivity (not a cognitive phenomenon) and the identity-allegiance level (1Jo 3:8 — of the devil — a constitutional identity rather than a cognitive assessment). The enslaving power operates below or beside the cognitive level. Noted.

**[CHAR-13]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals an asymmetry between divine and human cognition of the record: God knows it fully (Amo 5:12 — "for I know how many are your transgressions and how great are your sins") while the human's cognitive access to their own record is partial and often distorted. This asymmetry is the characteristic's epistemic structure: the record is fully known to God and partially (or wrongly) known to the person. Isa 58:1 — the prophetic function is precisely to bridge this asymmetry: "declare to my people their transgression, to the house of Jacob their sins."

**[CHAR-14]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that the characteristic is not anti-rational: the seeking requires cognitive recognition of sin (Lev 4:14), cognitive engagement with the prophetic testimony (Act 10:43), and cognitive reorientation through repentance (Act 2:38). But cognition alone does not complete the characteristic: Exo 32:30 — Moses knowing the sin and going up to seek atonement does not guarantee forgiveness; he says "perhaps I can make atonement" — the cognitive-volitional seeking is necessary but the divine response is not mechanical.

**[CHAR-15]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that generational sin impairs not raw cognitive capacity (the people perceived the wonders) but *cognitive-moral integration*: the capacity to interpret what is cognitively registered in light of the correct moral-theological framework. Psa 78:32's unbelief despite wonders is a failure of moral-theological cognition rather than sensory cognition. The generational pattern corrupts the interpretive framework through which evidence is processed rather than eliminating the capacity to perceive evidence.

**[CHAR-16]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals an asymmetry in the sinner-identity's cognitive effects: applied to the self by the honest conscience, the sinner-label is accurate (Luk 5:8; Luk 18:13; 1Ti 1:15 — Paul's "foremost sinner"); applied to others by the self-righteous, it is a tool of false categorisation (Joh 9:24 — Jesus wrongly labelled). The cognitive faculty is most accurate when the sinner recognises their own condition (self-directed cognition) and least accurate when it is deployed to identify and exclude others (other-directed cognition from a position of self-righteousness).

**[CHAR-17]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that guilt-as-inner-state is not exclusively a feeling but has a specific cognitive structure: it requires knowledge to activate (Lev 5:2/3/4 — "when he comes to know"), generates retrospective causal reasoning (Gen 42:21 — connecting past guilt to present suffering), and can distort prospective interpretation (Eze 9:9; Eze 21:23). The cognitive faculty is the gateway to guilt-recognition and is itself shaped (both clarified and distorted) by the guilt it mediates.

**[CHAR-18]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that iniquity-as-accumulated-crime is not cognitively self-disclosing: the person does not automatically know their iniquity-accumulation through unaided reason. Gen 15:16 — the Amorites are presumably unaware their iniquity is being measured toward completion; Jer 16:10 — "what is our iniquity? What is the sin that we have committed?" — the cognitively unaware community cannot identify its own crime without prophetic disclosure. The cognitive faculty requires external input (divine revelation, prophetic word, conscience-strike) to accurately assess the iniquity-account.

**[CHAR-19]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals the most distinctive analytical finding for CHAR-19: transgression requires cognition (Rom 4:15 — law must be known) yet progressively suppresses the cognitive capacity to accurately assess the transgression being committed (Isa 46:8; Pro 28:24). The knowing that makes transgression possible is the same knowing that transgression systematically undermines. The paradox of CHAR-19's cognitive dimension: it requires knowledge to begin and produces ignorance to sustain itself.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The cognitive pattern confirms that CHAR-2 is an *information-deficit phenomenon*: the characteristic exists because of the creature's epistemic limitation, not because of the will's defection. Where CHAR-1 shows the cognitive faculty present but overridden (knowing and sinning anyway), CHAR-2 shows the cognitive faculty present but uninformed (not knowing and sinning inadvertently). This distinction is the analytical key: the cognitive faculty's state — informed vs uninformed — is what separates CHAR-1 from CHAR-2, not the moral weight of the act or the objective liability it creates.

**[CHAR-20]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that faithlessness is particularly damaging to the cognitive faculty's self-assessment function: the faithless person cannot accurately read the signal that distress sends (2Ch 28:22) and cannot accurately present themselves to others (Jer 12:6 — friendly words masking treachery). The cognitive function is co-opted: used to plan treachery (Psa 59:5) rather than to assess covenant loyalty honestly. The corrective is Ezr 10:2 — "we have broken faith with our God" — the honest cognitive confession that accurately names what the person has done.

**[CHAR-21]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that perversion produces a two-stage cognitive corruption: (1) primary cognitive faculty impairment (1Ti 6:5 — mind depraved) and (2) consequent truth-deprivation (1Ti 6:5 — "deprived of the truth"). The depraved mind cannot self-correct because the very faculty of self-assessment is what has been corrupted. Isa 29:16's creator-denial confirms: perversion corrupts cognition at the most fundamental level — the capacity to know the source of one's existence. The cognitive pattern makes CHAR-21 the most epistemically devastating characteristic in M10.

**[CHAR-22]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals two levels: (1) *Surface-level misdirection* — the mind is fully deployed but toward wrong ends (Psa 64:6 — diligent search for injustice); (2) *Foundation-level deficit* — the God-knowledge that would anchor just cognition is absent (Job 18:21). The most analytically significant finding: Psa 64:6 — "for the inward mind and heart of a man are deep" — Scripture itself acknowledges the cognitive depth from which injustice's devising emerges; the deep mind is the site of injustice's planning.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that the *precision of confession reflects the depth of cognitive engagement with sin*. Exo 9:27 (Pharaoh — brief, unprecise) represents minimal cognitive engagement; Dan 9:5–15 (extended, multi-dimensional) represents maximal. The characteristic invites and rewards cognitive deepening — the person who confesses more specifically is engaging their mind more fully with the moral reality of what they have done. This confirms that confession is not merely an emotional or volitional act but a cognitive-moral event.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that conscience suppression is an *epistemic moral failure*: it is what happens when the mind's knowledge of God (1Cor 15:34) and the mind's self-directed moral reasoning (Jer 16:10) both fail. The cognitive failure is not general unintelligence but a specific blindness in the self-moral-assessment domain. This is why Paul's cure for the cognitive failure is not clever argument but "knowledge of God" (1Cor 15:34) — the cognitive faculty needs its fundamental reference point (God) restored before accurate moral self-cognition becomes possible.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals a critical distinction within CHAR-5: the Heb 10:26 mode shows the will acting against correct knowledge (knowledge present, will bypasses it), while the 1Ki 16:31 mode shows the will enabled by distorted knowledge (knowledge corrupted by minimisation). In both cases the will refuses, but the cognitive configuration differs: in one, the problem is purely volitional (know but don't turn); in the other, the problem combines volitional and cognitive failure (don't turn partly because know wrongly).

**[CHAR-6]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals a critical distinction between general cognition (which may be intact) and God-knowledge (which is impaired). 1Jo 3:6's "never known him" is not a general intelligence statement but a theological-relational one: the habitual sinner may be intelligent and capable, but their cognitive access to the knowledge of Christ is blocked by or correlates with the habitual sinning pattern. This reveals that correction of habitual defection requires specifically the restoration of God-knowledge, not merely cognitive information about right behaviour. 1Jo 3:6's abiding relationship is the knowledge-condition that breaks the pattern.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that contagious sin is partly a cognitive phenomenon: the community's knowledge base about right worship and conduct is being shaped by the transmitted sinning content (Deu 20:18 — taught abominable practices). The cognitive corruption is why structural dismantling (2Ki 23:15 — demolishing the altar) must accompany inner moral renewal: if the altar remains, the community's cognitive framework continues to receive sinning content from its presence; both the structural and cognitive sources of the transmitted sinning must be addressed.

**[CHAR-8]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that the corpus is not primarily concerned with the inner cognitive processes of political revolt but with its political-historical outcomes. The cognitive engagement implied (political calculation, strategic assessment) is the background condition for revolt, not the corpus's explicit focus. The corpus's literary form (regnal narrative and historical summary) describes political facts rather than cognitive processes.

**[CHAR-9]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that sinful speech operates within and deepens cognitive distortion: accurate cognition of God's identity and moral reality would prevent sinful speech (1Ti 1:13 — the ignorance was the enabling condition; receiving knowledge/mercy reversed it). The corrective for sinful speech is therefore not merely behavioural but cognitive-theological: the person must come to know what they do not currently know. This is why 1Ti 1:13's reversal by mercy is possible — the ignorance-ground of blasphemy is addressable by the knowledge of God that mercy brings.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The cognitive engagement pattern reveals that wickedness-as-settled-person-identity has occupied the reasoning faculty and redirected it toward the person's corrupt ends. The wicked person is not cognitively absent — they plot (Psa 37:12: "the wicked plots against the righteous"), devise (Jer 5:26: "wicked men… set a trap; they catch men"), and counsel (Pro 12:5) — the cognitive faculty is active. But it is active in the service of wickedness rather than truth. This reveals that wickedness is not a passive deficit but an active redirection of the person's cognitive resources toward corrupt ends. The characteristic co-opts the reasoning faculty rather than simply eliminating it.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that constitutional inner evil co-opts the thinking faculty and redirects it toward three specific corruptions: hostile assessment (Col 1:21), suspicious reasoning (1Ti 6:4), and evil thought-generation (Mat 9:4). The pattern confirms that the characteristic is not a passive inner state but an active generator — it actively produces evil thoughts through the cognitive faculty. This explains why the NT's remedial commands are so often cognitive: Col 1:21's "hostile in mind" context requires a transformed mind (Rom 12:2 — though outside this corpus); the active cognitive generation of evil requires active cognitive renewal.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that abomination operates within the cognitive faculty in three specific corruptions: deliberate thought-generation of abominable content (Pro 15:26 — VCG-02), perversion of the moral-evaluative cognitive faculty (Pro 17:15 — VCG-01 — justifying/condemning inverted), and cognitive bypass of reflective consideration that would name the abomination (Isa 44:19 — VCG-05). These three show the characteristic as corrupting the cognitive faculty at the levels of content (what thoughts are generated), assessment (how moral reality is evaluated), and reflection (whether the person considers what they are doing). Cognition is present and active in abomination but systematically misdirected.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that idolatrous abomination specifically suppresses the two cognitive functions most needed to arrest it: gravity-assessment and covenantal memory. The person who cannot assess the gravity of their abomination (Eze 8:17 — VCG-05) and cannot remember the covenantal origins that would motivate departure (Eze 16:22 — VCG-05) is cognitively disarmed against the characteristic. This explains why external prophetic intervention (naming the abominations — Eze 16:2 — VCG-05; confronting with the knowledge of fathers' abominations — Eze 20:4 — VCG-05) is the necessary corrective — the person's own cognitive faculties can no longer perform this function.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that iniquity as active scheming specifically co-opts the highest-level cognitive faculties (deliberate planning, premeditated devising, counsel-giving — Eze 11:2 — VCG-02; Mic 2:1 — VCG-02) while leaving the moral-evaluative cognitive function non-functional (Psa 14:4 — VCG-03: no knowledge). This creates an inner cognitive profile distinctive to the characteristic: high planning-scheming capacity, low moral-knowledge capacity. The person is cognitively sophisticated in evil production but cognitively blind to moral reality. This explains why the characteristic is so damaging: it weaponises the most capable cognitive faculties against others.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals that the characteristic exploits cognitive gaps — where understanding fails, blasphemous contempt fills the void (Jude 10 — VCG-01). This is analytically significant: the characteristic is not primarily a product of cognitive error (misunderstanding) but of the refusal to acknowledge what might be understood, and of contempt substituting for the understanding that is absent. The cognitive bypass (Jude 10 — VCG-01) reveals that the characteristic operates at a level below rational moral comprehension — it is a sub-rational expression of inner moral rejection, not a rationally considered position.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's cognitive pattern reveals that M10b inner evil does not produce cognitive incapacity but cognitive misdirection: the cognitive faculties remain operational but are systematically oriented away from truth, moral reality, and divine presence. This is most clearly evidenced by Char 5 (active cognitive scheming — the planning faculty working at full capacity for evil production) and Char 6 (blasphemy directed at specific targets requires cognitive targeting, not cognitive failure). The cluster reveals M10b evil as involving intelligent, purposeful cognitive activity — the evil is not stupid but strategically directed against the good.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The characteristic is constitutively cognitive — it cannot operate without categorical knowledge. The person must know which animals are categorically clean or unclean (Lev 11 corpus, M10c-A-VCG-02), what disease markers indicate leprous defilement (Lev 13 corpus, M10c-B-VCG-02), how contamination transmits through which contact pathways (M10c-A-VCG-06 and -07). The characteristic is thus a system that requires cognitive formation to navigate. This reveals that the characteristic is not merely a bodily-mechanism condition but an intellectually structured domain: a person cannot adequately manage the ritual defilement-state without the cognitive equipment provided by the purity laws.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The cognitive impairment pattern reveals the characteristic as epistemically corrupting: sustained moral-inner defilement does not merely produce wrong behaviour but wrong moral cognition — the person cannot correctly assess the moral character of actions, things, or their own inner condition. This reveals the characteristic as striking at the root of moral reasoning rather than merely redirecting the will.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The cognitive pattern reveals the characteristic as dependent on institutional knowledge transmission: the clean/unclean distinction is a taught faculty (Eze 44:23 — priests must teach it; Eze 22:26 — priests have failed to teach it). When the cognitive-formative institution (priesthood) fails, the community's capacity for the self-knowledge that would interrupt the defilement-cycle is lost. The characteristic propagates in part through the collapse of institutional cognition.

**[CHAR-4]** S — The silence on cognitive engagement reveals that the characteristic does not target the cognitive faculty specifically; it operates through will-domination and faculty-suppression rather than through cognitive distortion. This contrasts with Characteristics 2 and 3 where defiled cognition and self-deception are part of the mechanism. Characteristic 4 bypasses the cognitive faculty rather than corrupting it.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's cognitive pattern reveals cognition as both the tool for managing defilement and the faculty most vulnerable to defilement's corruption. Characteristics 1 and 3 show cognition as a taught, institutional faculty — the clean/unclean distinction must be transmitted (Lev 10:10 for Char 1; Eze 44:23 for Char 3). When the institutional transmission fails (Eze 22:26 for Char 3; Peter's categorical resistance for Char 1 at the NT revision point), the cognitive capacity for managing defilement collapses. Characteristics 2 and 3 show cognition as self-corruptible: the advanced defilement-state produces a person and community who cannot correctly cognise their own condition. The cluster's institutional insight: the cognitive faculty is not individually self-generating — it requires institutional formation and transmission. When the forming institution fails, the faculty degrades. This insight is most fully developed in Characteristic 3 (Eze 22:26 — priestly cognitive failure as propagation mechanism) but is present across the cluster.

questions.question_text: In this verse, does the characteristic engage the memory faculty — the holding and retrieving of inner-being reality across time — and if so, how? Record none if it does not.
questions.review_note: [2026-09-08: retired per researcher verdict, escalation #1598 Phase D (iba/docs/1598-phase-d-faculties-provenance-v1-20260908.md). Faculties are real but not directly derivable from any verse; the terminology is foreign to the Bible; no individual faculty exists or operates on its own -- it may only emerge from a collection of characteristics' own operations. Verdict: no harm to characteristic analysis or to final inner-being assembly if omitted. Retired with no replacement yet decided; the parties/players/operations/movements/outcomes work (escalation #1598) is the active priority instead.]

findings.session_b_note:
Yes — memory is one of the most directly engaged faculties in the forgiveness corpus, and the engagement is explicit:

**Divine memory addressed:** Jer 31:34 — "I will remember their sin no more." The divine memory faculty is the specific target of the forgiveness act in this verse. God's memory of sin against the person is what forgiveness terminates. OBS-064-017: "the debt is not merely cancelled but rendered non-recallable." Memory is not merely erased but structured so the record cannot be retrieved — it is rendered non-recallable.

**Human memory implied:** The parable logic of Mat 18 involves retained memory — the unforgiving servant remembers his debt, acts on that memory by seizing the fellow servant, and refuses to release what he holds in memory. The parable's ethical force depends on the contrast between received forgiveness (the master released him) and retained grievance (the servant cannot release). Memory is the mechanism of retained grievance.

**Luk 7:47 — the depth of received forgiveness:** "She loved much because she was forgiven much." The awareness of forgiveness received (a form of remembered reality — the contrast between former guilt-state and present release) generates the love-orientation. Memory of the forgiven-state is the ground of the ongoing relational disposition.

findings.session_b_note:

However: SD029 (Rom 8:32 inference-structure): assurance derived from grace depends on remembering what God has done — the supreme grace-event functions as a remembered ground for current confidence. findings.session_b_note:
Yes — the data reveals a specific and significant engagement with memory, operating in two directions.

**Memory as the appeal ground in supplication:** The supplication vocabulary (H8467 techinah, H8469 tahanun, H2603A chanan as XREF) names the inner act of earnest appeal to God for compassion. Psa 25:7 (group 1633-003): "Remember not the sins of my youth or my transgressions; according to your steadfast love remember me, for the sake of your goodness, O Lord!" The petition explicitly asks God to remember the person through the lens of chesed rather than through the lens of the person's sin-history. This is a direct engagement with God's memory as the ground of compassion's extension: the appeal asks that divine memory selectively retrieve the covenantal loyalty rather than the moral record.

**God's remembering as compassion-act:** The inverse is also present — God remembering with compassion is a specific inner act. Psa 25:7 treats divine memory as something that can be oriented differently depending on whether it operates through chesed or through the record of transgressions. This makes memory a structural component of compassion's operation in the divine-human relationship.

**Memory as the context of compassion's sustaining:** Psa 48:9 (group 1633-003): "We have thought on your steadfast love, O God, in the midst of your temple." Meditating on God's chesed is named as a sustained inner act — holding the memory of divine compassion-love in the mind as an orienting reality. This is memory in service of compassion's sustaining effect: remembering the divine compassion shapes the inner life of the one who remembers.

findings.session_b_note:
Memory is engaged implicitly in contrition's penitential-relational mode but is not explicitly named in the verse evidence. The contrite person's knowledge of what they have done ("I know my transgressions" — Psa 51:3 context) requires memory — the holding of the moral event in the inner being's register. Contrition cannot arise about a past event unless that event is available to inner remembrance.

The verse evidence does not develop a memory-contrition relationship explicitly. The closest implicit evidence: OBS-030-001 notes that contrition is "the interior grief of having actually caused harm or broken trust" — which implies the harm is held in memory. The groaning of Psa 38:8 ("I groan because of the tumult of my heart") implies an ongoing inner registration of something that produces continuous distress — which may be memory-related.

*Partial: memory is implicitly required for contrition but is not explicitly addressed in the verse evidence.*

findings.session_b_note:
**Memory as witness-preservation:** 1Jo 1:3 — *that which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you* — the fellowship-chain depends on memory: what has been seen and heard must be retained (memory) and then proclaimed (testimony). The fellowship is extended through the memory of the witness. Without memory of the seen-and-heard, the proclamation chain breaks.

**Memory in covenantal companionship:** Mal 2:14 — *the Lord was witness between you and the wife of your youth* — the faithlessness in view is against the companionship of the wife of one's *youth* — a temporal reference that requires memory to sustain the relational bond. The covenant companion relationship must be remembered and sustained over time.

**Leopard-spots — inverted memory:** Jer 13:23 (group 7573-001) — *can the leopard change his spots?* — the indelibility of character is precisely the constitutional permanence of what has been formed. The fellowship-vocabulary here points to a form of constitutional "memory" — the inner person retains (constitutionally) what it has been shaped into.

**New finding:** Memory plays a structural role in two fellowship modes: as the vehicle that sustains and extends righteous fellowship through time (testimony, covenantal loyalty), and as the inverse — constitutionally retained moral character that cannot easily be changed. Fellowship is partly a *time-extended* phenomenon whose continuity depends on memory.

findings.session_b_note: Memory is substantively engaged. Eze 36:31 ("Then you will remember your evil ways, and your deeds that were not good, and you will loathe yourselves") names memory as the faculty through which moral awareness of not-goodness is produced. The sequence is: memory activated → deeds recalled as not-good → self-loathing as moral response. Memory is the trigger for the moral-recognition that precedes transformation. Jos 23:14 also activates memory: "you know in your hearts and souls... that not one word has failed" — the covenantal knowing of God's goodness is held in the inner being through remembered experience of his faithfulness. Goodness engages memory in both its positive and negative registers: remembering God's faithfulness (covenantal knowing) and remembering one's own not-goodness (moral reckoning). (OBS-067-OBS-034, OBS-067-OBS-035)

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-067-003: T3 reveals that goodness is the most comprehensively faculty-engaging characteristic in the programme's current analytical record. Every faculty except creativity (T3.5 — silence confirmed) shows subs…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals that goodness is the most comprehensively faculty-engaging characteristic in the programme's current analytical record. Every faculty except creativity (T3.5 — silence confirmed) shows substantive engagement: perception (tasting and seeing goodness), cognition (moral evaluation and ranking), memory (covenantal knowing and moral reckoning), affect (stable rooted gladness vs fragile surface gladness), volition (reconstituted toward the good), agency (active expression required and enabled), moral evaluation (goodness as the normative anchor of the evaluative faculty), conscience (goodness calibrates the conscience's standard), conscientiousness (integration of all faculties into sustained moral expression), and relational capacity (dual-directional overflow). The tier as a whole reveals that goodness is not a specialist characteristic — it is an integrating one. The person who possesses genuine goodness has every faculty engaged and aligned. This comprehensive faculty-engagement is what distinguishes genuine goodness from its surface forms: surface goodness (the Haman problem) engages affect without engaging conscience or volitional alignment; genuine goodness integrates all.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-067-014: T2 identified the constitutional movement of goodness from Spirit-level through soul and heart to outward expression (six-step sequence, Q&A-064). T3 names the faculty operations at each level: Spirit…
findings.finding_value: T2 identified the constitutional movement of goodness from Spirit-level through soul and heart to outward expression (six-step sequence, Q&A-064). T3 names the faculty operations at each level: Spirit-level corresponds to Spirit-production (T2.1) → T3.6 volitional reconstitution (the Spirit enables the resolve for good); soul-level seeking (T2.2) → T3.1 perceptual encounter (tasting and seeing); heart-level knowing and gladness (T2.3) → T3.3 memory and T3.4 affect; evaluative-cognitive function (T2.4) → T3.2 cognition and T3.8 moral evaluation; outward expression (T2.10) → T3.7 agency and T3.11 relational capacity. The two tiers together reveal that the constitutional movement is not an abstract structural description but a faculty-by-faculty account of how goodness moves through the person. Each constitutional level corresponds to specific faculty engagements. The T3 faculty map gives content to the T2 constitutional architecture.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-067-020: T3 identified three faculty engagements that are particularly significant for transformation: memory (Eze 36:31 — memory activates moral recognition, Q&A-072), affect (stable vs fragile gladness diagn…
findings.finding_value: T3 identified three faculty engagements that are particularly significant for transformation: memory (Eze 36:31 — memory activates moral recognition, Q&A-072), affect (stable vs fragile gladness diagnostic, Q&A-077), and moral evaluation (conscience calibration, Q&A-089-090). T5's three transformation mechanisms (encounter, Spirit-infusion, recognition-confrontation — Q&A-129) map onto these faculty engagements. The recognition-confrontation mechanism (Eze 36:31 / Rom 2:4) operates specifically through the memory faculty (recall of deeds) and the conscience-moral evaluation faculty (recognition as not-good and self-loathing). The encounter mechanism operates through the perceptive faculty (tasting — Q&A-066) and the affective faculty (trust, gladness — Q&A-075). The Spirit-infusion mechanism produces faculty-level transformation: it reconstitutes the volitional faculty (Q&A-082), enables agency (Q&A-085), and generates stable affect (Q&A-076). T5's mechanisms are faculty-specific operations — each mechanism transforms the person by engaging specific faculties in specific ways. This is the most analytically precise inter-tier connection so far.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-103-003: Love engages all eleven inner faculties, but five show the richest engagement: (1) Identity and self-understanding — love is the primary faculty through which the person knows who they are: being-love…
findings.finding_value: Love engages all eleven inner faculties, but five show the richest engagement: (1) Identity and self-understanding — love is the primary faculty through which the person knows who they are: being-loved (agapētos) constitutes identity from the outside; what-one-loves constitutes identity from the inside. The person is doubly defined by love. (2) Relational capacity — love is the faculty's active content: it builds (Joh 13:34), sustains (Lam 3:22), and restores (Luk 15:20) relational capacity. (3) Memory — love's sustaining faculty: love without memory cannot maintain itself through absence (Jer 31:20 — 'I do remember him still'). (4) Moral sensitivity — love calibrates what the inner person registers as morally significant; the love-of-God requirement generates the hate-evil requirement (Psa 97:10). (5) Attention — love determines what the person perceives as worth attending to (Phili 4:8 — think on what is lovely). The weaker engagements: creativity (indirect, evidenced through Song-form) and conscience (inferred, not directly named). Overall: love is the faculty-most-engaged characteristic in the programme, operating through perception, reason, memory, imagination, desire, emotion, moral sensitivity, conscience (indirectly), identity, and relational capacity simultaneously.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-103-002: Love's definition as directed-attachment-toward-an-object generates a characteristic pattern of faculty engagement. Because love is always toward an object, it necessarily engages attention (what is a…
findings.finding_value: Love's definition as directed-attachment-toward-an-object generates a characteristic pattern of faculty engagement. Because love is always toward an object, it necessarily engages attention (what is attended to is the beloved — Phili 4:8), reason (judgment of the object's worth and the hierarchy of competing loves — Mat 10:37), memory (remembering the beloved sustains love — Jer 31:20), and identity (what is loved constitutes who one is — Q&A-075). The definition's object-determination principle (moral quality determined by object) maps onto the moral sensitivity faculty: the faculty that calibrates moral perception is calibrated by love's direction — you notice what you love, and what you love as most important determines what you register as morally significant (Psa 97:10 — love-of-God generates hate-of-evil). The definition's tripartite structure (disposition/act/condition) maps onto the faculty architecture: disposition engages the will and conscience; act engages the relational capacity and body; condition engages identity and emotion. No faculty operates independently of love's fundamental structure.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-103-012: The faculty engagement pattern in T3 is produced by and oriented toward the relational interfaces in T4. Love's identity-faculty (T3.10) is constituted through the relational interface: being-loved by…
findings.finding_value: The faculty engagement pattern in T3 is produced by and oriented toward the relational interfaces in T4. Love's identity-faculty (T3.10) is constituted through the relational interface: being-loved by God (GOD→HUMAN axis) establishes the identity of agapētos; what-one-loves (active direction) establishes identity through the chosen object. The relational capacity faculty (T3.11) is the faculty through which the three relational axes are exercised: the GOD→HUMAN axis engages the relational capacity as receiver; the HUMAN→GOD axis engages it as giver; the HUMAN→HUMAN axis engages it in both directions simultaneously. Memory (T3.3) sustains the relational interface: love toward God is sustained through remembering his chesed (Jer 31:20); love in community is sustained through shared history. Moral sensitivity (T3.8) is calibrated by the relational interface structure: love-of-God calibrates the moral perception of what is evil (Psa 97:10); love-of-neighbour calibrates the perception of what is just. The deepest inter-tier finding: the faculty engagement pattern is not incidental — it is precisely the faculty configuration required by the relational architecture. The relational structure generates the faculty requirements.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-103-013: Formation in T5 operates through the same faculties identified in T3, producing their development. Memory is formed through the covenantal story — Israel's memory of God's love (Jer 2:2 — 'I remember …
findings.finding_value: Formation in T5 operates through the same faculties identified in T3, producing their development. Memory is formed through the covenantal story — Israel's memory of God's love (Jer 2:2 — 'I remember the devotion of your youth') is the ground for love's formation in both directions; formation requires knowing the love-history. Imagination is formed through eschatological vision: the forward-projection of love's fullness (Psa 27:13, Jer 31:34) orients present formation toward its goal. Identity formation is the T3.10/T5 overlap: being-named-beloved (Mat 3:17, Rom 1:7) is the formation's constitutive moment — identity received through love is the ground from which love-acts are exercised. The relational capacity faculty (T3.11) is the faculty that formation produces: the formation process (Spirit infusion, obedience-purification, training) produces a person with increasing relational capacity for love's three directional axes. The community's role in formation (Q&A-097) corresponds to the relational capacity faculty's communal engagement: the faculty cannot develop in isolation because love cannot exist without a beloved.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-103-014: The faculty engagement breadth in T3 is consistent with love's structural position as the programme's central sequential node in T6. A characteristic that engages all eleven faculties will necessarily…
findings.finding_value: The faculty engagement breadth in T3 is consistent with love's structural position as the programme's central sequential node in T6. A characteristic that engages all eleven faculties will necessarily stand at the intersection of the programme's full inner-being vocabulary — because any characteristic that engages one faculty will co-occur with love insofar as love also engages that faculty. The memory-faculty engagement explains part of the co-occurrence with despair (R044 — 55 shared verses): lament appeals to the memory of God's love (Lam 3:22) as its ground. The identity-faculty engagement explains the co-occurrence with calling (R019 — 51 shared): identity-as-beloved and identity-as-called are grammatically co-ordinate (Rom 1:7). The moral-sensitivity engagement explains co-occurrence with guilt (R073 — 32 shared): moral sensitivity calibrated by love recognises guilt as the state that precedes the forgiveness that generates love (Luk 7:47). Faculty engagement and structural relationships thus form a coherent explanatory system: the faculty profile generates the co-occurrence pattern.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-064-003: T3 reveals forgiveness as uniquely faculty-comprehensive — it engages more named faculties with greater specificity than any other characteristic reviewed in this revision series. Memory is explicitly…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals forgiveness as uniquely faculty-comprehensive — it engages more named faculties with greater specificity than any other characteristic reviewed in this revision series. Memory is explicitly named (Jer 31:34 — divine memory as the content of forgiveness) and distinctively: forgiveness transforms memory in both directions — God's memory of sin is set aside permanently; the human forgiver releases the active use of memory against the offender. Affect is bidirectionally engaged: as prerequisite (somatic compassion, Mat 18:27) and as product (love, Luk 7:47; reverence, Psa 130:4). Conscience is addressed and purified by forgiveness (Heb 9:14). Volition is constitutive (the heart-level release is chosen). Cognition is enabled (Jer 31:34 — forgiveness → knowing God). The single silence is creativity (T3.5). T3's synthesis: forgiveness is the most faculty-comprehensive characteristic in the current review set — it reaches every major faculty with specific evidenced content, most strikingly in the memory domain.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-009: T1's four modes explain T3's faculty engagement pattern. The covenantal-objective mode (no inner-being prerequisite) corresponds to T3's absence of any faculty requirement for that mode. The divine re…
findings.finding_value: T1's four modes explain T3's faculty engagement pattern. The covenantal-objective mode (no inner-being prerequisite) corresponds to T3's absence of any faculty requirement for that mode. The divine relational-personal mode (faith, repentance, confession as access-postures) engages volition, conscience, and cognition. The human horizontal mode ("from your heart") requires volition, conscience, and moral evaluation. The intercessory mode requires the dependence-posture that engages cognition (accurate assessment of the grounds of the plea — God's character, not human merit) and volition. T1's definition of forgiveness as transitional (not terminal) is confirmed by T3's finding that every faculty engaged by forgiveness is deepened toward further engagement — not closed by the act but opened by it.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-014: T2's constitutional locations map onto T3's faculty engagements. The heart-locus (T2.3 — Mat 18:35) corresponds to T3's volition, moral evaluation, and conscience faculties — all heart-level. The cogn…
findings.finding_value: T2's constitutional locations map onto T3's faculty engagements. The heart-locus (T2.3 — Mat 18:35) corresponds to T3's volition, moral evaluation, and conscience faculties — all heart-level. The cognition-locus (T2.4 — Jer 31:34) corresponds to T3's cognition and memory faculty engagements. The somatic-compassion locus (T2.5 — splagchnizomai) corresponds to T3's affect faculty at its somatic depth. The constitutional movement (T2.10 — guilt-bearing → forgiveness → love) is the sequence in which T3's faculties are engaged: conscience identifies the guilt → volition releases the claim → affect produces the love-response. Constitutional location determines faculty engagement sequence.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-019: T3's faculty engagements all point in the same relational directions that T4 identifies as primary. Conscience (T3.9) is engaged in both the seeking-forgiveness direction (human-to-God: confession as …
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty engagements all point in the same relational directions that T4 identifies as primary. Conscience (T3.9) is engaged in both the seeking-forgiveness direction (human-to-God: confession as conscience's public verdict) and the giving direction (human horizontal: the conscience that recognises the offence to be released). Memory (T3.3) is engaged in the God-to-human direction (divine "remember no more" — Jer 31:34) and the human-giving direction (releasing the memory's active use against the offender). Volition (T3.6) drives the giving direction (heart-level release is chosen). The vertical-horizontal interdependence (T4 structural claim) is the relational expression of T3's conscience-and-volition faculty account: the person whose conscience has accurately received the magnitude of divine forgiveness has the volitional capacity to extend horizontal forgiveness.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-020: T3's faculty deepenings (cognition enabled — Jer 31:34; love produced — Luk 7:47; conscience purified — Heb 9:14; volition redirected) are T5's formation products described at the faculty level. The f…
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty deepenings (cognition enabled — Jer 31:34; love produced — Luk 7:47; conscience purified — Heb 9:14; volition redirected) are T5's formation products described at the faculty level. The formation sequence (T5) is the longitudinal account of which T3's faculty engagements are the synchronic snapshots. The commanded forgiveness as sanctification discipline (T5.5 — Eph 4:32) is the formation vehicle through which the volitional faculty (T3.6) is habituated and the moral evaluation faculty (T3.8) is deepened. T3 and T5 together reveal the full formation arc: T3 shows what happens to each faculty in the moment of forgiveness; T5 shows what sustained habitual forgiveness does to the person over time.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-021: T3's memory faculty finding (Jer 31:34 — divine "remember no more") explains the R160 thought/knowledge co-occurrence at that verse: the divine cognitive act of non-remembering and the human cognitive…
findings.finding_value: T3's memory faculty finding (Jer 31:34 — divine "remember no more") explains the R160 thought/knowledge co-occurrence at that verse: the divine cognitive act of non-remembering and the human cognitive outcome of knowing God meet in the same verse because they are structurally connected — the guilt-barrier's removal (forgiveness) enables the cognitive-relational access (knowing God). T3's affect-faculty finding (love produced — Luk 7:47) explains the R103 love co-occurrence (8 shared verses) — love is the affective downstream product of forgiveness. T3's conscience faculty finding confirms the R073 guilt structural partnership — guilt is what conscience identifies as the prior condition that forgiveness addresses. Faculty engagements (T3) and structural co-occurrences (T6) are mutually explanatory.

findings.finding_value: T7's literary forms explain why T3 finds different faculty engagements in different evidential contexts. The cultic-legal corpus (Lev 4:20) — covenantal-objective mode — requires no named faculty engagement (T3 finds no faculty requirement for this mode). The prophetic corpus (Jer 31:34) primarily engages cognition and memory (T3.2, T3.3). The Synoptic narrative corpus (Luk 7:47, Mat 18:27, Mat 18:35) engages affect, volition, and conscience most richly. The apostolic letter corpus (Eph 1:7, Eph 4:32) grounds the formation dimension (T3.10 conscientiousness, T5.5 sanctification). Each literary form carries specific faculty registers — T7's literary analysis explains T3's faculty engagement distribution.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-003: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion re…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion responds, it does not originate or create. It is the most responsive of the faculties-engaging characteristics. Second, affect and moral action are structurally unified in compassion — not sequentially related but simultaneous. Affect is the mechanism of movement (splanchnizō is both the felt inner event and the cause of the action), not a precursor or accompaniment. This is unique among the characteristics reviewed: in most other registries, affect and volition are distinguishable stages; in compassion, the felt movement is already the morally motivated action beginning. A third distinctive finding: compassion converts moral knowledge into motivated action — it is the motivational ground of conscientiousness, not a product of it. The conscience faculty engagement reveals compassion as conscience-healing: it addresses the pitiable condition that conscience perceives as a moral claim, resolving the tension between moral knowledge and moral incapacity. The three relational modes (building/sustaining — chesed; restoring/repairing — splanchnizō; extending across difference — Good Samaritan) are a new finding not in the instruction typology.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-003: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked …
findings.finding_value: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I but the grace of God that is with me." Agency is not displaced but constituted by grace. This relationship holds in paradox that the T3.6 prompt options (enable/deepen/bypass/impair) cannot accommodate — a prompt design limitation noted for catalogue revision. Second, grace produces moral clarity (T3.8 — sharpens moral evaluation rather than bypassing it): the person who recognises grace has made a precise moral evaluation (they know they received what they did not deserve). Third, grace and conscience are mutually necessary: grace is the condition within which conscience can operate fully without destroying the person; conscience without grace produces condemnation; grace without conscience produces presumption (T3.9). Fourth, grace is the primary relational faculty developer in the registry's evidence — it reaches every relational register (vertical access, horizontal forgiving, speech-grace) and enables each one. Creativity (T3.5) is the one genuinely silent faculty — not an impairment but a non-engagement: grace receives and constitutes, it does not create.

findings.session_b_note: Yes — memory is one of the most structurally prominent inner faculties in the covenant vocabulary, operating in both directions. God's active remembering of the covenant is the guarantee of its continuing operation — divine memory is the sustaining mechanism of covenant faithfulness. (2) Human covenant-memory: Deu 4:23 — "Take care, lest you forget the covenant of the Lord your God" (Group 765-002 — command to remember); Deu 8:18 — "remember the Lord your God... that he may confirm his covenant." The covenant meal is structured as a memorial act — covenant and memory are architecturally linked through the liturgical practice of remembering.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-099-003: T3 reveals that kindness engages a remarkably wide range of inner faculties — nine of eleven are evidenced with at least partial engagement. The two genuine absences (imagination and creativity) are s…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals that kindness engages a remarkably wide range of inner faculties — nine of eleven are evidenced with at least partial engagement. The two genuine absences (imagination and creativity) are structurally coherent: kindness is relational and loyally directed, not generative. The most significant faculty engagements are: (a) volition — kindness is chosen, not merely felt; the "put on" and "love kindness" language makes this constitutive; (b) agency — chrēsteuomai names love actively exercising kindness — kindness is enacted, not passive; (c) relational capacity — kindness constitutes relationships in their quality, not merely accompanies them; (d) conscientiousness — the chasid represents the full integration of moral awareness, will, and action in consistent reliable pattern; (e) taste as the primary perceptive mode — "tasted that the Lord is good" establishes that kindness is encountered experientially before it is understood conceptually. The pattern across all engaged faculties: kindness integrates the whole inner person — it does not operate as a single-faculty characteristic but as a whole-person orientation. T3's most significant intra-tier finding: kindness is a multi-faculty characteristic whose breadth of engagement reflects its status as a constitutive relational orientation rather than a single affective or volitional act.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-099-022: T3's finding that taste is the primary perceptive faculty for kindness (1Pet 2:3 — "tasted that the Lord is good / chrēstos") is grounded in T7's lexical finding that chrēstos itself carries the quali…
findings.finding_value: T3's finding that taste is the primary perceptive faculty for kindness (1Pet 2:3 — "tasted that the Lord is good / chrēstos") is grounded in T7's lexical finding that chrēstos itself carries the quality of agreeable goodness — something that can be tasted and found to be of a certain quality. The word chrēstos, which names the characteristic, contains an implicit sensory metaphor: it is the kind of characteristic that one encounters through experience (taste) before grasping conceptually. T7's lexical finding that chesed's semantic range includes goodness/faithfulness — not merely kindness — maps onto T3's cognition finding (T3.2 — Hos 6:6 pairing chesed with knowledge of God): genuine chesed requires a cognitive grasp of who God is, which is consistent with chesed carrying a knowledge-dimension in its semantic range. T7's most useful human science framework (developmental psychology/attachment theory) connects with T3's relational capacity finding: attachment theory explains the faculty-level mechanism by which the "secure base" of divine chesed enables the human person to exercise relational capacity toward others.

findings.session_b_note: Yes — in its negative form most directly. Lam 3:17 ("my soul is bereft of peace; I have forgotten what happiness is") — peace-deprivation produces the loss of remembered happiness. The person bereft of shalom cannot recall what flourishing was like — memory of wellbeing is inaccessible in the peaceless condition. This is a striking data point: peace's absence disrupts not only the present experience but the person's ability to remember peace. Conversely: Isa 38:17 ("it was for my welfare that I had great bitterness") — Hezekiah's retrospective memory of peace-through-suffering suggests that the person who has received peace carries a memory of its arrival that shapes their understanding of God.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-117-002: T1 names peace as integrative wholeness; T3 specifies how each inner faculty is engaged. The convergence: peace is integrative precisely because it engages all faculties — perception (enabling divine …
findings.finding_value: T1 names peace as integrative wholeness; T3 specifies how each inner faculty is engaged. The convergence: peace is integrative precisely because it engages all faculties — perception (enabling divine hearing), cognition (right orientation), memory (recovering forgotten happiness), affect (holding feeling rightly), volition (the most constitutive engagement — peace is chosen and refused), agency (liberated by authentic peace), moral evaluation (right judgment), conscience (gateway faculty), conscientiousness (integrated response enabled), and relational capacity (co-constitutive with interiority). The faculty engagement pattern confirms: peace is integrative because it involves every inner capacity simultaneously. The faculty that can most destroy peace (suppressed conscience) and most enable it (exercised conscience) is not the most obviously prominent but the most structurally foundational.

findings.finding_value: T3's faculty findings and T5's developmental findings illuminate each other. Memory (T3.3) connects to T5's sequence finding: the Lam 3 pathway (peaceless → remember → hope → wait) uses memory as the specific faculty through which the peaceless person recovers peace. Volition (T3.6) connects to T5's mechanism: the deliberate re-direction of the mind (Isa 26:3) is both a volitional act (T3.6) and the cognitive-orientation mechanism (T5.3) by which peace is received. Conscience (T3.9) connects to T5's transformation: the confession that exercises conscience (T3.9) is simultaneously the mechanism (T5.3) by which the suppressed-conscience peacelessness is resolved. Each faculty engagement is also a developmental mechanism.

findings.session_b_note: Yes — memory is structurally engaged in the covenantal giving register (872-001). Neh 9:15 ("you told them to go in to possess the land that you had sworn to give them") invokes the memory of the wilderness generation as the basis of current covenant identity. The covenantal giving narrative is a memory-saturated structure: each giving builds on and recalls prior giving.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-060-003: T3 as a whole reveals that this characteristic engages virtually every inner faculty in the programme's 11-faculty model — the only consistent gap is creativity (T3.5, S across three prompts). The pat…
findings.finding_value: T3 as a whole reveals that this characteristic engages virtually every inner faculty in the programme's 11-faculty model — the only consistent gap is creativity (T3.5, S across three prompts). The pattern of engagement is not uniform: perception is engaged as precondition (God hears before giving); cognition is constituted (wisdom is given, not generated); memory is deepened (the narrative-temporal dimension of covenantal giving); affect is the source of giving (compassion, anger) and the target of transformation (mourning→gladness); volition is called forth and elevated (genuine giving cannot be coerced); agency is the bridge between disposition and act; moral evaluation both produces and is produced by the characteristic; conscience is engaged indirectly through Spirit-forming and prophetic warning; conscientiousness at the human apex is the full integration of all three (moral awareness, will, act). Relational capacity is intrinsic — every mode is two-party. What T3 reveals as a whole: faithfulness-as-giving is not a faculty-specific characteristic but a whole-person characteristic — it recruits and integrates all active faculties into a unified inner-being act. The creativity silence is the only dimension where the data cannot confirm engagement.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-007: The constitutional locations (T2 — spirit, heart, soul, hidden inner parts, body) and the inner faculties (T3 — perception, cognition, memory, affect, volition, agency, moral evaluation, relational ca…
findings.finding_value: The constitutional locations (T2 — spirit, heart, soul, hidden inner parts, body) and the inner faculties (T3 — perception, cognition, memory, affect, volition, agency, moral evaluation, relational capacity) are not independent — they occupy the same inner-being territory from two different analytical perspectives. T2 asks where; T3 asks which faculty. Reading them together reveals: the heart (leb, T2.3) is the location of affect-volition integration (T3.4, T3.6) — where compassion (affect) determines giving (volitional act). The hidden inner parts (tukhoth, T2.5) are the constitutional home of the cognitive-formative faculty (T3.2 — the wisdom that is given there). The body (T2.6-7) is the somatic site of agentive expression (T3.7 — agency expresses through the body). The spirit (ruach, T2.1) is both the object of constitutive giving and the faculty whose depletion the eschatological giving addresses — connecting to the agency and relational capacity faculties that cannot operate from a faint spirit. What this pair reveals: constitutional location and faculty engagement are two descriptions of the same inner-being event. The characteristic is located constitutionally precisely where the relevant faculties operate.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-013: The faculty engagement pattern (T3) and the formation arc (T5) are directly linked: the faculties engaged by the characteristic are precisely the faculties that are formed through it. Cognition is bot…
findings.finding_value: The faculty engagement pattern (T3) and the formation arc (T5) are directly linked: the faculties engaged by the characteristic are precisely the faculties that are formed through it. Cognition is both constituted by endowing giving (T3.2 — wisdom deposited) and is the target of formation (T5.5 — Spirit given to instruct shapes over time). Memory is engaged by the covenantal mode (T3.3 — narrative-temporal dimension) and is the sustained environment of covenantal formation (T5.5 — the history of received giving shapes identity). Agency is both the bridge between disposition and act (T3.7) and is restored/enabled by eschatological giving (T3.7 Q&A-087 — depressed agency is renewed). Suffering reveals (T5.4 — tests the characteristic) and tests affect, volition, and conscientiousness (T3.4, T3.6, T3.10). What this pair reveals: the characteristic forms the person by engaging and developing the same faculties it requires for its own expression. Formation is circular in this characteristic: it needs faculties to be enacted, and its enactment develops those faculties further.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-015: The faculty engagement pattern (T3 — hearing precedes giving, memory is narrative-temporal, affect is at source and target, conscientiousness is the apex) and the methodological-evidential analysis (T…
findings.finding_value: The faculty engagement pattern (T3 — hearing precedes giving, memory is narrative-temporal, affect is at source and target, conscientiousness is the apex) and the methodological-evidential analysis (T7 — virtue ethics illuminates, attachment theory illuminates, both diverge at critical points) converge in an analytically productive way. Virtue ethics (T7.3) addresses the same faculties that T3 identifies: moral evaluation, volition, agency, conscientiousness are the virtue-ethics faculties. The virtue-ethics framework illuminates T3 findings precisely because both are addressing the same inner-being territory. The divergence (T7.3.3 — virtue ethics cannot account for the constitutive primacy of received divine giving) maps onto the T3 finding that cognition is constituted by endowing giving (Q&A-071) rather than generated by the person. Attachment theory illuminates the hearing-precedes-giving pattern (T3.1 — God hears inner suffering) and the restoration of relational responsiveness (T3.11 — relational capacity restored). What this pair reveals: the human-science frameworks are useful precisely because they address the same inner-being faculties, and limited precisely where they diverge from the biblical account of those faculties' grounding.

Memory is central to the persistence of hatred, particularly in group 1200 (sa.tam — grudge-bearing). Gen 27:41: Esau remembers the blessing theft. Gen 50:15: Joseph's brothers remember what they did to him — and fear he remembers it too. The grudge lives in memory; without memory it cannot persist. Sa.tam is essentially hatred preserved in memory across time — the grudge is the memory of the wound kept alive in the inner being.
