The retrospective lament of Pro 5:12 ("how I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof") — here memory perceives retrospectively what the contempt cost. Memory is the faculty that looks back on the contempt and names its damage, but not the faculty that sustains the contempt itself.

The eschatological permanence of de.ra.on (Dan 12:2) is not a memory-sustained state but a permanent condition.
Memory is not visibly engaged in M06-D. Cruelty is not characteristically sustained by memory of a wound — it operates as a settled character condition independently of specific memories.

Isa 54:4: "you will forget the shame of your youth, and the reproach of your widowhood you will remember no more" — the explicit naming of forgetting as what restoration requires shows that memory is the organ through which reproach is carried beyond its immediate experience. Psa 89:50: "I bear in my heart the insults of all the many nations" — the bearing is a memory-carrying function.
Memory is not prominently engaged in M06-F. The adversary relationship is present-active rather than memory-sustained.

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** Yes — "future generations shall proclaim it" (Psa 22:31, VSG M26-A1-005); "your righteousness shall be proclaimed to a people yet to be born" (Psa 22:31). The proclamation of God's righteousness across generations requires memory — the community holds the testimony of what God has done and passes it on. The psalmist who declares God's righteousness "all day" (Psa 35:28; 71:24; 145:7) is drawing on remembered encounters with God's righteousness.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Yes — memory is used against the righteous person and in favor of them. "None of the righteous deeds that he has done shall be remembered" (Eze 18:24, VSG M26-A2-002) — in the Ezekiel forfeiture material, righteousness is non-accumulative: past righteous deeds are not held in God's memory when the person turns to wickedness. Conversely, "none of the transgressions he has committed shall be remembered against him" (Eze 18:22, VSG M26-A2-002) when the wicked person repents. Memory — specifically God's remembering or not remembering — is the mechanism by which righteousness is assessed in the Ezekiel material.

**[C — Justification]** Yes — "as David also speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works" (Rom 4:6, VSG 3410-001). The appeal to David and Abraham (Rom 4:3–9) is an appeal to remembered precedent: the historical instances of credited righteousness are held in memory and applied as typological patterns. Justification by faith is not a novelty — Paul argues from remembered Scripture.
**[D — Avenging Justice]** Memory is not a primary engagement in D's verse evidence. Silence.

**[E — Condemnation]** Yes — the Ninevites' repentance is held in memory and applied as a standard of condemnation for the present generation (Mat 12:41, VSG 4846-001). The memory of past righteous responses condemns present unrighteous non-response.
**[F — Moral Reckoning]** The reckoning faculty is a present-deliberative act — it operates in the present moment of counting, not through memory retrieval. Silence.
**[G — Structural Opposites]** Memory is not a primary engagement in G's verse evidence. Silence.

**[CLUSTER — T3.3]** E. Memory engages the cluster specifically in: (1) the communal transmission of testimony to God's righteousness (A1); (2) the assessment of past righteous deeds in the Ezekiel forfeiture mechanism (A2); (3) the typological appeal to Abraham and David as remembered precedents for faith-righteousness (C); and (4) the use of past righteous responses as standards of condemnation (E). The cluster reveals that righteousness is not ahistorical — it accumulates testimony and creates a remembered pattern that the community carries forward.

findings.finding_value: Memory is implicitly engaged in M46-A through its failure. The prosperity-apostasy pattern requires the person to forget what God has done: Deu 32:15 (Jeshurun "forsook God who made him") implies forgetting the God of their making. Neh 9:25-26 narrates the pattern explicitly: Israel received the land, ate, were filled, delighted — and then "were disobedient and rebelled against you and cast your law behind their back and killed your prophets." The casting behind the back is a memory-rejection: what God has done is actively put behind attention.

findings.finding_value: M01-A engages memory in its formation: Deu 31:12-13 (public Torah-reading produces fear in children who have not yet heard — fear is formed through cumulative hearing and memory of God's word); 1Sa 12:24 ("fear of the Lord is commanded as an all-heart devotion **grounded in memory of God's great deeds**" — memory grounds reverential fear); 2Ki 17:38 ("correct inner fear is inseparable from **memory and loyalty**; forsaking the covenant opens the heart to misplaced reverence").

M01-B engages memory as a preventive or corrective: Deu 7:18 ("Israel is told not to be afraid of the nations they must displace — the inward dread of numerous enemies is to be **replaced by memory of what God did to Pharaoh**, grounding courage in historical experience"); Isa 33:18 (M01-C-VCG-04: "the heart will **muse on the past terror** after the enemy is gone — the inner faculty of reflection revisits the dread once it has passed"). Memory of God's past acts counters present fear.

M01-F engages memory in a specific way: Job 21:6 (M01-E-VCG-05: "shuddering takes hold of Job's flesh the **moment memory brings dismay**" — memory triggering somatic fear response); Deu 28:60 (M01-F-VCG-02: "Israel's former terror of Egypt's diseases is recalled — God will bring back the very afflictions they once dreaded, **exploiting that deep-seated fear**" — memory as the site of embedded anticipatory dread).

Memory is engaged across M01 in three distinct modes: (1) **formative** — fear of God is built by cumulative memory of his acts (M01-A); (2) **corrective** — memory of past divine deliverance counters present acute fear (M01-B); (3) **triggering** — memory of past fear retrieves that fear in the present (M01-F-VCG-02). Memory is not a dominant faculty engagement in M01 but it is consistently present as a mediating element.

Yes. Heb 3:11 and 4:3 (M02-A-VCG-01) deploy the wilderness generation's wrath-experience as a canonical memory that functions normatively for future generations — the oath of wrath is remembered and its memorial function is explicit in how Hebrews uses it. Deu 9:7 (M02-A-VCG-04): "Remember how you provoked God to wrath" — memory of past divine anger is commanded as a formative inner exercise for the present generation.

Rev 16:19 (M02-A-VCG-03): God's wrath toward Babylon is described as "remembered, purposeful divine disposition that delivers the full penalty long stored up" — the wrath itself is a form of divine memory, holding the record of accumulated offenses until their full reckoning.

Yes, prominently. Memory is a recurring trigger for grief in M03-A. The exiles' communal grief sitting by Babylon's waters is triggered by remembering Zion (Psa 137:1 — M03-A-VCG-03): grief arises when the lost past is brought into present awareness through memory. Old men weeping when the new temple foundation is laid, because they remember the former one (Ezr 3:12 — M03-A-VCG-01): grief triggered by memory of what has been lost. Rachel's inconsolable weeping (Jer 31:15 — M03-A-VCG-01) arises from the knowledge of irreversible loss — memory of what was but is no longer. In M03-BOUNDARY, Joseph's naming his son Manasseh because God made him forget his hardship (Gen 41:51) shows grief diminishing when the painful memory is released.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. The dominant pattern of exultation in the Psalms is directed at God's past acts of salvation: Psa 9:14 (exultation anticipated in the future but grounded in God's known character); Psa 31:7 (rejoicing in steadfast love because "you have seen my affliction"); Psa 35:9 (soul's exultation at "his salvation" — the whole history of God's saving acts). The eschatological exultation passages (Isa 65:18–19; Zep 3:17) also engage a remembered pattern — God's past covenant faithfulness is the warrant for future exultation.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes. Psa 66:6 — "they passed through the river on foot. There did we rejoice in him" — the memory of the Exodus crossing is the ground for present communal rejoicing; the joy is retrospective and memory-anchored. Psa 106:5 — "that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation" — the psalmist desires to enter into the joy of the nation's memory of God's acts. Psa 137:6 — "if I do not set Jerusalem above my highest joy" — the memory of Jerusalem as the place of joy is the psalmist's highest value. Psa 51:12 — "restore to me the joy of your salvation" — David's memory of pre-sin joy is the reference point for what he asks restored. The M04-E-VCG-01 restoration joy (sa.s.von) is essentially the promised restoration of what was and is remembered: Jer 33:11 (the voice of gladness returning after judgment silenced it) — memory of pre-judgment joy is the criterion of restoration.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Partially. Joh 8:56 (Abraham's anticipatory joy at Christ's day) involves a prophetic forward-memory — the faith-memory of a promised future. Act 2:26 (Peter quoting Psalm 16 — "my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced") is a memory-act — the NT church's appropriation of David's hope as the basis for present confidence. The memory of Christ's suffering and resurrection (1Pe 4:13 — "share Christ's sufferings") grounds present Suffering-Joy in the remembered pattern of Christ's own suffering-to-glory.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. M04-O-VCG-02 (better-than comparatives) frequently engages retrospective memory: Hos 2:7 ("it was better for me then than now") — comparison of present adversity to remembered better past; Jon 4:3, 8 (Jonah's despairing comparison) — past memory of expectations shaping present evaluation. M04-O-VCG-04 (covenantal promise-goodness) engages a different memory: Jos 21:45 ("not one word of all the good promises had failed") — the cumulative memory of God's faithfulness is the ground for present confidence. M04-L-VCG-01's doxological praise formula ("for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever") is itself a memory-rehearsal — the Psalms' repeated ki-tov declarations sustain communal memory of divine goodness.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes: (1) **The Psa 119 sha.a pairings** — Psa 119:16 ("I will delight in your statutes; I will not forget your word") — Delight and memory are explicitly paired; the opposite of Delight in God's word is forgetting it; (2) **Jer 31:20** ("as often as I speak against him, I do remember him still") — God's sha.a.shu.im in Ephraim as a darling child sustains memory even through rebuke; divine Delight functions as a memory-anchor for the beloved; (3) **Hos 2:7** (adjacent — the people remembering that "it was better for me then than now" — the memory of former delight driving return); (4) **Psa 37:4** — "he will give you the desires of your heart" — the heart's desires shaped by Delight in God require memory of what God has given as a sustaining reference.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Partially: (1) **2Sa 1:26** — David's lament for Jonathan recalls the pleasantness of their relationship; memory of pleasantness is what makes grief acute; (2) **Jer 51:34** — Jerusalem's delicacies devoured by Nebuchadnezzar — the memory of former pleasantness intensifies the sense of loss; (3) **Psa 77:11** (in M04-I, not directly Pleasure but adjacent) — the act of remembering pleasant past experiences of God sustains present endurance.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes — memory is Wonder's second most prominent faculty: (1) **"Remember the wondrous works"** (1Ch 16:12; Psa 105:5; 111:4) — deliberate memory-engagement as a core Wonder-practice; (2) **"The wonders of old"** (Psa 77:11) — retrospective memory of past wonders as the inner strategy for sustaining faith through present distress; (3) **"Did not consider your wondrous works"** (Neh 9:17; Psa 106:7) — memory-failure as Wonder-failure; (4) **"He has caused his wondrous works to be remembered"** (Psa 111:4) — God himself ensuring his wonders remain in memory; (5) **"Do not hide them from their children"** (Psa 78:4) — generational memory-transmission as the Wonder-preserving act.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Memory is engaged across all seven characteristics, with Wonder (Char 6) as the most memory-dependent and Suffering-Joy (Char 7) as the most distinctive in its memory-mode: (1) **Most memory-dependent**: Wonder (Char 6) — the Tell-Remember-Meditate triad is the cluster's most explicit memory-practice; the entire 61-verse VCG-01 proclamatory corpus is a sustained communal memory exercise; Wonder-failure equals memory-failure (Neh 9:17; Psa 78:11); (2) **Memory as sustaining resource**: Joy (Char 2) — the feast-joy is constitutively memorial (Deu 16:11 — "rejoice in all that the Lord your God has blessed you"); Psa 51:12 (restored joy sought using the memory of pre-sin joy as reference point); (3) **Memory as the Delight-anchor**: Delight (Char 4) — Psa 119:16's "I will delight in your statutes; I will not forget your word" pairs Delight and memory as mutually sustaining; God's sha.a.shu.im in Ephraim sustains God's own memory through rebuke (Jer 31:20); (4) **Christological-eschatological memory** (unique to Suffering-Joy Char 7): the memory of Christ's suffering and resurrection as the formative ground for present Suffering-Joy — a specifically theological-historical memory rather than biographical memory.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, explicitly. Eze 16:61 (vc=38511): "then you will *remember* your ways and be ashamed" — memory activating shame. Eze 16:63 (vc=65575) — "that you may *remember* and be confounded" — memory paired with the shame-silencing. The generational dimension of shame (Ezr 9:7 — "from the days of our fathers") shows shame carried in collective memory. Isa 54:4 (vc=34838) — "you will *forget* the shame of your youth" — God's promise directly addresses the memory-load of shame, promising its dissolution. Shame and memory are structurally linked: shame is partly constituted by memory (the remembered failure or wound) and is resolved when memory is reoriented (forgetting the shame, or remembering it differently under atonement).

**[CHAR-2]** E — VCG-04 evidence (Eze 32; Jer 23:40) shows CHAR-2 engaging memory through its persistence: "perpetual shame, which shall not be forgotten" — the humiliation is branded into the identity-record. Warriors who bear shame into the pit carry a memory of their defeat outlasting their life. Memory in CHAR-2 operates as the vehicle for the enduring burden.

**[CHAR-4]** S — Not directly evidenced in the 16-verse corpus. Silent.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Memory is engaged in CHAR-5 through the accumulated identity-formation of sustained contempt. Bartimaeus's beggar-identity (Mar 10:50) is a memory-constituted condition: the accumulated contempt of years has deposited into a self-understanding that the person carries as their ongoing identity. The throwing off of the cloak is a memory-renunciation act — a decisive abandonment of the shame-identity that contempt has written into the person's inner record.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Memory is engaged in CHAR-6 through the psalmist's appeal to his maintained moral record: "I have kept my heart clean" (Psa 73:13) is a memory-claim about sustained moral integrity. The psalmist's maintenance of innocence is something he remembers and can appeal to as a sustained pattern, not merely a momentary state.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Memory is engaged across Chars 1, 2, 5, and 6. Char 1 shows shame feeding on memory and God's promise addressing the memory-load (Isa 54:4 — "you will forget the shame of your youth"). Char 2 shows shame persisting as a permanent identity-record beyond death (Eze 32:24-30). Char 5 shows accumulated contempt depositing into a shame-identity (Bartimaeus's beggar-cloak — Mar 10:50). Char 6 shows the psalmist's appeal to sustained moral record ("I have kept my heart clean" — Psa 73:13). Cluster-level pattern: shame accumulates in memory (Chars 1, 2, 5) and innocence makes a memory-claim (Char 6). The cluster's most significant memory-promise — Isa 54:4's divine dissolving of the shame of youth — is M07's eschatological answer to the memory-problem that shame creates. Chars 3 and 4 do not directly evidence memory-engagement; silent for those two characteristics.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, primarily by disabling specific memory. Deu 8:14 (vc=34223, M08-A1-VCG-01): "your heart will be lifted up and you forget the Lord your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery" — the heart-lift directly produces forgetfulness of God's redemptive history; the memory of divine provision and deliverance is the specific content that CHAR-1 displaces. Hos 13:6 (vc=34232, M08-A1-VCG-01): "when they had grazed, they became full, they were filled, and their heart was lifted up; therefore they forgot me" — the same sequence: prosperity → heart lifted → God forgotten. 2Ch 32:25 (vc=34045, M08-A1-VCG-01): "Hezekiah's heart was proud rather than grateful — inner self-exaltation displaced proper thankfulness for divine benefit" — CHAR-1 displaces the memory-sustained gratitude that divine benefit should generate.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes. The Neh 9 corpus (vc=34125, vc=34120, vc=34126, M08-B-VCG-01) evidences the specific memory failure that characterises CHAR-2 at the communal level: Israel "acted presumptuously" despite the memory of God's prior redemptive acts (Neh 9:10: "you performed signs and wonders") and prior covenant commands. The repeated pattern ("even after warnings, they acted presumptuously again" — Neh 9:29) confirms that CHAR-2 operates despite available memory of divine action, not in its absence.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, partially. 1Ki 20:11 (vc=33353, M08-C-VCG-01): "let not him who puts on his armour boast like him who takes it off" — premature boasting involves forgetting (or ignoring) that the outcome is not yet achieved; the memory of past uncertainties would prevent the boast. 1Cor 4:7 (vc=33871): boasting "as if you did not receive it" — the memory of the reception of one's goods (and their source) is precisely what the boaster has failed to hold. CHAR-3 in its VCG-01 form operates by setting aside the memory of received goods and uncertain futures.

**[CHAR-4]** S — The verse evidence in §3.C is silent on CHAR-4 engaging the memory faculty. No verse addresses memory retention or forgetfulness in relation to vain conceit. The epistemic failure of 1Ti 6:4 ("understanding nothing") may imply a form of active non-retention, but this is not explicitly evidenced.

**[CHAR-5]** S — The verse evidence in §3.D is largely silent on CHAR-5 engaging the memory faculty directly. The closest evidence is the general pattern of CHAR-1's memory-displacement (forgetting God after prosperity), which CHAR-5 participates in through the ease/prosperity trigger, but §3.D does not explicitly name forgetting in relation to CHAR-5 specifically.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The memory faculty is engaged by CHAR-1, CHAR-2, and CHAR-3, but silent for CHAR-4 and CHAR-5. CHAR-1: bypasses memory of divine provision (Deu 8:14, M08-A1-VCG-01: "you forget the Lord your God"; Hos 13:6, M08-A1-VCG-01: "they forgot me"). CHAR-2: overrides the memory of covenantal history and its obligations (Neh 9:16/29, M08-B-VCG-01: repeated presumption despite remembered covenant history). CHAR-3: bypasses the memory of the received quality of goods (1Cor 4:7, M08-C-VCG-01: "as if you did not receive it") and the memory of future uncertainty (Pro 27:1, M08-C-VCG-01: boasting about tomorrow). CHAR-4 and CHAR-5 are silent on memory-engagement. The cluster-synthesis: M08's memory-engagement is concentrated in the three characteristics with Hebrew OT primary corpora (CHAR-1, CHAR-2, CHAR-3) and is notably absent from the two NT-heavy or NT-only characteristics (CHAR-4 entirely NT; CHAR-5 primarily OT but non-Deuteronomic). This may reflect the Deuteronomic tradition's particular emphasis on memory as the antidote to pride (Deu 8:14's "forget the Lord" being the defining memory-failure for CHAR-1).

**[CHAR-2]** E — Memory engagement is present but implicit. 2Cor7:15 — Titus's "deepened affection" is stirred by "recalling the Corinthians' obedience" — the memory of the community's past obedience functions as the affective prompt for renewed relation. Phile21 — Paul's confidence in Philemon's obedience is based on a known track-record (a memory-informed character assessment). The characteristic's sustained formation (Phili2:12 — "always obeyed") implies a memory-function in tracking the consistency of the inner disposition across time.

**[CHAR-3]** S — The two-verse corpus does not directly evidence engagement with the memory faculty. Psa34:18 and Isa57:15 address the present state of contrition and God's response to it without naming memory as an engaged faculty.

**[CHAR-4]** S — The two-verse corpus does not directly evidence engagement with the memory faculty. The shared-weakness ground of Heb5:2 may implicitly involve the memory of one's own past failures or experiences of weakness, but this is inferred beyond the text.

**[CHAR-5]** S — The three-verse corpus does not directly evidence engagement with the memory faculty by semnotēs. The characteristic is addressed as a present character quality without memory-function engagement named.

**[CHAR-6]** S — The five-verse corpus does not directly evidence engagement with the memory faculty. Psa51:12's penitential context implies retrospective awareness of past failure, but the willing spirit sought is a forward-oriented gift rather than a memory-function.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Memory engagement is implicit rather than explicit in the corpus. The ka.na narrative pattern (Israel's repeated failures and humblings across Chronicles) suggests that the absence of humility involves a failure of moral memory — not retaining the lessons of prior judgment. 2Ch33:19 records Manasseh's humbling as a "turning point" in his biography, suggesting the memory-function of marking and retaining the significance of an inner event. However, the corpus does not directly name the memory faculty as engaged by humility. The clearest implicit memory connexion is 2Ch33:23 (Amon's failure to humble as Manasseh his father had) — the comparison implies that Manasseh's example was available as a remembered model which Amon refused to follow.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Memory engagement is implicit rather than explicit across the cluster; no characteristic directly evidences memory as a primary faculty. CHAR-1 has the clearest indirect evidence: the Chronicles narrative's repeated-humbling pattern implies a moral-memory function (Amon's failure to humble as Manasseh had — 2Ch33:23 — implies Manasseh's example was available as a remembered model). CHAR-2: Phile21 (Paul's confidence in Philemon's obedience based on known track-record) implies memory-informed character assessment. CHAR-3 through CHAR-6: largely silent on memory. Cluster-level: M09's silence on memory as a primary faculty reflects the cluster's present-tense orientation — these are characteristics of how the person is before God and others *now*, not characteristics primarily mediated through retrospective memory. The cluster's engagement with the past is through moral self-knowledge (CHAR-3 — confronting one's own failure) rather than through memory as a primary constitutional faculty. This distinguishes M09 from clusters where remembrance or historical consciousness is central.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The memory faculty is engaged in two directions. (1) *Pre-act memory as deterrent*: Psa 119:11 ("I have stored up your word in my heart") — the word memorised is what prevents sinning; the memory faculty holds the moral resource that deters the will. (2) *Post-act memory as reckoning*: Gen 42:22 — Reuben's retrieval of his past warning ("Did I not tell you not to sin against the boy?") in the present moment of distress shows memory connecting the past act of sinning to present consequence. The cultic-atonement corpus (VCG-04: Lev 4:23 — "the sin which he has committed is made known to him") shows memory-retrieval as the trigger for cultic obligation when the sin surfaces to conscious recollection.

**[CHAR-10]** S — The 5-verse corpus does not explicitly engage the memory faculty in connection with any of the three mechanisms. The characteristic's focus is on present-tense processes (being enticed, acting hypocritically, forsaking) rather than on memory retrieval or retention.

**[CHAR-11]** E — Memory is engaged through the ledger/accounting dimension of the condition. Rom 4:8 — "blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin" — sin is "counted" against the person; the divine memory of the person's sin-condition constitutes the ledger. Act 3:19 — "that your sins may be blotted out" — blotting out is a memory-erasure metaphor: the divine record is cleared. 1Ti 5:24 — "the sins of some people are conspicuous, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others appear later" — the temporal dimension of when the condition's recorded content appears implies a memory-record that either surfaces now or at judgment.

**[CHAR-12]** S — The 9-verse corpus does not explicitly engage the memory faculty in connection with sin as enslaving power. The characteristic's focus on present-tense practice, structural imprisonment, and constitutional identity does not engage memory processes.

**[CHAR-13]** E — The memory faculty is the primary faculty engaged — on both the divine and human sides. (1) *Divine memory*: Jer 14:10 — "he will remember their iniquity and punish their sins"; Hos 8:13 — "now he will remember their iniquity and punish their sins" — the divine memory retains the record and triggers judgment from it. The liberation metaphors are memory-erasure metaphors: Isa 43:25 — "I will not remember your sins"; Jer 31:34 — "I will remember their sin no more." (2) *Human memory*: Gen 41:9 — "I remember my offenses today" — the cupbearer's memory of past failure resurfaces; Psa 25:7 — "Remember not the sins of my youth" — the psalmist pleads for God not to hold the past record in memory against him.

**[CHAR-14]** E — Yes — through the Day of Atonement's memorial function. Exo 30:16 — "that it may bring the people of Israel to remembrance before the Lord, so as to make atonement for your lives" — the atonement money brings Israel to God's remembrance; the memorial function is part of the seeking mechanism. Gen 41:9 (CHAR-13 corpus — same root) — "I remember my offenses today" — the memory of past failure that triggers the seeking. In the characteristic itself: the annual kip.pu.rim cycle (VCG-01) operates as a rhythmic memorial practice — annual remembrance that the sin-record requires covering.

**[CHAR-15]** E — Yes — through the explicit memory-failure dimension. Psa 78:32 — "despite his wonders, they did not believe" — and the broader Psalm 78 context (a historical recital of God's acts that Israel failed to remember — the psalm's genre is anamnesis, calling the community to remember what was forgotten). Isa 64:5 — "those who remember you in your ways" — the positive foil states that *remembering* God's ways is what the generational sinning-pattern fails to do; the inherited condition is characterised by a failure of covenantal memory.

**[CHAR-16]** E — Memory engages through the persistent reputation and the sin-accumulation dimensions. Num 16:38 — "these men who have sinned at the cost of their lives... shall be a sign to the people of Israel" — the sinners' identity is permanently memorialised in the bronze altar covering; their sinner-character is preserved as a communal memory-warning; Luk 7:37 — the woman "of the city, who was a sinner" — the city's corporate memory has fixed her identity as "a sinner"; Psa 51:13 — "sinners will return to you" — the memory of what the sinner was (before return) is the implicit backdrop of the return.

**[CHAR-17]** E — Yes — centrally. Eze 21:23/24 — "he brings their guilt to remembrance... because you have made your guilt to be remembered" — God's recall of guilt from memory is the mechanism of judgment; the guilt-record exists in God's memory; Eze 21:24 — "your transgressions are uncovered, so that in all your deeds your sins appear" — the guilt becomes visible when God's memory re-activates it. Gen 42:21 — the brothers' own memory of their past cruelty activates their guilt-recognition; their guilt is memory-mediated.

**[CHAR-18]** E — Yes — centrally through the divine memory register (VCG-03). Hos 13:12 — "the iniquity of Ephraim is bound up; his sin is kept in store" — God's memory is the storage medium for the iniquity-record; Hos 9:9 — "he will remember their iniquity; he will punish their sins" — divine memory is the mechanism that activates judgment; Psa 79:8 — "do not remember against us our former iniquities" — the plea asks God's memory not to function against them. Human memory also engages: Lev 26:40/41 — "confess their iniquity and the iniquity of their fathers" — the generational confession requires memory of ancestral crimes.

**[CHAR-19]** E — Yes — through both divine memory and human memory. (1) *Divine memory of transgression*: Isa 43:25 — "I will not remember your sins" — forgiveness is defined as divine memory-non-retention; the default is that God remembers; Dan 9:24 — "to finish the transgression" — a temporally bounded divine memory; (2) *Human memory of transgression*: Isa 46:8 — "recall it to mind, you transgressors" — human memory of the transgressing condition is required; Psa 25:7 — "remember not the sins of my youth or my transgressions" — the plea for God not to remember the speaker's early transgressions.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Memory is engaged in two directions. (1) *Pre-act memory failure*: unintentional sinning can occur when a known prohibition fails to be recalled at the moment of action — the person may have been taught the commandment but did not retrieve it in the moment (Lev 4:2 — the commandments "about things not to be done" presupposes prior instruction; the sinning occurs despite that instruction, implying a memory-retrieval gap). (2) *Post-act memory activation*: the realisation phase (Lev 5:5 — "when he realizes his guilt") involves the person connecting the past act to its moral status — a retrospective memory-event where the act is re-evaluated in light of newly available information.

**[CHAR-20]** E — Yes — through the communal memory and the eschatological forgetting dimensions. (1) *Communal warning-memory*: 2Ch 30:7 — "do not be like your fathers and your brothers, who were faithless to the Lord God of their fathers, so that he made them a desolation, as you see" — the appeal to visible historical memory of what faithlessness produced; (2) *Eschatological resolution of memory*: Eze 39:26 — "they shall forget their shame and all the treachery they have practiced against me, when they dwell securely" — the eschatological promise is that the memory of treachery will be eclipsed by secure dwelling; (3) *Divine covenant-memory triggered by confession*: Lev 26:42 — "I will remember my covenant with Jacob" — God's covenant-memory is reactivated by the confession of treachery.

**[CHAR-21]** E — The memory faculty is engaged through the forgetting-God pattern. Jer 3:21 — "they have perverted their way; they have forgotten the Lord their God" — the perversion of the way is explicitly linked to forgetting God; memory of God is what the perversion eliminates. Pro 2:17 (cross-context) — forgetting covenant; Deu 32:20 — the perverse generation — "children in whom is no faithfulness" — the absence of faithfulness implies the forgetting of the covenant-bond that faithfulness maintained.

**[CHAR-22]** E — Yes — through divine memory and communal warning-memory. (1) *Divine memory*: Rev 18:5 — "God has remembered her iniquities" — God's memory retains the accumulating record of injustice; (2) *Memory of God's justice*: Psa 107:42 — "the upright see it and are glad, and all wickedness shuts its mouth" — the righteous remember God's just acts which silence wickedness; (3) *Communal warning-memory*: 2Sa 7:10 — "violent men shall afflict them no more, as formerly" — the memory of past injustice informs the promise.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. Memory is engaged in confession's retrospective orientation — confession names what was *done*, requiring retrieval of the past act. Neh 1:6 — "confessing the sins... which we have sinned against you. Even I and my father's house have sinned" — requires memory spanning generations. Psa 106:6 — "Both we and our fathers have sinned" — memory of ancestral sin extended to the present generation. Dan 9:11 — the curse written in Moses's Law "have been poured out upon us, because we have sinned against him" — historical memory of the Mosaic covenant's terms. Confession thus requires an active memory faculty that retrieves both the specific past acts and the longer moral history they belong to.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Memory is implicitly engaged through the *failure to hold the moral record*. Jer 16:10 — "what sin have we committed against the Lord our God?" — the people cannot retrieve (or perhaps never encoded) the moral record of their accumulated sinning. The memory faculty that should hold the history of what was done is either not functioning or not accessing the relevant record. Jer 2:35 — "I have not sinned" — the active denial may involve suppression of the memory of specific sins: the person cannot (or will not) retrieve what their conscience should hold before them.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Memory is implicitly engaged through the inherited-pattern dimension. 2Ki 15:9 — "as his fathers had done" — the son who follows his fathers in not departing from Jeroboam's sins carries the memory of his fathers' pattern as the inherited moral framework. The memory of "this is how things have been done" provides the cognitive-memorial basis for the inherited refusal. Neh 9:29 — the corporate prayer recites the history of Israel's stubborn refusal over generations — the memory faculty holds this history as the community's self-understanding.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Memory is implicitly engaged through the historical-persistence evidence. Hos 10:9 — "from the days of Gibeah, you have sinned, O Israel; there they have *continued*" — the sinning has persisted across a history that extends from Gibeah to the present; the habitual pattern is maintained across time, which requires that the sinning orientation be preserved in the community's moral memory and practice. 2Ki 17:7 — "the people of Israel had sinned against the Lord their God, who had brought them up out of Egypt" — the forgetting of the redemptive history (the Exodus) is the memory-failure that enables the habitual sinning: the memory of what God did is not operational as a corrective in the will's direction.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Memory is engaged through the historical-generational persistence of the Jeroboam pattern. 1Ki 22:52 — Ahaziah followed "the way of his father and... his mother and... Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin" — the memory of the transmitted sinning pattern is held across three named generations and referenced as the operative moral precedent. The memory faculty carries the Jeroboam-pattern as the received moral heritage; each subsequent generation's reception of the pattern requires the memory of what prior generations did.

**[CHAR-8]** E — Memory is engaged through the "to this day" markers. 1Ki 12:19 / 2Ch 10:19 — "Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day" — the narrator's memory holds the revolt as a persistent present reality; the community's corporate memory carries the fact of the revolt and its ongoing consequence. 2Ki 8:22 / 2Ch 21:10 — "Edom revolted from the rule of Judah to this day" — similarly. The memory faculty holds the revolt in the historical-political consciousness, making the broken relationship a known and named part of the political identity.

**[CHAR-9]** S — The 22-verse corpus does not explicitly engage the memory faculty in connection with sinful speech. No verse addresses the retention or retrieval of past sinful speech or the role of memory in enabling or preventing it.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The memory faculty is engaged through its absence and its consequences. The core practical-atheism evidence (Psa 9:17 — VCG-02 — "the wicked… all the nations that forget God") explicitly identifies forgetting as the wicked person's defining cognitive-memorial act. God-forgetting is the characteristic's memorial mode: the wicked person's memory retains everything except the orientation toward God. The legacy of the wicked is also addressed through memory's inverse: Pro 10:7 (VCG-09): "the name of the wicked will rot" — their memory is corrupted at the social level; what will be remembered of them is dishonour. Psa 9:5 (VCG-05): "you have blotted out their name forever and ever" — divine judgment is described as the ultimate erasure of the wicked person's memorial existence. The characteristic engages memory by displacing the God-memory that should be foundational and corrupting the social memory that will survive the person.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The evidence engages memory primarily through its consequences rather than the memory faculty directly. Heb 8:12 (vc=14342 — VCG-06): "I will remember their sins no more" — God's gracious choice not to remember the iniquities (adikia) implies that the iniquities exist as a moral record; the constitutional inner evil generates a record of offenses that divine memory could hold. Rom 1:18 (vc=14336 — VCG-05): unrighteousness "suppresses the truth" — the suppression implies a knowing that is actively being denied, which involves a form of distorted memorial function (the person knows truth but refuses to remember it or act on it). The characteristic engages memory through suppression (denying what is known) rather than through positive memorial content.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. Memory is engaged through a specific restoration dynamic in VCG-04. Eze 36:31 (vc=1681 — VCG-04): "Then you will remember your evil ways and your deeds that were not good, and you will loathe yourselves for your iniquities and your abominations." The memory faculty is the mechanism through which the awakened conscience re-engages with past abominations — restored memory produces self-loathing. The verse shows memory not merely as a neutral cognitive recall but as the morally laden faculty that, when restored to function, enables genuine conscience engagement with past abominable acts.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes. Memory is engaged through its systematic failure. Eze 16:22 (vc=65985 — VCG-05): "in all your abominations and your whorings you did not remember the days of your youth, when you were naked and bare, wallowing in your blood" — the covenantal memory of origins (the founding divine care) is precisely what is suppressed. Eze 16:43 (vc=65987 — VCG-05): "because you have not remembered the days of your youth" — the memorial failure is stated as the cause of enraging the divine. Eze 6:9 (vc=1697 — VCG-05): "those of you who escape will remember me among the nations" — post-judgment restoration of memory is what produces conscience-reactivation and self-loathing. Memory's engagement with the characteristic is through its suppression: the characteristic operates by preventing the recall of what would arrest it.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes. Memory appears primarily in the context of iniquity's accumulation and the divine record of it. Job 21:19 (vc=38209 — VCG-04): "God stores up their iniquity for their children" — God's moral memory retains accumulated iniquity beyond the individual's lifespan. Psa 94:23 (vc=38249 — VCG-03): "He will bring back on them their iniquity" — the divine memory brings the person's own iniquity back as judgment; the judgment is precisely the return of what was done, implying a stored moral record. Psa 125:5 (vc=38382 — VCG-03): those who turn aside "to their crooked ways" — the crooked ways as a remembered moral trajectory that has been followed. The human memory faculty also appears in the evidence for the suppression of instruction-memory: Job 22:15 (vc=38210 — VCG-04): "the old way that wicked men have trod" — the memory of this worn path perpetuates the characteristic.

**[CHAR-6]** S — The 17-verse corpus does not directly evidence the memory faculty's engagement with this characteristic. No verse addresses what the blaspheming or falsely accusing person remembers or fails to remember in the course of the characteristic's operation. This silence is noted. The closest proximity to memory appears in the VCG-01 sequence (Rev 16:9/11/21) where repeated divine judgments apparently fail to leave a corrective moral memory — but this is inferential rather than directly evidenced.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Memory engagement is evidenced in four of six characteristics. Char 4 provides the richest memory evidence: Eze 16:22 (VCG-05 — "in all your abominations and your whorings you did not remember the days of your youth") and Eze 6:9 (VCG-05 — survivors will "remember me among the nations") — showing the characteristic's suppression of covenantal memory and its restoration enabling conscience-reactivation. Char 3 (Eze 36:31 — memory restored producing self-loathing) confirms the memory-restoration pattern. Char 1 (Psa 9:17 — "the nations who forget God") shows memory failure as a characteristic marker. Char 5 notes the divine-memory pattern (Job 21:19 — God stores up iniquity for children; Psa 94:23 — returns iniquity upon the practitioner). Chars 2 and 6 are relatively silent on memory specifically.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Memory is engaged in the cognitive-formation role: the categorical system must be remembered and applied consistently. Lev 11:47 (M10c-B-VCG-01) names the purpose of all purity laws as cultivating active moral discernment — a capacity that can only function through memory of what is clean and what is unclean. Peter's Act 10:14 conviction — "I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean" — is the product of memory: a lifetime of categorical observance retained as a deeply embedded inner rule. Memory in this characteristic functions as the repository of the categorical system that the person draws on in each encounter with a potential defiling agent.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, at two evidenced points. 2Cor 12:21 (VCG-02): Paul speaks of "those who sinned earlier and have not repented of the impurity... that they have practiced" — the memory of past impurity as practiced sin is the frame for the present unrepented state. The memory of what has been practiced (the history of the defilement-state) is part of what Paul expects repentance to engage. Rom 6:19 (VCG-02): "just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity" — the memory of the prior condition is the rhetorical frame for the call to a new orientation; the person is asked to remember what they were to understand what they are being called away from.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, centrally and uniquely. Eze 20:43 (VCG-02) is the most important evidence: "there you shall remember your ways and all your deeds with which you have defiled yourselves, and you shall loathe yourselves for all the evils that you have committed." The memory of corporate defilement is the named mechanism of the characteristic's eschatological resolution — the community's future remembering of its defilement-state will generate the self-loathing that is the inner mechanism of repentance. No other verse in the 83-verse corpus provides this direct evidence of memory as the defilement-state's resolution mechanism.

**[CHAR-4]** S — The 21-verse corpus does not evidence engagement with the memory faculty. The characteristic is focused on present domination rather than on memory's holding of inner-being reality across time.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster reveals a striking pattern: 3 E : 1 S — Characteristics 1, 2, and 3 engage the memory faculty; Characteristic 4 does not. Characteristic 1 engages memory in the categorical-formation role (Act 10:14 — Peter's lifetime of categorical observance retained as a deeply embedded inner conviction; the timing requirements of defilement resolution require tracking when the condition was incurred). Characteristic 2 engages memory as a faculty that exists but fails in the advanced state: 2Cor 12:21 — the memory of past impurity exists but does not produce repentance. Characteristic 3 engages memory as the designed mechanism of future eschatological resolution: Eze 20:43 — "there you shall remember your ways and all your deeds with which you have defiled yourselves, and you shall loathe yourselves." Characteristic 4 bypasses the memory faculty entirely — the condition is temporally immediate (seizure and domination), with no engagement of the person's inner history. The cluster's memory pattern: memory is a faculty that the M10c cluster consistently engages in three of four characteristics, but with very different functions (formation, failed repentance-summons, eschatological resolution-mechanism).

findings.session_b_note:
The data supports a precise and previously unassembled answer:

**Terminates divine memory of sin:** Jer 31:34 — divine forgiveness actively terminates the divine memory of the specific wrong. This is not impairment of memory in general but targeted cessation of one specific memory-function: holding sin against the person.

**Transforms human memory of guilt:** The condition of being forgiven (afesis — the release-state) changes the person's relationship to their own memory of guilt. The guilt-state is what forgiveness addresses; once addressed, the memory of the former guilt-state becomes the ground of gratitude and love-orientation (Luk 7:47 — "she loved much because she was forgiven much"). Memory is not erased but **reframed**: the remembering of forgiveness-received becomes an ongoing motivational ground.

**Impaired memory as blockage:** The withholder's inner life is "poisoned" (OBS-064-001) by the retained memory of the wrong — the grievance held in memory. Unforgiveness may therefore be characterised as **memory operating in a destructive mode** — the record kept and rehearsed, preventing the release that forgiveness would bring.

*New finding:* The data implies a three-stage memory dynamic in relation to forgiveness: (1) memory holds the record of wrong (pre-forgiveness); (2) forgiveness terminates the memory of the wrong as a legal claim (at the divine level) and releases the human person from the guilt-state; (3) the memory of being forgiven becomes the ongoing ground of love and gratitude (post-forgiveness). This three-stage memory arc has not been assembled in the existing observations and is analytically significant.

findings.session_b_note:
**Compassion enables and orients memory:** The supplication pattern shows that the person who approaches God for compassion does so by invoking specific memories — God's past acts of chesed, the person's own history of need and divine response. Compassion is sought through memory and is itself a form of remembering (God "remembering" the person through chesed). The receipt of compassion deepens the person's capacity to return to that memory as a sustaining resource (Psa 48:9 — meditation on steadfast love).

**The womb-memory connection:** Groups 1613-001 and 1613-002 describe the womb as the origin of human existence and the space from which God's compassionate sovereignty begins. Psa 22:10 — "from my mother's womb you have been my God" — grounds the appeal in an origin-memory: the relationship with God predates conscious memory. This is the deepest form of memory — the inner-being knowing that one has been held by God before one could remember being held.

**What is missing (P):** The data does not address whether receiving compassion heals or restores damaged memory — whether, for example, the person whose history is marked by the absence of compassion (neglect, abandonment) is restored at the level of memory when they receive it. This is a gap; no SD pointer addresses it.

findings.session_b_note: Goodness enables and deepens memory in its truthful operation. The covenantal knowing of Eze 23:14 (God's faithfulness held in memory) is a deepened form of inner-being knowledge held over time. The moral reckoning of Eze 36:31 (remembering deeds as not-good) is memory enabled by an act of God — the divine work that brings the person to genuine self-recognition includes activating memory truthfully. Conversely, the self-justifying memory of Jer 44:17 ("when we burned incense to the queen of heaven, we had plenty of food and prospered") is an impaired memory — goodness misidentified produces false memory of what the good was. Genuine goodness enables truthful memory; false goodness impairs it. (OBS-067-OBS-034, OBS-067-OBS-035, OBS-067-OBS-043)

findings.session_b_note: Love **deepens and sustains** memory. Jer 31:20 (OBS-103-117): 'I do remember him still' — God's love for Ephraim persists as memory even through judgment-speech. The love-relationship makes the beloved unforgettable: the nephesh cannot forget the one it loves (Jer 12:7 — 'beloved of my soul'). Jer 2:2 (OBS-103-098): God's memory of Israel's early love ('the devotion of your youth') shows love as the content of sustained divine memory. Conversely, the threat to love is forgetting: Hos 2:13 (implied in the prophetic love-vocabulary) — Israel forgot God. Lovelessness leads to forgetting the love-relationship; love sustains memory of the beloved across time and distance. Love deepens memory because the beloved is the content of what is held across time. Love cannot maintain itself without memory — the love that forgets is the love that fails.

findings.session_b_note: Mercy operates in the memory faculty in two opposing movements: (1) Divine memory-bypass — Heb 8:12 ("I will remember their sins no more") — mercy as the wilful erasure of the divine memory-record of sin. (2) Human memory-deepening — Eze 16:63 — received mercy does not erase human memory of sin but activates it: the person remembers what they have done precisely because mercy was given for it. *New finding: mercy creates an asymmetric memory structure — divine forgetting and human remembering are the two poles of the mercy event. God no longer holds the record; the person is left holding the memory of what was forgiven.* OBS-111-035, OBS-111-039.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-111-003: Reading T3 as a whole reveals mercy as a faculty-activating characteristic — it does not primarily engage one or two faculties but activates the inner-being faculty system comprehensively. The pattern…
findings.finding_value: Reading T3 as a whole reveals mercy as a faculty-activating characteristic — it does not primarily engage one or two faculties but activates the inner-being faculty system comprehensively. The pattern: mercy enables perception (face-access), opens cognition in both directions (upward to divine knowledge; downward to self-knowledge), creates an asymmetric memory structure (divine forgetting / human remembering), engages affect as its native register, expands volition (received mercy increases mercy-capacity), demands agency, reframes moral evaluation (mercy as higher-order moral evaluation), presupposes and deepens conscience, enables conscientiousness, and constitutes relational capacity. The single faculty not evidenced is creativity (T3.5.2 — S status). Reading T3 together: mercy is characterised by faculty-comprehensiveness; its absence (mercilessness in Rom 1:31) appears alongside affective incapacity (*astorgos*) and other faculty-failures — confirming that mercy's presence is correlated with full faculty activation and its absence with faculty contraction.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-014: T2 maps mercy's constitutional locations (soul, mind, heart, body, spirit-soul interface) and T3 maps its faculty engagements. Reading together: the constitutional locations and the faculty engagement…
findings.finding_value: T2 maps mercy's constitutional locations (soul, mind, heart, body, spirit-soul interface) and T3 maps its faculty engagements. Reading together: the constitutional locations and the faculty engagements are co-extensive. Soul-level location (T2) corresponds to conscience and moral evaluation faculty engagement (T3) — the soul is where guilt resides and where conscience/moral evaluation operate. Mind-level location (T2, memory-erasure) corresponds to memory faculty engagement (T3, asymmetric memory structure). Heart/splanchna location (T2) corresponds to affect faculty (T3). The receiving-before-generating origin (T2) corresponds to relational capacity as foundational enabler (T3.11). T2 and T3 together: constitutional location and faculty engagement are two descriptions of the same inner-being reality — where mercy operates constitutionally (T2) is where it activates faculties (T3).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-020: T3's finding that mercy deepens conscience (Q&A-093) and expands volitional capacity (Q&A-084) maps to T5's finding that mercy produces ongoing character formation (Q&A-138 — mercy as first inner garm…
findings.finding_value: T3's finding that mercy deepens conscience (Q&A-093) and expands volitional capacity (Q&A-084) maps to T5's finding that mercy produces ongoing character formation (Q&A-138 — mercy as first inner garment in the formation arc). Reading T3 and T5 together: the faculty deepening identified in T3 (conscience deepened, volition expanded, relational capacity constituted) is the mechanism through which T5's formative arc operates. Mercy forms character (T5) by deepening and expanding the inner faculties (T3) — the formation is not abstract but faculty-specific. The suffering-mercy connection (T5.4) also corresponds to T3's conscience presupposed (Q&A-092) — suffering activates the conscience that generates authentic mercy-seeking.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-022: T7's primary anchor verse identification (Psa 78:38) and its confirmation of mercy's cross-genre literary evidence maps to T3's faculty engagement profile. Psa 78:38 (T7, Q&A-185) contains within it a…
findings.finding_value: T7's primary anchor verse identification (Psa 78:38) and its confirmation of mercy's cross-genre literary evidence maps to T3's faculty engagement profile. Psa 78:38 (T7, Q&A-185) contains within it a four-stage inner sequence (compassion → atoning act → anger restraint → wrath modulation) that traverses multiple faculties: affect (compassion), agency (atoning act), moral evaluation (anger restraint as moral-evaluative act), and volition (not stirring up wrath). The verse T7 identifies as primary anchor encodes the T3 faculty engagement in concentrated form. T7's human-science divergence finding (Q&A-189 — mercy grounded in prior reception, not autonomous moral development) is the methodological form of T3's receiving-before-generating faculty activation pattern.

findings.session_b_note: Forgiveness transforms memory in both directions. Divine: God's memory of sin is permanently set aside in forgiveness (Jer 31:34). Human: the act of forgiving requires the offended person to release the claim held in memory — not to deny the memory but to choose not to hold it against the offender. Unforgiveness is precisely the continuing active use of memory against the offender (the "tormentors" of Mat 18:34 image the inner state of one whose memory continues to exact the debt). OBS-064-017, OBS-064-032.

findings.finding_value: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion responds, it does not originate or create. It is the most responsive of the faculties-engaging characteristics. Second, affect and moral action are structurally unified in compassion — not sequentially related but simultaneous. Affect is the mechanism of movement (splanchnizō is both the felt inner event and the cause of the action), not a precursor or accompaniment. This is unique among the characteristics reviewed: in most other registries, affect and volition are distinguishable stages; in compassion, the felt movement is already the morally motivated action beginning. A third distinctive finding: compassion converts moral knowledge into motivated action — it is the motivational ground of conscientiousness, not a product of it. The conscience faculty engagement reveals compassion as conscience-healing: it addresses the pitiable condition that conscience perceives as a moral claim, resolving the tension between moral knowledge and moral incapacity. The three relational modes (building/sustaining — chesed; restoring/repairing — splanchnizō; extending across difference — Good Samaritan) are a new finding not in the instruction typology.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-003: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked …
findings.finding_value: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I but the grace of God that is with me." Agency is not displaced but constituted by grace. This relationship holds in paradox that the T3.6 prompt options (enable/deepen/bypass/impair) cannot accommodate — a prompt design limitation noted for catalogue revision. Second, grace produces moral clarity (T3.8 — sharpens moral evaluation rather than bypassing it): the person who recognises grace has made a precise moral evaluation (they know they received what they did not deserve). Third, grace and conscience are mutually necessary: grace is the condition within which conscience can operate fully without destroying the person; conscience without grace produces condemnation; grace without conscience produces presumption (T3.9). Fourth, grace is the primary relational faculty developer in the registry's evidence — it reaches every relational register (vertical access, horizontal forgiving, speech-grace) and enables each one. Creativity (T3.5) is the one genuinely silent faculty — not an impairment but a non-engagement: grace receives and constitutes, it does not create.

findings.session_b_note: Covenant structures and disciplines memory — it does not bypass it. (1) Covenant enables and deepens memory in those who maintain it: the covenantal commands to remember (Deu 4:23; 8:18) orient the inner memory faculty toward God's acts and commitments. The covenant creates a framework within which memory is directed and disciplined — festivals, signs (rainbow, circumcision, Sabbath, Eucharist), and written law all serve as memory aids that structure the inner faculty's operation. (2) Covenant breach is associated with forgetting: "Take care, lest you forget the covenant" — the drift from covenant faithfulness begins in the memory faculty's failure to hold covenantal reality. The covenant-breaker is characterised by forgetting God's covenant (2Ki 17:38: "you shall not forget the covenant that I have made with you"). (3) The new covenant does not abolish the memory structure but reorients it: the Eucharistic "do this in remembrance of me" establishes a covenantal memory practice centred on Christ's death rather than Sinai's law-giving. Memory is retained and redirected, not bypassed.

findings.session_b_note: Peace-deprivation impairs memory (Lam 3:17 — forgotten happiness); peace-restoration enables retrospective memory of God's faithfulness. The Lam 3 context is particularly rich: the movement from Lam 3:17 ("forgotten") to Lam 3:21-22 ("but this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: the steadfast love of the Lord never ceases") — the act of remembering God's hesed breaks through the peaceless condition and restores hope. The memory of God's covenant faithfulness is the cognitive act that enables the return to peace. Peace and memory have a mutual relationship: peace enables the memory of grace; the memory of grace enables the recovery of peace.

findings.session_b_note: The characteristic deepens memory in its covenantal mode: the accumulated record of divine giving across generations forms the memory-structure of Israel's inner-being identity. Each new giving adds to the memory of prior giving, deepening the narrative foundation of trust. Neh 9 (the long Levitical prayer) is itself a memory-act: reciting the history of divine giving as the basis of present covenantal renewal. Hos 2:15 invokes Exodus memory as the ground of eschatological hope — the memory of what God gave before shapes the expectation of what he will give again. The characteristic does not impair memory in any evidenced instance; it is constitutively tied to the faithfulness of remembered giving.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** The Ezekiel material reveals a specific mode: righteousness is forfeitable in God's memory — past righteous deeds are not counted when the person turns to wickedness (Eze 18:24). This is not memory impairment in the person but a statement about how God's judicial memory functions. God's judicial memory does not accumulate righteousness as credit; it assesses the current state.

**[CLUSTER]** E. The cluster engages memory primarily in the communal-testimonial and judicial-historical modes. Righteousness enables testimonial memory (the psalmist's sustained declaration); the forfeiture mechanism (A2) reveals how God's judicial memory functions differently from human accumulative memory.
