findings.finding_value:
M01-A engages the affective faculty in a complex way. Reverential fear itself is an affective state — it is a felt orientation, not merely a cognitive assessment. But M01-A shows the affect paired with joy: Psa 2:11 ("fear of the Lord coexists with joy, shaping worship as a **reverent, trembling delight** rather than casual confidence"); Heb 12:28 (fear and awe as "the fitting inner disposition for approaching God in worship, prompted by gratitude"). Fear-as-reverence is an affective state that is not mutually exclusive with positive affect.

**[Folded from wa_session_b_findings.id=38; finding_id=DIM-11-001; registry=awe]**
Awe spans both Affective/Emotional and Spiritual/God-ward dimensions. God-ward groups (1682-001, 1682-003, 703-002, 703-003) show that the deepest fear/awe content is Spiritual/God-ward rather than merely affective. Session B should examine whether awe functions as a distinct inner-being category integrating affective intensity and God-ward orientation — the two are inseparable in the data.

M01-B engages the affective faculty centrally — acute fear is by definition an intense affective experience. The range includes: alarm (Gen 32:7), awe-mingled-dread (Mar 4:41), social anxiety (Joh 7:13), and relief-producing fear (Psa 105:38: Egypt's terror "produced gladness at their departure"). Mat 28:8 (women departing "holding **fear and great joy simultaneously**") is the most vivid example of complex affective coexistence.

M01-D engages the affective faculty through the dismay-experience: Psa 6:3 (the psalmist's soul "greatly dismayed — profound turmoil driving the anguished cry to God"). The affective content is anguish, horror, and internal upheaval.

M01-F's affective content is sustained apprehension: de.a.gah (H1674) anxiety as a weighing-down burden on the heart (Pro 12:25); the anticipatory dread of M01-F-VCG-03 as unrelenting anguish that "distorts the experience of time" (Deu 28:67).

The affective faculty is the primary dimension of M01 across all sub-groups. Fear is constitutively affective. The affective range across the cluster is wide: from reverent delight (M01-A, Psa 2:11; Heb 12:28) through acute alarm (M01-B) to overwhelming anguish (M01-D, F) to horror (M01-C). The characteristic's affective diversity reflects the cluster's seven-sub-group structure.

The affective faculty is the primary faculty engaged — this characteristic is constitutively affective. All the thermal vocabulary (burning, kindling, filling, pouring) names affective states of high arousal. Eze 3:14 (M02-B-VCG-03): rage as felt inner heat in the spirit — the felt quality of the experience is central to what the term names. Dan 3:19: filling with fury — a fully affective state visibly transforming the person.

2Cor 7:11 (M02-C-VCG-02): indignation as one of several strong inner responses produced by godly grief — the affective register of indignation is explicitly named as a moral-emotional response to an encounter with wrongdoing. The affective faculty is engaged as the resonance chamber for moral assessment.

M03 is by far the most affectively concentrated cluster in the programme. Every sub-group is primarily affective. The ya.gon and tu.gah corpus (M03-C-VCG-01) names grief as a settled affective condition of the heart. The weeping corpus (M03-A) names the somatic overflow of intense feeling. The distress corpus (M03-D) names the affective quality of being overwhelmed and pressed. The groaning/sighing corpus (M03-E) names the vocal-somatic expression of deep feeling. The bitterness corpus (M03-G) names the qualitative texture of felt inner experience. This is the cluster whose primary mode of inner-being reality is affective.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes — exultation is the affective faculty in its most elevated and directed expression. The soul exults (Psa 35:9; Isa 61:10), the heart is glad (Psa 16:9; 13:5), the whole being rejoices (Psa 16:9), the bones are asked to rejoice (Psa 51:8), and the person is "jubilant with joy" (Psa 68:3). The affective faculty is the primary vehicle of exultation.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Joy is the affective faculty in its most fully-engaged participatory expression. The heart's gladness (consistently across both OT and NT), the whole being's rejoicing (Psa 16:9), the Spirit's joy overflowing into the community (Act 13:52; 1Th 1:6), Mary's spirit-rejoicing (Luk 1:47), the inexpressible joy filled with glory (1Pe 1:8) — all are primary affective events. Joy is not primarily cognitive or volitional (though it engages both) but fundamentally affective: a positive, engaged inner feeling directed at its object.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Yes — Suffering-Joy is primarily affective in its intense form: 1Pe 1:8 ("inexpressible and filled with glory") — the affective quality is named first and most prominently; Act 16:34 (the jailer "rejoiced along with his entire household") — an intense affective event in a crisis context; Luk 1:47 (Mary's spirit exults — an intense affective inner event in a vulnerable context); Luk 10:21 (Jesus' rejoicing in the Holy Spirit — an affective event in the Spirit). M04-F (ba.lag) is also primarily affective — the desired brightening of the inner person's felt condition.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, in the M04-O register. The "good news refreshing the bones" (Pro 15:30), Saul "refreshed and well" (1Sa 16:23), the men of Jabesh "glad when they heard" (1Sa 11:9), the makarismos blessedness (Rom 4:6, 9; Gal 4:15 — a felt inner state of divine-favour happiness), and Lam 3:26's "wait quietly" (a gentle, sustained affective posture) are all affective in character. The M04-L-VCG-01 ki-tov declarations also have an affective dimension — gratitude is a felt inner state.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes — Delight's M04-G register (sha.a.shu.im, sha.a, a.nog) is primarily affective: (1) **sha.a.shu.im** (Psa 119 series) — the multiple-intensity noun for pleasurable cherishing; (2) **sha.a** (Psa 94:19 — "your consolations cheer my soul"; Isa 66:12 — bounced on knees) — affective carefree-pleasure quality; (3) **a.nog** (Psa 37:4 — "delight yourself in the Lord"; Isa 58:14 — "take delight in the Lord"; Isa 66:11 — drink deeply with delight) — luxuriating, resting, pleasurable affect; (4) **sunēdomai** (Rom 7:22 — "I delight in the law of God") — synergistic joy in, the most explicitly affective NT term for Delight in the inner being; (5) **che.med** (Eze 23:12 — lustful desirability) — affective captivation in the corrupt register.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes — this is the primary faculty of Pleasure: (1) **M04-J-VCG-02's relational pleasantness** — 2Sa 1:26 (the affective warmth of Jonathan's companionship); Song 1:16; 7:6 (the lover's affective appreciation of the beloved's beauty); Psa 133:1 (the affective exclamation of communal pleasantness); (2) **Pro 2:10** (knowledge pleasant to the soul — a felt affective quality); (3) **Pro 16:24** (gracious words as sweetness — affective nourishment); (4) **Gen 8:21** (God's inner calmed, settled affective response to the soothing aroma); (5) **Psa 16:11** (pleasures forevermore — the affective quality of God's presence).

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes, in the arrest-astonishment register: (1) **thambeō** (Mar 1:27; 10:24; 10:32) — the most affectively intense Wonder term: the disciples are seized with astonishment (an inner feeling state of overwhelming surprise); (2) **"I marvelled greatly"** (Rev 17:6) — John's intense inner feeling-response to the vision; (3) **VCG-03's dark astonishment** — Job 10:16 (wonders worked against Job); Gal 1:6 ("I am astonished") — Paul's troubled inner affective state; (4) **"Fearfully and wonderfully made"** (Psa 139:14) — the awe-component of Wonder at one's own creation is affective.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All seven engage the affective faculty, with markedly different profiles: (1) **Affective-primary**: Exultation (Char 1) — "the soul exults, the heart is glad, the whole being rejoices, the bones are asked to rejoice" — the affective faculty at its most elevated expression; Joy (Char 2) — the heart as primary constitutional seat; Suffering-Joy (Char 7) — 1Pe 1:8's "inexpressible and filled with glory" names the affective quality as primary; (2) **Affective-receptive**: Pleasure (Char 5) — the most affective-receptive of the seven — the ambient felt pleasantness of what is agreeable; (3) **Affective-resting**: Delight (Char 4) — the characteristic that settles the affective faculty into a specific treasured object, producing stability rather than surge; (4) **Affective-secondary (cognition primary)**: Gladness (Char 3) — affective in the M04-O register (warm inner response) but cognitively-primary overall; Wonder (Char 6) — affective arrest is real and present but secondary to cognitive encounter with limits; (5) **Affective-dual-layer**: Suffering-Joy (Char 7) — the natural grief and the Spirit-produced joy operate simultaneously at different constitutional levels; this dual-layer is the characteristic's distinctive affective feature.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Shame is itself primarily an affective phenomenon — the felt collapse of dignity is an affective event. The evidence is uniformly phenomenological across the corpus: "I am filled with disgrace" (Job 10:15); "shame has covered my face" (Psa 44:15); "she groans and turns her face away" (Lam 1:8); "Jonathan rose from the table in fierce anger... for he was grieved" (1Sa 20:34 — vc=38502, shame producing emotional pain in a third party). The M07-A material is particularly rich in affective texture: the mother who has "grown feeble and fainted" from shame (Jer 15:9), the farmers covering their heads in shame before drought (Jer 14:3-4). Affect is CHAR-1's primary mode.

**[CHAR-2]** E — CHAR-2 produces strong negative affect: dismay, confusion, wailing (Jer 48:20 — "wail and cry"), fear (Jer 49:23 — "melt in fear"), and derision in the observer. The cosmic register (Isa 24:23 — moon and sun ashamed before divine glory) extends the affective dimension. CHAR-2 impairs positive affect by stripping the inner confidence from which positive states arise.

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — The affective dimension of CHAR-3 is present but secondary — in the VCG-01 active mode, the dishonorer's inner disposition of contempt or self-righteousness (Luk 18:9 in CHAR-5) carries an affective component. Paul's reception of dishonour "without altering inner integrity" (2Cor 6:8) implies the affective faculty has been stabilised against the dishonour signal.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — VCG-03 engages affect in the inverted mode: "they glory in their shame" (Phili 3:19) — the affective response to shamefulness is joy/pride rather than recoil. VCG-02's "dishonorable passions" (Rom 1:26) and "consumed with passion" (Rom 1:27) show affect in its disordered form as the engine of the shameful conduct. Functioning CHAR-4 produces recoil as its affective response to the shameful.

---

**[CHAR-5]** E — CHAR-5 is primarily an affective phenomenon in its received form: the shame produced by contempt is felt — it wounds the person's sense of worth and produces the inner pain of being treated as nothing. Psa 14:6's shaming of the poor's "plans" targets their inner affective confidence (their hope and aspiration). 1Pe 3:9's call to bless rather than retaliate shows the affective pull toward retaliatory anger that verbal contempt produces.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — The affective dimension of CHAR-6 is engaged in Psa 73:13's lament: the psalmist's maintained innocence is accompanied by existential suffering — the emotion of frustrated confidence in innocence's protective value. The affect here is not the joy that innocence should ideally produce (access to God, Psa 26:6) but the anguish of apparent futility. CHAR-6's affective register includes both the confidence of VCG-01 and the anguish of VCG-02's questioning.

---

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's affective engagement is extensive. Char 1 is primarily affective — the felt collapse of dignity is the central phenomenological event. Chars 2, 3, and 5 carry strong affective secondary dimensions (dismay, wailing, turmoil in Char 2; the woundedness of worth-denial in Char 3; the pain of contempt-rejection in Char 5). Char 4's affective dimension appears primarily in the inverted-conscience's perverted joy (Phili 3:19 — "glory in their shame"). Char 6 carries affect in Psa 73:13's existential pain of maintained innocence that seems futile. Cluster-level: M07 is one of the most affectively rich clusters in the programme. Shame's felt dimension runs through five of six characteristics, being the primary dimension of Char 1. The one exception where shame-associated affect becomes perverted (Char 4's VCG-03 glorying in shame) is the cluster's most extreme pathological form.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — The verse evidence engages affect primarily from the perspective of those who encounter CHAR-1's contempt, not from the perspective of the proud person's own felt experience. Psa 123:4 (vc=33953, M08-A4-VCG-03): "our soul has had more than enough of the scorn of those who are at ease, of the contempt of the proud" — the victim's inner experience of CHAR-1 is one of overwhelming affective saturation under contempt. Psa 13:2 (vc=34241, M08-A4-VCG-03): the enemy's exaltation produces "sorrow in my heart all the day" in the psalmist. Jer 13:17 (vc=34091, M08-A3-VCG-03): "my soul will weep in secret for your pride" — the observer's affective response is grief. From within the proud person's own register, Psa 73:6 (vc=33959, M08-A2-VCG-02) — "pride is their necklace" — suggests the proud person carries their arrogance as an ornament, implying a degree of satisfaction or pleasure in the display, but the evidence does not name a felt emotional state explicitly.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The zid vocabulary carries an affective dimension in its root meaning: boiling, seething — the metaphor implies an inner agitation or heat that propels the will's transgression. Exo 18:11 (vc=34121, M08-B-VCG-01): "Egypt's arrogant dealing with Israel is described with a term for boiling insolence" — the affective quality is heated intensity of inner arrogance. 2Pe 2:10 (vc=4670, M08-B-VCG-03): the "bold man" who is "bold in blasphemy" carries an affective register of reckless daring that the tolmētēs root names.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. 2Cor 7:4 (vc=33917, M08-C-VCG-03): "I am overflowing with joy in all our affliction" — the affective experience of boasting/glorying in the community is joy overflowing even amid suffering; the God-directed boasting of VCG-03 has a direct and evidenced affective dimension of joy. Rom 5:2–3 (vc=33874, vc=33875, M08-C-VCG-03): "we rejoice in hope of the glory of God... we rejoice in our sufferings" — the examined kauchaomai is paired with rejoicing. For VCG-01: the boasting of Pro 20:14 (vc=33357) — buyer boasting of a bargain — implies satisfaction; the inner pleasure of self-glorification is the characteristic's affective reward.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes, by displacing appropriate affect. 1Cor 5:2 (vc=33940, M08-D-VCG-01): "you are arrogant [fusioō]. Ought you not rather to mourn?" — CHAR-4 prevents the appropriate affective response (grief over a community moral failure) that the situation demands. The puffed-up cognitive self-picture produces a sense of superiority that displaces the grief that accurate self-assessment (of the community's actual moral state) would generate.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes. Isa 47:8 (vc=9563, M08-E-VCG-02): a.din (voluptuous ease, self-indulgence) — the affective register of sensory pleasure and ease is explicitly named as the inner companion of CHAR-5's self-declaration. Eze 16:49 (vc=33979, M08-E-VCG-01): "prosperous ease" (shalvah) paired with Sodom's pride — the affective experience of ease and material comfort is the companion-condition of power-pride. CHAR-5 is distinctively connected to affective ease and pleasure as the felt inner condition that sustains and reinforces the proud self-sufficiency claim.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All five characteristics engage the affective faculty, and the cluster comparison reveals a consistent pattern: each characteristic is associated with ease and satisfaction as its affective ground, not with suffering. CHAR-1: positive affective experiences (prosperity, beauty, military success) trigger the pride disposition. CHAR-2: the zid "boiling" energy implies an affective heat, though the evidence for the boiling-will's felt experience is sparse. CHAR-3: the satisfaction of social recognition is the VCG-01 affective reward; VCG-03 generates explicit joy (2Cor 7:4, M08-C-VCG-03). CHAR-4: the felt competence of knowledge-possession and the community's felt ease (1Cor 5:2, M08-D-VCG-01: puffed-up instead of mourning). CHAR-5: a.din (Isa 47:8, M08-E-VCG-02: voluptuous ease) and prosperous ease (Eze 16:49, M08-E-VCG-01). The cluster-synthesis: M08 characteristics are characteristically generated in conditions of positive affective experience (ease, satisfaction, felt competence). The cluster's affective relationship to its generating conditions is distinctively positive — pride is a prosperity-adjacent disorder, not a suffering-adjacent one.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes. The most direct affective engagement is in Phili2:12 — "with fear and trembling" — fear as the reverential affect accompanying genuine submission of will. Col3:22 — "fearing the Lord" — the same reverential affect as the motivational ground. 2Cor7:15 — "with fear and trembling" as the affective expression of the Corinthians' obedient reception of Titus. 1Pe1:22 — obedience to truth producing "sincere brotherly love from a pure heart" — love is the affective fruit produced in the person by sustained submission to truth. Affective engagement is both at the origin of the submission (reverential fear as motivator) and at its fruit (love as product).

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, as its primary constitutional dimension (T1.8.1). Psa34:18 — "brokenhearted" — the heart's breaking is an acute affective event; the brokenness of the heart is fundamentally an emotional-experiential state. Isa57:15 — "contrite spirit" — the spirit's crushed state is an affectively-loaded condition. The characteristic is constitutively affective: it is an inner suffering, a genuine grief over one's condition before God, not merely a cognitive self-assessment.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes, and this is the most analytically interesting dimension of metriopatheō. The term compound (metrios + patheō) names a *measured experience of passion/feeling* — affective engagement within measure. Heb5:2 — "he can deal gently with the ignorant and wayward, since he himself is beset with weakness" — the shared-weakness ground is affectively resonant: the high priest feels something of the erring person's condition through his own experience of limitation. The characteristic is affectively engaged (feeling with/compassion) but in a calibrated form — not feeling so much that objectivity is lost, nor so little that coldness replaces compassion. Metriopatheō is thus the measure-of-affect characteristic.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Semnotēs engages the affective faculty in the sense that the settled gravity it names has an affective tone: sober, weighty seriousness (1Ti2:2 — "sober, weighty seriousness of character") is not emotionally cold but carries the settled, composed affective quality of genuine inner gravitas. The characteristic excludes both excessive emotional display and cold affective detachment — it is the composed, settled affective tone of genuine moral gravity. 1Ti3:4 — the orderly compliance produced in children by the overseer's dignity implies an affective response of appropriate regard that the dignity evokes.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes, as part of the primary volitional-affective dimension (T1.8.1). Psa51:12 — "restore to me the joy of your salvation, and uphold me with a willing spirit" — the willing spirit is paired directly with the joy of salvation; the characteristic has an affective dimension of gladness and joy. The freely-moved heart of VCG-01 (Exo35:5/22; 2Ch29:31) carries an implicit affective quality: the "spontaneous, internally-motivated generosity" (2Ch29:31 Pass A meaning) is not affectively neutral but joyfully motivated. The characteristic is the will and the joy together — the gladly-willing rather than the grimly-compliant.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, significantly. The ka.na corpus repeatedly pairs humbling with weeping: 2Ki22:19 — "you have torn your clothes and wept before me"; 2Ch34:27 — "you have torn your clothes and wept before me." The weeping is the affective correlate of genuine humbling — the inner act of self-lowering produces or is accompanied by grief over one's situation before God. 2Cor12:21 names the grief Paul anticipates if God humbles him before the congregation — "I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned." Phili4:12 names the inner experience of "being brought low" — a felt state of deprivation that Paul has learned to navigate with contentment. Act20:19 names "tears" as the accompaniment of sustained humility in ministry.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All six characteristics engage the affective faculty, but with different affective registers. *Grief and tenderness* (CHAR-1 and CHAR-3): the cluster's most grief-adjacent affectives. Genuine humbling is accompanied by weeping and heart-tenderness (2Ki22:19; 2Ch34:27); contrition is constitutively the most grief-loaded inner state in the cluster (CHAR-3's primary dimension). *Reverential fear* (CHAR-2): Phili2:12 — "fear and trembling" — reverential awe as the primary affective companion of genuine submission. *Measured compassion* (CHAR-4): metriopatheō — calibrated feeling-within-bounds — the cluster's most explicitly calibrated affective register. *Composed gravity* (CHAR-5): semnotēs carries a settled, sober affective tone — not cold but composed. *Joy-adjacent gladness* (CHAR-6): Psa51:12 pairs the willing spirit directly with the joy of salvation — the cluster's most joyfully-affective characteristic. Cluster-level: the affective range of M09 spans from grief and contrition (CHAR-3) to joyful gladness (CHAR-6), with reverential fear (CHAR-2), calibrated compassion (CHAR-4), and composed gravity (CHAR-5) in between. The cluster's affective register is not single-toned but richly varied — confirming that non-self-assertive inner existence is not affectively flat.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. The affective faculty is engaged in several registers. (1) *Fear as affective deterrent*: Exo 20:20 ("that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin") — fear of God is an affective state that prevents sinning. (2) *Social fear as sinning-enabler*: 1Sa 15:24 ("I feared the people") — fear of social consequence is the affective state that produces capitulation to sinning. (3) *Anger as sinning-risk*: Psa 4:4 ("be angry, and do not sin; ponder in your own hearts") — anger is the affective state that creates risk of sinning. (4) *Contempt as sinning-mode*: Isa 1:4 ("they have despised the Holy One of Israel") — despising is an affective act that functions as sinning.

**[CHAR-10]** E — The affective faculty is engaged primarily through enticement. Jam 1:14 — "his own desire" — the desire-faculty is inherently affective: it is a faculty of appetite, longing, and motivational pull. 2Pe 2:14 — "insatiable for sin" — the insatiability is an affective state of unquenched appetition. 2Pe 2:18 — "sensual passions of the flesh" — the sensual passions are explicitly affective. Hypocrisy (Gal 2:13) engages affect through the social-belonging dimension — the desire for peer acceptance is an affective motivation. Apostasy (Act 21:21) engages affect through the covenantal allegiance that is being abandoned.

**[CHAR-11]** E — The affective faculty is engaged through the passions and desires that the condition activates. Rom 6:12 — "let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions" — the condition operates through bodily passions as its affective instruments of rule; sin reigns by making the person obey affective desires rather than God. Rom 7:5 — "our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members" — the sinful passions are the affective-level instruments through which the condition operates within the fleshly state. 2Ti 3:6 — "led astray by various passions" — the condition-burdened person is susceptible to multiple affective passions that lead them further from God.

**[CHAR-12]** E — The affective faculty is engaged through Eph 4:26 — "be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger" — anger is an affective state that can become sin if sustained; the verse engages the affective-to-sin transition. The broader corpus also implies affective engagement: the practice of sinning (Joh 8:34) involves affective desires that drive the sinning practices; the enslaving power operates through what the person is affectively drawn to.

**[CHAR-13]** E — Yes — the record produces affective responses when conscience-accessible. Psa 38:18 — "I am sorry for my sin" — the record produces sorrow as its affective consequence; Neh 9:2 — "stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers" — the corporate assembly's affective posture before the record is penitential standing. Psa 38:3 — the physical consequences of the record ("no health in my bones") produce what is implicitly an affective state of illness and distress. Eze 33:10 — "our sins are upon us, and we rot away because of them. How then can we live?" — the affective dimension is despair: the weight of the record produces hopelessness.

**[CHAR-14]** E — Yes — centrally on the receiving side. Luk 7:47 — "her sins, which are many, are forgiven — for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little" — love is the affective response that forgiveness received produces; the magnitude of love is proportional to the magnitude of forgiveness. Lev 23:27 — "you shall afflict yourselves" — the self-affliction on the Day of Atonement is an affective-penitential posture required on the seeking side. The characteristic thus engages affect at both ends: self-affliction in seeking; love in receiving.

**[CHAR-15]** E — The affective faculty is engaged through the doom-despair dimension. Jer 8:14 — "the Lord our God has doomed us to perish and has given us poisoned water to drink, because we have sinned against the Lord" — the corporate recognition of doom produces an affective state of hopelessness: "why do we sit still?" — paralysis and despair. Isa 64:5 — "and shall we be saved?" — the question expresses an affective state of uncertainty about whether salvation is possible after the long duration of the sinning-condition.

**[CHAR-16]** E — Yes — on both the sinner's and the observer's side. (1) *Sinner's affect*: Isa 33:14 — "sinners in Zion are afraid; trembling has seized the godless" — dread and trembling are the affective response of the sinner-identity confronting divine holiness; Luk 18:13 — beating the breast is an affective-penitential act expressing grief over the sinner-identity; (2) *Observer's affect*: Pro 23:17 — "let not your heart envy sinners" — the observer's affective response to the sinner's apparent prosperity is envy; Psa 26:9 — "do not sweep my soul away with sinners" — the affective response is fear of being swept into the sinner's fate.

**[CHAR-17]** E — Yes — as one of its primary inner-being dimensions. Ezr 9:6 — "I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you, my God" — shame and blush are the affective responses to guilt-recognition; Ezr 9:6 — this is the corpus's most explicit affect description; Gen 4:13 — "my punishment is greater than I can bear" — despair/overwhelm is the affective experience of guilt-as-punitive-weight; Hos 5:5 — "shall stumble in his guilt" — the stumbling includes an affective dimension of moral unsteadiness. 1Sa 25:31 — pu.qah — "pangs of conscience" — the term directly names the affective-experiential dimension of conscience-stagger under guilt.

**[CHAR-18]** E — Yes — through the weight-experience and the sorrow dimension. Psa 38:4 — "like a heavy burden, they are too heavy for me" — the iniquity-weight produces an affective experience of overwhelm; Psa 38:18 — "I am sorry for my sin" — the affect of sorrow accompanies confession of iniquity; Ezr 9:6 — "I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you" — shame is the primary affective response to the recognised accumulation. Psa 40:12 — "my heart fails me" — the iniquities overtaking the person produce an affective collapse.

**[CHAR-19]** E — Yes — through the love-of-transgression dimension and the weight-grief dimension. (1) *Affection toward transgression*: Pro 17:19 — "whoever loves transgression loves strife" — the inner affective capacity of love is directed toward transgression itself; the positive emotional orientation toward transgression is a distinct inner condition; (2) *Grief and collapse under transgression's weight*: Lam 1:22 — "my heart is faint" — the affective collapse under accumulated transgressions; Eze 33:10 — "how then can we live?" — the desperate affective response to the burden of accumulated transgressions.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The affect evidence is limited but present in the post-act realisation phase. Lev 5:5 ("when he realizes his guilt... and confesses") — the realisation of guilt involves an affective component: guilt-as-felt-state is the affective register of the cognitive recognition. Num 22:34 (Balaam — "I have sinned, for I did not know... if it is evil in your sight, I will turn back") — the offer to turn back carries an affective quality of contrition, though the text does not name the affective state explicitly. In VCG-02 (cultic-purification), affect is absent — the ritual purification of an altar or sanctuary is a procedural act without named inner emotional register.

**[CHAR-20]** E — Yes — through the grief-of-witness and the desolation-of-victim dimensions. (1) *Grief of witness*: Ezr 9:4 — Ezra "sat appalled" and fasted; Ezr 10:6 — "mourning over the faithlessness of the exiles, neither eating bread nor drinking water" — the spiritually attuned person's affective response to witnessing faithlessness is deep grief; (2) *Desolation of victim*: Lam 1:2 — "she weeps bitterly in the night, with tears on her cheeks; all her friends have dealt treacherously with her; they have become her enemies" — weeping bitterly as the victim's affective experience; (3) *Desire as faithlessness-driver*: Pro 11:6 — "the treacherous are taken captive by their lust" — the craving-affect is the inner driver of the faithlessness.

**[CHAR-21]** E — Yes — in both the affective-attraction-to-perversion and the affective-distress-under-perversion directions. (1) *Affective attraction*: Pro 2:14 — "who rejoice in doing evil and delight in the perverseness of evil" — the will and emotion are positively oriented toward what is morally inverted; delight and rejoicing are the named affective states toward perversity; (2) *Affective distress*: Psa 38:6 — "I am utterly bowed down and prostrate; all the day I go about mourning" — the person under the weight of their own perversity mourns; the affect is grief and prostration.

**[CHAR-22]** E — Yes — through the God-hatred of injustice and the human affective responses. (1) *Divine affect*: Isa 61:8 — "I the Lord love justice; I hate robbery and wrong" — God's love and hatred as the defining affective standard; (2) *Righteous person's fretful response*: Psa 37:1 — "fret not yourself because of evildoers; be not envious of wrongdoers" — the inner fretfulness and envy that injustice's apparent prosperity evokes in the righteous; (3) *Victim's pleading response*: Job 6:29 — "let no injustice be done... my vindication is at stake" — the urgency of the plea; Psa 43:1 — "deliver me from the deceitful and unjust man" — the affect of urgent appeal.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The affective faculty is engaged in confession's shame and sorrow dimensions. Jer 3:25 — "Let us lie down in our shame, and let our dishonor cover us" — shame is the affective state that accompanies and frames the confession: the people are willing to accept shame as the appropriate inner-outer condition for what they have done. Dan 9:8 — "To us, O Lord, belongs open shame, to our kings, to our princes, and to our fathers, because we have sinned against you" — shame is specifically named as the appropriate affective consequence of the named sin. Lam 5:7 — "Our fathers sinned... and we bear their iniquities" — the emotional weight of bearing inherited iniquity carries grief-adjacent affect.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The affective faculty is engaged through its *distorted operation* in conscience suppression. Ecc 8:12 — the sinner who "prolongs his life" while "doing evil a hundred times" presumably experiences some form of positive affect (satisfaction, comfort) that reinforces the suppression — the absence of the fear of God means the negative affect (shame, fear) that should accompany sinning is absent. Jer 2:35 — "surely his anger has turned from me" — the person feels secure (positive affective state) where the appropriate state would be concerned awareness of divine anger. The affective faculty produces false peace where appropriate fear should exist.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The affective faculty is engaged in the dulling mode. 1Ki 16:31 — "as if it had been a light thing" — the affective register of moral gravity is dulled: Jeroboam's sins, which should produce moral revulsion or at least serious concern, produce only a light response. 2Ki 3:3's "clung to" (*davaq*) carries an attachment dimension — the will has an affective bond with the sinful course, making departure emotionally as well as volitionally difficult. 1Ti 5:20 — "so that the rest may stand in fear" — the public rebuke is aimed at producing the affect of fear in the community, implying that appropriate moral fear is what refusal to repent lacks.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The affective faculty is engaged through the *misdirected allegiance* that 2Ki 17:7 names. "Sinned against the Lord their God... and had *feared* other gods" — the fear-as-reverence is an affective-volitional state: their reverence, loyalty, and emotional allegiance has been transferred from the Lord to other gods. The habitual defection in this instance is constituted by an affective misdirection: the emotional-devotional capacity is operating toward wrong objects. Ecc 7:26 — "the sinner is taken" — the sinner's entrapment has an affective dimension: the seductive snare works through the affective pull of what the trap offers, and the sinner lacks the God-oriented affect that would enable escape.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The affective faculty is engaged through the relational provocation dimension. 1Ki 14:22 — "they provoked him to jealousy with their sins" — the community's transmitted sinning provokes God's jealousy: a relational-affective response from God to the breach of covenant loyalty. 1Ki 16:13 — "provoking the Lord God of Israel to anger with their idols" — the idolatrous direction transmitted through contagious sin produces the affective-relational provocation of God. On the community side, the affective allegiance (reverential fear/love) has been diverted: 2Ki 17:7 — "feared other gods" — the affective devotion is redirected through the transmitted sinning to wrong objects.

**[CHAR-8]** S — The 9-verse corpus contains no explicit affective vocabulary in connection with political revolt. The characteristic is described through political-action language (rebelled, revolted, set up a king) without named affective states of the revolting parties.

**[CHAR-9]** E — The affective faculty is engaged through the emotional states that generate sinful speech. Eph 4:31 — slander is listed alongside "bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor" — the affective states of bitterness, wrath, and anger are the emotional context within which slander arises. Col 3:8 — "anger, wrath, malice, slander" — the emotional sequence culminates in slander. 1Ti 6:4 — "unhealthy craving for controversy" — a diseased affective appetite drives the slanderous speech. The characteristic is affectively driven: the corrupted emotional register generates the sinful words.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. The affective faculty is engaged and corrupted. Evidence across VCGs: (1) Pride as an affective disposition — Pro 21:4 (VCG-03): "haughty eyes and a proud heart" name an affective posture of self-elevation; (2) inner hostility — Psa 37:12 (VCG-03): "gnashes his teeth" — a visceral affective expression of hostility toward the righteous; (3) exultation that is momentary — Job 20:5 (VCG-10): "the exulting of the wicked is short" — an affective high that cannot sustain itself; (4) soul-level desire as affect — Pro 21:10 (VCG-09): "the soul of the wicked desires evil" — desire is the affective dimension of this soul-level orientation; (5) inner fear — Pro 10:24 (VCG-06): "what the wicked dreads will come upon him" — the characteristic produces chronic inner dread; (6) inner anguish — Job 15:20 (VCG-06): "the wicked man writhes in pain all his days."

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes. Affective engagement is documented across multiple VCGs. Mat 20:15 (vc=14460 — VCG-06): the evil eye as inner envy and grudging resentment — envy is a direct affective expression of the constitutional evil. Jam 4:16 (vc=14472 — VCG-06): boasting from arrogance declared evil — the affective disposition of pride expressing outward through self-aggrandizing speech. Joh 3:19 (vc=14448 — VCG-04): people "loved the darkness" — love is here an affective orientation toward moral concealment; the characteristic has corrupted the affective faculty of love to attach to darkness. 1Cor 13:6 (vc=14341 — VCG-06): unrighteousness is something that could draw "inner delight" — the affective capacity for delight is capable of being attracted to wrongdoing.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, extensively. The characteristic is constitutively affective on the divine side (revulsion, loathing, hatred — Pro 6:16: "hates"; Pro 11:20 — VCG-01: contrasted with "delight") and generates specific human affective responses. On the human side, when conscience is functional: Eze 9:4 (vc=1698 — VCG-04): "sigh and groan" — grief and anguish as the affective response to perceived abomination; Eze 36:31 (vc=1681 — VCG-04): "you will loathe yourselves" — self-loathing as the affective response to remembered abomination. When conscience is silenced: the affective faculty of shame is entirely absent — Jer 6:15; 8:12 (VCG-04): no shame, no blushing — the affective moral faculty that should register the abomination produces nothing. Pro 13:19 (vc=1687 — VCG-05): the fool experiences turning from evil as affectively abominable — an inverted moral affect.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes. The affective faculty is centrally and definitionally engaged. Isa 66:3 (vc=1633 — VCG-04): "their soul delights in their abominations" — the delight faculty is inverted: attached to abominations rather than to God. Deu 32:16 (vc=65938 — VCG-02): "they stirred him to jealousy with strange gods; with abominations they provoked him to anger" — the relational affect of jealousy on the divine side and of provocative betrayal on the human side. Eze 7:20 (vc=65909 — VCG-05): "His beautiful ornament they used for pride" — pride as an affective disposition drives the characteristic. Eze 16:36 (vc=65986 — VCG-05): "your lust was poured out" — intense desire as the affective fuel of idolatrous abomination.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes. The affective faculty appears in its inverted form. Isa 66:3 (vc=38204 — VCG-04): "their soul delights in their abominations" — the delight-faculty is attached to their iniquitous self-chosen ways. Pro 19:28 (vc=38220 — VCG-03): "the mouth of the wicked devours iniquity" — devouring implies an inner craving and appetite for iniquity; this is an affective desire-state, not merely a cognitive or volitional choice. Pro 21:15 (vc=38221 — VCG-03): "when justice is done, it is a joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers" — the evildoer's affective response to justice is terror (dread), revealing that the inner affective faculty is so aligned with iniquity that right judgment produces fear rather than relief. Psa 55:3 (vc=38188 — VCG-01): enemies "in anger they bear a grudge" — the affective state of sustained anger and grudge-bearing sustains the iniquity directed at others.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes. The affective faculty appears in the contempt-register of VCG-01. Rev 13:6 (vc=14356 — VCG-01): sustained deliberate blasphemy against God's name and dwelling — the sustained quality of the blasphemy reveals contempt as a deep affective inner orientation, not a momentary emotional outburst. Rev 16:9/11/21 (VCG-01): people under catastrophic judgment curse God — the cursing carries intense affective hostility: anger and defiance directed toward God. Jude 8 (vc=14354 — VCG-01): "defile the flesh" alongside authority-rejection and blasphemy — the sensory/fleshly self-indulgence accompanies the blasphemous expression, showing that affective self-indulgence and contemptuous speech are paired inner states.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All six characteristics engage the affective faculty, with consistent inversion across the cluster. Char 4 provides the most extreme affective evidence: Isa 66:3 (VCG-04 — "their soul delights in their abominations") — the delight-faculty attached to abominations. Char 5 (Pro 19:28 — "mouth devours iniquity" showing inner craving) and Char 6 (Rev 16:9/11/21 — contemptuous hostility toward God as the dominant affective state) provide the strongest sustained-affect evidence. Char 3 (Eze 9:4 — sighing and groaning as the grieving conscience's affective response to perceived abomination) and Char 1 (Psa 11:5 — God's soul hates the wicked) both evidence affect at the divine response level rather than the human-practitioner level.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, at two documented points. First, grief at exclusion: Num 9:7 (M10c-A-VCG-07) — the men rendered unclean through corpse-contact "said to him, 'We are unclean through touching a dead body. Why are we kept from bringing the Lord's offering at its appointed time among the people of Israel?'" The grief of desire blocked by an involuntary condition is directly named. Second, the distress of enforced isolation: Lev 13:45-46 (M10c-B-VCG-03) — the person with skin disease must live alone outside the camp for the entire duration of the condition. The cumulative isolation of a sustained defilement state is a condition of relational deprivation that engages the affective faculty, though the verses do not use emotional vocabulary directly.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes. Paul's anticipated mourning at 2Cor 12:21 (VCG-02) — "I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier" — shows that the unrepented impurity produces grief in the pastoral observer who perceives the condition. The affective register of grief is the proper response of one who sees the condition clearly. The positive-inverse in VCG-05 engages affect differently: Rev 14:4 — "they follow the Lamb wherever he goes" — the undefiled inner state is characterised by devotion and following, which is an affective orientation toward Christ. Isa 6:5 (VCG-01) — "woe is me! For I am lost" — the prophet's recognition of his moral-inner defilement produces the affective response of lostness-distress.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. Three affective registers are evidenced. (1) Simmering grief and restrained anger: Gen 34:5 (VCG-01) — Jacob's immediate affective response to the violation of Dinah is restrained awareness; the brothers' affective response (Gen 34:13: "the sense of violated honour drives a calculated, vengeful will") is controlled outrage. (2) Jealousy: Num 5:14 (VCG-01) — "if the spirit of jealousy comes over him" — covenantal betrayal generates jealousy as the immediate affective inner response. (3) Future self-loathing: Eze 20:43 (VCG-02) — "you shall loathe yourselves for all the evils that you have committed" — the anticipated eschatological affect is self-loathing generated by the memory of defilement. (4) Moral revulsion: Eze 36:17 (VCG-04) — God's perception of the community's conduct as "like the uncleanness of a woman in her menstrual impurity" — the language of moral revulsion describes God's affective response to the corporate defilement.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes, indirectly — through the response of those around the affected person. Mar 7:25 (VCG-01): "immediately a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit... came and fell down at his feet" — the mother's urgent, prostrate supplication shows intense affective response generated by the child's condition. Act 5:16 (VCG-02): "people gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits" — the corporate affective response of concern and care. The affected person's own affect is not narrated (dominated and suppressed), but the affect of those who love them is strongly engaged.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All four characteristics engage the affective faculty, but the form and direction of affective engagement differ. Characteristic 1: grief at blocked worship desire (Num 9:7 — "why are we kept from bringing the Lord's offering?") and the affective cost of enforced isolation (Lev 13:45-46). Characteristic 2: the prophet's distress-recognition (Isa 6:5 — "woe is me!"), Paul's anticipated pastoral grief (2Cor 12:21 — "I may have to mourn"), the devotional affect of the undefiled (Rev 14:4 — following the Lamb). Characteristic 3: simmering grief and restrained anger (Gen 34:5), jealousy (Num 5:14), future self-loathing (Eze 20:43), God's moral revulsion (Eze 36:17). Characteristic 4: the affected person's own affect bypassed (structurally inaccessible); intense affect generated in those who love the possessed (Mar 7:25 — mother's prostrate urgency; Luk 9:42 — father receiving his son back). Cluster affective pattern: every characteristic generates grief or distress in those who perceive the condition correctly. The characteristic's affective register is universally negative — no characteristic generates positive affect in relation to the defilement-state itself (only the positive-inverse — the undefiled state — generates positive affect such as the Rev 14:4 devotional following).

findings.session_b_note:
The data supports a differentiated answer across three modes:

**Enables and deepens affect (in the receiver):** Forgiveness received generates love (Luk 7:47) and reverential awe (Psa 130:4) — affective states that are named as outcomes of the forgiveness-encounter. The depth of the affective response is proportional to the depth of forgiveness received ("forgiven much → loved much") — forgiveness deepens the affective capacity by the scale of what is released.

**Transforms affect (in the forgiver):** The act of forgiving releases the withheld grievance — a negative affective state — and replaces it with the inner freedom described in the data. The withholder's "poisoned" inner life (OBS-064-001) implies that withholding sustains a destructive affective state; forgiving releases it.

**Incorporates affect as precondition (in the forgiver):** The visceral compassion (Mat 18:27) functions as the affective prerequisite of the act. Forgiveness is not a cold volitional transaction — the affective faculty (compassion, gut-level responsiveness to the other's condition) is engaged as the motivating ground. Affect is not bypassed but enrolled.

findings.session_b_note:
Enables and deepens. Zec 12:10: grace outpoured produces mourning — the capacity to grieve what grace has cost. SD020: charis/chairo root-sharing — grace is inherently joy-productive, the ground of joy as a sustained inner state. Eph 4:32: eusplanchnos — grace softens the inner person affectively, enabling compassion-feeling. Grace enables appropriate affect: fear, mourning, and joy and peace are all appropriate responses to different aspects of grace.

*Adds structure: the enabling of appropriate affect — the specific affects corresponding to each encounter with grace — is a significant T3 finding.*

findings.session_b_note:
**Compassion enables affect — the eusplanchnos quality:** 1 Pet 3:8 — "tender heart" (eusplanchnos) — names the inner constitution that is open to affective movement. Compassion both requires and, over time, enables a tenderness of inner being that makes affective movement possible. The person formed in compassion becomes more affectively open, not less.

**Compassion deepens affect toward the suffering other:** The splanchnizō pattern shows that compassion does not merely acknowledge suffering intellectually — it is moved by it. The movement deepens the affective engagement with the other's condition: the person who is splanchnizō toward the widow of Nain (Luke 7:13) is not merely noting her grief but is affected by it in the body. Compassion deepens affect by requiring the person to be genuinely present to the other's emotional reality.

**The metriopatheō exception:** G3356 metriopatheō (Heb 5:2) names a form of compassion in which the affective response is moderated. This is not impairment of affect but calibration — compassion shaped by wisdom rather than overwhelmed by feeling. The data explicitly regrounds this moderation in shared vulnerability rather than philosophical suppression, which preserves the affective dimension while giving it appropriate form. Compassion does not bypass affect even when it moderates it.

findings.session_b_note:
Contrition **deepens and authenticates** affect. The registry description distinguishes genuine contrition from surface shame — the distinction is between deep interior grief (authentic affective engagement with the reality of harm done) and surface shame (social/reputational affect without genuine inner engagement). Contrition enables the affective faculty to engage with genuine depth rather than remaining at the surface of social self-presentation.

The movement from contrition toward joy (Psa 51:8 — "let the bones that you have broken rejoice") suggests that contrition, paradoxically, enables a deeper and more authentic experience of joy than is available to the person who has not passed through it. The contrite person longs for joy from a position of real need; when it comes (through divine revival), it will be received at the full depth of the inner being.

findings.session_b_note:
**Enabling positive affect:** Righteous fellowship (Psa 119:63, Ecc 4:10, 1Jo 1:3) enables hope, belonging, and comfort. The person in genuine fellowship has their affective capacity supported and amplified by the relational bond.

**Enabling sorrow as fellowship:** Phili 3:10 — the fellowship of suffering is an affective engagement: the person participates in the suffering of Christ affectively, not only philosophically or theologically. Fellowship can encompass sorrow as a genuine affective participation.

**Impairing affect through wrong fellowship:** The co-occurrence with R051 (distress, 3 shared verses) and the spiritual bondage of idolatrous joining (Hos 4:17) suggest that wrong fellowship impairs the affective capacity — the person joined to idols is in a condition of divine abandonment that produces not comfort but distress.

**Gap:** The precise affective sequence of fellowship — what the person feels when entering, sustaining, and losing fellowship — is not systematically mapped in the data.

findings.session_b_note: Goodness enables and deepens affect when genuine. Genuine encounter with divine goodness produces trust, praise, and gladness rooted in God — these are authentic affective states produced by the encounter. The comparative wisdom mode also has an affective dimension: the person who genuinely values "better than" outcomes experiences a right ordering of their desires and affections. Distorted goodness impairs affect: Haman's gladness-of-heart (tov-lev, Est 5:9) is genuine affect but immediately destroyed — it is affect without its proper root, which renders it constitutionally fragile. The diagnosis is that goodness properly produces deep, stable, rooted affective states; goodness-mimicry produces shallow, fragile affective states. (OBS-067-OBS-040, OBS-067-OBS-041, OBS-067-OBS-029)

findings.session_b_note: Love **deepens and intensifies** affect rather than bypassing or impairing it. The love-vocabulary's emotional range is the widest in the programme (OBS-103-051 — from deepest joy to deepest grief). Specific deepening evidence: Song 5:6 (OBS-103-062) — love's absence produces soul-failing, one of the most acute affective states in the corpus. 2Sa 1:26 (OBS-103-095) — love measured by its grief: 'your love was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women.' The intensity of love produces intensity of affect — not merely as a side-effect but as love's evidence and measure. Love also enables affect that would otherwise be inaccessible: love of enemy (Mat 5:44) enables compassion where enmity would produce contempt; love of God enables the reverential joy of Psa 63:3 ('better than life'). Disordered love distorts affect: love-of-money produces 'many pangs' (1Ti 6:10, OBS-103-132) — the wrong love generates the wrong affective outcomes.

findings.session_b_note: Mercy deepens affect in both the seeking and receiving directions: seeking mercy is accompanied by intensified emotional expression (breast-beating, persistent cry against opposition); received mercy produces affective depth (joy, shame, wonder, silence). The mercilessness catalogue (Rom 1:31 — OBS-111-034) pairs mercilessness with *astorgos* (heartless/affectionless) — the absence of mercy is associated with affective incapacity. Mercy thus enables affect; its absence impairs it. OBS-111-034, OBS-111-047, OBS-111-054.

findings.session_b_note: Contrition deepens affect in two directions simultaneously: it deepens grief (the weight of having caused harm is fully felt) and deepens longing (the desire for restoration and joy is intensified by the depth of the brokenness). The affective range of the contrite person is not narrowed but expanded — they feel their failure fully and their longing for restoration fully. *New finding: contrition produces affective depth in both directions — grief at the bottom and longing at the horizon — without numbing either.* OBS-030-001, OBS-030-055.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-030-020: The faculty tier (T3) shows that contrition deepens every faculty without impairing any; the formative tier (T5) shows that this deepening accumulates into settled character over time. T3's snapshot (…
findings.finding_value: The faculty tier (T3) shows that contrition deepens every faculty without impairing any; the formative tier (T5) shows that this deepening accumulates into settled character over time. T3's snapshot (what contrition does to the faculties in the moment) and T5's longitudinal account (what repeated contrition produces in the person over time) together yield a complete picture: the opening of perception, cognition, affect, volition, agency, conscience, conscientiousness, and relational capacity that contrition produces in the moment (T3) becomes, through repetition, the settled character of the person who habitually trembles at God's word (T5 — Isa 66:2). The character of lowliness is the long-term form of the faculty-opening that contrition produces in the short term.

findings.session_b_note: Fellowship deepens affect — shared suffering produces shared comfort (2Cor 1:7); shared hope (Ecc 9:4) is the affective product of existential fellowship. The affective deepening is proportionate: "as you share in our sufferings, so also you share in our comfort" — the depth of shared suffering determines the depth of shared comfort. OBS-062-031.

OBS-064-029, OBS-064-032.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-003: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion re…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion responds, it does not originate or create. It is the most responsive of the faculties-engaging characteristics. Second, affect and moral action are structurally unified in compassion — not sequentially related but simultaneous. Affect is the mechanism of movement (splanchnizō is both the felt inner event and the cause of the action), not a precursor or accompaniment. This is unique among the characteristics reviewed: in most other registries, affect and volition are distinguishable stages; in compassion, the felt movement is already the morally motivated action beginning. A third distinctive finding: compassion converts moral knowledge into motivated action — it is the motivational ground of conscientiousness, not a product of it. The conscience faculty engagement reveals compassion as conscience-healing: it addresses the pitiable condition that conscience perceives as a moral claim, resolving the tension between moral knowledge and moral incapacity. The three relational modes (building/sustaining — chesed; restoring/repairing — splanchnizō; extending across difference — Good Samaritan) are a new finding not in the instruction typology.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-009: T1's four kinds explain T3's most distinctive finding: that affect and moral action are structurally unified rather than sequential. In T1 terms, compassion-as-inner-event (splanchnizō) and compassion…
findings.finding_value: T1's four kinds explain T3's most distinctive finding: that affect and moral action are structurally unified rather than sequential. In T1 terms, compassion-as-inner-event (splanchnizō) and compassion-as-externalised-act are not two separate kinds but a continuous movement — the felt-movement is the beginning of the act. T3 confirms this: affect is the mechanism of movement, not its precursor. T1's finding that compassion converts moral knowledge into motivated action (the unique position as motivational ground of conscientiousness) maps onto T3.10's finding of the same: the definitional claim (T1) that compassion is constitutively outward-facing explains T3's finding that it is the driving faculty between moral knowledge and moral action.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-014: T2's four-stage constitutional movement sequence (somatic arousal → soul engagement → volitional engagement → outward action) maps directly onto T3's faculty engagement sequence. The somatic-arousal s…
findings.finding_value: T2's four-stage constitutional movement sequence (somatic arousal → soul engagement → volitional engagement → outward action) maps directly onto T3's faculty engagement sequence. The somatic-arousal stage (T2.6 — gut stirring, splanchnizō) corresponds to T3.1's perceptive-trigger stage (sight activates the somatic response) and T3.4's affect stage (the stirring is the affective movement). The soul-engagement stage (T2.2 — chesed as soul-character) corresponds to T3.8 moral evaluation (the soul assesses the need) and T3.9 conscience (the conscience activates the response). The volitional-engagement stage (T2.3 — heart-locus as deliberative site) corresponds to T3.6 volition (the will directs the action). The outward-action stage corresponds to T3.7 agency. T2 and T3 describe the same movement sequence from two perspectives: T2 maps the constitutional levels; T3 maps the faculties active at each level.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-019: T3's perceptive-trigger finding (compassion is activated by sight — splanchnizō is perceptively dependent) and T4's scope-by-need finding (scope is determined by perceived need, not covenantal standin…
findings.finding_value: T3's perceptive-trigger finding (compassion is activated by sight — splanchnizō is perceptively dependent) and T4's scope-by-need finding (scope is determined by perceived need, not covenantal standing) are the same finding from two analytical perspectives. T3 names the faculty (perception) and its function (triggering compassion by seeing the pitiable condition); T4 names the relational consequence (scope defined by what is seen). The cross-boundary extension in T4 (Nineveh, Samaritan/Jew) is the relational expression of T3's merit-independence: compassion is perceptively dependent (it must see the need) but merit-independent (it does not assess the moral standing of the one seen). The three relational modes in T3.11 (building/sustaining, restoring/repairing, extending across difference) correspond precisely to T4's chesed/splanchnizō/cross-boundary structure.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-020: T3's affect-moral-action unity (affect is the mechanism, not the precursor) and T5's formation finding (compassion is simultaneously character target and motivational ground) are structurally connecte…
findings.finding_value: T3's affect-moral-action unity (affect is the mechanism, not the precursor) and T5's formation finding (compassion is simultaneously character target and motivational ground) are structurally connected. T5 names compassion as the motivational ground that makes the sanctification arc survivable through failure and return — but T3 has already established that affect is the mechanism of this motivational ground: the character formation that T5 describes is accomplished through the affective mechanism that T3 identifies. The person who is formed into compassionate character (T5) is the person whose affective faculty has been trained to respond immediately and morally to perceived suffering (T3). T3's finding that affect and moral action are unified is T5's mechanism of formation: the person becoming compassionate is the person in whom the affective-moral unity is deepening and stabilising.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-021: T3's finding that compassion is the motivational ground of conscientiousness explains the co-occurrence pattern in T6. Conscience (T3.9) and moral evaluation (T3.8) are the faculties that register the…
findings.finding_value: T3's finding that compassion is the motivational ground of conscientiousness explains the co-occurrence pattern in T6. Conscience (T3.9) and moral evaluation (T3.8) are the faculties that register the pitiable need as a moral claim; compassion is the affective-motivational response that converts that moral knowledge into action. The co-occurrence of will (R173 — 25 verses) and surrender (R156 — 21 verses) in T6 is the co-occurrence expression of T3's volitional faculty finding: compassion engages and redirects the will toward the suffering other. The sequential relationship confirmed in T6 (compassion → mercy — constitutionally causal) is the relational expression of T3's finding that compassion converts moral knowledge into motivated action: the mercy-act is the action that compassion's motivation produces.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-022: T3's perceptive-trigger and affect-mechanism findings are grounded in T7's primary anchor evidence. The Synoptic pattern of splanchnizō — always triggered by sight, always preceding action — is the te…
findings.finding_value: T3's perceptive-trigger and affect-mechanism findings are grounded in T7's primary anchor evidence. The Synoptic pattern of splanchnizō — always triggered by sight, always preceding action — is the textual ground for T3.1's finding (compassion is perceptively dependent) and T3.4's finding (affect is the mechanism of movement). T7's argument structure finding (Matt 9:36 — compassion as the theological engine of missional response) is the evangelist's literary expression of T3.10's analytical claim (compassion converts moral knowledge into motivated action). T7's framework divergences (human science frameworks failing at sovereignty, cross-boundary extension, and purposive suffering) correspond to the three areas where T3's faculty analysis finds its most distinctive results: the sovereign freedom of divine compassion exceeds the natural automaticity of empathic response; the cross-boundary extension exceeds natural empathic scope; the purposive suffering (T5.4/T5.5) requires the teleological frame that T7.3 identifies.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-003: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked …
findings.finding_value: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I but the grace of God that is with me." Agency is not displaced but constituted by grace. This relationship holds in paradox that the T3.6 prompt options (enable/deepen/bypass/impair) cannot accommodate — a prompt design limitation noted for catalogue revision. Second, grace produces moral clarity (T3.8 — sharpens moral evaluation rather than bypassing it): the person who recognises grace has made a precise moral evaluation (they know they received what they did not deserve). Third, grace and conscience are mutually necessary: grace is the condition within which conscience can operate fully without destroying the person; conscience without grace produces condemnation; grace without conscience produces presumption (T3.9). Fourth, grace is the primary relational faculty developer in the registry's evidence — it reaches every relational register (vertical access, horizontal forgiving, speech-grace) and enables each one. Creativity (T3.5) is the one genuinely silent faculty — not an impairment but a non-engagement: grace receives and constitutes, it does not create.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-009: T1's immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response) is the affective-volitional expression of T3's faculty engagement at the moment grace arrives. T3…
findings.finding_value: T1's immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response) is the affective-volitional expression of T3's faculty engagement at the moment grace arrives. T3.4 (affect is the first named faculty engaged by grace) and T3.6 (the agency-constituting paradox of 1Cor 15:10) together explain why T1.5 finds the creaturely recognition response before positive states settle: grace first produces the affective recognition (fear, mourning) before constituting the agency through which the person responds (prostration as the body enacting the inner posture that grace has produced). T1's finding that grace requires creaturely recognition to complete its operation (T1.7) is T3.1's finding at the faculty level: grace requires and enables perception simultaneously.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-014: T2's constitutional movement (spirit reception → soul standing → capacity → character expression) maps onto T3's faculty engagement sequence. The spirit-reception stage (T2.1) corresponds to T3.1 (per…
findings.finding_value: T2's constitutional movement (spirit reception → soul standing → capacity → character expression) maps onto T3's faculty engagement sequence. The spirit-reception stage (T2.1) corresponds to T3.1 (perception — grace enabling the inner sight and hearing that receives it). The soul-standing stage (T2.2) corresponds to T3.9 (conscience — grace as the condition within which conscience can operate without destruction) and T3.8 (moral evaluation — the standing produces the clarity of moral self-assessment). The capacity-gifting stage (T2.1 — spirit level) corresponds to T3.7 (agency — capacity given constitutes agency for the task). The character-expression stage (T2.7 — outward through body-soul) corresponds to T3.10 (conscientiousness — the integrated moral-action expression of received grace-character). T2 maps the constitutional space; T3 maps the faculties active at each spatial level; the two tiers describe the same movement from orthogonal perspectives.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-020: T3's faculty findings are the synchronic expression of T5's diachronic formation arc. The creaturely recognition response (T5.2 — fear → mourning → prostration as the consistent transitional state in …
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty findings are the synchronic expression of T5's diachronic formation arc. The creaturely recognition response (T5.2 — fear → mourning → prostration as the consistent transitional state in all grace-sequences) is the affective-faculty event (T3.4) at the moment of grace-arrival, which then constitutes the volitional-faculty alignment (T3.6 — the agency-constituting paradox) that enables the conscientious expression (T3.10). T5's formation arc (sustained work producing character-quality) is the longitudinal development of T3.9's finding (conscience operating fully within grace) into T3.10's finding (conscientiousness as the integrated moral character that grace constitutes over time). The person who has been formed by grace through the T5 formation arc is the person in whom T3's faculty engagements have been progressively deepened and integrated.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-022: T3's faculty findings are grounded in and confirmed by T7's primary anchor evidence. The perceptive-faculty finding (T3.1 — grace requires and enables perception) is grounded in the eye-formula of che…
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty findings are grounded in and confirmed by T7's primary anchor evidence. The perceptive-faculty finding (T3.1 — grace requires and enables perception) is grounded in the eye-formula of chen (SD041), Zec 12:10's grace-produced vision, and SD012's hearing-receptivity pattern. T7's argument structure for Zec 12:10 (grace outpoured → "when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced") confirms T3.1 precisely: the grace-event produces and requires the inner sight that recognises what grace has cost. T3.6's agency-constituting paradox (1Cor 15:10) is T7.3's most significant framework-divergence point: at the moment of constitutional incapacity, all human science frameworks assume the person has some prior agency; the biblical account holds the paradox of grace-constituted agency that is genuinely human while grace-originated. This is the methodological divergence T7.3 identifies and T3.6 establishes as the operative finding.

findings.session_b_note: The evidence suggests that covenant structures the context within which affect operates rather than producing or impairing it directly. (1) Enabling: covenant inclusion enables hope and security (Eph 2:12 reversed — being included produces hope that exclusion destroys — OBS-034-060); the new covenant enables a knowing of God (Jer 31:34) that carries affective depth — knowing a person involves emotional engagement. The covenant of hesed (love) names the affective quality of the relationship it structures. (2) The adjuration register (3308-004 — OBS-034-056) shows that covenant language is taken up into the register of intense emotional longing — covenant is not affectively flat but can carry the whole emotional range of intimate relationship. Gap: the data does not directly address whether covenant enables or deepens affect as a distinct inner-being operation. The clearest evidence is that covenant shapes the conditions within which affect is experienced (inclusion → hope; exclusion → desolation; breach → grief), but whether covenant produces affect independent of these conditional states is not directly stated.

findings.session_b_note: Kindness primarily enables and deepens affect — it does not bypass or impair it. Three patterns are evidenced. (a) Enables affect: the person who has received divine chesed acquires an affective capacity that exceeds what they would otherwise have — Lam 3:22–23 situates hope (an affective orientation) in the context of Lamentations (total devastation) specifically because chesed is inexhaustible [XREG: H2617A, OBS-099-085]. The receipt of kindness opens an affective register that devastation alone would close. (b) Deepens affect: the chasid formation arc [XREG: H2623, OBS-099-094] — the person shaped by chesed over a lifetime — develops deeper affective sensitivity to the relational world. The paired term in Eph 4:32 (eusplanchnoi — compassionate hearts) suggests that the formation of kindness goes alongside deepening affective resonance with others. (c) The counterfeit (chrēstologia — Rom 16:18 [OBS-099-074]) reveals what bypassed affect looks like: pleasant words without inner disposition is the pathology of kindness-form without affective substance. Genuine kindness cannot be bypassed from affect — the counterfeit that does so is named and condemned.

findings.session_b_note: Peace enables positive affect and resolves negative affect. Evidence: (1) Judg 6:23 — "Peace be to you. Do not fear" — divine peace directly displaces terror; (2) Est 9:22 — "sorrow turned into gladness and mourning into a holiday" (in the context of Purim rest/peace); (3) 1Sa 1:17-18 — Hannah went away and "her face was no longer sad" after Eli's peace-blessing; (4) Phili 4:7 — peace guards the heart against anxiety (Phili 4:6 context: "do not be anxious about anything... and the peace of God will guard"). Peace is the affective resolution of anxiety, fear, and sorrow. Its sustained presence does not bypass affect — peace-bearing people still weep, still feel — but it prevents affect from becoming debilitating or destructive. The person in peace can feel sorrow without being overwhelmed by it.

findings.session_b_note: The characteristic both enables and transforms affect. In its eschatological mode (872-007): the transformative giving directly replaces negative affect (mourning, faint spirit) with positive affect (gladness, praise) — Isa 61:3 (OBS-060-048). This is direct affective transformation: the giving enables new affective states that were previously absent or depleted. In its responsive mode (872-002): the divine affective state (rahamim, compassion — Hos 11:8, OBS-060-038) is itself what the giving expresses — the characteristic does not bypass affect but is grounded in it. The human relinquishing mode (Job 1:21, OBS-060-044) shows affect operating under the characteristic: blessing and worship under devastating loss is an affective act, not a stoic suppression of affect. The characteristic does not impair affect in any evidenced instance; where it fails to operate (glory withheld from God), affect is disordered (Jer 13:16 — darkness, stumbling). Affect is constitutively engaged throughout.

In the concealment register: impairs honest affective expression — the person must suppress the true affective state and perform its opposite (false peace). In group 1200 (sa.tam): transforms affect from acute anger into sustained smouldering state — the heat of the moment becomes the cold persistence of the grudge.

Contempt is characteristically affectively flat — the cool dismissal. It does not intensify affect but evacuates it: what should produce respect and reverence produces nothing. It impairs the affective registering of worth.

Abhorrence is affectively intense — it amplifies the moral-disgust register of the affective faculty. Righteous abhorrence deepens the affective response to moral violation; inverted abhorrence redirects that intensity toward what should be welcomed.

Cruelty impairs the compassion-register of affect — the affective response to another's suffering that would normally trigger mercy is absent. Pro 12:10: even the cruel person's mercy-attempts are shaped by the underlying cruelty.
Reproach impairs — it produces a sustained state of shame, fear, and despair that reshapes the whole affective orientation of the person toward their social environment.
Sharpens urgency — the adversary relationship heightens affective alertness.

Inverts — the normally aversive affective response to another's suffering (compassion, sorrow) is replaced by pleasure and joy. The affective faculty is operating but in the most complete inversion possible.

Affect is the primary faculty for M05-B (compassion) and M05-F (comfort), the most important secondary faculty for M05-A (love), and a real but tertiary faculty for M05-C, D, E, G. The cluster's characteristics engage the affective faculty differentially: the suffering-triggered characteristics (B, F) are constitutively affective; the moral-quality characteristics (D, E) are peripherally affective; the relational characteristics (A, G) span both. This pattern reveals that M05 is not uniformly affective — it ranges from the constitutively somatic-affective (M05-B) to the substantially non-affective (M05-D, G in their primary registers).

**[CLUSTER]** E. Righteousness enables specific positive affects (gladness, hope, zeal, relief) and re-orients potentially destructive affects (the recontextualization of suffering through reckoning in F; the entrusting of vengeance rather than the destructive weight of self-executed resentment in D). Wickedness impairs the healthy affects (the hardened heart cannot feel appropriate fear or compunction, G). The cluster reveals that righteousness is an affective organiser — it enables right affects and orients potentially destructive ones toward productive outcomes.
Wisdom produces affect secondarily: wisdom-as-character produces peace (via right orientation), but is not itself affective.

findings.finding_value: M01-A **deepens** affect by integrating fear with joy, delight, and confidence. Psa 2:11 (trembling delight), Pro 14:26 (fear as "foundation of strong confidence, not anxiety"), Neh 1:11 (fearing God's name as "something the servants delight in — a willing, joyful inner devotion rather than reluctant dread"). Reverential fear does not flatten the affective life but deepens and integrates it.

M01-B acute fear, M01-C terror, and M01-D dismay **overwhelm** affect in their extreme forms. The sheer intensity of the experience monopolises the inner life: Dan 5:6 (dismay striking so violently that color changes and limbs fail — all other affect is displaced). Mat 28:8 (fear and joy coexisting) is the exception rather than the rule in the acute register.
