findings.finding_value: T3 reveals forgiveness as uniquely faculty-comprehensive — it engages more named faculties with greater specificity than any other characteristic reviewed in this revision series. Memory is explicitly named (Jer 31:34 — divine memory as the content of forgiveness) and distinctively: forgiveness transforms memory in both directions — God's memory of sin is set aside permanently; the human forgiver releases the active use of memory against the offender. Affect is bidirectionally engaged: as prerequisite (somatic compassion, Mat 18:27) and as product (love, Luk 7:47; reverence, Psa 130:4). Conscience is addressed and purified by forgiveness (Heb 9:14). Volition is constitutive (the heart-level release is chosen). Cognition is enabled (Jer 31:34 — forgiveness → knowing God). The single silence is creativity (T3.5). T3's synthesis: forgiveness is the most faculty-comprehensive characteristic in the current review set — it reaches every major faculty with specific evidenced content, most strikingly in the memory domain.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-009: T1's four modes explain T3's faculty engagement pattern. The covenantal-objective mode (no inner-being prerequisite) corresponds to T3's absence of any faculty requirement for that mode. The divine re…
findings.finding_value: T1's four modes explain T3's faculty engagement pattern. The covenantal-objective mode (no inner-being prerequisite) corresponds to T3's absence of any faculty requirement for that mode. The divine relational-personal mode (faith, repentance, confession as access-postures) engages volition, conscience, and cognition. The human horizontal mode ("from your heart") requires volition, conscience, and moral evaluation. The intercessory mode requires the dependence-posture that engages cognition (accurate assessment of the grounds of the plea — God's character, not human merit) and volition. T1's definition of forgiveness as transitional (not terminal) is confirmed by T3's finding that every faculty engaged by forgiveness is deepened toward further engagement — not closed by the act but opened by it.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-019: T3's faculty engagements all point in the same relational directions that T4 identifies as primary. Conscience (T3.9) is engaged in both the seeking-forgiveness direction (human-to-God: confession as …
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty engagements all point in the same relational directions that T4 identifies as primary. Conscience (T3.9) is engaged in both the seeking-forgiveness direction (human-to-God: confession as conscience's public verdict) and the giving direction (human horizontal: the conscience that recognises the offence to be released). Memory (T3.3) is engaged in the God-to-human direction (divine "remember no more" — Jer 31:34) and the human-giving direction (releasing the memory's active use against the offender). Volition (T3.6) drives the giving direction (heart-level release is chosen). The vertical-horizontal interdependence (T4 structural claim) is the relational expression of T3's conscience-and-volition faculty account: the person whose conscience has accurately received the magnitude of divine forgiveness has the volitional capacity to extend horizontal forgiveness.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-020: T3's faculty deepenings (cognition enabled — Jer 31:34; love produced — Luk 7:47; conscience purified — Heb 9:14; volition redirected) are T5's formation products described at the faculty level. The f…
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty deepenings (cognition enabled — Jer 31:34; love produced — Luk 7:47; conscience purified — Heb 9:14; volition redirected) are T5's formation products described at the faculty level. The formation sequence (T5) is the longitudinal account of which T3's faculty engagements are the synchronic snapshots. T3 and T5 together reveal the full formation arc: T3 shows what happens to each faculty in the moment of forgiveness; T5 shows what sustained habitual forgiveness does to the person over time.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-022: T7's literary forms explain why T3 finds different faculty engagements in different evidential contexts. The cultic-legal corpus (Lev 4:20) — covenantal-objective mode — requires no named faculty enga…
findings.finding_value: T7's literary forms explain why T3 finds different faculty engagements in different evidential contexts. The cultic-legal corpus (Lev 4:20) — covenantal-objective mode — requires no named faculty engagement (T3 finds no faculty requirement for this mode). The prophetic corpus (Jer 31:34) primarily engages cognition and memory (T3.2, T3.3). The Synoptic narrative corpus (Luk 7:47, Mat 18:27, Mat 18:35) engages affect, volition, and conscience most richly. The apostolic letter corpus (Eph 1:7, Eph 4:32) grounds the formation dimension (T3.10 conscientiousness, T5.5 sanctification). Each literary form carries specific faculty registers — T7's literary analysis explains T3's faculty engagement distribution.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-003: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion re…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion responds, it does not originate or create. It is the most responsive of the faculties-engaging characteristics. Second, affect and moral action are structurally unified in compassion — not sequentially related but simultaneous. Affect is the mechanism of movement (splanchnizō is both the felt inner event and the cause of the action), not a precursor or accompaniment. This is unique among the characteristics reviewed: in most other registries, affect and volition are distinguishable stages; in compassion, the felt movement is already the morally motivated action beginning. A third distinctive finding: compassion converts moral knowledge into motivated action — it is the motivational ground of conscientiousness, not a product of it. The conscience faculty engagement reveals compassion as conscience-healing: it addresses the pitiable condition that conscience perceives as a moral claim, resolving the tension between moral knowledge and moral incapacity. The three relational modes (building/sustaining — chesed; restoring/repairing — splanchnizō; extending across difference — Good Samaritan) are a new finding not in the instruction typology.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-009: T1's four kinds explain T3's most distinctive finding: that affect and moral action are structurally unified rather than sequential. In T1 terms, compassion-as-inner-event (splanchnizō) and compassion…
findings.finding_value: T1's four kinds explain T3's most distinctive finding: that affect and moral action are structurally unified rather than sequential. In T1 terms, compassion-as-inner-event (splanchnizō) and compassion-as-externalised-act are not two separate kinds but a continuous movement — the felt-movement is the beginning of the act. T3 confirms this: affect is the mechanism of movement, not its precursor. T1's finding that compassion converts moral knowledge into motivated action (the unique position as motivational ground of conscientiousness) maps onto T3.10's finding of the same: the definitional claim (T1) that compassion is constitutively outward-facing explains T3's finding that it is the driving faculty between moral knowledge and moral action.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-014: T2's four-stage constitutional movement sequence (somatic arousal → soul engagement → volitional engagement → outward action) maps directly onto T3's faculty engagement sequence. The somatic-arousal s…
findings.finding_value: T2's four-stage constitutional movement sequence (somatic arousal → soul engagement → volitional engagement → outward action) maps directly onto T3's faculty engagement sequence. The somatic-arousal stage (T2.6 — gut stirring, splanchnizō) corresponds to T3.1's perceptive-trigger stage (sight activates the somatic response) and T3.4's affect stage (the stirring is the affective movement). The soul-engagement stage (T2.2 — chesed as soul-character) corresponds to T3.8 moral evaluation (the soul assesses the need) and T3.9 conscience (the conscience activates the response). The volitional-engagement stage (T2.3 — heart-locus as deliberative site) corresponds to T3.6 volition (the will directs the action). The outward-action stage corresponds to T3.7 agency. T2 and T3 describe the same movement sequence from two perspectives: T2 maps the constitutional levels; T3 maps the faculties active at each level.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-020: T3's affect-moral-action unity (affect is the mechanism, not the precursor) and T5's formation finding (compassion is simultaneously character target and motivational ground) are structurally connecte…
findings.finding_value: T3's affect-moral-action unity (affect is the mechanism, not the precursor) and T5's formation finding (compassion is simultaneously character target and motivational ground) are structurally connected. T5 names compassion as the motivational ground that makes the sanctification arc survivable through failure and return — but T3 has already established that affect is the mechanism of this motivational ground: the character formation that T5 describes is accomplished through the affective mechanism that T3 identifies. The person who is formed into compassionate character (T5) is the person whose affective faculty has been trained to respond immediately and morally to perceived suffering (T3). T3's finding that affect and moral action are unified is T5's mechanism of formation: the person becoming compassionate is the person in whom the affective-moral unity is deepening and stabilising.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-003: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked …
findings.finding_value: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I but the grace of God that is with me." Agency is not displaced but constituted by grace. This relationship holds in paradox that the T3.6 prompt options (enable/deepen/bypass/impair) cannot accommodate — a prompt design limitation noted for catalogue revision. Second, grace produces moral clarity (T3.8 — sharpens moral evaluation rather than bypassing it): the person who recognises grace has made a precise moral evaluation (they know they received what they did not deserve). Third, grace and conscience are mutually necessary: grace is the condition within which conscience can operate fully without destroying the person; conscience without grace produces condemnation; grace without conscience produces presumption (T3.9). Fourth, grace is the primary relational faculty developer in the registry's evidence — it reaches every relational register (vertical access, horizontal forgiving, speech-grace) and enables each one. Creativity (T3.5) is the one genuinely silent faculty — not an impairment but a non-engagement: grace receives and constitutes, it does not create.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-009: T1's immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response) is the affective-volitional expression of T3's faculty engagement at the moment grace arrives. T3…
findings.finding_value: T1's immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response) is the affective-volitional expression of T3's faculty engagement at the moment grace arrives. T3.4 (affect is the first named faculty engaged by grace) and T3.6 (the agency-constituting paradox of 1Cor 15:10) together explain why T1.5 finds the creaturely recognition response before positive states settle: grace first produces the affective recognition (fear, mourning) before constituting the agency through which the person responds (prostration as the body enacting the inner posture that grace has produced). T1's finding that grace requires creaturely recognition to complete its operation (T1.7) is T3.1's finding at the faculty level: grace requires and enables perception simultaneously.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-014: T2's constitutional movement (spirit reception → soul standing → capacity → character expression) maps onto T3's faculty engagement sequence. The spirit-reception stage (T2.1) corresponds to T3.1 (per…
findings.finding_value: T2's constitutional movement (spirit reception → soul standing → capacity → character expression) maps onto T3's faculty engagement sequence. The spirit-reception stage (T2.1) corresponds to T3.1 (perception — grace enabling the inner sight and hearing that receives it). The soul-standing stage (T2.2) corresponds to T3.9 (conscience — grace as the condition within which conscience can operate without destruction) and T3.8 (moral evaluation — the standing produces the clarity of moral self-assessment). The capacity-gifting stage (T2.1 — spirit level) corresponds to T3.7 (agency — capacity given constitutes agency for the task). The character-expression stage (T2.7 — outward through body-soul) corresponds to T3.10 (conscientiousness — the integrated moral-action expression of received grace-character). T2 maps the constitutional space; T3 maps the faculties active at each spatial level; the two tiers describe the same movement from orthogonal perspectives.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-019: T3's agency-constituting finding (grace constitutes rather than replaces agency — 1Cor 15:10) and T4's human-to-God direction (supplication as the human posture of appeal — requiring genuine human age…
findings.finding_value: T3's agency-constituting finding (grace constitutes rather than replaces agency — 1Cor 15:10) and T4's human-to-God direction (supplication as the human posture of appeal — requiring genuine human agency in the act of plea) are structurally aligned. The constituted agency (T3.7) is precisely the agency that supplication requires: the creature must genuinely appeal, not merely receive passively. T3's finding that grace and conscience are mutually necessary (T3.9) corresponds to T4's relational-access finding: grace transforms the threshold of human-to-God approach (prosagōgē — SD035) from impassable to open, which is the relational expression of T3.9's constitutional finding that grace creates the condition within which conscience can operate fully without destruction. T3 names the inner-being event; T4 names the relational consequence of the same event.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-020: T3's faculty findings are the synchronic expression of T5's diachronic formation arc. The creaturely recognition response (T5.2 — fear → mourning → prostration as the consistent transitional state in …
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty findings are the synchronic expression of T5's diachronic formation arc. The creaturely recognition response (T5.2 — fear → mourning → prostration as the consistent transitional state in all grace-sequences) is the affective-faculty event (T3.4) at the moment of grace-arrival, which then constitutes the volitional-faculty alignment (T3.6 — the agency-constituting paradox) that enables the conscientious expression (T3.10). T5's formation arc (sustained work producing character-quality) is the longitudinal development of T3.9's finding (conscience operating fully within grace) into T3.10's finding (conscientiousness as the integrated moral character that grace constitutes over time). The person who has been formed by grace through the T5 formation arc is the person in whom T3's faculty engagements have been progressively deepened and integrated.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-022: T3's faculty findings are grounded in and confirmed by T7's primary anchor evidence. The perceptive-faculty finding (T3.1 — grace requires and enables perception) is grounded in the eye-formula of che…
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty findings are grounded in and confirmed by T7's primary anchor evidence. The perceptive-faculty finding (T3.1 — grace requires and enables perception) is grounded in the eye-formula of chen (SD041), Zec 12:10's grace-produced vision, and SD012's hearing-receptivity pattern. T7's argument structure for Zec 12:10 (grace outpoured → "when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced") confirms T3.1 precisely: the grace-event produces and requires the inner sight that recognises what grace has cost. T3.6's agency-constituting paradox (1Cor 15:10) is T7.3's most significant framework-divergence point: at the moment of constitutional incapacity, all human science frameworks assume the person has some prior agency; the biblical account holds the paradox of grace-constituted agency that is genuinely human while grace-originated. This is the methodological divergence T7.3 identifies and T3.6 establishes as the operative finding.

The covenant-making act is the volitional commitment of the inner person. (2) The Sinai covenant is structured around bilateral volitional obligation: Exo 19:5 — "if you will indeed obey my voice" — the covenant condition is framed as volitional compliance (OBS-034-039). (3) Group 765-002 (76 relevant verses, Volition) is the largest group in the registry — the Sinai/Mosaic covenant is comprehensively Volition-dimensioned, reflecting that this covenant primarily calls for human volitional obedience. (4) The all-heart covenant-making (3304-002 — OBS-034-047) — "with all his heart" — represents total volitional mobilisation. (5) Prohibited covenant (3304-003 — OBS-034-048) is volitionally framed: making covenant with false parties is a volitional misdirection that must be avoided by deliberate volitional choice.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-034-003: T3 as a whole reveals that covenant comprehensively engages the inner faculties but with a specific structural bias: the faculties it most deeply and richly engages are those oriented toward the Other…
findings.finding_value: T3 as a whole reveals that covenant comprehensively engages the inner faculties but with a specific structural bias: the faculties it most deeply and richly engages are those oriented toward the Other (relational capacity, memory, cognition as knowing-God, moral evaluation, conscientiousness) rather than those oriented inward (creativity, which is notably absent). This faculty-engagement pattern is coherent with covenant's relational-disposition primary classification — covenant is constitutively Other-oriented and therefore engages the Other-oriented faculties most richly. The deepest T3 finding is the developmental one: the old covenant calls for volition from outside (demands obedience); the new covenant transforms volition from inside (liberates and enables faithfulness through Spirit). This volitional trajectory is confirmed across T3.6 (volition) and T3.7 (agency) and is the faculty-level expression of the same transformation that T2 identified at the constitutional-movement level and T5 identifies at the mechanism level. All three tiers point to the same inner-being reality from different analytical vantage points.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-034-009: T1 defines covenant as architecturally prior to other characteristics — the structure that makes other inner-being realities possible. T3 reveals which inner faculties this architectural priority enga…
findings.finding_value: T1 defines covenant as architecturally prior to other characteristics — the structure that makes other inner-being realities possible. T3 reveals which inner faculties this architectural priority engages: relational capacity (T3.11 — covenant is form; relational capacity is content), conscientiousness (T3.10 — covenant is the primary structuring reality for conscientious inner life), memory (T3.3 — covenant is constitutively temporal and requires memory to be held active), and volition (T3.6 — covenant calls for volition from within the old structure and transforms volition from within the new). The T1 × T3 synthesis: covenant's architectural character (T1) is instantiated through a specific set of inner faculties (T3) — the faculties it most deeply engages are precisely those that operate in the time-extended, Other-oriented, and morally structured modes that covenant's form requires. The characteristic is defined by the faculties it constitutes.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-034-019: T3 reveals that the inner faculties covenant most deeply engages are Other-oriented (relational capacity, conscience, moral evaluation, memory). T4 reveals that covenant's relational interfaces are as…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals that the inner faculties covenant most deeply engages are Other-oriented (relational capacity, conscience, moral evaluation, memory). T4 reveals that covenant's relational interfaces are asymmetric (God initiates; human responds; horizontal is grounded in vertical). The T3 × T4 synthesis: the Other-oriented faculty bias (T3) and the asymmetric relational structure (T4) are coherently related — the inner faculties that covenant engages are precisely those required for the kind of asymmetric responsive relationship that covenant constitutes. The relational capacity (T3.11) is the constitutional equipment for genuine connection; the covenant's relational interfaces (T4) are the actual connections that this capacity enables. The inner posture required for human-to-God covenant movement (T4.2 — Q&A-106: reverent fear, love, all-heart, hearing orientation) corresponds directly to the inner faculties that covenant engages: fear engages moral evaluation (T3.8), love engages affect and relational capacity (T3.4, T3.11), all-heart engages volition (T3.6), and hearing engages perception (T3.1). T3 and T4 are two analytical views of the same responsive inner-being structure.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-099-003: T3 reveals that kindness engages a remarkably wide range of inner faculties — nine of eleven are evidenced with at least partial engagement. The two genuine absences (imagination and creativity) are s…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals that kindness engages a remarkably wide range of inner faculties — nine of eleven are evidenced with at least partial engagement. The two genuine absences (imagination and creativity) are structurally coherent: kindness is relational and loyally directed, not generative. The most significant faculty engagements are: (a) volition — kindness is chosen, not merely felt; the "put on" and "love kindness" language makes this constitutive; (b) agency — chrēsteuomai names love actively exercising kindness — kindness is enacted, not passive; (c) relational capacity — kindness constitutes relationships in their quality, not merely accompanies them; (d) conscientiousness — the chasid represents the full integration of moral awareness, will, and action in consistent reliable pattern; (e) taste as the primary perceptive mode — "tasted that the Lord is good" establishes that kindness is encountered experientially before it is understood conceptually. The pattern across all engaged faculties: kindness integrates the whole inner person — it does not operate as a single-faculty characteristic but as a whole-person orientation. T3's most significant intra-tier finding: kindness is a multi-faculty characteristic whose breadth of engagement reflects its status as a constitutive relational orientation rather than a single affective or volitional act.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-099-009: T1's finding that kindness is primarily a disposition (not merely an act) is confirmed and deepened by T3's faculty analysis. The disposition identified in T1 requires the full engagement of multiple …
findings.finding_value: T1's finding that kindness is primarily a disposition (not merely an act) is confirmed and deepened by T3's faculty analysis. The disposition identified in T1 requires the full engagement of multiple faculties — volition (it is chosen), agency (it is enacted), conscientiousness (moral awareness + will + action integrated), and relational capacity (it constitutes relationship quality) — which together explain why it is dispositional rather than episodic: a characteristic that engages this many faculties simultaneously is, by its nature, a settled whole-person orientation rather than a single-faculty response. T1's three-mode finding (disposition / deliberate act / Spirit formation) is reflected in T3's faculty pattern: the dispositional mode engages conscientiousness and relational capacity; the deliberate act mode engages volition and agency; the Spirit-formation mode produces the integrated faculty engagement over time. The counterfeit (chrēstologia — T1.4.3 / Q&A-024) maps onto T3's faculty analysis as the pathology of the speech-mode: it engages the communicative faculty while bypassing genuine moral evaluation and conscientiousness — presence of outward form without inner faculty integration.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-099-014: T2's finding that kindness is located in the heart and moves outward through a constitutional trajectory (Spirit → heart → disposition → acts) connects structurally with T3's finding that kindness eng…
findings.finding_value: T2's finding that kindness is located in the heart and moves outward through a constitutional trajectory (Spirit → heart → disposition → acts) connects structurally with T3's finding that kindness engages the heart's integrating faculties — volition, agency, conscientiousness, moral evaluation, relational capacity, and conscience. The heart in T2 is not merely a location label but the integrating site where all these faculties converge (T2.3.2 — Q&A-045). The constitutional movement pattern in T2 (downward-outward from Spirit to acts) is powered by the multi-faculty engagement that T3 documents: the Spirit-formation produces the heart-level disposition, but the heart exercises volition (choosing to be kind), agency (enacting kindness), and conscientiousness (sustaining kindness reliably over time) to move the disposition into action. The T3 finding that kindness engages taste as the primary perceptive faculty (1Pet 2:3 — "tasted that the Lord is good") is the perceptive entry point for the T2 constitutional movement: the person first tastes divine kindness, then the Spirit forms it in the heart, then the heart's faculties exercise it outward. The two tiers together describe a complete inner-to-outer movement with both location (T2) and mechanism (T3) identified.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-099-020: T3's faculty findings and T5's formation findings reveal a bidirectional relationship: the faculties that kindness engages are both the tools through which formation occurs and the products of formati…
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty findings and T5's formation findings reveal a bidirectional relationship: the faculties that kindness engages are both the tools through which formation occurs and the products of formation. Volition (T3) is exercised in the deliberate acts of kindness (Rut 3:10, 2Sa 10:2) that form the chasid's character — formation happens partly through the repeated exercise of volitional kindness. Conscientiousness (T3) is both engaged by kindness and deepened through its practice — "let not steadfast love forsake you" (Pro 3:3) implies that conscientiousness requires maintenance, and that maintenance in turn deepens conscientiousness. The T5 finding that suffering does not impair kindness formation (Lam 3:22, Job 6:4, Gen 44:29/32) maps onto the T3 faculty engagement in suffering contexts: conscience (T3.9 — the burden of Judah's surety-pledge), moral evaluation (T3.8 — Hos 6:6's priority ranking), and relational capacity (T3.11 — Moses's intercessory solidarity) are all engaged precisely in the suffering mode of kindness. The two tiers together: the inner faculties are both the instruments and the beneficiaries of kindness formation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-099-021: T3's finding that kindness engages volition, agency, and conscientiousness as an integrated whole maps onto T6's causal network in a specific way: it is precisely these three faculties operating toget…
findings.finding_value: T3's finding that kindness engages volition, agency, and conscientiousness as an integrated whole maps onto T6's causal network in a specific way: it is precisely these three faculties operating together that make the T6 causal chain function. The T6 finding that received human kindness causes its reproduction (2Sa 10:2 — "as his father dealt loyally with me, so I will deal loyally") requires all three: the cognition (knowing what was done), the moral evaluation (recognising the obligation), and the agency (acting on it). The T6 co-occurrence finding that kindness clusters with faithfulness, patience, and humility maps onto T3's multi-faculty profile: faithfulness requires conscientiousness; patience requires impulse-control at the volitional level; humility requires conscience and moral evaluation. The T3 finding that imagination and creativity are absent connects with T6's finding that kindness is a central node in a relational-moral web — it is constitutively oriented toward the actual other, not toward the imagined or created.

findings.session_b_note: Yes — prominently. The volitional engagement of peace is one of its most theologically significant features. Evidence: (1) The refusal-of-peace pattern (Q&A-026): Isa 30:15 ("but you were unwilling") — the will actively refuses the peace God offers; Isa 28:12 ("they would not hear"), Jer 6:16 ("we will not walk in it") — peace is declined by volitional act; (2) The pursuit-of-peace pattern: Psa 34:14 ("seek peace and pursue it") — peace requires active volitional seeking; G1514 eirēneuō ("live peaceably with all") — the volitional act of choosing peace; (3) Psa 120:7 ("I am for peace") — the identity-level volitional commitment to peace as a fundamental choice of orientation; (4) H2790B group 408-001 — "holding silence in response to emotional provocation" — the volitional restraint of impulse in service of peace. Peace is not only received but chosen and refused.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-117-002: T1 names peace as integrative wholeness; T3 specifies how each inner faculty is engaged. The convergence: peace is integrative precisely because it engages all faculties — perception (enabling divine …
findings.finding_value: T1 names peace as integrative wholeness; T3 specifies how each inner faculty is engaged. The convergence: peace is integrative precisely because it engages all faculties — perception (enabling divine hearing), cognition (right orientation), memory (recovering forgotten happiness), affect (holding feeling rightly), volition (the most constitutive engagement — peace is chosen and refused), agency (liberated by authentic peace), moral evaluation (right judgment), conscience (gateway faculty), conscientiousness (integrated response enabled), and relational capacity (co-constitutive with interiority). The faculty engagement pattern confirms: peace is integrative because it involves every inner capacity simultaneously. The faculty that can most destroy peace (suppressed conscience) and most enable it (exercised conscience) is not the most obviously prominent but the most structurally foundational.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-117-012: T3 maps inner faculty engagement; T4 maps relational directions. The synthesis: the relational capacity (T3.11) and the relational interfaces (T4) describe the same reality from different angles — the…
findings.finding_value: T3 maps inner faculty engagement; T4 maps relational directions. The synthesis: the relational capacity (T3.11) and the relational interfaces (T4) describe the same reality from different angles — the inner equipment (T3.11) and its external directions (T4). The conscience (T3.9 — gateway faculty for peace) connects directly to T4.2 (human to God): the human's movement toward God in confession (T4.2) is precisely the conscience-exercise that opens the peace-channel (T3.9). The volitional faculty (T3.6) connects to T4.3 (giving): genuine extension of peace requires authentic inner orientation (T4.3.2) — which is exactly the T3.6 finding that the giving of peace is a volitional act flowing from identity (Psa 120:7). Inner faculty and relational direction are structurally interconnected throughout.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-117-013: T3's faculty findings and T5's developmental findings illuminate each other. Memory (T3.3) connects to T5's sequence finding: the Lam 3 pathway (peaceless → remember → hope → wait) uses memory as the …
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty findings and T5's developmental findings illuminate each other. Memory (T3.3) connects to T5's sequence finding: the Lam 3 pathway (peaceless → remember → hope → wait) uses memory as the specific faculty through which the peaceless person recovers peace. Volition (T3.6) connects to T5's mechanism: the deliberate re-direction of the mind (Isa 26:3) is both a volitional act (T3.6) and the cognitive-orientation mechanism (T5.3) by which peace is received. Conscience (T3.9) connects to T5's transformation: the confession that exercises conscience (T3.9) is simultaneously the mechanism (T5.3) by which the suppressed-conscience peacelessness is resolved. Each faculty engagement is also a developmental mechanism.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-117-014: T3's volitional finding (peace is chosen and refused, T3.6) connects to T6's causal sequences (trust → peace, T6.2) — trust is the volitional act that enables the causal chain; the refusal of peace (I…
findings.finding_value: T3's volitional finding (peace is chosen and refused, T3.6) connects to T6's causal sequences (trust → peace, T6.2) — trust is the volitional act that enables the causal chain; the refusal of peace (Isa 30:15) is the volitional act that interrupts it. T3's conscience-gateway finding (T3.9) connects to T6's peace-is-produced-by findings (T6.3.2 — confession produces peace) — conscience exercise is the specific faculty engagement that makes the Psa 32 causal sequence possible. T3's moral evaluation finding (T3.8 — authentic peace enables right judgment) connects to T6's shared anchor Isa 59:8 (the way of peace they do not know) — the morally disordered person cannot find the peace-way because moral disorder corrupts the evaluative faculty.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-117-015: T3's faculty findings are validated and illuminated by T7's methodological analysis. T3's attachment-theory insight (Psa 131:2 — weaned child posture as attachment security) is the human science frame…
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty findings are validated and illuminated by T7's methodological analysis. T3's attachment-theory insight (Psa 131:2 — weaned child posture as attachment security) is the human science framework most appropriate to the relational capacity faculty (T3.11) and the soul's quiet (T2.2). T3's conscience-gateway finding (Psa 32:3-5) is the verse that T7.2.3 classifies as exhibiting the conditional-causal argument structure: the logical structure (suppressed conscience → deterioration → confession → peace) is both a faculty engagement pattern (T3.9) and a coherent causal argument (T7.2.3). The faculty map and the lexical-literary analysis describe the same biblical reality through different analytical lenses.

findings.session_b_note: Yes — volition is central to the characteristic in multiple modes. (1) Divine giving as volitional act: the giving of land and covenant is an act of divine will — God chose to give, to whom, and what. The covenantal giving is a decision, not a mechanical output. Most explicitly in Hos 11:8 (OBS-060-038): "How can I give you up?" — the divine volition is in tension with itself, resolved by compassion. The heart-recoiling is a volitional-affective movement. (2) Human self-giving (872-005): Job 1:21 (OBS-060-044) — the decision to bless God under devastating loss is a volitional act of the highest order. Isa 50:6 (OBS-060-045) — "I gave my back" — active volitional self-offering. (3) The imperative in Jer 13:16 ("give glory to the Lord your God") directly addresses human volition — the giving of glory is commanded, presupposing that it can be chosen or refused.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-060-003: T3 as a whole reveals that this characteristic engages virtually every inner faculty in the programme's 11-faculty model — the only consistent gap is creativity (T3.5, S across three prompts). The pat…
findings.finding_value: T3 as a whole reveals that this characteristic engages virtually every inner faculty in the programme's 11-faculty model — the only consistent gap is creativity (T3.5, S across three prompts). The pattern of engagement is not uniform: perception is engaged as precondition (God hears before giving); cognition is constituted (wisdom is given, not generated); memory is deepened (the narrative-temporal dimension of covenantal giving); affect is the source of giving (compassion, anger) and the target of transformation (mourning→gladness); volition is called forth and elevated (genuine giving cannot be coerced); agency is the bridge between disposition and act; moral evaluation both produces and is produced by the characteristic; conscience is engaged indirectly through Spirit-forming and prophetic warning; conscientiousness at the human apex is the full integration of all three (moral awareness, will, act). Relational capacity is intrinsic — every mode is two-party. What T3 reveals as a whole: faithfulness-as-giving is not a faculty-specific characteristic but a whole-person characteristic — it recruits and integrates all active faculties into a unified inner-being act. The creativity silence is the only dimension where the data cannot confirm engagement.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-002: The disposition-in-action definition (T1) requires the full inner faculty set to be operational (T3). The triadic architecture (source → act → object) maps directly onto faculty engagement: the source…
findings.finding_value: The disposition-in-action definition (T1) requires the full inner faculty set to be operational (T3). The triadic architecture (source → act → object) maps directly onto faculty engagement: the source requires affect (compassion/anger motivating), volition (choosing to give), and moral evaluation (assessing rightness); the act requires agency (initiating the transfer); the object requires relational capacity (attending to the other's condition). No individual faculty is the characteristic — but the characteristic integrates all of them in a coordinated whole. What this pair reveals: the definition of faithfulness-as-giving is not an abstract proposition but a faculty-integration event. The characteristic exists only when the full inner-being architecture — affective, volitional, agentive, relational — is engaged together. This is why the apex instance (Job 1:21, Isa 50:6) represents the highest form: all faculties operating in unified inner-being act.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-012: The faculty engagement pattern (T3 — perception, affect, volition, relational capacity all engaged) and the relational interface structure (T4 — God-to-human, human-to-God) reveal a faculty-interface …
findings.finding_value: The faculty engagement pattern (T3 — perception, affect, volition, relational capacity all engaged) and the relational interface structure (T4 — God-to-human, human-to-God) reveal a faculty-interface correspondence. In the God-to-human direction: divine hearing (T3.1 — perception) precedes compassionate giving (T4.1 — responsive basis); divine affect (T3.4 — rahamim, leb) determines the direction of giving (T4.1 — basis of extension); divine relational capacity (T3.11) is the prior orientation that makes the giving possible. In the human-to-God direction: human perception (Q2 — recognising divine sovereignty), human affect (blessing under loss), human volition (choosing to give glory), and human relational capacity (genuine correspondence) are all required for the giving to be genuine (T4.2 — inner posture). What this pair reveals: the relational interfaces are not external channels through which giving flows; they are relational events in which the inner faculties of both parties are engaged simultaneously and correspondingly. The correspondence is not mechanical but genuinely personal.

Contempt organises the will away from the despised object. Gen 25:34: Esau's despising of the birthright produces a volitional act — he eats, drinks, rises, goes his way. The will acts in accordance with the verdict that the birthright has no binding claim. Cruelty organises the will toward unrestrained destructive action. The volitional impact of reproach is primarily in the paralysis or constraint it produces. Job 31:34: "because I stood in great fear of the multitude, and the contempt of families terrified me, so that I kept silence, and did not go out of doors" — the reproach-fear produced volitional paralysis. The counter-volitional response: 1Th 2:2: Paul had "boldness in our God to declare the gospel" despite shameful treatment — the volitional choice to continue speaking despite reproach is grounded in God.

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** Yes — the human person can choose to submit to God's righteousness or resist it. "Seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God's righteousness" (Rom 10:3, VSG M26-A1-006). The volitional choice of submission or resistance to the divine standard is the central volitional engagement of A1 with the human person.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Yes — hunger and thirst (Mat 5:6, VSG M26-A2-006) names an active volitional orientation: the person chooses to pursue righteousness, to hunger for it, not to settle for its absence. The Ezekiel material (A2-002) reveals that the forfeiture of righteousness involves a volitional turning: "when a righteous person turns away from his righteousness" (Eze 18:24) — the turning is a volitional act. Righteousness in A2 is sustained by volitional commitment; it can be forfeited by volitional abandonment.

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** Yes — walking in uprightness is a volitional choice: "who forsake the paths of uprightness to walk in the ways of darkness" (Pro 2:13, VSG 1211-002). The person chooses to walk in or to forsake the path of uprightness. The disposition is inner, but its maintenance involves ongoing volitional commitment.

**[C — Justification]** Yes — receiving justification by faith is a volitional act: "justified by faith" presupposes the volitional act of believing and trusting. The alternative — "severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law" (Gal 5:4, VSG 3194-001) — names the volitional choice that short-circuits justification. Reception requires the will's cooperation in faith.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** Yes — the relinquishment of personal vengeance (Rom 12:19, VSG 6841-002) is an explicitly volitional act: "never avenge yourselves." The person must choose not to execute vengeance personally. The persistent widow's appeal (Luk 18:3, VSG 944-001) is volitional persistence — she will not give up.

**[E — Condemnation]** Yes — "judge not, and you will not be judged; condemn not, and you will not be condemned" (Luk 6:37, VSG 3201-001). The act of condemning is volitional; the choice not to condemn is equally volitional. The hypocritical judge (Rom 2:1) chose to pass judgment — the choice is the problem.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** Yes — "count yourselves dead to sin" (Rom 6:11). The counting is a volitional act: the person is commanded to reckon, implying that they have the capacity to choose to do so or not. The consequent "therefore do not let sin reign" (Rom 6:12) is also volitional. The reckoning faculty requires the will to engage it.

**[G — Structural Opposites]** Yes — "when a righteous person turns away from his righteousness and does injustice" (Eze 18:24, VSG M26-A2-002, G-adjacent). Wickedness involves volitional turning: the hard and impenitent heart (Rom 2:5) is hard because the person has not chosen to repent. Wickedness is not merely weakness — it is volitional resistance.

**[CLUSTER — T3.6]** E. Volition is engaged throughout the entire cluster — every sub-group involves volitional choices. The volitional dimensions span: choosing to submit to or resist God's righteousness (A1), choosing to pursue or forfeit righteousness (A2), choosing to walk in uprightness or devious paths (B), choosing to receive justification by faith or resist it (C), choosing to entrust vengeance to God or execute it personally (D), choosing to condemn or not to condemn (E), choosing to reckon (F), and choosing to repent or harden (G). Volition is one of the most pervasively engaged faculties in this cluster.

findings.finding_value: M01-A engages the volitional faculty pervasively. Reverential fear governs the will's choices across all ethical and covenant contexts: Lev 19:14 (fear preventing the will from exploiting the vulnerable — the will restrained by the inner reverential disposition); Deu 6:24 (fear as the inner posture "that produces obedience" — directly governing the will); Pro 16:6 ("fear of the Lord is an operative inner force that **turns the person away from evil**, functioning as the moral agent that drives ethical avoidance"). The will is fear-of-God's primary operating theatre.

M01-B engages the volitional faculty through will-governance: Gen 32:7 (fear "immediately drives strategic action" — the will is channelled by fear); 1Sa 17:24 (all men of Israel flee "without deliberation" — fear overrides the deliberative will); Joh 19:38 (Joseph's discipleship was hidden because "fear of the Jews **governed** his public behavior"). Fear in M01-B systematically governs or overrides the will.

M01-C engages the volitional faculty by paralyzing or redirecting it: Gen 35:5 (terror "paralyzing the will to pursue Jacob's sons"); Est 9:3 (dread of Mordecai "redirected the will of those in authority" — the will of officials redirected by fear of Jewish power); Deu 11:25 (dread of Israel "placed in enemies' hearts so no one can withstand them" — the will to resist neutralized by divinely-imposed dread).

M01-D engages the volitional faculty by dissolving it: Isa 21:3 (dismay so complete that the prophet cannot see — the will to perceive has collapsed); Eze 7:27 ("dismay so overwhelms the people that **their hands are paralyzed**" — the will to act physically disabled); Gen 45:3 (brothers "cannot answer" — the will to speak is shut down).

M01-G is definitionally volitional: timidity is a failure of the will to act faithfully under pressure. Mat 25:25 (the will choosing passive self-preservation over faithful risk); Joh 14:27 (the heart commanded not to "yield to that fearful recoiling" — the will choosing to resist or surrender to timidity); Rev 21:8 (the will choosing apostasy under sustained threat).

The volitional faculty is the most consistently engaged inner faculty across all M01 sub-groups. Fear governs, channels, overrides, paralyses, or dissolves the will across every sub-group. The cluster's unifying feature is volitional impact: all seven sub-groups describe how fear determines what the person does or fails to do. The volitional faculty is M01's primary operating theatre.

Hos 10:9 — "there they have *continued*" — the continuation is volitional persistence: the will sustains its sinning orientation without requiring a new decision at each moment. Exo 9:34 — "sinned yet again and *hardened* his heart" — the hardening is a volitional self-formation: the will contributes to its own increasing rigidity.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The volitional faculty is the primary faculty engaged at both ends of the contagious sin structure. In the leader: "walked in the way of Jeroboam" (1Ki 16:26) — the will's personal commitment to the sinning course; "made Israel to sin" (Hiphil causative) — the will's causative exercise of authority toward transmitting the sinning direction. In the community: 2Ki 17:21 — "drove Israel from following the Lord" — the community's will is redirected from God-following to the sinning direction. The volitional engagement is real at both ends: the leader's will causes the transmission; the community's will is reshaped by it.

**[CHAR-8]** E — Yes — the volitional faculty is the primary faculty engaged. Pa.sha is a deliberate wilful act: the decision to break submission and act on that decision is constitutively volitional. 2Ki 1:1 / 3:5 — "Moab rebelled against Israel" — the rebellion is an act of the Moabite community's political will. 2Ki 8:20 / 2Ch 21:8 — "Edom revolted... and set up a king of their own" — both the breaking from and the establishing of new governance are volitional acts. 2Ch 21:10's causal chain shows volition operating at both the ruler level (Jehoram's volitional forsaking of the Lord) and the political level (Edom's and Libnah's volitional revolt).

**[CHAR-9]** E — Yes. The volitional faculty is engaged at the point of externalisation. Jude 9 — Michael "did not *presume* to pronounce a blasphemous judgment" — the restraint is a volitional act; the will withholds the word. Rev 13:5 — the beast's blasphemous words are a sustained willed production ("it was allowed to exercise authority for forty-two months"). 1Ti 6:4 — the "craving for controversy" is a volitional appetite for the conditions that produce sinful speech. The will either restrains (Jude 9) or enables and sustains (Rev 13:5) sinful speech.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. Volition is the primary faculty engaged by wickedness-as-settled-person-identity (confirming T1.8.1). The Ezekiel corpus (VCG-07, 22V) is the definitive evidence: wickedness is consistently addressed as a "way" the wicked person is "on" and can "turn from" (Eze 3:18; 18:21; 33:11-19). The volitional faculty is engaged by: (1) the initial directional choice ("enter the path of the wicked" — Pro 4:14 — a volitional entry); (2) the sustained volitional refusal to turn (Eze 3:19; 33:9 — "he does not turn from his way"); (3) the active inner renunciation of God (Psa 10:13 — "renounce God"; Psa 9:17 — "forget God"); (4) the willed entry into alliance with the wicked (Psa 1:1 — walking, standing, sitting — three progressively deeper volitional stages of alignment). The characteristic is constituted and sustained by volitional acts.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, though the volitional dimension is secondary to the constitutional-structural primary classification (T1.8.1). The will is engaged in several registers: (1) active preference — Joh 3:19 (vc=14448 — VCG-04): people "loved the darkness" — the will chose moral concealment; (2) active suppression — Rom 1:18 (vc=14336 — VCG-05): "suppress the truth" — the will is actively engaged in preventing truth's operation; (3) obedience to unrighteousness — Rom 2:8 (vc=14338 — VCG-05): "do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness" — the will's allegiance is given to the constitutional evil rather than truth; (4) knowing non-compliance — Luk 19:22 (vc=14447 — VCG-04): "you knew…and still refused" — the will operates despite knowledge to withhold faithful action.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. Volition is directly engaged across multiple VCGs. Deu 25:16 (vc=65936 — VCG-01): "all who act dishonestly" — the abominable quality arises from chosen habitual behaviour. Eze 14:6 (vc=65984 — VCG-04): "repent and turn away from your idols, and turn away your faces from all your abominations" — the call to repentance addresses the will directly: the abominations are things the will is currently oriented toward, and repentance requires volitional redirection. Pro 13:19 (vc=1687 — VCG-05): "to turn away from evil is an abomination to fools" — the will's resistance to departure from evil is the distinctive volitional engagement; the fool's will is so bonded to evil that the idea of turning is experienced as repugnant. Deu 27:15 (vc=65937 — VCG-04): the person "makes" and "sets it up in secret" — volitional acts producing abomination while knowing it is wrong.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes. Volition is the primary faculty engaged (confirming T1.8.1). The Deuteronomic VCG-02 (14V) addresses the will directly throughout: "you shall not covet" (Deu 7:25 — VCG-02), "you shall not learn to follow" (Deu 18:9 — VCG-02), "you shall not worship" (Deu 12:31 — VCG-02). The Ezekiel corpus (VCG-05) shows the will in its hardened state: Eze 20:8 (vc=65911 — VCG-05): "they rebelled against me and were not willing to listen to me. None of them cast away the detestable things" — volitional refusal is the precise characterisation. Isa 66:3 (vc=1633 — VCG-04): "they have chosen their own ways" — volitional choice as the constitutive act of the characteristic.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes. Volition is the primary faculty engaged, as confirmed by the characteristic's primary classification. Job 36:21 (vc=38216 — VCG-04): "do not turn to iniquity, for this you have chosen rather than affliction" — volitional choice is the stated mechanism of the characteristic's entry and persistence. Psa 36:4 (vc=38235 — VCG-02): "he sets himself in a way that is not good; he does not reject evil" — the refusal to reject evil is a volitional act of sustained commitment. Mic 2:1 (vc=38217 — VCG-02): "when the morning dawns, they perform it, because it is in the power of their hand" — the "power of their hand" shows the will's execution capacity aligned with the scheming. 1Sa 15:23 (vc=38185 — VCG-02): "presumption" called iniquity — self-assertive will elevating its own judgment above the divine word.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes. Volition is the primary faculty — the characteristic is constituted by the will's expression of wickedness through speech. Rev 16:9 (vc=14352 — VCG-01): "they did not repent and give him glory" — the refusal to repent is the defining volitional act; the cursing of God's name is the positive volitional expression. Jude 8 (vc=14354 — VCG-01): "reject authority and blaspheme the glorious ones" — authority-rejection is explicitly volitional. Rev 13:6 (vc=14356 — VCG-01): "opened its mouth to utter blasphemies" — the deliberate opening of the mouth is a volitional act. Joh 18:30 (vc=14378 — VCG-03): the accusers deliberately formulate and deliver the false charge — a volitional speech act. The characteristic is volitionally active throughout: it requires deliberate choice at multiple levels (refusing repentance, choosing the speech act, choosing the content of the false accusation).

**[CLUSTER]** E — Volition is the cluster's most universal and deeply evidenced inner faculty — all six characteristics evidence substantial volitional engagement. This confirms the cluster's primary dimension (T1.8.1) as predominantly volitional. Char 1: the settled volitional orientation that constitutes the wicked person's "way" (Eze 3:18 — the wicked person refusing to turn from their way). Char 4: the will's deliberate devotional choice and sustained commitment to idols (Eze 20:8 — "not willing to listen; none of them cast away"). Char 5: explicitly named as chosen (Job 36:21 — "this you have chosen rather than affliction"). Char 6: the will refusing repentance under judgment (Rev 16:9/11 — "they did not repent"). Chars 2 and 3 show volition through the will's refusal of departure: Char 2 (the constitutional evil from which the will can turn but doesn't without divine help); Char 3 (Eze 14:6 — "repent and turn away from your abominations" addressed to the will).

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, substantially. The volitional faculty is engaged at multiple points: (1) volitional avoidance: Lev 11:43-44 (M10c-A-VCG-04) — "you shall not defile yourselves with any swarming thing that crawls on the ground." The person is commanded to refuse defiling contact; this requires the will's active choice not to touch or eat the defiling agent. (2) Volitional pursuit of remedy: Lev 15:11 (M10c-A-VCG-06) — "if the one with the discharge touches someone without first rinsing his hands in water"; the washing of hands is a volitional act that prevents transmission. Num 19:19-20 (M10c-A-VCG-07) — the prescribed cleansing requires the person to present themselves for sprinkling. (3) Volitional refusal of remedy: Num 19:20 (M10c-A-VCG-07) — "if the man who is unclean does not cleanse himself" — the will's refusal of the appointed remedy is the decisive moral fault.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, centrally. Rom 6:19 (VCG-02): "slaves to impurity" — the will is bound under the condition; the slavery metaphor names the will as the faculty constrained by the defilement. Eph 4:19 (VCG-02): "given themselves up to sensuality" — a volitional act of self-surrender that entrenches the condition. 2Cor 12:21 (VCG-02): those who "have not repented" — the will's refusal of repentance as the maintenance mechanism of the defilement-state. Rev 14:4 (VCG-05): "they follow the Lamb wherever he goes" — the will's positive orientation in the non-defiled state, following as an active volitional posture. The volitional faculty is the primary theatre in which the characteristic's progress or resolution is determined.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, centrally. The volitional faculty is the primary generating force of the characteristic. Eze 22:3 (VCG-02): the city "makes idols to defile herself" — purposeful, self-directed volitional act of desecration. Eze 20:7/18/30 (VCG-02): the repeated commands "do not defile yourselves with the idols of Egypt / your fathers / your fathers' manner?" all presuppose volitional capacity — the command is possible because the will can choose. Jer 7:30 (VCG-03): "they have set their detestable things in the house that is called by my name, to defile it" — the phrase "to defile it" names the will's purpose; the desecration is intentional. Lev 18:20 (VCG-01): "you shall not lie sexually with your neighbor's wife and so make yourself unclean with her" — the prohibition addresses the will directly.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes, centrally — through domination. Luk 8:29 (VCG-01): "he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the desert" — the person's will is overridden; the body acts on the demon's impulse. The will is not eliminated but subjugated: the person exists as a will but cannot express it in their own direction. The contrast between the demon's will (driving the man) and the human person's will (which human restraint attempted to support but failed) reveals the will as the primary contested faculty.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All four characteristics engage the volitional faculty, with dramatically different modes. Characteristic 1: will engaged at the perimeter (avoidance discipline — Lev 11:43-44; remedy-seeking — Lev 15:11; refusal of remedy — Num 19:20); the will does not generate the condition but manages the person's relationship to it. Characteristic 2: will engaged as the generating force (the condition produced through volitional desire-following and habituation — Eph 4:19) and then bound by the condition it helped produce (Rom 6:19 — "slaves to impurity"). Characteristic 3: will engaged as the corporate generating force of deliberate, purposeful defection (Eze 22:3 — "a city that makes idols to defile herself"; Jer 7:30 — "set their detestable things in the house... to defile it"). Characteristic 4: will overridden entirely by the external spirit (Luk 8:29 — "driven by the demon"). The cluster's volitional gradient: will engaged-at-perimeter (Char 1) → will generating-then-bound (Char 2) → will deliberately-defecting-corporately (Char 3) → will completely-overridden-externally (Char 4).

findings.session_b_note:
**Capacity:** Forgiveness received **enables** the volitional capacity for horizontal forgiveness — F-003 establishes this: vertical reception structurally enables horizontal extension. The person who has received forgiveness has a volitional capacity they did not have before (or not in the same measure). Conversely, the withholding of forgiveness **constrains** the will — the unforgiving person's inner life is "poisoned" (OBS-064-001), suggesting the retained grievance limits the will's freedom.

**Interaction with other characteristics:** The volitional act of forgiving interacts with:
- Compassion (splagchnizomai — the affective impulse that motivates the volitional act, Mat 18:27)
- Repentance (in horizontal forgiveness — Luk 17:3-4, the offender's repentance as the stated condition)
- Love (Luk 7:47 — the love produced by received forgiveness then motivates further volitional generosity)

**Constraints:** The outer limit (Mar 3:29) names the one constraint that permanently forecloses the volitional capacity to receive forgiveness — the Spirit's work permanently rejected. Within that limit, no other constraint on the volitional capacity to forgive or receive forgiveness is absolute.

findings.session_b_note:
**Compassion engages and tests volitional capacity:** The judicial-prohibition pattern shows that suppressing compassion requires a willed act — the capacity to choose is actively exercised. This tests volitional capacity: the person must choose to override a strong natural impulse. The frequency with which this prohibition is stated (seven times in Ezekiel alone — Pass 3 analysis) suggests that the volitional suppression of compassion is genuinely difficult — it must be repeatedly commanded because the will's natural inclination runs the other way.

**Compassion interacts with justice and righteousness at the volitional level:** The constraints under which volitional compassion operates are named in the data. Justice (Reg 98) and righteousness (Reg 139) are the characteristics that interact with compassion at the volitional level — they are what constrain or redirect the will when compassion would otherwise operate unchecked (SD-018). The volitional engagement is therefore not between compassion and absence of compassion but between compassion and other moral characteristics that lay claim on the will simultaneously.

**Compassion enables bold volitional action:** Mark 1:41 — compassion produces the crossing of the ritual-purity boundary. Luke 10:33 — the Good Samaritan stops, approaches, touches, and invests in the wounded stranger. Compassion appears to enable volitional acts that self-protective or socially-conventional inner states would not produce. The characteristic enables a quality of volitional boldness directed specifically toward the suffering other.

findings.session_b_note:
Contrition **redirects and reorients** volition. The volitional movement of contrition is from self-assertion (the will seeking its own aims, defending its own position) toward self-disclosure and openness before God (the will bringing its broken condition without defending it). The contrite person's will has been redirected from the assertive posture toward the receptive posture.

The Hithpael "allowing oneself to be crushed" is the key data point: this is not the will being bypassed or destroyed but the will actively consenting to its own reduction. The volitional faculty is not impaired by contrition but redirected — from self-protective assertion to open acknowledgment. This is a thoroughgoing reorientation of the will's directionality.

*New finding: contrition involves a specific volitional movement — the will's active consent to its own lowering. This is distinct from passive reception of crushing and distinct from volitional destruction. The will remains active but its direction changes: from self-assertion to self-surrender. This connects to the Session D synthesis question about the relationship between volition and creaturely dependence.*

findings.session_b_note:
**Enabling volition through companionship:** Righteous fellowship enables the person's will by providing moral support and alignment — the companions who fear God strengthen the person's own moral orientation. The will is supported and shaped by the fellowship community.

**Constraining volition through constitutional formation:** Jer 13:23 (group 7573-001) — the leopard's indelible spots image — suggests that sustained fellowship (particularly with wickedness, given its context) produces a constitutional fixity that *constrains* future volition. The person who has been deeply formed by wrong fellowship finds the will diminished in its capacity to choose righteously.

**Bypassing volition:** The divine nature participation mode (2Pe 1:4) and the community restoration mode (Eze 37:19) are not primarily volitional on the human side — God grants the promises, God joins the sticks. The human receives, but the originating act bypasses human volition at the highest fellowship register.

**New finding:** Fellowship exercises a paradoxical relationship with volition: it requires volition at the point of choice (whom to companion with), while at the same time shaping and constraining future volition through the constitutional formation that sustained fellowship produces (Jer 13:23). Fellowship chosen in freedom can produce a condition in which freedom narrows.

findings.session_b_note: Goodness reconstitutes volition rather than bypassing or overriding it. 2Th 1:11 makes this precise: "may God fulfil every resolve for good" — the human resolve is real and operative; God's power fulfils it (does not replace it). The structure is: Spirit-produced goodness produces a genuine resolve in the human will → God's power fulfils that resolve → the human agent acts. The will's capacity is enabled (Spirit-production enables the resolve), the will's interaction with other characteristics is shaped (goodness reconstitutes what the will chooses as its object), and the will operates under the constraint of the good as revealed (Mic 6:8 — "He has told you what is good" sets the constraint within which the will's proper operation is defined). Volition without this reconstitution produces self-direction (Isa 65:2) or wilful refusal (Jer 6:16) — the will's natural operation in the fallen condition is away from the good. (OBS-067-OBS-014, OBS-067-OBS-039, OBS-067-OBS-040, SBF-067-Q040)

findings.session_b_note: Love **enables and expands** the volitional capacity. Evidence: (a) Capacity — love of God produces the capacity for commandment-keeping (Joh 14:15, OBS-103-140) — love gives the will the motivation it needs to sustain obedience. Without love, will-alone cannot sustain the commandment-pattern; with love, the will is equipped. (b) Interaction with other characteristics — love interacts with will positively: Mat 10:37 (OBS-103-151) — the will must choose which love ranks highest; this choice-act is love's volitional exercise. (c) Constraints — enemy-love (Mat 5:44, OBS-103-143) operates against the constraint of natural antipathy; love expands the volitional range by enabling choices that natural feeling would block. Disordered love **impairs** volition by narrowing its range: love-of-money produces craving (OBS-103-132) — the will is progressively constrained toward the money-object and away from faith-objects.

findings.session_b_note: Mercy enables volition in the receiver: received mercy does not constrain future choice but expands the moral capacity to choose mercy toward others. Mat 18:33 implies that received mercy should have generated the volitional capacity to show mercy — the failure is in not exercising this enabled volition. Conversely, mercilessness (Rom 1:31 — OBS-111-034) appears alongside faithlessness — the merciless person's volitional capacity is compromised. *New finding: mercy is a volitional enabler — received mercy expands the person's capacity to make merciful choices; mercilessness marks a contracted volitional capacity for compassionate action.* OBS-111-034, OBS-111-055.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-111-003: Reading T3 as a whole reveals mercy as a faculty-activating characteristic — it does not primarily engage one or two faculties but activates the inner-being faculty system comprehensively. The pattern…
findings.finding_value: Reading T3 as a whole reveals mercy as a faculty-activating characteristic — it does not primarily engage one or two faculties but activates the inner-being faculty system comprehensively. The pattern: mercy enables perception (face-access), opens cognition in both directions (upward to divine knowledge; downward to self-knowledge), creates an asymmetric memory structure (divine forgetting / human remembering), engages affect as its native register, expands volition (received mercy increases mercy-capacity), demands agency, reframes moral evaluation (mercy as higher-order moral evaluation), presupposes and deepens conscience, enables conscientiousness, and constitutes relational capacity. The single faculty not evidenced is creativity (T3.5.2 — S status). Reading T3 together: mercy is characterised by faculty-comprehensiveness; its absence (mercilessness in Rom 1:31) appears alongside affective incapacity (*astorgos*) and other faculty-failures — confirming that mercy's presence is correlated with full faculty activation and its absence with faculty contraction.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-019: T3 shows mercy activating the full faculty system (perception, cognition, memory, affect, volition, agency, moral evaluation, conscience, conscientiousness, relational capacity) and T4 shows mercy ope…
findings.finding_value: T3 shows mercy activating the full faculty system (perception, cognition, memory, affect, volition, agency, moral evaluation, conscience, conscientiousness, relational capacity) and T4 shows mercy operating across three relational directions (God→human, human→God, human→human). Reading together: the faculty activations in T3 are the inner capacities that each T4 relational direction requires. God→human mercy (T4.1) engages mercy's receptive faculty complex — conscience, moral evaluation, affect, memory (asymmetric structure). Human→God mercy (T4.2 — mercy-seeking) engages volition, agency, affect, conscience, and perception (face-toward-God). Human→human mercy (T4.3) engages moral evaluation, agency, volition, and relational capacity. The three relational directions of T4 are served by the specific faculty subsets activated in T3.

findings.finding_value: T3's finding that mercy deepens conscience (Q&A-093) and expands volitional capacity (Q&A-084) maps to T5's finding that mercy produces ongoing character formation (Q&A-138 — mercy as first inner garment in the formation arc). Reading T3 and T5 together: the faculty deepening identified in T3 (conscience deepened, volition expanded, relational capacity constituted) is the mechanism through which T5's formative arc operates. Mercy forms character (T5) by deepening and expanding the inner faculties (T3) — the formation is not abstract but faculty-specific. The suffering-mercy connection (T5.4) also corresponds to T3's conscience presupposed (Q&A-092) — suffering activates the conscience that generates authentic mercy-seeking.

The contrite person's volitional capacity is not destroyed but re-aimed: Psa 51:10 (in context — "create in me a clean heart") is a volitional request directed toward God. The contrite will is a willing-toward-God rather than a willing-for-self. OBS-030-052, OBS-030-055.

findings.session_b_note: Forgiveness redirects volition — from claim-retention toward claim-release.
