findings.finding_value: M01-A **enables and deepens** agency. The ethical courage of the midwives (Exo 1:17), Nehemiah's wall-building despite threats (Neh 4:14; 6:9-14), and Job's sustained integrity despite suffering (Job 1:8; 2:3) all show fear of God enabling courageous, initiative-taking action against opposition.

M01-C and D **bypass and impair** agency. Terror-as-force bypasses the person's deliberative agency entirely (God's terror produces immediate paralysis, Gen 35:5). Dismay impairs agency by dissolving the physical and volitional capacity to act (Eze 7:27; Job 32:15).

M01-C and D **bypass and impair** agency. Terror-as-force bypasses the person's deliberative agency entirely (God's terror produces immediate paralysis, Gen 35:5). Dismay impairs agency by dissolving the physical and volitional capacity to act (Eze 7:27; Job 32:15).
M01-G **suppresses** agency by channelling it toward passive self-preservation rather than initiative.
Ordered fear enables agency; disordered fear suppresses or destroys it. The pattern is consistent across all sub-groups.

Righteous anger enables agency where there would otherwise be inaction. Nehemiah, hearing oppression, becomes angry — and acts (Neh 5:6–12). Samuel, angry at Saul's disobedience, intercedes all night — the anger drives sustained agential intercession. The characteristic is an agency-enabler for the person who would otherwise not act.

Possessing rage produces driven agency that bypasses self-governance: Dan 3:13 (M02-B-VCG-03) — the command "demands instant compliance." The agency of those around the enraged person is also constrained — they must comply immediately. The driven agency of possessing rage bypasses others' agency as well.

2Sa 13:21 (M02-B-VCG-02) provides a counter-evidence: David's great anger at Amnon's rape of Tamar "does not translate into action or discipline, leaving the incensed state inwardly contained and unresolved." Here anger impairs agency — the inner state fires but the will does not act. The failure of anger to issue into agency can itself be a moral failure.

Grief can impair agency: anguish seizing the person so that hands fall helpless (Jer 4:31 — BOUNDARY; Jer 50:43 — M03-D-VCG-04). Overwhelming distress disabling the will to act (1Sa 13:6 — M03-D-VCG-04). Prolonged parental grief threatening to immobilise the prophet (1Sa 16:1 — M03-B-VCG-02). Grief can enable agency: Esther's grief-driven intercession (Est 8:3 — M03-A-VCG-02); Hannah's bitter weeping driving prayer (1Sa 1:10 — M03-A-VCG-02). The enabling pattern appears when grief is directed outward toward God or toward redemptive action; the impairing pattern appears when grief is overwhelming or misdirected.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Exultation enables and motivates agency: Isa 64:5 names "him who joyfully works righteousness" — exultation in God produces active righteous conduct. Hab 3:18 shows the exulting prophet in a posture of perseverance. Exultation does not impair agency.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Joy enables and motivates agency: the consistent pattern is that the inner state of gladness produces outward action (singing, going, giving, dancing, proclaiming). There is no evidence of Joy impairing agency except in the comic instance of Act 12:14 (Rhoda's joy briefly overriding practical action of opening the gate — quickly resolved). The general pattern is joy → enabled, motivated action.

The characteristic's most distinctive feature of agency is Isa 30:22 (VCG-02): the future act of declaring the idols defiled — the same agency that was directed toward idolatry is redirected toward active rejection of those idols.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The characteristic suppresses and displaces the person's agency, substituting the spirit's agency for the person's own. The person's body acts under the spirit's direction, not their own. Human restraint attempts to compensate (Luk 8:29 — chains and shackles) but fails. Only divine authority expelling the spirit (Mar 5:8 — the command; Act 8:7 — expulsion) effectively restores agency (Luk 9:42 — "gave him back to his father").

**[CLUSTER]** E — The four agency-impact modes reveal the cluster's range of agency engagement. Characteristic 1: structures and obligates agency without impairing it (the remedial system prescribes required agency-acts). Characteristic 2: misdirects agency while preserving its capacity (the person actively pursues defilement — Eph 4:19 — fully agentic but wrongly directed). Characteristic 3: misdirects corporate agency toward defilement-generating acts (the community's full agentic capacity is engaged in deliberately defiling the sacred environment), with the prospect of agency redirected toward rejection of idols (Isa 30:22). Characteristic 4: displaces and replaces agency — the most radical form of agency-impairment in the cluster; the person is acted upon, not acting (Luk 8:29 — driven, not driving; Luk 9:42 — thrown, not throwing).

findings.session_b_note:
The motivational engagement pattern reveals something structurally significant: forgiveness is **both a motivational product and a motivational producer** within the same inner-being system.

- It is a **product** of prior motivational states: compassion (splagchnizomai) motivates the act of forgiving; love motivates the woman's acts of devotion.
- It is a **producer** of subsequent motivational states: received forgiveness generates love, reverence, hope — all of which then motivate further acts.

This circular motivational structure — compassion → forgiving act → love-orientation → further relational generosity → (compassion again) — is not assembled in the existing observations. *New finding:* Forgiveness occupies a **hub position** in the inner motivational economy: it receives motivational input (compassion) and generates motivational output (love, reverence, hope). This hub-position is structurally significant and likely a Session D synthesis point.

findings.session_b_note:
The consistent agency-generation pattern reveals that compassion is not a terminal inner state — it does not complete itself in feeling. It completes itself in action directed toward the one who is suffering. The registry description captures this precisely: "Compassion always faces outward toward the one suffering and produces action."

This has significant implications for the programme's understanding of the relationship between inner being and outward behaviour. Compassion is the clearest example in the data of a characteristic that structurally requires an outer expression to be fully itself. A compassion that feels but does not act is, in the terms of the data, incomplete. This places compassion in a structurally distinct category: it is a characteristic whose inner reality is constitutively incomplete without its outward expression. The eleēmosunē evidence confirms this from the social side: compassion that does not give has not fully arrived (Pass 1, term 20).

findings.session_b_note: The pattern confirms that fellowship operates partly through human agency (choice, proclamation, companionship-seeking) and partly through divine agency that bypasses or exceeds human agency (divine nature grant, divine joining, divine witness). At the highest register (ontological participation), human agency receives but does not originate. At the horizontal register (companionship, mutual support), human agency is fully engaged and constitutive of the fellowship. Agency in fellowship is therefore register-dependent: the higher the fellowship register, the more dominant divine agency becomes.

findings.session_b_note: The agency engagement pattern reveals that love is the programme's primary motivating ground for ethical action. The pattern across the anchor verse corpus is consistent: love generates acts that exceed what duty, fear, or self-interest could reliably produce. Joh 15:13 names the limit: 'greater love has no one than this.' The greatest act of agency (dying for another) is grounded in and produced by love — not by command or duty alone. This reveals love's relationship to the rest of the ethical life: love is not simply an inner feeling that happens to produce acts. It is the constitutive motivational source from which the full range of agentive expression flows. The ethical architecture implied: acts without love are inadequate (1Cor 13:1-3 — tongues, prophecy, self-sacrifice without love = nothing); acts from love are constitutively different because their source is different.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-003: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion re…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion responds, it does not originate or create. It is the most responsive of the faculties-engaging characteristics. Second, affect and moral action are structurally unified in compassion — not sequentially related but simultaneous. Affect is the mechanism of movement (splanchnizō is both the felt inner event and the cause of the action), not a precursor or accompaniment. This is unique among the characteristics reviewed: in most other registries, affect and volition are distinguishable stages; in compassion, the felt movement is already the morally motivated action beginning. A third distinctive finding: compassion converts moral knowledge into motivated action — it is the motivational ground of conscientiousness, not a product of it. The conscience faculty engagement reveals compassion as conscience-healing: it addresses the pitiable condition that conscience perceives as a moral claim, resolving the tension between moral knowledge and moral incapacity. The three relational modes (building/sustaining — chesed; restoring/repairing — splanchnizō; extending across difference — Good Samaritan) are a new finding not in the instruction typology.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-003: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked …
findings.finding_value: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I but the grace of God that is with me." Agency is not displaced but constituted by grace. This relationship holds in paradox that the T3.6 prompt options (enable/deepen/bypass/impair) cannot accommodate — a prompt design limitation noted for catalogue revision. Second, grace produces moral clarity (T3.8 — sharpens moral evaluation rather than bypassing it): the person who recognises grace has made a precise moral evaluation (they know they received what they did not deserve). Third, grace and conscience are mutually necessary: grace is the condition within which conscience can operate fully without destroying the person; conscience without grace produces condemnation; grace without conscience produces presumption (T3.9). Fourth, grace is the primary relational faculty developer in the registry's evidence — it reaches every relational register (vertical access, horizontal forgiving, speech-grace) and enables each one. Creativity (T3.5) is the one genuinely silent faculty — not an impairment but a non-engagement: grace receives and constitutes, it does not create.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-019: T3's agency-constituting finding (grace constitutes rather than replaces agency — 1Cor 15:10) and T4's human-to-God direction (supplication as the human posture of appeal — requiring genuine human age…
findings.finding_value: T3's agency-constituting finding (grace constitutes rather than replaces agency — 1Cor 15:10) and T4's human-to-God direction (supplication as the human posture of appeal — requiring genuine human agency in the act of plea) are structurally aligned. The constituted agency (T3.7) is precisely the agency that supplication requires: the creature must genuinely appeal, not merely receive passively. T3's finding that grace and conscience are mutually necessary (T3.9) corresponds to T4's relational-access finding: grace transforms the threshold of human-to-God approach (prosagōgē — SD035) from impassable to open, which is the relational expression of T3.9's constitutional finding that grace creates the condition within which conscience can operate fully without destruction. T3 names the inner-being event; T4 names the relational consequence of the same event.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-021: T3's faculty findings explain several patterns in T6's co-occurrence landscape. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (R140 — 40 verses) is partly explained by T3.6's agency-constituting finding: seekin…
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty findings explain several patterns in T6's co-occurrence landscape. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (R140 — 40 verses) is partly explained by T3.6's agency-constituting finding: seeking requires the constituted agency that grace provides for its own reception (SD026 — grace giving the capacity for supplication). The power cluster co-occurrences (strength R187 — 15 verses, might R198 — 10 verses) confirm T3.7's agency-constituting finding at the cross-registry level: grace producing agency is registered as co-occurring with power/strength across the corpus. T3.8's moral clarity finding explains the guilt co-occurrence (R073 — 10 verses): the moral clarity grace produces is most visible at the point of moral failure, and the co-occurrence reflects this — grace and guilt appear together because grace produces the moral clarity that accurately names the guilt it addresses.

findings.session_b_note: The pattern reveals that covenant is always an agency-involving reality — it is never passive or automatic in its human dimension. Even the new covenant, which is constituted by divine initiative and Spirit-agency, calls for human responsive agency: entry (Neh 10:29 — OBS-034-035), keeping (the moral-character mode of covenant faithfulness — OBS-034-053), and transmission (Isa 59:21 — the covenant word carried forward through the mouth across generations — OBS-034-051). Covenant does not produce passive recipients but active participants. The asymmetry is structural: divine agency first, human agency responsive — not because human agency is diminished but because covenant is a relationship, and in this relationship God is always the initiating party.

findings.session_b_note: The agency pattern reveals that authentic peace is not passive or quietist but enables robust, courageous action in the world. The peaceful person is not inactive — Mordecai seeks welfare, the peacemakers sow righteousness, Christ makes peace through the cross. The silence/stillness vocabulary names the inner orientation that enables agency, not the absence of agency. The contrast with complacent ease (H7600 413-001) is decisive: the person who is "at ease in Zion" (Amo 6:1) is precisely the person who does not act when they should — complacency impairs agency. ### T3.8 — Moral Evaluation
findings.notes: DIR-20260514-004 (Phase 9 findings load 2026-05-14); source: WA-M39-consolidated-findings-v1-20260514-part3-T3-T4.md; catalogue: v2.1-2026-05-13; obslog: wa-obslog-M39-sessionb-v1-20260514.md

findings.finding_value: Agency is consistently engaged across all four sub-groups, but its direction varies entirely. Inner closure and hardness mis-direct or disengage agency. Ordered character and voluntary release fully exercise and direct agency rightly. The wealth domain reveals the person's fundamental agency orientation — it does not merely test the will but exposes the habitual direction of the whole acting self.

findings.finding_value: The pattern confirms that fear is an agency-shaping characteristic at its core: what the person fears determines what they are willing to do and what they are too afraid to do. Ordered fear (M01-A) produces the most courageous agency in the cluster — the midwives defy Pharaoh, Nehemiah builds in the face of death threats. Disordered fear produces the most paralysed or suppressed agency (M01-D hands paralysed; M01-G burying the talent). The inverse relationship between ordered fear of God and suppression of human-threat agency is a significant structural finding: the more a person genuinely fears God, the less they fear human opposition (Deu 7:21; 1Ch 22:13; Neh 4:14).

**Contrast: B-VCG-04 vs B-VCG-02:** The characteristic's relationship to agency reveals its defining moral role: anger is designed to be the inner energy of just action. When it issues appropriately into agency (righteous anger → just act), the divine image is functioning. When it drives ungoverned agency (possessing rage → destructive act) the image is distorted. When it fires without issuing into agency (2Sa 13:21 — David's contained anger → no action), the moral failure is the disconnection of anger from its agency-function.

Grief's relationship with agency mirrors its relationship with volition. The characteristic is not inherently enabling or impairing of agency — the outcome depends on the grief's orientation. Grief directed toward God in prayer activates agency; grief that overwhelms and paralyses disables it. The evidence suggests that grief functioning within the Godward prayer pattern (M03-D-VCG-01) is the context in which grief most consistently enables rather than impairs agency.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Exultation is an agentive characteristic — it issues in action. The inner surge overflows into the shout, the song, the righteous work, the approach to God's presence. This is consistent with the kinetic root meaning of gil (spinning, leaping movement).

**[CHAR-2]** E — Joy is agentively generative: persons in the full experience of Joy characteristically act from it — they go, they give, they sing, they proclaim, they persist. This makes Joy a reliable formation resource for agency: communities whose inner life is characterized by Joy will be communities that act, serve, and persist.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Suffering-Joy is agentively generative precisely because it removes the circumstantial dependency of motivation. Where Joy (Characteristic 2) produces agency through the energy of gladness in what is good, Suffering-Joy produces agency through the freedom from requiring the presence of the good before acting. This is the characteristic's most distinctive contribution to the inner being's agency.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Gladness functions as a moral-clarity and confidence-generating characteristic that enables agency: the person and community that accurately assess God's goodness and their own moral situation are those who can act from a stable, informed inner base. Gladness does not generate the impulse to action in the same way Joy does (Joy's energy propels action); rather, Gladness provides the stable cognitive-affective foundation from which reliable action proceeds.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Delight is the most agentively-powerful characteristic in M04: it directly energises the will and produces action without requiring intermediate steps. This is why the misdirection of Delight is so dangerous (M04-P, M04-H-VCG-04) — the same agency-generating power that in the righteous person drives obedience and mission drives the unrighteous person toward destruction with equal energy. Delight does not produce tentative or half-hearted action; Gen 34:19's "did not delay" and God's "he does all that he pleases" are at the same ends of the spectrum — both show Delight as immediately and fully agentive.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Pleasure is not primarily an agentive characteristic but it motivates agency toward its object: what is experienced as pleasant draws the person toward it. The ni.cho.ach corpus's link between obedient sacrificial action and divine Pleasure shows the most direct Pleasure-agency relationship: right worship-action produces the Pleasure-quality of the aroma; the action and the Pleasure are inseparable.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Wonder is the characteristic most agentively directed toward proclamation and teaching: the primary action it generates is not service or justice (Delight's obedience modes) but declaration — going out to tell, proclaim, sing, and pass on. Wonder's agency is inherently communicative and missional.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's agency pattern reveals that positive inner-being states in Scripture are not private spiritual experiences but agentively generative realities. Every characteristic in M04 produces outward action as a natural consequence: the exultant person cries out; the joyful person sings, dances, gives, and persists; the glad person builds (Neh 2:18); the delightful person acts immediately; the wondering person proclaims; the Suffering-Joyful person continues to teach (Act 5:41). The cluster categorically refuses any inner-spirituality that does not flow outward into action.

**[CHAR-1]** E — That CHAR-1 is fundamentally an agency-impairment phenomenon in its ordinary operation, and that the characteristic's resolution is tied to the restoration of agency. The shame-lifting promises are not merely about dignity restored in the abstract — they are about the concrete capacity to stand, speak, and act in the world and before God being restored to the person from whom shame had taken it.

**[CHAR-2]** E — CHAR-2 withdraws or collapses the recipient's agency: they cannot speak (Mat 22:12), cannot re-enter public space (2Sa 10:5), must retreat (Jer 48:39). In VCG-03, God is the agent; the proud person's agency is precisely what is overridden. CHAR-2 is the enforced withdrawal of agency from the person whose pride had inflated it beyond its proper scope.

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — The dishonorer exercises agency in the act of worth-denial (VCG-01). The dishonoured's agency may be affected when dishonour restricts their relational capacity (the poor man whose case cannot receive justice, Jam 2:6). The structural mode (VCG-02) restricts the recipient's agency in terms of what they can access or what roles they can occupy.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4's functioning enables the exercise of principled moral agency — the person who recognises and renounces the shameful can act with integrity. The inverted conscience (VCG-03) produces misdirected agency — the person acts, but in the direction of what is actually shameful. VCG-02's disordered desire overwhelms agency with appetite.

---

**[CHAR-5]** E — Agency is impaired in the recipient by CHAR-5: Psa 14:6 — the plans of the poor are shamed (targeted for dismissal) — their capacity to act on their own plans and hopes is suppressed by the contempt. Paul's concern that contempt toward Timothy (1Cor 16:11) would "devalue his ministry and undermine his standing" shows agency-impairment as the downstream effect of sustained CHAR-5. Conversely, the act of throwing off the cloak (Mar 10:50) is the regaining of agency in response to a stronger worth-assignment from Jesus.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — CHAR-6 enables agency: the person with clean hands and a blameless heart can approach God's altar (Psa 26:6) — the agency of worship is enabled by CHAR-6. The incapacity for innocence (Hos 8:5) impairs agency in the specific domain of approach to God — the people cannot exercise the agency of genuine covenant approach because innocence-capacity has been lost.

---

**[CLUSTER]** E — The most consistent cluster-level finding on agency: the shame-characteristics impair agency (Chars 1, 2, 3, 5 all show shame withdrawing the capacity to act, speak, and present oneself); the counter-characteristics restore or protect agency (Char 6 enables the agency of approach to God; Char 4's functioning conscience enables principled moral agency). The cluster's agency-narrative: the shame-field takes agency from the person; the positive moral conditions (innocence, functioning conscience) return it. The christological dimension is critical: Jesus's voluntary acceptance of shame (Chars 1 and 5 in the passion narrative) demonstrates that agency can be maintained within the shame-condition — his "despising the shame" (Heb 12:2) is the highest form of volitional agency over against shame's impairing pull. The resurrection's reversal (Act 4:11 — the rejected cornerstone; 1Cor 15:43 — raised in glory) is the eschatological restoration of full agency from the shame-field's impairment.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — The pattern reveals that CHAR-1 is an energising characteristic — it generates active inner drive that moves outward as aggression, domination, oppression, and rebellion. Job 41:34 (vc=12089, M08-A4-VCG-04): Leviathan is "king over all the sons of pride" — pride as the defining quality of those with fierce, dominating self-assertion. Psa 36:11 (vc=33966, M08-A4-VCG-03): arrogance personified as foot and hand — agency metaphors for the active force of pride. This energising quality distinguishes CHAR-1 from a passive conceit or self-regarding mood: it generates initiative, force, and organised action in service of the self's elevation above others. The agency finding also illuminates why CHAR-1 and CHAR-2 (presumptuous defiance) are constitutively related: CHAR-1's volitional-agency energy is what generates CHAR-2's specific defiant acts against authority.

**[CHAR-2]** E — CHAR-2 reveals that unconstrained agency is dangerous rather than liberating: the more fully the will's agency is freed from legitimate constraint, the more directly it produces harm — murder (Exo 21:14), oppression of the poor (Psa 119:85, vc=34102), abuse of fellow servants (Mat 24:49, vc=55613), social strife (Pro 13:10, vc=34113). CHAR-2's energised agency is what makes it socially and relationally destructive.

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3's agential pattern reveals that the boasting-act itself is a deliberate social initiative — one chooses to boast, chooses the content, chooses the audience. This deliberate quality is what makes the VCG-02 discipline possible (if boasting were involuntary, it could not be examined and constrained) and what makes VCG-01 morally culpable (if it were involuntary, it could not be prohibited).

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4's agency pattern reveals that the characteristic produces actions that consistently exceed actual capacity and standing — the hallmark of an inflated self-picture operating as the basis for action. 1Cor 4:19 (vc=33939): Paul's exposure of the inflated persons will reveal the gap between their agency-claims (talk) and their actual power — this gap is what CHAR-4 generates at the agency level.

**[CHAR-5]** E — CHAR-5's agency pattern reveals that structural power generates a distinctive form of energised, unconstrained agency: the proud-might nation and the wealth-proud individual both have real structural capacity behind their agency, making CHAR-5 the most practically powerful of the M08 characteristics in terms of agency-impact. The damage CHAR-5 causes (to the poor — Eze 16:49; through unjust gain — Hab 2:9) is enabled by the actual structural power that the characteristic claims as its ground.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The agency pattern confirms M08 as an action-producing cluster. The cluster's characteristics are not merely felt inner states — they are inner orientations that reliably produce specific types of action in the social world (predation — CHAR-1; transgression — CHAR-2; social self-promotion — CHAR-3; intellectual combat — CHAR-4; exploitation and self-securing — CHAR-5). The cluster-synthesis: understanding M08 requires attending to the action-signatures of each characteristic as much as to the inner states they name.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The agency pattern reveals that submission is not a passive characteristic. The will actively yields; the person actively receives the authority's claim and actively orients toward it. Phile21 (going beyond the minimum) and 1Pe1:22 (earnest love from a pure heart) confirm that genuine submission produces rather than suppresses genuine agency. The characteristic is the inner posture that rightly orients agency rather than eliminating it.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The pattern reveals that contrition operates as a suspension and renewal of agency rather than a permanent impairment: the crushed spirit's self-asserting agency is suspended, and God's reviving restores a cleaner form of inner vitality and capacity. The characteristic is thus a transitional state for agency — passing through rather than ending in.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The agency pattern reveals that meekness and gentleness are agency-enabling rather than agency-suppressing: the meek/gentle person is not a passive non-actor but one whose agency is appropriately calibrated and immediately responsive. The characteristic enables the full and appropriate exercise of agency without the distortions of reactive severity or self-protective hesitation.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The pattern reveals that semnotēs is an *agency-enabling character quality* — it provides the inner ground from which effective, credible agentive action flows. Leadership and teaching agency without semnotēs may technically occur but lacks the character-grounded effectiveness that the characteristic enables. The characteristic is thus the inner enabling condition for the agency of leadership and instruction to be genuinely effective.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The pattern reveals that willing-heartedness is an *agency-maximising quality* — where it is present, the person gives more than required (2Ch29:31 — beyond-required offerings), serves fully (1Ch28:21 — wholly at command), and acts immediately without friction (Exo35:22 — brought). The characteristic is what enables human agency to reach its fullest expression in giving and service, and its absence (Psa51:12 — requiring restoration) is what limits that expression.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The agency pattern reveals that humility is an *active* rather than passive characteristic. The M09-B evidence (experienced lowliness — Phili4:12; 2Cor7:6) shows the passive register, but even there, what is commended is the cultivated active response of contentment (Phili4:12 — "I have learned the secret"). Humility is not the suppression of agency but its reorientation: the will acts, but it acts toward God and others rather than toward its own elevation. This distinguishes humility from quietism (the passive suppression of will and agency) and from servility (agency-absence from external pressure).

**[CLUSTER]** E — The agency pattern reveals that M09 characteristics are active rather than passive. Even Contrition (CHAR-3) — the most condition-like and state-like characteristic — involves agency in the form of remaining open to God's reviving rather than fleeing into hardening. Dignity (CHAR-5)'s ordered agency (leadership through character gravity rather than force) and Willing-heartedness (CHAR-6)'s maximised agency (beyond-required giving) confirm that the cluster's most settled and most spontaneous characteristics are both fully agentive. The cluster's anti-agency patterns — self-protective withdrawal of hesitation (against CHAR-4), compelled compliance at the minimum (against CHAR-6) — consistently evidence agency that is inhibited or constrained by self-protective concerns. M09 characteristics universally produce agency that exceeds minimums and moves without self-protective friction.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — The agency pattern confirms that wilful sinning is a *responsible act* — the corpus never excuses it as compelled or inevitable (even Saul's self-excuse in 1Sa 15:24 is narratively presented as inadequate: Samuel does not accept it as a valid defence). The moral accountability in Eze 18:4/20, the personal confession in Jos 7:20, and the deterrence corpus all presuppose that agency is real and operative. The characteristic is constituted by genuine agency — which is precisely why it is morally serious.

**[CHAR-10]** E — The agency pattern reveals that CHAR-10's mechanisms engage agency across a spectrum: enticement progressively captures agency through desire (the person becomes less free as the desire deepens — 2Pe 2:14 "insatiable for sin"); hypocrisy misdirects agency through social pressure (Gal 2:13 — led astray); apostasy exercises agency in departure (Act 21:21). The most severe form for agency is the trained-greed enticement: the person whose heart has been "trained in greed" has an agency that is now shaped by the training — their choices naturally move toward the sinful appetite because the agency-forming process has been captured.

**[CHAR-11]** E — The agency pattern reveals that the universal sin-condition does not render persons passive recipients but *active participants* in their own enslavement: "you present your members to sin as instruments" (Rom 6:13) — the person is doing the presenting. The condition's enslavement operates through the person's own agentive acts, which are the form the enslavement takes. This has a significant implication: the condition is not external imposition but internal captivity that operates through and as the person's own actions — making moral accountability real (they sin — Rom 3:23) even within the context of structural enslavement.

**[CHAR-12]** E — The agency pattern reveals that sin's enslaving power does not render the person passive but captures active agency and deploys it within the sin-domain. The practicing-sinner is agentively sinning (Joh 8:34); the enslaving power captures and redirects what remains an active agentive capacity. This is why the enslaving power is so difficult to escape from within: the person's agency is engaged, not dormant — but it operates within the master's domain rather than toward freedom. Liberation requires an external intervention (new birth — 1Jo 3:9; Christ's protection — 1Jo 5:18) that restructures the agency's constitutional direction.

**[CHAR-13]** E — The agency pattern reveals that sin as divine record is the product of genuine human agency: the record is filled by real agentive choices (drawing sin, adding sin, walking in sin, not departing). This is what makes the record a moral account rather than a fatalistic condition: each entry was made by the person's own agency. This agency-grounding of the record is also what makes genuine penitential agency possible: the turn of Eze 18:21 is meaningful precisely because the prior record was genuinely the person's own.

**[CHAR-14]** E — The agency pattern reveals that the characteristic is not a passive reception of divine action but a genuine agentive co-participation: the person must act (repent, believe, bring the offering, lay hands) for the forgiveness-transaction to be enacted. The divine side is equally agentive (God forgives, Christ's blood is poured out), but the human agency is not bypassed. The characteristic is thus a cooperative agentive event: human agency in seeking + divine agency in granting = forgiveness sought and received.

**[CHAR-15]** E — The agency pattern reveals that generational sin is not passive reception of a condition but requires active volitional-agentive participation: each generation actively rebels (Psa 78:17 — "rebelling") and "sins still more" (Psa 78:32). The generational pattern is thus sustained by genuine human agency at each stage, which is why the response also requires genuine agency — the active heart-turning (1Ki 8:47) rather than passive waiting for the inherited condition to dissolve.

**[CHAR-16]** E — The agency pattern reveals that the sinner as moral character is an *active* rather than passive identity: sinners entice others (Pro 1:10), direct hostility against Christ (Heb 12:3), speak harsh things against God (Jude 15), and lend/do good/love within their radius (Luk 6:32/33/34). The sinner-identity is not a condition of passivity or mere moral weakness but a constituted inner orientation that actively expresses itself in agentive ways — both against God (Heb 12:3; Jude 15) and within the self-interest radius (Luk 6:32/33/34).

**[CHAR-17]** E — The agency pattern reveals the characteristic's most productive inner dynamic: guilt-recognition produces a specific agentive sequence — bringing an offering → confession → restitution — that is the conscience-to-action pipeline. The guilt-state is the inner impetus that keeps the pipeline flowing; without guilt-recognition, the agentive repairs would not occur. This is the characteristic's designed function (T0.2.1): equipping the person to recognise moral failure and initiate repair.

**[CHAR-18]** E — The agency pattern reveals CHAR-18's most distinctive feature: the transformation of the person from active agent of iniquity (Isa 5:18 — drawing iniquity) to passive subject of iniquity's power (Isa 64:6/7 — taken away, melted in its hand). The accumulated iniquity reverses the agency relationship: the person who chose the crime is eventually chosen by it — ensnared (Pro 5:22), swept away (Isa 64:6), and melted (Isa 64:7). Only external divine agency can reverse this (Mic 7:19 — God treads iniquities underfoot; Zec 3:9 — removes iniquity in a single day).

**[CHAR-19]** E — The agency pattern confirms the volitional-enslavement dynamic: the person who actively transgressed (agentive commission) is progressively incapacitated in their agency (Pro 29:6 — ensnared; Psa 19:13 — dominion threatened). The active agency at commission (Amos 4:4 — "come and transgress") is replaced by the passivity of being held in transgression's grip (Pro 29:6). This is the characteristic's most significant inner-being consequence: the agent of the crossing becomes the captive of what they crossed into.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The agency pattern confirms that moral accountability in the Levitical framework is based on *agency*, not on *intentionality*. The fact that the person acted (exercised agency) is sufficient to create moral liability, regardless of the inner quality of the will at the moment of action. This is a foundational principle of Lev 4:2 and Num 15:27/28: agency creates liability; intentionality differentiates the *kind* and *scale* of the remedy required, not whether a remedy is required at all.

**[CHAR-20]** E — The agency pattern confirms CHAR-20's distinctive communal-reach: the agency of a single faithless person implicates and damages the agency of the whole community (Jos 7:1 — Achan; 1Ch 10:13 — Saul's faithlessness affecting all Israel). This communal-agency reach distinguishes CHAR-20 from characteristics whose consequences remain primarily individual. The leader's faithlessness (2Ch 28:22 — Ahaz; 2Ch 26:16 — Uzziah; 2Ch 36:14 — priests and people) consistently radiates to the community, showing that the agency of CHAR-20's faithlessness is constitutively social.

**[CHAR-21]** E — The agency pattern reveals CHAR-21's most distinctive inner-being arc: the transition from active evil-devising agent (Pro 6:14; Isa 32:7) to passive instinct-driven captive (Jude 10 — destroyed by instinct; 2Pe 2:19 — enslaved). The reversal of agency — from the person who perverts to the person destroyed by their own perversion — is CHAR-21's defining developmental trajectory. The perverter becomes the perverted-by-their-own-perversion.

**[CHAR-22]** E — The agency pattern reveals that CHAR-22 is M10's most agentively other-directed characteristic: every expression of injustice requires a victim and an agent. Job 29:17 — "I broke the fangs of the unrighteous" — the metaphor names the unjust as a predatory agent; Psa 58:2 — "your hands deal out violence on earth" — the active distribution of violence across the earth. CHAR-22's agent is not merely a person who does wrong but a person who systematically does wrong *toward* others — its defining agentive orientation is harm-toward-persons.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The agency pattern reveals that confession is an *agency-claiming event*: it requires the person to identify themselves as the agent of the sin rather than displacing responsibility. This is why genuine confession is morally demanding — it requires claiming full personal or corporate agency for what was done (1Ch 21:17; 2Sa 24:17; Dan 9:5 — "we have sinned"). The moral demand is proportional to how clearly the agency-claim is owned. Hollow confession (Deu 1:41) shows the failure: the verbal claim of agency for the sin does not produce ownership of agency for the remedy.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The agency pattern reveals that conscience suppression is *an agency-disinhibition event*: it does not restrict the person's capacity to act but removes the moral framework within which acting should occur. The person's agency becomes fully operational without its governing moral check — which is precisely why conscience suppression is dangerous. The agency continues to produce actions (including evil ones — Ecc 8:12) that accumulate liability (Jer 2:35 — judgment) while the person remains unaware of the liability being created.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The agency pattern reveals that refusal to repent is an *agency-investment process*: each agentive act performed within the sinful course (serving Baal, walking in Jeroboam's sins) represents an investment of agency in the wrong direction. The accumulation of these investments makes the sinful course progressively more entrenched — the person has more of themselves invested in it, making departure ever more demanding. This is why long-established refusal to repent (lifetime — 2Ki 15:18; generational — 2Ki 15:9) is harder to reverse than recent refusal: more of the person's agency-history is invested in the sinful course.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The agency pattern reveals that habitual defection is *agentively productive in the wrong direction*: the habitually sinning person builds, invests, and institutionalises — their agency is not diminished but its outputs are wrong. Hos 8:11 is the paradigm: full agentive investment in altars produces the self-reinforcing sinning structure. This reveals that breaking habitual defection requires redirecting a fully operative agentive capacity, not simply restoring an impaired one. The difficulty of breaking habitual defection is partly the difficulty of redirecting an established agentive investment pattern rather than initiating agency from scratch.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The agency pattern reveals that contagious sin produces *collective moral agency shaped toward sin*: the community is not merely influenced but is agentively sinning together, provoking God through their collective action (1Ki 14:22 — "provoked him to jealousy with their sins"). The communal scale of the agency (a whole nation sinning together through collective agentive action) makes contagious sin's moral consequence larger than any individual's sinning. Ecc 9:18 (CHAR-6 corpus adjacent) — "one sinner destroys much good" — is the wisdom-register observation about a related pattern: the contagious sin corpus demonstrates this through the specifics of national-scale moral consequence.

**[CHAR-8]** E — The agency pattern reveals that political revolt is fundamentally an *assertion of political agency*: the revolting community reclaims governing self-determination by breaking submission and establishing independent rule. The pa.sha act is the form through which political agency asserts itself against an established governing relationship. This explains why revolt is more than passive non-compliance — it is an active assertion of independent agency through the decisive act of breaking submission and constructing alternative governance.

**[CHAR-9]** E — The agency pattern reveals that sinful speech is a fully agentive act for which the speaker is accountable: Mat 26:65 — "He has uttered" — the utterance is attributed to the speaker as a deliberate agentive act. This is why Mat 12:31's unforgivable blasphemy against the Spirit is foregrounded as such: it is a specific, deliberate agentive speech-act that carries permanent consequence. Sinful speech is not accidental or non-agentive; it is a chosen deployment of speech-agency in the wrong direction, for which the agent bears full accountability.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The agency pattern reveals that wickedness-as-settled-person-identity is not a passive condition — it is an active posture that generates harm in the social world. The wicked person is not merely morally deficient in their inner being; they produce measurable damage in their communities (Pro 11:11 — cities overthrown), legal systems (Isa 5:23 — justice perverted), and interpersonal relationships (Psa 28:3 — speaking peace while harboring evil). The characteristic's agency-activation pattern explains its social dangerousness and why the corpus addresses it with divine judgment: an active harmful agency that shapes communities requires termination, not merely internal correction.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The agency pattern reveals that evil as constitutional inner nature is not a passive state but an active generative engine that produces ongoing social harm through fully operational agency. The constitutionally evil person is not incapacitated — they are energised by their constitutional condition toward harm. This explains the NT's urgency about the characteristic: a fully agentic person constitutionally oriented toward evil is not merely a passive problem but an active danger to communities (1Cor 5:13 — VCG-04: the community must expel the evil person precisely because their active agency is corrupting the whole). The agency pattern confirms the need for transformation at the constitutional level, not merely behavioural restraint.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The agency pattern reveals that abomination requires active sustained agency for its production. It is not a passive inner state — it is actively generated by the dishonest dealer (Deu 25:16 — VCG-01), the offering-bringer (Pro 15:8 — VCG-03), the idol-maker (Deu 27:15 — VCG-04). The characteristic therefore has a sustained-agency component: the abominable inner condition is continuously enacted through habitual practice, not merely held as a static quality. This accounts for the evidence's emphasis on turning from abominations (Eze 14:6 — VCG-04) — the agency must be actively redirected rather than merely the inner state addressed.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The agency pattern reveals that idolatrous abomination is sustained through organised, persistent, publicly visible agency: high places constructed, idols installed in temples, national practices reformed. The characteristic is not a private inner state but an energetically enacted social phenomenon. This explains why the evidence so consistently frames the response as equally active and public: reform requires removing, destroying, and purging with equal organising energy to what installed the abomination (2Ki 23:24 — VCG-03: comprehensive Josiah reform). The agency pattern confirms that CHAR-4 is a characteristically activist deviation — driven by the same inner-being capacity for agency as the reforms that must oppose it.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The agency pattern reveals that iniquity as active scheming is constitutively agentive: it requires and deploys full agency for its realisation. Job 4:8 (VCG-04): "plow iniquity and sow trouble" — the agricultural labour metaphor shows that iniquity requires sustained effort, like farming. The characteristic is therefore not a passive moral failure but an energetically sustained practice. The agency pattern also reveals why the characteristic is so harmful to others: the full agency of the person (power to make things happen, institutional authority in Isa 10:1 — VCG-02) is directed against the weak and innocent. Addressing the characteristic must therefore involve the redirection of agency, not its elimination.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The agency pattern reveals that evil expressed through speech is an agentive choice at every level: choosing to open the mouth (Rev 13:6 — VCG-01), choosing the content of the speech (cursing God's name — Rev 16:9 — VCG-01), choosing to formulate the false charge (Joh 18:30 — VCG-03). The characteristic is not an involuntary expression but an agentively produced and delivered speech act. This full-agency character makes the characteristic specifically morally culpable — it is not the overflow of emotion beyond the person's control but a deliberate, agentively executed expression of inner wickedness. Rom 3:8 (vc=14358 — VCG-02): "their condemnation is just" — the justness of condemnation presupposes the agentive character of the slanderous speech.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's agency pattern confirms the theological seriousness of M10b characteristics: each is agentively enacted, requiring the person's full capacity to act, initiate, and sustain. This agentive character grounds the moral culpability of M10b evil across all six characteristics. Char 6's explicit condemnation (Rom 3:8 — "their condemnation is just" for slanderous speech) expresses this culpability principle at the cluster's most explicit level.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The extensive prescribed agency-acts reveal that the characteristic is not passive — the person in the defilement-state is not merely a subject of a condition but an active participant in its resolution. The entire remedial system (washing, waiting, examination, water of impurity, self-declaration, removal of contaminated material) requires sustained agency. This reveals the characteristic as a condition that mobilises the person's agency toward resolution — the defilement-state is designed to be managed, not simply suffered.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The agency pattern reveals the characteristic as operating through the redirection of human capacity rather than its elimination. The person in moral-inner defilement is not incapacitated but actively moving in the wrong direction. This reveals the characteristic as a condition of misdirection rather than nullification — the inner person retains agency and uses it, but under the condition of the defilement-state the direction of agency is toward corruption rather than holiness.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The agency pattern reveals the characteristic as the domain where the community's sacral stewardship responsibility is exercised or betrayed. The land, sanctuary, and divine name are entrusted to the community as objects of their agency; the corporate/covenantal defilement-state is the result of agency directed against those objects rather than in their service. The characteristic thus reveals the stakes of human agency in the covenantal domain: agency directed toward sacred objects determines their condition.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The agency pattern reveals the characteristic as uniquely agency-displacing: the person's agency is not corrupted (Characteristic 2) or misdirected (Characteristic 3) but replaced by the spirit's agency. The person becomes the site through which an alien agency operates — both present as a person and absent as an agent. This is the most radical form of agency impairment in the M10c cluster and the basis for the characteristic's classification as defilement by external agency.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's agency pattern reveals a critical distinction between two types of agency-engagement: constitutive agency (the person's own will generating action through their own inner constitution — Chars 1, 2, 3) and displaced agency (the person's agency replaced by an alien agency — Char 4). Characteristics 1, 2, and 3 all preserve the person's constitutive agency even while engaging defilement: in all three, the person or community is an agent — avoidance (Char 1), misdirected pursuit (Char 2), deliberate desecration (Char 3). Characteristic 4 is the only characteristic where the person is not an agent but a site through which an alien agency operates. This confirms the cluster's taxonomy: self-generated defilement (Chars 1-3) preserves agency; externally-imposed defilement (Char 4) replaces it. Restoration in Characteristics 1-3 requires the person's own agency to participate (washing, repenting, turning from idols); restoration in Characteristic 4 requires divine authority to remove the alien agency, after which the person's own agency is returned.

findings.session_b_note:
Yes — moral evaluation is structurally embedded in the nature of forgiveness from the outset:

**The legitimacy of the claim:** The registry description states: "the release of a **legitimate** claim." Forgiveness presupposes moral evaluation — the wrong done must be assessed as genuinely wrong, the claim as genuinely legitimate, before it can be released. Forgiveness is not moral indifference (overlooking without moral engagement) but moral seriousness followed by volitional release.

**The standard named in the vocabulary:** The salach-root operates within the covenantal-moral framework — sin is the transgression of God's law; atonement is required because the moral order has been violated. Forgiveness addresses a moral reality (sin, debt, trespass) assessed against a moral standard.

**The parable's moral calculus (Mat 18):** The parable structures the ethical argument around moral comparison — the scale of debt received vs. the scale of debt withheld. The moral evaluation faculty is engaged by the parable in order to produce recognition of the incoherence: the servant who received much and gave nothing is morally inconsistent.

**The unforgivable sin (Mar 3:29):** The permanent moral boundary — the one condition in which forgiveness is permanently withheld — implies a moral evaluation at the deepest level: the rejection of the Spirit's work is assessed as the most severe moral condition the vocabulary names.

findings.session_b_note:
Yes — moral evaluation is engaged at several points in the compassion data.

**The judicial-prohibition pattern:** The chus vocabulary in judicial contexts presupposes a moral evaluation: the law identifies cases in which the compassion-impulse is morally wrong to follow (Deut 7:16; 19:13 — the cases of idolaters, murderers). The moral evaluation faculty is what identifies these as cases where justice requires the suppression of compassion. Compassion interacts with moral evaluation by providing an impulse that moral evaluation then assesses as appropriate or inappropriate to the context.

**Compassion as the moral standard in the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:33):** In the parable, compassion (splanchnizō) is the moral criterion by which the Samaritan is judged to have acted rightly and the priest and Levite are judged to have acted wrongly. The moral evaluation faculty in the hearer (and the lawyer asking the question) is asked to assess the three travellers, and compassion is the standard by which the assessment is made. Compassion here is not only an inner experience — it is a moral norm.

**The chesed-as-moral-requirement vocabulary:** Mic 6:8 — "love kindness" (chesed) — places the chesed-compassion quality within an explicit moral framework alongside doing justice and walking humbly. Moral evaluation of one's life includes the assessment of whether one has practised chesed. The Hos 6:6 anchor — "I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice" — makes chesed the moral standard by which ritual observance is evaluated. Compassion is the measure of authentic moral life.

findings.session_b_note:
Yes — moral evaluation is central to the penitential-relational mode of contrition. The contrite person has made a moral assessment: they have recognised that what they did was wrong, that it caused harm or broke trust, and that they stand accountable before God. This requires the moral evaluation faculty to be active and operative.

The verse evidence supports this: the broader Psa 51 context (the penitential psalm from which anchor verse Psa 51:17 is drawn) is built on moral evaluation — David's assessment of his actions against God's standard. Isa 66:2's "trembles at my word" implies that God's word provides the evaluative standard to which the contrite person is attentive.

findings.session_b_note:
Yes. Moral evaluation is central to fellowship's proper operation.

**Evaluation of fellowship-object:** 2Cor 6:14 — the person must evaluate the moral character of potential fellowship partners: righteousness vs. lawlessness, light vs. darkness. The moral evaluation faculty determines who the person can genuinely be in fellowship with.

**Evaluation of self in fellowship-context:** Mat 23:30 — the Pharisees' moral self-assessment (*we would not have taken part*) is an act of moral evaluation applied to the self in the fellowship context. The person evaluates their own hypothetical fellowship choices.

**Standard of moral evaluation:** Psa 119:63 — the standard for choosing companions is *fear of God* and *keeping of precepts*. The moral evaluation faculty applies this standard to potential fellowship partners.

**Moral evaluation of complicity:** Finding 062-SD003 (fellowship as moral complicity mechanism) specifically targets the way fellowship language relates to moral responsibility and guilt-by-association — a moral evaluation problem.

findings.session_b_note: Moral evaluation is one of the most extensively engaged faculties. The not-good verdict mode (884-006, 22 verses) is itself a sustained moral evaluation activity — the prophetic and wisdom literature applies the standard of the good to conduct and names the verdict. The comparative wisdom mode (884-004) engages moral evaluation in its comparative form — ranking goods hierarchically. Eze 36:31 engages moral evaluation in the person's own self-assessment: the person comes to evaluate their own deeds as not-good. Gen 1:31 (884-007) is a divine moral evaluation — "God saw that it was good." Mic 6:8 presents goodness as the criterion against which conduct is evaluated. Moral evaluation is both engaged by goodness (goodness calibrates the moral evaluation faculty) and expressed through goodness (the good person applies the standard rightly). (OBS-067-OBS-012, OBS-067-OBS-035, OBS-067-OBS-036, SBF-067-Q065)

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-067-003: T3 reveals that goodness is the most comprehensively faculty-engaging characteristic in the programme's current analytical record. Every faculty except creativity (T3.5 — silence confirmed) shows subs…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals that goodness is the most comprehensively faculty-engaging characteristic in the programme's current analytical record. Every faculty except creativity (T3.5 — silence confirmed) shows substantive engagement: perception (tasting and seeing goodness), cognition (moral evaluation and ranking), memory (covenantal knowing and moral reckoning), affect (stable rooted gladness vs fragile surface gladness), volition (reconstituted toward the good), agency (active expression required and enabled), moral evaluation (goodness as the normative anchor of the evaluative faculty), conscience (goodness calibrates the conscience's standard), conscientiousness (integration of all faculties into sustained moral expression), and relational capacity (dual-directional overflow). The tier as a whole reveals that goodness is not a specialist characteristic — it is an integrating one. The person who possesses genuine goodness has every faculty engaged and aligned. This comprehensive faculty-engagement is what distinguishes genuine goodness from its surface forms: surface goodness (the Haman problem) engages affect without engaging conscience or volitional alignment; genuine goodness integrates all.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-067-009: T1 identified goodness as an integrating characteristic with 12 modes of operation. T3 confirms the mechanism of integration: goodness is integrating because it engages and aligns every inner faculty …
findings.finding_value: T1 identified goodness as an integrating characteristic with 12 modes of operation. T3 confirms the mechanism of integration: goodness is integrating because it engages and aligns every inner faculty simultaneously. The T1 finding that goodness has a communicative mode (doxological declaration and divine revelatory speech — Q&A-024) connects to T3's perceptual (Q&A-066) and relational (Q&A-096) faculty findings: the communicative mode of goodness engages perception (tasting and seeing), activates conscience (the divine word naming what is good calibrates the conscience's standard), and builds relational capacity (community-forming declaration). The T3 finding that goodness is fundamentally integrating (Q&A-095) is what makes its T1 multi-modality coherent: the 12 modes are not fragmented operations but facets of a single faculty-integrating reality.

findings.session_b_note: Yes — love is the primary shaper of moral sensitivity in the data. Psa 97:10 (OBS-103-115): 'O you who love the Lord, hate evil' — love of God directly produces moral sensitivity to evil (the capacity to hate what is wrong). Lev 19:17 (OBS-103-114): the prohibition on hating the brother in the heart implies that moral sensitivity recognises inner hate as morally significant. 1Cor 13:6 (within OBS-103-127): love 'does not rejoice in wrongdoing' — love shapes the moral sensitivity that recognises wrongdoing as something not to be celebrated. Pro 10:12 (OBS-103-097): love's moral sensitivity distinguishes between hatred-that-stirs-strife and love-that-covers — the faculty that makes this distinction is morally sensitised by love. Love functions as the moral-sensitivity calibrator: it determines what the inner person registers as morally significant and how they register it.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-103-003: Love engages all eleven inner faculties, but five show the richest engagement: (1) Identity and self-understanding — love is the primary faculty through which the person knows who they are: being-love…
findings.finding_value: Love engages all eleven inner faculties, but five show the richest engagement: (1) Identity and self-understanding — love is the primary faculty through which the person knows who they are: being-loved (agapētos) constitutes identity from the outside; what-one-loves constitutes identity from the inside. The person is doubly defined by love. (2) Relational capacity — love is the faculty's active content: it builds (Joh 13:34), sustains (Lam 3:22), and restores (Luk 15:20) relational capacity. (3) Memory — love's sustaining faculty: love without memory cannot maintain itself through absence (Jer 31:20 — 'I do remember him still'). (4) Moral sensitivity — love calibrates what the inner person registers as morally significant; the love-of-God requirement generates the hate-evil requirement (Psa 97:10). (5) Attention — love determines what the person perceives as worth attending to (Phili 4:8 — think on what is lovely). The weaker engagements: creativity (indirect, evidenced through Song-form) and conscience (inferred, not directly named). Overall: love is the faculty-most-engaged characteristic in the programme, operating through perception, reason, memory, imagination, desire, emotion, moral sensitivity, conscience (indirectly), identity, and relational capacity simultaneously.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-103-002: Love's definition as directed-attachment-toward-an-object generates a characteristic pattern of faculty engagement. Because love is always toward an object, it necessarily engages attention (what is a…
findings.finding_value: Love's definition as directed-attachment-toward-an-object generates a characteristic pattern of faculty engagement. Because love is always toward an object, it necessarily engages attention (what is attended to is the beloved — Phili 4:8), reason (judgment of the object's worth and the hierarchy of competing loves — Mat 10:37), memory (remembering the beloved sustains love — Jer 31:20), and identity (what is loved constitutes who one is — Q&A-075). The definition's object-determination principle (moral quality determined by object) maps onto the moral sensitivity faculty: the faculty that calibrates moral perception is calibrated by love's direction — you notice what you love, and what you love as most important determines what you register as morally significant (Psa 97:10 — love-of-God generates hate-of-evil). The definition's tripartite structure (disposition/act/condition) maps onto the faculty architecture: disposition engages the will and conscience; act engages the relational capacity and body; condition engages identity and emotion. No faculty operates independently of love's fundamental structure.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-103-012: The faculty engagement pattern in T3 is produced by and oriented toward the relational interfaces in T4. Love's identity-faculty (T3.10) is constituted through the relational interface: being-loved by…
findings.finding_value: The faculty engagement pattern in T3 is produced by and oriented toward the relational interfaces in T4. Love's identity-faculty (T3.10) is constituted through the relational interface: being-loved by God (GOD→HUMAN axis) establishes the identity of agapētos; what-one-loves (active direction) establishes identity through the chosen object. The relational capacity faculty (T3.11) is the faculty through which the three relational axes are exercised: the GOD→HUMAN axis engages the relational capacity as receiver; the HUMAN→GOD axis engages it as giver; the HUMAN→HUMAN axis engages it in both directions simultaneously. Memory (T3.3) sustains the relational interface: love toward God is sustained through remembering his chesed (Jer 31:20); love in community is sustained through shared history. Moral sensitivity (T3.8) is calibrated by the relational interface structure: love-of-God calibrates the moral perception of what is evil (Psa 97:10); love-of-neighbour calibrates the perception of what is just. The deepest inter-tier finding: the faculty engagement pattern is not incidental — it is precisely the faculty configuration required by the relational architecture. The relational structure generates the faculty requirements.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-103-014: The faculty engagement breadth in T3 is consistent with love's structural position as the programme's central sequential node in T6. A characteristic that engages all eleven faculties will necessarily…
findings.finding_value: The faculty engagement breadth in T3 is consistent with love's structural position as the programme's central sequential node in T6. A characteristic that engages all eleven faculties will necessarily stand at the intersection of the programme's full inner-being vocabulary — because any characteristic that engages one faculty will co-occur with love insofar as love also engages that faculty. The memory-faculty engagement explains part of the co-occurrence with despair (R044 — 55 shared verses): lament appeals to the memory of God's love (Lam 3:22) as its ground. The identity-faculty engagement explains the co-occurrence with calling (R019 — 51 shared): identity-as-beloved and identity-as-called are grammatically co-ordinate (Rom 1:7). The moral-sensitivity engagement explains co-occurrence with guilt (R073 — 32 shared): moral sensitivity calibrated by love recognises guilt as the state that precedes the forgiveness that generates love (Luk 7:47). Faculty engagement and structural relationships thus form a coherent explanatory system: the faculty profile generates the co-occurrence pattern.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-103-015: The vocabulary evidence grounds the faculty claims with lexical precision. Identity faculty (T3.10): agapētos (person-type of being-loved), chasid (person-type of chesed), filos (person-type of phileō…
findings.finding_value: The vocabulary evidence grounds the faculty claims with lexical precision. Identity faculty (T3.10): agapētos (person-type of being-loved), chasid (person-type of chesed), filos (person-type of phileō) — all three are lexically grounded person-type terms (Q&A-127). Moral sensitivity faculty (T3.8): the hate-vocabulary embedded as OWNER (H8130 sane — Q&A-126) grounds the claim that love requires and produces righteous hatred — the structural opposite provides the moral sensitivity calibration. Memory faculty (T3.3): the verb-form analysis (Q&A-123) shows that chesed as noun-primary form implies a dispositional quality that persists — memory is the chesed-noun's faculty correlate. Attention faculty (T3.1): phileō's etymology (from philos — friend) implies a relational salience structure — the one who is phileō-loved becomes salient to the lover's attention-field. The vocabulary's etymological structure (Q&A-122) is thus the lexical ground of the faculty engagement pattern: the root meanings point toward the faculties each term primarily activates.

findings.session_b_note: Yes — mercy engages moral evaluation in a complex way. Jam 2:13 (mercy triumphs over judgment — OBS-111-070) places mercy in explicit relation to the moral-evaluative process: judgment is the conclusion of moral evaluation; mercy overrides it. Mat 23:23 (justice, mercy, faithfulness as weightier matters of the law — SD003) places mercy as a component of the moral law itself. Dan 4:27 (practicing righteousness and showing mercy as parallel — OBS-111-062) makes mercy a moral obligation assessed against a standard. *New finding: mercy is not opposed to moral evaluation but is itself a moral evaluation — specifically, the evaluation that sets the claims of the other's need above the calculus of strict retributive accountability.* OBS-111-070, OBS-111-062.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-111-003: Reading T3 as a whole reveals mercy as a faculty-activating characteristic — it does not primarily engage one or two faculties but activates the inner-being faculty system comprehensively. The pattern…
findings.finding_value: Reading T3 as a whole reveals mercy as a faculty-activating characteristic — it does not primarily engage one or two faculties but activates the inner-being faculty system comprehensively. The pattern: mercy enables perception (face-access), opens cognition in both directions (upward to divine knowledge; downward to self-knowledge), creates an asymmetric memory structure (divine forgetting / human remembering), engages affect as its native register, expands volition (received mercy increases mercy-capacity), demands agency, reframes moral evaluation (mercy as higher-order moral evaluation), presupposes and deepens conscience, enables conscientiousness, and constitutes relational capacity. The single faculty not evidenced is creativity (T3.5.2 — S status). Reading T3 together: mercy is characterised by faculty-comprehensiveness; its absence (mercilessness in Rom 1:31) appears alongside affective incapacity (*astorgos*) and other faculty-failures — confirming that mercy's presence is correlated with full faculty activation and its absence with faculty contraction.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-009: T1 identifies the enabling conditions for mercy-reception (guilt-awareness, humility, persistence, soul-affliction) and T3 maps mercy's faculty engagements. Reading T1 and T3 together: the enabling co…
findings.finding_value: T1 identifies the enabling conditions for mercy-reception (guilt-awareness, humility, persistence, soul-affliction) and T3 maps mercy's faculty engagements. Reading T1 and T3 together: the enabling conditions for mercy-reception (T1) are precisely the conditions that require the full faculty activation identified in T3. Guilt-awareness requires conscience (T3.9) and moral evaluation (T3.8); humility requires affect (T3.4) and embodied posture; persistence requires volition (T3.6) and agency (T3.7); soul-affliction requires affect (T3.4) and relational capacity (T3.11). T1's enabling conditions are T3's faculty activation in a single moment — mercy-reception requires the whole inner faculty system to be engaged.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-021: T3 shows mercy as a faculty-comprehensive characteristic and T6 shows mercy as a structurally integrative hub characteristic. Reading together: the faculty-comprehensiveness (T3) is what enables the s…
findings.finding_value: T3 shows mercy as a faculty-comprehensive characteristic and T6 shows mercy as a structurally integrative hub characteristic. Reading together: the faculty-comprehensiveness (T3) is what enables the structural hub position (T6). A characteristic that activates all (or nearly all) inner faculties is positioned to connect to the widest range of adjacent characteristics — which is exactly what T6's co-occurrence and cross-registry data shows. Mercy's structural hub position in T6 is the cross-registry expression of its faculty-comprehensiveness in T3. The one missing faculty (creativity, T3.5.2 — S) corresponds to the one connection not evidenced in T6 — creative production is not a named output of mercy in the cross-registry data.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-022: T7's primary anchor verse identification (Psa 78:38) and its confirmation of mercy's cross-genre literary evidence maps to T3's faculty engagement profile. Psa 78:38 (T7, Q&A-185) contains within it a…
findings.finding_value: T7's primary anchor verse identification (Psa 78:38) and its confirmation of mercy's cross-genre literary evidence maps to T3's faculty engagement profile. Psa 78:38 (T7, Q&A-185) contains within it a four-stage inner sequence (compassion → atoning act → anger restraint → wrath modulation) that traverses multiple faculties: affect (compassion), agency (atoning act), moral evaluation (anger restraint as moral-evaluative act), and volition (not stirring up wrath). The verse T7 identifies as primary anchor encodes the T3 faculty engagement in concentrated form. T7's human-science divergence finding (Q&A-189 — mercy grounded in prior reception, not autonomous moral development) is the methodological form of T3's receiving-before-generating faculty activation pattern.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-030-003: Reading T3 as a whole reveals that contrition engages virtually every inner faculty — with one exception (creativity, T3.5 — data silent). The pattern across the engaged faculties is consistent: contr…
findings.finding_value: Reading T3 as a whole reveals that contrition engages virtually every inner faculty — with one exception (creativity, T3.5 — data silent). The pattern across the engaged faculties is consistent: contrition deepens and opens rather than impairs or bypasses. It deepens perception (opens to divine address), deepens cognition (enables accurate self-knowledge), deepens affect (makes grief and longing both fuller), redirects volition (from self-assertion to God-direction), converts agency (from self-directed to God-seeking), deepens moral evaluation (requires and enables accurate self-assessment), deepens conscience (allows conscience's verdict to reach the spirit/heart), deepens conscientiousness (grounds it in inner reality rather than performance), and enables relational capacity (specifically for divine nearness). The single thread running through all faculty engagements is: contrition removes self-protective barriers — it is the inner-being event in which every protective reflex is dissolved, leaving the person fully exposed and open. This is why it enables rather than impairs every faculty: openness is the condition in which all faculties function most truthfully.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-030-009: The definition tier (T1) establishes contrition as a passive inner condition produced by encounter; the faculty tier (T3) shows that this passivity simultaneously opens every inner faculty. The connec…
findings.finding_value: The definition tier (T1) establishes contrition as a passive inner condition produced by encounter; the faculty tier (T3) shows that this passivity simultaneously opens every inner faculty. The connection between T1 and T3 is that contrition's defining feature — the dissolution of self-protection — is precisely what enables the faculties. T1's structural negative (inner self-enclosure as the opposite of contrition, Q&A-033) is T3's impairment condition: the self-enclosed person has every faculty partially closed. Contrition's definition therefore predicts its faculty effects: a characteristic that is constitutively about removal of self-protective barriers will enable every faculty that self-protection would otherwise restrict.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-030-022: The faculty tier (T3) shows that contrition deepens conscience, moral evaluation, and cognition; the evidential tier (T7) identifies the primary literary form as penitential psalm and prophetic addres…
findings.finding_value: The faculty tier (T3) shows that contrition deepens conscience, moral evaluation, and cognition; the evidential tier (T7) identifies the primary literary form as penitential psalm and prophetic address — both forms that are constitutively about honest self-knowledge before God. The Psa 51 genre (penitential psalm — T7.2) is the literary vehicle for contrition in the conscience-and-cognition registers (T3.8, T3.9): the psalm form presupposes accurate self-assessment and directed it to God. The prophetic form (Isa 57:15, 66:2 — T7.2) is the vehicle for contrition in the volitional and relational registers (T3.6, T3.11). T7's literary analysis explains why T3 finds that different faculties are engaged in different evidential contexts.
