findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-062-003: Reading T3 as a whole reveals that every faculty engagement with fellowship runs in both directions — right fellowship deepens and enables; wrong fellowship degrades and constrains. Perception, cognit…
findings.finding_value: Reading T3 as a whole reveals that every faculty engagement with fellowship runs in both directions — right fellowship deepens and enables; wrong fellowship degrades and constrains. Perception, cognition, moral evaluation, conscience, conscientiousness, and relational capacity are all deepened by rightly directed fellowship and progressively impaired by wrongly directed fellowship. The single exception is creativity (T3.5 — data silent). The pattern is systematic: fellowship is not merely a relational characteristic but a faculty-shaping characteristic — it progressively shapes every inner faculty in conformity with its object. This makes the choice of fellowship objects one of the most consequential inner-being decisions a person makes: the consequences extend through every faculty across time.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-062-009: T1 establishes that fellowship is object-determined and progressively constitutional; T3 shows that fellowship shapes every inner faculty in conformity with its object. These are two descriptions of t…
findings.finding_value: T1 establishes that fellowship is object-determined and progressively constitutional; T3 shows that fellowship shapes every inner faculty in conformity with its object. These are two descriptions of the same reality: "object determines character" (T1) is the principle; "every faculty shaped by fellowship direction" (T3) is the mechanism. The five-mode structure (T1) explains why T3 finds diverse faculty effects: existential mode primarily engages affect and relational capacity; companionship mode primarily engages volition, moral evaluation, and conscientiousness; suffering mode primarily engages affect and agency; ontological mode primarily engages relational capacity at its deepest level.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-062-014: T2's constitutional locations map directly onto T3's faculty engagements. The desire-faculty location (T2.5) corresponds to T3.6 volition and T3.7 agency — desire and will are structurally adjacent in…

The soul-level (T2.2 — Ecc 9:4) corresponds to T3.4 affect — the existential fellowship produces hope as an affective state at the soul level. findings.finding_value: T3's faculty engagements all run in the same relational direction that T4 identifies as primary (vertical — human toward God). Perception, volition, moral evaluation, conscientiousness, and relational capacity are all deepened when directed toward the right fellowship object (God and God-fearers). T3's bilateral finding (right fellowship deepens; wrong fellowship degrades) explains T4's structural negative (misdirected fellowship is more dangerous than absence — Hos 4:17, Mat 23:30): when every faculty is progressively shaped by the fellowship object, misdirected fellowship progressively degrades every faculty, not just the relational capacity.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-062-020: T3's snapshot (what fellowship does to faculties in the moment) and T5's longitudinal account (what habitual fellowship produces over time) together reveal that faculty deepening (T3) is the process o…
findings.finding_value: T3's snapshot (what fellowship does to faculties in the moment) and T5's longitudinal account (what habitual fellowship produces over time) together reveal that faculty deepening (T3) is the process of which constitutional character formation (T5) is the endpoint. The right-direction faculty deepening (T3 — perception, cognition, conscience, moral evaluation each deepened by right fellowship) accumulates over time into the fixed character of Psa 119:63's declared God-fearer companion, which is on its way to Jer 13:23's constitutional formation. T3 → T5 is the moment-to-character arc.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-062-022: T7's literary forms explain why T3 finds different faculty engagements in different evidential contexts. The wisdom poetry setting (Psa 119:63, Jer 13:23, Ecc 9:4) engages primarily the volitional, co…

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-064-003: T3 reveals forgiveness as uniquely faculty-comprehensive — it engages more named faculties with greater specificity than any other characteristic reviewed in this revision series. Memory is explicitly…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals forgiveness as uniquely faculty-comprehensive — it engages more named faculties with greater specificity than any other characteristic reviewed in this revision series. Memory is explicitly named (Jer 31:34 — divine memory as the content of forgiveness) and distinctively: forgiveness transforms memory in both directions — God's memory of sin is set aside permanently; the human forgiver releases the active use of memory against the offender. Affect is bidirectionally engaged: as prerequisite (somatic compassion, Mat 18:27) and as product (love, Luk 7:47; reverence, Psa 130:4). Conscience is addressed and purified by forgiveness (Heb 9:14). Volition is constitutive (the heart-level release is chosen). Cognition is enabled (Jer 31:34 — forgiveness → knowing God). The single silence is creativity (T3.5). T3's synthesis: forgiveness is the most faculty-comprehensive characteristic in the current review set — it reaches every major faculty with specific evidenced content, most strikingly in the memory domain.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-021: T3's memory faculty finding (Jer 31:34 — divine "remember no more") explains the R160 thought/knowledge co-occurrence at that verse: the divine cognitive act of non-remembering and the human cognitive…
findings.finding_value: T3's memory faculty finding (Jer 31:34 — divine "remember no more") explains the R160 thought/knowledge co-occurrence at that verse: the divine cognitive act of non-remembering and the human cognitive outcome of knowing God meet in the same verse because they are structurally connected — the guilt-barrier's removal (forgiveness) enables the cognitive-relational access (knowing God). T3's affect-faculty finding (love produced — Luk 7:47) explains the R103 love co-occurrence (8 shared verses) — love is the affective downstream product of forgiveness. T3's conscience faculty finding confirms the R073 guilt structural partnership — guilt is what conscience identifies as the prior condition that forgiveness addresses. Faculty engagements (T3) and structural co-occurrences (T6) are mutually explanatory.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-003: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion re…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion responds, it does not originate or create. It is the most responsive of the faculties-engaging characteristics. Second, affect and moral action are structurally unified in compassion — not sequentially related but simultaneous. Affect is the mechanism of movement (splanchnizō is both the felt inner event and the cause of the action), not a precursor or accompaniment. This is unique among the characteristics reviewed: in most other registries, affect and volition are distinguishable stages; in compassion, the felt movement is already the morally motivated action beginning. A third distinctive finding: compassion converts moral knowledge into motivated action — it is the motivational ground of conscientiousness, not a product of it. The conscience faculty engagement reveals compassion as conscience-healing: it addresses the pitiable condition that conscience perceives as a moral claim, resolving the tension between moral knowledge and moral incapacity. The three relational modes (building/sustaining — chesed; restoring/repairing — splanchnizō; extending across difference — Good Samaritan) are a new finding not in the instruction typology.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-003: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked …
findings.finding_value: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I but the grace of God that is with me." Agency is not displaced but constituted by grace. This relationship holds in paradox that the T3.6 prompt options (enable/deepen/bypass/impair) cannot accommodate — a prompt design limitation noted for catalogue revision. Second, grace produces moral clarity (T3.8 — sharpens moral evaluation rather than bypassing it): the person who recognises grace has made a precise moral evaluation (they know they received what they did not deserve). Third, grace and conscience are mutually necessary: grace is the condition within which conscience can operate fully without destroying the person; conscience without grace produces condemnation; grace without conscience produces presumption (T3.9). Fourth, grace is the primary relational faculty developer in the registry's evidence — it reaches every relational register (vertical access, horizontal forgiving, speech-grace) and enables each one. Creativity (T3.5) is the one genuinely silent faculty — not an impairment but a non-engagement: grace receives and constitutes, it does not create.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-009: T1's immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response) is the affective-volitional expression of T3's faculty engagement at the moment grace arrives. T3…
findings.finding_value: T1's immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response) is the affective-volitional expression of T3's faculty engagement at the moment grace arrives. T3.4 (affect is the first named faculty engaged by grace) and T3.6 (the agency-constituting paradox of 1Cor 15:10) together explain why T1.5 finds the creaturely recognition response before positive states settle: grace first produces the affective recognition (fear, mourning) before constituting the agency through which the person responds (prostration as the body enacting the inner posture that grace has produced). T1's finding that grace requires creaturely recognition to complete its operation (T1.7) is T3.1's finding at the faculty level: grace requires and enables perception simultaneously.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-021: T3's faculty findings explain several patterns in T6's co-occurrence landscape. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (R140 — 40 verses) is partly explained by T3.6's agency-constituting finding: seekin…
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty findings explain several patterns in T6's co-occurrence landscape. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (R140 — 40 verses) is partly explained by T3.6's agency-constituting finding: seeking requires the constituted agency that grace provides for its own reception (SD026 — grace giving the capacity for supplication). The power cluster co-occurrences (strength R187 — 15 verses, might R198 — 10 verses) confirm T3.7's agency-constituting finding at the cross-registry level: grace producing agency is registered as co-occurring with power/strength across the corpus. T3.8's moral clarity finding explains the guilt co-occurrence (R073 — 10 verses): the moral clarity grace produces is most visible at the point of moral failure, and the co-occurrence reflects this — grace and guilt appear together because grace produces the moral clarity that accurately names the guilt it addresses.

findings.session_b_note: Yes — moral evaluation is deeply engaged by covenant. (1) Covenant defines the moral standard against which inner fidelity is assessed: the covenant's terms (law, commandments, statutes) provide the content of moral evaluation (Deu 7:9 — OBS-034-039; 2Ki 23:3 — OBS-034-047). Living within covenant means living under a defined moral evaluative framework. (2) Covenant breach is a moral failure assessed by the moral evaluation faculty: Dan 9:11 — "we have sinned against him" (OBS-034-036) — Daniel's prayer of confession is a moral self-assessment in covenantal categories. (3) The oath/curse structure (H0423 — OBS-034-007) embeds a moral assessment mechanism in the covenant itself: the covenant includes its own evaluation criterion and sanction for breach. (4) G0802 (asunthetos — OBS-034-057): Paul's taxonomy in Rom 1:31 names covenant-breaking as a moral defect — the moral evaluation faculty of the apostle and of Scripture judges covenant-breaking as character vice.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-099-003: T3 reveals that kindness engages a remarkably wide range of inner faculties — nine of eleven are evidenced with at least partial engagement. The two genuine absences (imagination and creativity) are s…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals that kindness engages a remarkably wide range of inner faculties — nine of eleven are evidenced with at least partial engagement. The two genuine absences (imagination and creativity) are structurally coherent: kindness is relational and loyally directed, not generative. The most significant faculty engagements are: (a) volition — kindness is chosen, not merely felt; the "put on" and "love kindness" language makes this constitutive; (b) agency — chrēsteuomai names love actively exercising kindness — kindness is enacted, not passive; (c) relational capacity — kindness constitutes relationships in their quality, not merely accompanies them; (d) conscientiousness — the chasid represents the full integration of moral awareness, will, and action in consistent reliable pattern; (e) taste as the primary perceptive mode — "tasted that the Lord is good" establishes that kindness is encountered experientially before it is understood conceptually. The pattern across all engaged faculties: kindness integrates the whole inner person — it does not operate as a single-faculty characteristic but as a whole-person orientation. T3's most significant intra-tier finding: kindness is a multi-faculty characteristic whose breadth of engagement reflects its status as a constitutive relational orientation rather than a single affective or volitional act.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-099-019: T3's faculty analysis and T4's relational interface analysis are structurally interdependent in a specific way: the faculties that kindness most strongly engages (volition, agency, relational capacity…
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty analysis and T4's relational interface analysis are structurally interdependent in a specific way: the faculties that kindness most strongly engages (volition, agency, relational capacity, conscientiousness) are precisely the faculties required for the T4 relational circuit to operate. Relational capacity (T3.11) is what makes the T4 interfaces possible at all — the person must have the constitutional equipment for genuine connection before kindness can flow in any direction. Agency (T3.7) is what makes the T4 giving direction concrete — not passive benevolence but enacted care. Conscientiousness (T3.10) is what makes the T4 circuit sustainable across time — the chasid who reliably keeps covenant. The T4 communal interface (Moses's intercession; the chasidim assembly) requires an intercessory capacity (T3 — memory + relational capacity) that knows how to appeal on behalf of others. The two tiers together describe a portrait of the whole inner person oriented outward: T3 names the inner equipment and T4 names the relational directions in which that equipment is deployed.

findings.session_b_note: Yes — extensively. Peace has a moral evaluation function: the presence or absence of shalom is a moral indicator. Evidence: (1) Isa 48:22, 57:21 — "there is no peace for the wicked" — moral condition is the determinative factor for peace's availability; (2) Isa 59:8 — "the way of peace they do not know" — moral disorder produces cognitive/perceptual blindness to peace's way; (3) Mal 2:6 — "walked with me in peace and uprightness" — shalom paired with uprightness as the moral-character portrait; (4) The false-peace pattern (Jer 6:14, Deu 29:19) — the moral faculty has been corrupted when false peace is claimed. Peace's connection to moral evaluation is among the richest in the programme: the peaceful person evaluates rightly; the wicked person cannot perceive peace's way; the self-deceived person evaluates falsely.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-117-003: T3 identifies conscience as peace's primary gateway faculty — the inner faculty whose state most directly determines whether genuine peace is constitutionally accessible. Three conscience-patterns: su…
findings.finding_value: T3 identifies conscience as peace's primary gateway faculty — the inner faculty whose state most directly determines whether genuine peace is constitutionally accessible. Three conscience-patterns: suppressed conscience destroys peace somatically (Psa 32:3 — bones wasting); exercised conscience restores peace through confession (Psa 32:5); bypassed conscience produces false peace (Deu 29:19). No other inner faculty has this bidirectional gateway function as clearly documented. The moral evaluation faculty (T3.8) confirms: authentic peace enables right moral judgment; false peace corrupts it. The practical implication: the route back from peacelessness is through conscience-exercise (confession, acknowledgment, remembering God's faithfulness), not through direct emotional management.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-060-003: T3 as a whole reveals that this characteristic engages virtually every inner faculty in the programme's 11-faculty model — the only consistent gap is creativity (T3.5, S across three prompts). The pat…
findings.finding_value: T3 as a whole reveals that this characteristic engages virtually every inner faculty in the programme's 11-faculty model — the only consistent gap is creativity (T3.5, S across three prompts). The pattern of engagement is not uniform: perception is engaged as precondition (God hears before giving); cognition is constituted (wisdom is given, not generated); memory is deepened (the narrative-temporal dimension of covenantal giving); affect is the source of giving (compassion, anger) and the target of transformation (mourning→gladness); volition is called forth and elevated (genuine giving cannot be coerced); agency is the bridge between disposition and act; moral evaluation both produces and is produced by the characteristic; conscience is engaged indirectly through Spirit-forming and prophetic warning; conscientiousness at the human apex is the full integration of all three (moral awareness, will, act). Relational capacity is intrinsic — every mode is two-party. What T3 reveals as a whole: faithfulness-as-giving is not a faculty-specific characteristic but a whole-person characteristic — it recruits and integrates all active faculties into a unified inner-being act. The creativity silence is the only dimension where the data cannot confirm engagement.

This is the faculty most centrally engaged in the righteous register. Pro 8:13: "the fear of the Lord is hatred of evil" — the moral evaluation of evil as evil is what produces the hatred. Psa 45:7: "you have loved righteousness and hated wickedness" — the moral evaluation of righteousness (as worthy of love) and wickedness (as worthy of hatred) is the operative faculty. In the disordered register: hatred bypasses or corrupts moral evaluation of the hated person (the hater cannot evaluate the hated person fairly because the hostile disposition prejudices the evaluation). Psa 36:2: the wicked "flatters himself in his own eyes" — his moral self-evaluation is corrupted by a related avoidance of having his iniquity "found out and hated."

The moral evaluation faculty is the primary operative faculty of contempt. Contempt is an act of moral evaluation — specifically, a wrong verdict rendered by the moral evaluation faculty. Every instance involves a wrong assessment of worth: Esau wrongly assesses the birthright as worth less than food; the priests wrongly assess God's name as not demanding honour; the comfortable person wrongly assesses the sufferer's misfortune as not deserving attention.

Moral evaluation is the faculty that names and confirms the abhorrence. The characteristic operates at a level deeper than moral evaluation (the visceral recoil precedes the verdict) but the moral evaluation faculty is what identifies the object as worthy of abhorrence and maintains the response as morally valid. Rom 2:22's challenge works precisely here: the claimed abhorrence of idols (a moral evaluation position) is exposed as not corresponding to an actual inner state.

The moral evaluation faculty is characteristically absent or impaired in M06-D. Pro 12:10: "the righteous has regard for the life of his beast" — the righteous person evaluates animal life as worthy of regard; the wicked person does not make this evaluation. The cruel person's moral evaluation faculty has ceased to register the worth of what would otherwise trigger mercy. The faculty is not inverted (as in M06-B's contempt of justice) but simply absent in its mercy-triggering function.

The moral evaluation faculty is engaged in cognitive resistance to reproach. Isa 51:7: "you who know righteousness, the people in whose heart is my law; fear not the reproach of man" — the internal moral knowledge (knowing righteousness) is the evaluative resource that enables the person to resist internalising the false social verdict. The faculty is called to evaluate the reproach itself as unjust and to maintain that evaluation against social pressure.

Moral evaluation is operative in the assessment of whether the adversary relationship is just: God's taking up of the adversary posture (Exo 23:22) is grounded in his moral evaluation of the situation. The human's appeal to God (Psa 35:1) implicitly calls on God's moral evaluation as the arbiter.

The moral evaluation faculty has been most completely corrupted in M06-G. Eze 36:5: "wholehearted joy and utter contempt" — the moral evaluation of the other's destruction as a positive good is the deepest cognitive distortion in M06. The faculty is operating but has evaluated destruction as good and the other's suffering as deserved and pleasurable.

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** Yes — God's righteousness is the standard of moral evaluation. "He does no injustice" (Zep 3:5); "he does wickedly, and the Almighty will not pervert justice" (Job 34:12, VSG 1225-001). God's righteousness is the measure by which all other moral claims are evaluated. The standard itself is the moral evaluation faculty at its source.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Yes — "the thoughts of the righteous are just" (Pro 12:5, VSG M26-A2-011). The righteous person's moral evaluation is accurate — they think justly. The testing of the righteous (Psa 7:9, VSG M26-A2-013: "O God who tests the minds and hearts") engages moral evaluation as the mode of divine assessment of the person.

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** Yes — uprightness enables moral evaluation of right paths (Pro 2:9). The person with uprightness can evaluate what is straight and what is crooked. Isa 30:10 (VSG 1214-001) shows the rejection of moral evaluation: "do not prophesy to us what is right; speak smooth things" — the demand for smooth things is a refusal of honest moral evaluation.

**[C — Justification]** Yes — "will you even put me in the wrong? Will you condemn me that you may be in the right?" (Job 40:8, VSG 1225-002). The moral evaluation of who is right — who can stand before God's standard — is the question that justification answers. Justification is God's moral evaluation of the person through Christ.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** Yes — "God's righteous judgment" (Rom 2:5, VSG 3207-001) engages moral evaluation: the identification of wrongdoing and the determination of appropriate retribution. D presupposes accurate moral evaluation as its precondition: the avenger must correctly identify wrong before acting.

**[E — Condemnation]** Yes — condemnation is the negative verdict of moral evaluation. "He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the righteous are both alike an abomination to the Lord" (Pro 17:15, VSG 1225-002). The accuracy of moral evaluation in E is critical — corrupt evaluation (condemning the righteous, justifying the wicked) is itself condemned.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** Yes — and centrally. The reckoning faculty in F is the moral evaluation faculty applied to specific questions: what is this worth? How does this compare? What is the standing of this person? Moral reckoning (F) is moral evaluation in its most explicitly cognitive and deliberative mode.

**[G — Structural Opposites]** Yes — but distorted. "They do not know how to do right" (Amo 3:10); "he who justifies the wicked and condemns the righteous" (Pro 17:15) — the sub-group names both the failure of moral evaluation (inability to do right) and its inversion (justifying the wicked, condemning the righteous). Wickedness distorts moral evaluation in both directions.

**[CLUSTER]** E. Righteousness enables and sharpens moral evaluation; wickedness distorts it (condemning the righteous, justifying the wicked). The cluster reveals that accurate moral evaluation is both an expression of righteousness and one of its primary functions. The person who is righteous evaluates rightly; the person who is wicked evaluates corruptly. Moral evaluation is the faculty most fundamentally at stake in the M26 cluster.

findings.finding_value: M01-A is the most morally evaluative sub-group in the cluster. Fear of God provides the interior moral standard against which the person's conduct is assessed in the absence of external accountability: Lev 19:14 (fear as the moral evaluator operating where "no human court can see"); Neh 5:9 (fear of God as "the inner ethical standard that should have restrained the leaders from oppressing their own people"); 2Ch 19:9 (judicial conduct governed by fear of the Lord "paired explicitly with faithfulness and whole-heartedness"). The moral evaluation faculty is the primary channel through which M01-A operates in practical contexts.

M01-A-VCG-05 (reorientation of fear) engages moral evaluation directly: the person must morally assess what they are fearing and judge whether the object is appropriate (God) or not (crowds, idols, human power). Isa 8:12-13 (the prophet commanded not to adopt the crowd's fear-object — a moral assessment of fear's direction is required).

M01-G timidity **impairs** moral evaluation: Rev 21:8 (cowardice listed alongside idolatry and murder — timidity is a moral failure); Mat 25:25 (the servant's misjudgment of the master's character drives the wrong decision — moral evaluation distorted by fear).

M01-B's social fear (B-VCG-04) **bypasses** moral evaluation: Gal 2:12 (Peter's social fear driving withdrawal "against conviction" — the person's own moral assessment is overridden by fear-of-crowd-opinion); 1Sa 15:24 (Saul confesses that "fear of the people was the inner motive behind his disobedience — human social dread displaced his fear of God and drove him to comply with the crowd" — moral evaluation suppressed by social fear).

The moral evaluation faculty is: **enabled and deepened** by M01-A (fear of God as the interior moral standard); **bypassed** by M01-B's social fear (crowd opinion overriding moral judgment); **impaired** by M01-G timidity (cowardly failure of moral discernment under pressure). Ordered fear activates and grounds moral evaluation; disordered fear bypasses or suppresses it.

Psa 7:11 (M02-C-VCG-01): God's indignation is a constant, daily disposition against wickedness — the indignation is the felt moral verdict of the righteous judge. Jam 1:20 (M02-A-VCG-04): human wrath "does not produce God's righteousness" — the moral evaluation faculty is explicitly invoked to assess the moral inadequacy of human anger.

Yes. Conscience-driven sighing (Eze 9:4 — M03-E-VCG-01) is the paradigmatic instance: grief arising from the moral evaluation of witnessed wickedness. Jesus's grief at the Pharisees' hardness of heart (Mar 3:5 — M03-C-VCG-02) is compassionate moral grief — grief arising from perceiving and evaluating the moral failure of others. Peter's grief (Joh 21:17 — M03-C-VCG-01) arises from conscience's moral evaluation of his own past denial. The entire godly grief passage (2Cor 7:9-11 — M03-C-VCG-02) shows grief as a morally evaluative response that leads to reformation.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. The evidence repeatedly shows that exultation requires and exercises moral evaluation — distinguishing its legitimate from its illegitimate forms. Pro 24:17 prohibits exultation over an enemy's fall; Pro 2:14 marks exultation in evil as a sign of moral corruption; Hos 9:1 prohibits Israel's exultation on moral grounds; Psa 13:4 frames enemy exultation over the righteous as a feared moral wrong. The person's moral evaluation of the appropriate objects of exultation is itself a moral act.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, bidirectionally. (1) **Moral evaluation enabling Joy** — 1Cor 13:6 ("rejoices with the truth") — love's Joy is morally constrained by the capacity to evaluate what is truly good; Psa 97:8 (joy at God's "judgments" — moral appreciation of divine justice produces joy); Job 31:25, 29 (Job denies having rejoiced in wealth or at enemy's ruin — negating morally problematic joy forms); (2) **Joy enabling moral evaluation** — Psa 58:10 ("the righteous will rejoice when he sees the vengeance") — the righteous person's joy at justice being done reflects and reinforces moral evaluation.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Partially. 1Cor 13:6 (love "does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth" — adjacent to M04-D but the "rejoices with the truth" in the sunchairo corpus is a moral-evaluative rejoicing about what is genuinely right). Jas 1:2's "trials of various kinds" presupposes the moral evaluation that trials are genuinely adverse and the counter-intuitive reframing that they are also genuinely beneficial (v.3–4). The moral evaluation faculty is engaged but not primary — the characteristic's defining feature is not its moral evaluation of suffering but its transcendence of circumstances through Spirit-enabled joy.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes — this is Gladness's most distinctive faculty engagement across the entire M04 cluster. M04-L-VCG-02 (45 verses) is almost entirely the moral evaluation faculty in operation: the systematic "is this good? is this not-good?" exercise of the Proverbs corpus; the comparative "better than" assessments; the "what is good?" investigations of Ecclesiastes; Mic 6:8's definitional statement of what human goodness is; Job 34:4's communal moral discernment process. Gladness in its evaluative-cognitive face IS the moral evaluation faculty as an inner-being characteristic.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes, in M04-G and M04-M: (1) **M04-G's law-delight** — Psa 119's Delight in God's statutes, testimonies, commandments is simultaneously moral engagement: the psalmist who delights in the law is engaging the moral evaluation faculty through pleasurable orientation; Psa 40:8 ("I delight to do your will, O my God") — delight as moral alignment; (2) **M04-M-VCG-02** — the series of "doing what is good and right in God's sight" texts (Deu 6:18; 12:28; 1Sa 15:22; Joh 8:29; 1Jo 3:22) — all engage moral evaluation as the faculty that identifies what is pleasing to God; (3) **M04-H-VCG-02** — God's moral preferences revealed: what God delights in (steadfast love, justice, righteousness — Jer 9:24; Mic 7:18; Hos 6:6) is a moral declaration; (4) **M04-H-VCG-04** — the corrupt-Delight instances (Isa 65:12; 66:3; 2Th 2:12) engage moral evaluation by negation — pleasure in what God condemns reveals the moral inversion.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes, primarily in M04-K-VCG-03: (1) **Psa 37:16** (little of righteous better than abundance of wicked — moral-comparative evaluation); (2) **Pro 15:16** (little with fear of Lord better than great treasure with trouble — moral priority); (3) **Pro 15:17** (dinner of herbs with love better than feast with hatred — moral-relational evaluation); (4) **Pro 16:32** (slow to anger better than mighty — inner character better than external power — shared anchor with anger registry); (5) **Pro 19:22** (steadfast love most desirable — moral evaluation of character-quality over material goods). M04-K-VCG-03 is essentially the moral evaluation faculty applied to material Pleasure — the wisdom literature training the evaluative faculty to prefer what is genuinely more pleasant.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Partially: (1) **Psa 118:23** ("this is the Lord's doing; it is marvellous in our eyes") — the evaluative act of recognising God as the agent of the marvellous is a form of moral-theological evaluation; (2) **Gal 1:6** — Paul's astonished moral evaluation of the Galatians' theological defection; his thauma is simultaneously a moral judgment that something wrong has happened; (3) **Rev 17:7** — the angel's "why do you marvel?" to John implies that some marvelling requires moral-evaluative redirection — not everything that produces Wonder deserves it; (4) **Psa 9:1** ("wonderful deeds" in the context of God's just judgment on the wicked — Psa 9:4–6) — Wonder at God's just judgments involves moral evaluation.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Moral evaluation engagement varies across the cluster: (1) **Constitutively moral**: Gladness (Char 3) — M04-L-VCG-02's 45-verse corpus is the moral evaluation faculty in operation; Gladness and moral evaluation are functionally co-constitutive in this characteristic; this makes Gladness the most morally-constituted positive characteristic in M04; (2) **Morally diagnostic**: the direction of each characteristic reveals the state of the person's moral evaluation: what one exults in (Char 1), rejoices in (Char 2), delights in (Char 4), finds pleasant (Char 5), and wonders at (Char 6) all diagnose the moral evaluation faculty's current orientation; (3) **Morally constraining**: Wonder (Char 6) — Rev 17:7's angel correcting John's marvelling at the harlot confirms that not all Wonder is morally appropriate; the angel is effectively applying moral evaluation to the Wonder-response; Joy (Char 2) — 1Cor 13:6 ("love does not rejoice at wrongdoing") is an explicit moral constraint on Joy; (4) **Morally co-constitutive**: Delight (Char 4) — the direction of Delight reveals the moral evaluation faculty's state more diagnostically than any other characteristic: "what a person delights in is what they judge to be good" (Char 4 T3.8.3 finding); (5) **Morally indirect**: Pleasure (Char 5) — morally engaged through the wisdom-comparative register (M04-K-VCG-03) rather than constitutively.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Pervasively. The moral evaluation faculty — the capacity to assess against a standard of right, good, and true — is the primary internal generator of shame in the M07-B and M07-C registers. Shame is what the moral evaluation faculty produces when it accurately registers failure. The Proverbs pattern (Pro 3:35; 6:33; 13:5; 13:18; 18:3; 18:13) consistently presents shame as the moral-evaluation output of specific failures: folly inherits disgrace, deception produces shame, wickedness generates dishonour. The M07-C guilt-shame register is entirely about the moral evaluation faculty registering the person's own sin before God's holiness. The M07-B seared-conscience register is about the destruction of the moral evaluation faculty: those who cannot blush have lost the capacity for moral evaluation that should produce shame.

**[CHAR-2]** E — In VCG-03, CHAR-2 is deeply morally evaluated: Pro 11:2 — "when pride comes, then comes disgrace" — is a wisdom-tradition moral evaluation of the pride to humiliation connection. God's abasing act is morally just. The VCG-01 and VCG-02 modes are more ambiguous morally — David's envoys were humiliated unjustly. The moral evaluation of CHAR-2 depends on whether the humiliation is just (corrective of pride) or unjust (inflicted on the innocent).

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3 is produced by failed moral evaluation (the worth-assessment capacity distorted). Eze 23:13 (VCG-02): "I saw that she was defiled" — God's moral evaluation of the community's condition as defiled, operating as the standard of assessment. Jer 2:23 (VCG-02): the community's self-evaluation ("I am not unclean") is contrasted with what prophetic moral evaluation reveals.

**[CHAR-4]** S — The 21-verse corpus does not evidence engagement with the moral evaluation faculty in the inhabited person. The characteristic operates through spiritual domination of will and faculties, not through distortion of moral assessment capacity. The spirits make one moral-evaluative declaration (Mar 3:11 — "You are the Son of God"), but this is the spirits' recognition of Christ's moral-ontological superiority, not the person's moral evaluation.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Characteristics 1, 2, and 3 engage the moral evaluation faculty substantially; Characteristic 4 does not. Characteristic 1: moral evaluation in the categorical-boundary maintenance mode (Lev 20:25 — the clean/unclean distinction as the basis of covenant identity; Deu 26:14 — integrity-assessment of one's own conduct within the ritual system). Characteristic 2: moral evaluation of one's own inner condition (Isa 6:5 — the prophet's self-evaluation as morally defiled before divine holiness; Mat 23:27 — Jesus's Woe pronouncement as authoritative naming of hidden defilement; Eph 5:5 — doctrinal-normative evaluation establishing the standard). Characteristic 3: moral evaluation as institutional vocation (Eze 22:26 — the priestly failure to distinguish holy from common; Eze 44:23 — the restored priests' vocation of teaching moral evaluation; Eze 23:13 — God's moral evaluation as the definitive standard against the community's self-deceptive denial — Jer 2:23). Characteristic 4: silent on moral evaluation — the characteristic operates prior to moral evaluation through direct spiritual domination.

findings.session_b_note:
**Enables more accurate moral self-assessment:** The parable of Mat 18 functions by sharpening the moral evaluation faculty — the servant's incongruence becomes visible only when the scale of received forgiveness is compared with the scale of withheld forgiveness. Received forgiveness creates the moral context for accurate self-assessment: "you have been forgiven enormously; you withhold a fraction."

**May impair moral evaluation if presumed upon:** Psa 130:4 — "that you may be feared" — the counterintuitive direction implies that a shallow reception of forgiveness (without the accompanying reverence) might impair moral seriousness. If forgiveness is received without the reverential fear it should produce, the moral evaluation faculty may be dulled — presuming on pardon rather than being sharpened by it.

*Gap noted:* Whether forgiveness consistently deepens or may sometimes impair moral evaluation is not fully explored in the data. The Psa 130:4 observation implies the risk of impairment; the parable of Mat 18 implies the enablement of sharper self-assessment. The data is partial on this question.

findings.session_b_note:
**Compassion deepens moral evaluation:** The Good Samaritan pattern shows that compassion produces a deeper moral perception — seeing the wounded man as a full person, a neighbour, worthy of complete investment. The compassion-movement enables the moral evaluation faculty to assess the situation rightly. Without it, the priest and Levite assessed incorrectly — they saw the situation through the lens of ritual risk and social distance rather than through the lens of human need.

**Compassion is the moral evaluative standard in key contexts:** Hos 6:6 — "I desire steadfast love (chesed) and not sacrifice" — places compassion above ritual observance as the moral norm. Jesus cites this verse twice (Matt 9:13; 12:7 — though these are not anchor verses in this registry, the Hos 6:6 anchor links to the Synoptic pattern). Compassion as moral standard deepens the moral evaluation of all other practices — sacrifice, ritual, observance — by providing the criterion against which they are measured.

**Compassion does not bypass moral evaluation:** The judicial prohibition pattern (chus — "shall not pity") shows that compassion can be assessed as morally wrong to follow in specific contexts. The moral evaluation faculty retains authority over the compassion-impulse. Compassion does not claim exemption from moral assessment — it is itself subject to the moral evaluation of whether and how it should be expressed.

findings.session_b_note:
Contrition **deepens and truthifies** moral evaluation. The registry description distinguishes genuine contrition from surface shame — the difference is precisely in the depth and accuracy of the moral evaluation: genuine contrition is the "interior grief of having actually caused harm" (accurate moral assessment) versus "surface shame of being caught" (reactive self-protection rather than genuine moral assessment). Contrition enables the moral evaluation faculty to see clearly and truthfully rather than defensively.

The contrast: the hardened posture of Jer 44:10 implies impaired moral evaluation — the people are not assessing their condition accurately against God's standard. The contrite condition produces and is constituted by accurate moral self-assessment.

*New finding: contrition is the inner-being condition that corresponds to accurate moral evaluation — it is both produced by and productive of honest moral self-assessment. The absence of contrition correlates with impaired moral evaluation (whether through self-deception, pride, or active resistance to divine assessment).*

findings.session_b_note:
**Deepening moral evaluation:** Righteous companionship (Psa 119:63, Isa 1:23 by contrast) provides a community context in which moral evaluation is sharpened. Being among those who fear God and keep precepts supports the person's own moral evaluation capacity.

**Bypassing moral evaluation (partially):** Idolatrous joining (Hos 4:17) and the constitutional fixity of wrong-formed character (Jer 13:23) suggest that sustained wrong fellowship can progressively impair the person's capacity to apply accurate moral evaluation — what has been joined to becomes the new standard. The person joined to idols may no longer accurately evaluate the wrongness of that joining.

**Gap:** The mechanism by which fellowship impairs moral evaluation (the process of normalization through wrong companionship) is not directly analysed in the data beyond Jer 13:23.

findings.session_b_note: Goodness enables and deepens moral evaluation when genuine; distorted goodness specifically impairs it. The enabling function: the standard of the good, as revealed and received (Mic 6:8 — "He has told you what is good"), calibrates the moral evaluation faculty. The person who possesses genuine goodness can accurately assess what is and is not good. The deepening function: the comparative wisdom mode actively trains the evaluative capacity — the better-than sayings develop discernment. The impairing function: Mal 2:17 / Jer 44:17 describe the condition where moral evaluation is inverted — the faculty is functioning but its standard has been corrupted. This is the most severe impairment: the evaluative faculty applied to a false standard produces confident but wrong moral verdicts. (OBS-067-OBS-012, OBS-067-OBS-021, SBF-067-Q065)

findings.session_b_note: Love **enables and calibrates** moral evaluation — it is the primary calibrator of the moral faculty's standards. Psa 97:10 (OBS-103-115): 'O you who love the Lord, hate evil' — love of God calibrates the moral evaluation that rightly identifies evil as what must be hated. Lev 19:17 (OBS-103-114): the prohibition on hating the brother 'in your heart' requires moral evaluation of inner states, not just outer acts — love enables the inner moral evaluation that reaches below behaviour to motivation. 1Cor 13:6 (within OBS-103-127): love 'does not rejoice in wrongdoing but rejoices with the truth' — love calibrates the moral evaluation faculty so that wrongdoing generates the correct response (non-rejoicing) and truth generates joy. Disordered love impairs moral evaluation: the Pharisees' love-of-money produced mockery of Jesus' teaching (Luk 16:14, OBS-103-136) — a distorted moral evaluation produced by a distorted love.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-003: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion re…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion responds, it does not originate or create. It is the most responsive of the faculties-engaging characteristics. Second, affect and moral action are structurally unified in compassion — not sequentially related but simultaneous. Affect is the mechanism of movement (splanchnizō is both the felt inner event and the cause of the action), not a precursor or accompaniment. This is unique among the characteristics reviewed: in most other registries, affect and volition are distinguishable stages; in compassion, the felt movement is already the morally motivated action beginning. A third distinctive finding: compassion converts moral knowledge into motivated action — it is the motivational ground of conscientiousness, not a product of it. The conscience faculty engagement reveals compassion as conscience-healing: it addresses the pitiable condition that conscience perceives as a moral claim, resolving the tension between moral knowledge and moral incapacity. The three relational modes (building/sustaining — chesed; restoring/repairing — splanchnizō; extending across difference — Good Samaritan) are a new finding not in the instruction typology.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-003: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked …
findings.finding_value: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I but the grace of God that is with me." Agency is not displaced but constituted by grace. This relationship holds in paradox that the T3.6 prompt options (enable/deepen/bypass/impair) cannot accommodate — a prompt design limitation noted for catalogue revision. Second, grace produces moral clarity (T3.8 — sharpens moral evaluation rather than bypassing it): the person who recognises grace has made a precise moral evaluation (they know they received what they did not deserve). Third, grace and conscience are mutually necessary: grace is the condition within which conscience can operate fully without destroying the person; conscience without grace produces condemnation; grace without conscience produces presumption (T3.9). Fourth, grace is the primary relational faculty developer in the registry's evidence — it reaches every relational register (vertical access, horizontal forgiving, speech-grace) and enables each one. Creativity (T3.5) is the one genuinely silent faculty — not an impairment but a non-engagement: grace receives and constitutes, it does not create.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-009: T1's immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response) is the affective-volitional expression of T3's faculty engagement at the moment grace arrives. T3…
findings.finding_value: T1's immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response) is the affective-volitional expression of T3's faculty engagement at the moment grace arrives. T3.4 (affect is the first named faculty engaged by grace) and T3.6 (the agency-constituting paradox of 1Cor 15:10) together explain why T1.5 finds the creaturely recognition response before positive states settle: grace first produces the affective recognition (fear, mourning) before constituting the agency through which the person responds (prostration as the body enacting the inner posture that grace has produced). T1's finding that grace requires creaturely recognition to complete its operation (T1.7) is T3.1's finding at the faculty level: grace requires and enables perception simultaneously.

findings.finding_value: T3's faculty findings explain several patterns in T6's co-occurrence landscape. The seeking co-occurrence dominance (R140 — 40 verses) is partly explained by T3.6's agency-constituting finding: seeking requires the constituted agency that grace provides for its own reception (SD026 — grace giving the capacity for supplication). The power cluster co-occurrences (strength R187 — 15 verses, might R198 — 10 verses) confirm T3.7's agency-constituting finding at the cross-registry level: grace producing agency is registered as co-occurring with power/strength across the corpus. T3.8's moral clarity finding explains the guilt co-occurrence (R073 — 10 verses): the moral clarity grace produces is most visible at the point of moral failure, and the co-occurrence reflects this — grace and guilt appear together because grace produces the moral clarity that accurately names the guilt it addresses.

findings.session_b_note: Covenant enables and structures moral evaluation; it does not bypass or impair it. (1) Enabling: the covenant provides the moral framework within which the person's actions and character can be assessed — covenant terms are the evaluative standard. Without the covenant's law-content, moral evaluation has no defined reference point in the OT framework. (2) Deepening: the new covenant deepens moral evaluation by internalising the evaluative standard — the law written on the heart (Heb 8:10) means the moral standard is not external to be measured against but internal, shaping moral perception from within. The new covenant person does not merely evaluate their actions against an external law but has the law's evaluative criteria as part of their inner constitution. (3) The covenant's curse-mechanism (alah — OBS-034-007) is the ultimate moral evaluation tool: it activates against the one who has failed the moral assessment built into the covenant oath.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-117-003: T3 identifies conscience as peace's primary gateway faculty — the inner faculty whose state most directly determines whether genuine peace is constitutionally accessible. Three conscience-patterns: su…
findings.finding_value: T3 identifies conscience as peace's primary gateway faculty — the inner faculty whose state most directly determines whether genuine peace is constitutionally accessible. Three conscience-patterns: suppressed conscience destroys peace somatically (Psa 32:3 — bones wasting); exercised conscience restores peace through confession (Psa 32:5); bypassed conscience produces false peace (Deu 29:19). No other inner faculty has this bidirectional gateway function as clearly documented. The moral evaluation faculty (T3.8) confirms: authentic peace enables right moral judgment; false peace corrupts it. The practical implication: the route back from peacelessness is through conscience-exercise (confession, acknowledgment, remembering God's faithfulness), not through direct emotional management.

findings.session_b_note: The endowing giving (872-003) enables moral evaluation: wisdom and understanding given to the inward parts (Job 38:36) constitute the cognitive capacity for right moral discernment. The eschatological giving restores the inner-being orientation from which moral evaluation flows — "oaks of righteousness" (Isa 61:3) names a stable moral identity restored by the giving. Covenantal giving (872-001) deepens moral evaluation by grounding the person's identity in the narrative of divine faithfulness — the memory of God's reliable giving provides the moral framework against which actions are assessed. In the failure direction: the judicial giving-over (872-004) may represent a consequence of failed moral evaluation (Israel's failure to assess rightly what faithfulness required), though the data is more explicit about the consequence than the prior failure.

Moral evaluation is a significant faculty across all sub-groups. The cluster's characteristics are morally evaluative in multiple senses: they are moral qualities themselves (subject to moral assessment); they require moral evaluation to be rightly practiced (discerning when compassion should be withheld, whether fellowship is genuine); and they serve as moral standards (love as the fulfilling of the law).
