findings.finding_value: M01-A **enables and deepens** moral evaluation by providing an interior standard (fear of God as inner ethical judge, Lev 19:14; Neh 5:15). The person who fears God has an interior moral referee that continues to operate even when external consequences are removed.

M01-B's social fear and M01-G timidity **bypass and impair** moral evaluation. Social fear substitutes crowd opinion for moral principle (Gal 2:12; 1Sa 15:24). Timidity substitutes self-preservation for moral faithfulness (Mat 25:25; Rev 21:8).

M01-B's social fear and M01-G timidity **bypass and impair** moral evaluation. Social fear substitutes crowd opinion for moral principle (Gal 2:12; 1Sa 15:24). Timidity substitutes self-preservation for moral faithfulness (Mat 25:25; Rev 21:8).

The pattern is the clearest moral-evaluation finding in the cluster: M01-A reverential fear is the foundation of interior moral evaluation; social fear (M01-B-VCG-04) and timidity (M01-G) are the systematic bypasses of it.

Possessing rage bypasses moral evaluation: Job 36:18 (M02-B-VCG-03) — "rage can seduce a person into scoffing, showing its capacity to distort judgment and lead the inner will astray." The possessing form corrupts the moral evaluation faculty, substituting rage-momentum for principled assessment.

Righteous anger deepens moral evaluation: 2Cor 7:11 (M02-C-VCG-02) — indignation as proof of genuine repentance shows that moral anger (indignation) is itself an evidence of the moral evaluation faculty working accurately — the person has correctly evaluated the wrong they did.

Righteous anger deepens moral evaluation: 2Cor 7:11 (M02-C-VCG-02) — indignation as proof of genuine repentance shows that moral anger (indignation) is itself an evidence of the moral evaluation faculty working accurately — the person has correctly evaluated the wrong they did.

Grief deepens moral evaluation: godly grief produces "indignation" as one of its moral fruits (2Cor 7:11 — M03-C-VCG-02) — a sharpened moral sensitivity toward the wrong that produced the grief. Conscience-driven sighing (Eze 9:4 — M03-E-VCG-01) is itself evidence of moral evaluation operating in the inner being. The absence of grief where grief is morally appropriate signals that moral evaluation is not functioning (1Cor 5:2; Amo 6:6 — M03-B-VCG-04, BOUNDARY). Grief does not bypass or impair moral evaluation; it is one of the primary signs that moral evaluation is active.

Grief deepens moral evaluation: godly grief produces "indignation" as one of its moral fruits (2Cor 7:11 — M03-C-VCG-02) — a sharpened moral sensitivity toward the wrong that produced the grief. Conscience-driven sighing (Eze 9:4 — M03-E-VCG-01) is itself evidence of moral evaluation operating in the inner being. The absence of grief where grief is morally appropriate signals that moral evaluation is not functioning (1Cor 5:2; Amo 6:6 — M03-B-VCG-04, BOUNDARY). Grief does not bypass or impair moral evaluation; it is one of the primary signs that moral evaluation is active.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Rightly-directed exultation deepens moral evaluation — Psa 97:8 shows the daughters of Judah rejoicing specifically because of God's "judgments," making moral appreciation of divine justice the ground of their joy. Misdirected exultation (Pro 2:14; Hos 9:1; 10:5) is associated with moral blindness and corruption. The characteristic both requires and reinforces moral discernment.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Rightly-directed Joy deepens moral evaluation: the person who rejoices in God's judgments (Psa 97:8) is thereby reinforcing their appreciation of divine justice. Misdirected Joy corrupts and bypasses moral evaluation: Pro 2:14 (those who "rejoice in doing evil") show Joy bypassing moral evaluation entirely; Eze 25:6 ("malice within your soul" as source of corrupt joy) shows Joy rooted in moral corruption producing perverse evaluation.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Suffering-Joy does not bypass moral evaluation of suffering — 1Pe 1:6 acknowledges the grief as genuine and the trials as actually grievous; Jas 1:2 does not say trials are good (evaluating them as the good) but says to count them AS joy because of what they produce. The moral faculty is not bypassed but the characteristic operates at a different level — not evaluation of the suffering's goodness but transcendence of the evaluation through Spirit-grounding.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Gladness deepens moral evaluation: the person whose inner life is settled in the recognition of what is genuinely good (M04-L-VCG-01 — divine character goodness as the standard) has the reference point from which all other moral evaluation proceeds. Distorted Gladness bypasses moral evaluation: Isa 41:7's craftsman saying "it is good" over an idol is a short-circuit of genuine moral evaluation.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Delight deepens moral evaluation when rightly directed: the person who delights in God's law meditates on its moral content continuously (Psa 1:2); the person who delights in doing God's will has an inward moral compass (Psa 40:8; Joh 8:29). Misdirected Delight impairs and bypasses moral evaluation: Isa 66:3 (soul delighting in abominations — the moral evaluation faculty overridden by the force of misdirected pleasure); 2Th 2:12 (pleasure in unrighteousness — those condemned had their moral evaluation replaced by an anti-moral Delight); Pro 18:2 (fool taking pleasure only in his own opinion — moral evaluation bypassed by self-referential delight).

**[CHAR-5]** E — Right Pleasure in wisdom enables and deepens moral evaluation: Pro 2:10's wisdom-in-heart producing Pleasure in knowledge enables the whole evaluative apparatus of wisdom including moral judgment. Wrong Pleasure bypasses moral evaluation: Pro 9:17's stolen-bread Pleasure makes the forbidden appear genuinely pleasant, preventing accurate moral evaluation of the act.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Wonder at God's justice (Psa 9) deepens moral evaluation: recognising God's acts as marvellous includes recognising that he acts with justice, which deepens the appreciation of moral reality. Rev 17:7's redirected wonder shows that Wonder can be applied inappropriately (marvelling at evil) — the angel's "why do you marvel?" is a moral-evaluative correction to misapplied Wonder. Genuine Wonder at the right object deepens moral evaluation; misapplied Wonder bypasses it.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The most significant cluster-level pattern on moral evaluation: (1) The characteristics whose direction is toward God's own moral preferences (steadfast love, justice, righteousness — Jer 9:24) deepen moral evaluation; (2) The characteristics whose direction is toward wrong objects (delight in abominations — Isa 66:3; rejoicing in evil — Pro 2:14) bypass and corrupt moral evaluation; (3) **Gladness (Char 3)** is the characteristic most directly formative of moral evaluation — Mic 6:8's "he has told you, O man, what is good" defines the standard by which all Gladness-evaluation operates; formation in the Gladness-evaluative faculty is formation in moral discernment.

**[CHAR-1]** E — In its corrective form, shame **enables and deepens** moral evaluation: entropē (1Cor 6:5; 15:34) uses shame to awaken the community's moral evaluation of their own failure. The gateway-of-shame passages (Eze 43:10-11) show shame as the precondition for the house of Israel receiving the moral design of the temple — shame clears the inner space for accurate moral perception. In its hardened form, shame's absence **impairs** moral evaluation catastrophically — the seared conscience neither evaluates nor corrects. In its acute wound-form (M07-A unjust shame), shame can **bypass** moral evaluation by arriving before it — the unjust wound produces shame regardless of what the moral evaluation faculty says about the person's actual standing.

**[CHAR-2]** E — In VCG-03, CHAR-2 is deeply morally evaluated: Pro 11:2 — "when pride comes, then comes disgrace" — is a wisdom-tradition moral evaluation of the pride to humiliation connection. God's abasing act is morally just. The VCG-01 and VCG-02 modes are more ambiguous morally — David's envoys were humiliated unjustly. The moral evaluation of CHAR-2 depends on whether the humiliation is just (corrective of pride) or unjust (inflicted on the innocent).

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3 is produced by failed moral evaluation (the worth-assessment capacity distorted). Rom 2:23 — boasting in the law while breaking it — is the clearest case of moral evaluation corrupted: the person evaluates themselves as honouring the law while their conduct denies it, and simultaneously dishonours God.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4 is constitutively the moral-evaluation faculty in its shame-recognitive mode. It is the characteristic most directly about moral evaluation. VCG-03 shows this faculty corrupted — the inverted conscience does evaluate, but by a wrong standard.

---

**[CHAR-5]** E — Moral evaluation is engaged in CHAR-5 through the contempt-er's distorted moral evaluation (treating persons as of less worth than they have) and through the community's moral evaluation of the contempt-act itself. The commands against despising (Rom 14:3; 14:10; 1Cor 16:11; 1Th 5:20) are moral-evaluative instructions: despising a brother is wrong, and the community's moral evaluation must recognise it as wrong.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — Moral evaluation is engaged in CHAR-6: the person who claims innocence (Gen 20:5; Psa 26:6) is making a moral-evaluative self-assessment — they are evaluating their own conduct against the standard of blameless moral integrity. God's confirmation of Abimelech's innocence (Gen 20:6) is the authoritative moral evaluation that validates the self-assessment. CHAR-6 depends on and engages the moral-evaluation faculty in its self-assessment mode.

---

**[CLUSTER]** E — The moral evaluation faculty runs through all six characteristics and is the constitutive faculty of Char 4. Cluster-level moral-evaluation map: the functioning conscience identifies the shameful (Char 4), registers guilt-shame (Char 1 M07-C), correctly assigns worth (Chars 3, 5 in their positive registers), and maintains the innocence that counters guilt-shame (Char 6). The corrupted conscience glories in shame (Char 4's VCG-03), produces self-righteous contempt (Char 5's generating mechanism — Luk 18:9), dishonours God through hypocrisy (Char 3 — Rom 2:23), and loses the capacity for moral purity (Char 6 — Hos 8:5). Cluster-level finding: the moral evaluation faculty's condition is the primary determinant of whether M07's characteristics function healingly or destructively. A properly calibrated moral evaluation faculty produces the shame that corrects, the conscience that identifies the shameful, and the innocence that enables approach to God. A corrupted moral evaluation faculty produces shame that paralyses, conscience that inverts, and incapacity for innocence that blocks approach.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — CHAR-1 impairs moral evaluation by displacing its reference point (God) and replacing it with the self's own evaluation of what is worthy. Psa 10:4 (vc=34074, M08-A2-VCG-02): "all his thoughts are, 'there is no God'" — eliminating the divine reference point removes the moral standard by which one's own position and actions should be assessed. Luk 16:15 (vc=60870, M08-A4-VCG-01): human moral evaluation prizes what God calls abomination — the two standards diverge so completely that CHAR-1 produces an inverted moral assessment framework. Eze 28:17 (vc=34047, M08-A1-VCG-02): wisdom corruption means the faculty that discerns right from wrong is damaged. The moral evaluation faculty is not absent in the proud person — it is active, but evaluating by the wrong standard (the self's elevation as the criterion of worth).

**[CHAR-2]** E — CHAR-2 bypasses moral evaluation. Jer 43:2 (vc=34105, M08-B-VCG-02): "the insolent men said to Jeremiah, 'You are telling a lie'" — they substitute their own evaluation for the divinely-mediated prophetic word, showing that CHAR-2 treats the self's assessment as the final moral authority. Psa 119:21 (vc=34098, M08-B-VCG-02): the arrogant "wander from your commandments" — the divine moral standard is treated as non-binding; the self's will replaces the commandment as the evaluative criterion.

**[CHAR-3]** E — VCG-01 impairs moral evaluation by producing a distorted self-assessment that overestimates the self's moral standing (Rom 2:23 — boasting in the law, breaking the law). VCG-02 engages and deepens moral evaluation: 2Cor 1:12 (vc=33912) — the boast grounded in conscience's testimony to "holiness and godly sincerity" requires active moral self-assessment. VCG-03 redirects moral evaluation outward to God as the proper object of glorying. CHAR-3's three registers demonstrate the full spectrum: moral-evaluation-distorting (VCG-01), moral-evaluation-engaging (VCG-02), moral-evaluation-transcending (VCG-03).

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4 severely impairs moral evaluation through the inflated self-picture that overrides accurate moral assessment. The puffed-up person evaluates themselves as competent (1Cor 4:19 — confident in talk), morally superior (1Cor 5:2 — not mourning the moral failure), and spiritually advanced (Col 2:18 — based on claimed spiritual experience) — all false evaluations generated by CHAR-4.

**[CHAR-5]** E — CHAR-5 bypasses and impairs moral evaluation through the self-sufficiency conviction it generates. Eze 16:49 (vc=33979, M08-E-VCG-01): the person or community with structural power sees themselves as complete and self-sufficient; the moral obligation to aid others arises only when one sees oneself as part of a shared community of need. CHAR-5's self-sufficiency claim ("I am, and there is no one besides me" — Isa 47:8, vc=9563) specifically removes the relational recognition that would ground moral obligation to others.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All five bypass and impair moral evaluation. The cluster comparison reveals that the impairment is most comprehensive in CHAR-4 ("understanding nothing") and CHAR-1 (functional atheism as the endpoint of full pride), and most specifically directional in CHAR-2 (the self's assessment substituted for the divinely-established standard) and CHAR-5 (moral obligation to the poor rendered invisible). CHAR-3 is distinctive: in its VCG-02 register, the moral evaluation faculty is actively engaged through conscience (2Cor 1:12, M08-C-VCG-02: "the testimony of our conscience" as the ground of examined boasting) — making CHAR-3 the only M08 characteristic that evidences the moral evaluation faculty functioning positively within the characteristic's own discourse.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Submission *enables and deepens* moral evaluation. Rom16:19 — Paul redirects the Romans' obedient disposition toward "wisdom as to what is good and innocence as to what is evil" — the obedient will is the posture from which genuine moral discernment grows. Gal2:5 — the willingness to withhold submission when the authority is illegitimate evidences that genuine submission presupposes and deepens moral evaluation (the person must be able to assess the authority's legitimacy). The submission that bypasses moral evaluation — yielding without assessing the authority's legitimacy — is the Milgram-style pathological compliance that the evidence (Gal2:5 as principled non-submission) specifically guards against.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Contrition *presupposes and validates* moral evaluation. The person who arrives at genuine contrition has allowed their moral evaluation faculty to function without self-protective distortion — the breaking is, in part, the event of genuine moral self-knowledge before God's holiness. The characteristic confirms and deepens accurate moral evaluation by its very existence: the crushed spirit is evidence that the moral evaluation faculty has genuinely perceived the person's condition rather than protecting the self from that perception.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Meekness/gentleness *deepens and calibrates* moral evaluation. The shared-weakness self-awareness (Heb5:2) that grounds metriopatheō prevents the moral evaluation faculty from operating with prideful distortion — the person who genuinely knows their own weakness assesses others' moral conditions more accurately. The characteristic enables the moral evaluation faculty to function without the distortion of assumed superiority that harshness introduces.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Semnotēs *enables and confirms* genuine moral evaluation in the sense that the person of genuine semnotēs is one whose moral seriousness is authentic rather than performed. Tit2:7 — teaching that has both integrity and dignity is teaching whose moral evaluation is genuine — the integrity is the moral content; the dignity is the character-gravity that confirms the moral content is genuinely held rather than performed. The characteristic thus confirms that the moral evaluation faculty is functioning genuinely rather than performing its function for display.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Willing-heartedness *enables genuine moral evaluation* to produce the appropriate response. The person whose inner will is freely-oriented toward God can respond genuinely to the moral evaluation's conclusion (giving is right and good) — the evaluation and the will's response are aligned. The person without willing-heartedness may evaluate giving as right but find their will unresponsive to the moral evaluation's conclusion — the moral evaluation faculty functions but the will does not follow.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Humility *enables and deepens* moral evaluation. Pro11:2 — "with the humble is wisdom" — and the evidence that the humble person can identify their own fault (Hezekiah in 2Ch32:26; Josiah in 2Ch34:27) suggest that the humble person's moral evaluation faculty operates without the distortion that pride introduces. Col2:18 identifies the "sensuous mind" operating beneath false humility as a site of distorted moral evaluation — the puffed-up person cannot accurately evaluate their own moral condition. Genuine humility enables accurate moral self-assessment because it does not require the protective distortions that maintain the illusion of rightness.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All six enable and deepen moral evaluation; none bypass or impair it. Humility (CHAR-1) enables accurate moral self-assessment — the humble person can identify their own fault (Hezekiah in 2Ch32:26; Josiah in 2Ch34:27); Col2:18's puffed-up sensuous mind confirms that performed humility distorts rather than enables moral evaluation. Submission (CHAR-2) enables moral evaluation of the authority's legitimacy as constitutive — Gal2:5 (withholding from false teachers) evidences that genuine submission requires moral evaluation of whether the authority is legitimate; Rom16:19 (wisdom as to what is good) confirms that submission produces rather than bypasses moral discernment. Contrition (CHAR-3) presupposes and validates accurate moral evaluation — the crushed spirit is evidence that the moral evaluation faculty has genuinely perceived the person's condition rather than protecting the self from that perception. Meekness and Gentleness (CHAR-4) calibrates moral evaluation of others' conditions through prior moral self-assessment (Heb5:2 — the self-knowledge of shared weakness precedes accurate judgment of the erring). Dignity (CHAR-5) confirms genuine conscience-function (Tit2:7 — integrity + semnotēs confirm the moral evaluation faculty is shaping the whole characterological manner). Willing-heartedness (CHAR-6) enables moral evaluation's conclusion to produce actual conduct rather than remaining in the knowing-good/not-doing-good gap. Cluster-level: M09 is a morally evaluative cluster — genuine possession of any characteristic requires and enables accurate moral evaluation.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — Wilful sinning *bypasses* moral evaluation in the act of commission. The will acts despite the available moral evaluation: Saul (1Sa 15:24) knew the command but obeyed the people's voice — the moral evaluation was available but overridden. Over time, sustained sinning *impairs* moral evaluation: Isa 1:4's people "despise the Holy One of Israel" — the moral evaluation faculty has become inverted, treating the holy as contemptible. This impairment trajectory from bypass (single act) to inversion (sustained pattern) is the moral-evaluation consequence of wilful sinning.

**[CHAR-10]** E — (1) *Enticement bypasses moral evaluation*: Jam 1:14 — desire engages before moral evaluation deliberates; the mechanism exploits the pre-deliberative desire-faculty to capture the person before moral evaluation can assess the situation. (2) *Hypocrisy distorts moral evaluation*: Gal 2:13 — collective hypocrisy corrupts the moral evaluation of the socially conforming individuals; the social weight of the group's behaviour overrides individual moral assessment. (3) *Apostasy reflects impaired moral evaluation*: Act 21:21 — the forsaking of Moses implies a moral evaluation that has incorrectly assessed the covenantal obligation — the moral evaluation faculty has produced a false conclusion about the covenantal commitment.

**[CHAR-11]** E — The condition *distorts and bypasses* moral evaluation. Heb 3:13 — "hardened by the deceitfulness of sin" — the hardening of the heart that sin's deceitfulness produces is a moral-evaluative hardening: the person's capacity to correctly evaluate their own condition is progressively diminished. Joh 9:41 — the Pharisees' false evaluation of their own seeing (while the condition persists) shows the condition distorting self-moral-evaluation: they evaluate themselves as seeing when the condition has produced blindness. The condition's self-concealing nature (perceptive pattern — T3.1.3) is also a moral-evaluative concealment.

**[CHAR-12]** E — The enslaving power *bypasses and distorts* moral evaluation: the enslaved person evaluates themselves as free (Joh 8:33 — "we have never been enslaved") while the enslaving power holds them. The moral evaluation faculty cannot accurately assess the enslaved condition from within it; the externally-declared moral assessment (Jesus in Joh 8:34; John in 1Jo 3:8) is required to supply what the enslaved person's own moral evaluation cannot generate.

**[CHAR-13]** E — The record *reveals the failure of the moral evaluation faculty* most precisely: Job 13:23 — Job cannot evaluate the extent of his own record; Jer 16:10 — the people under judgment cannot evaluate their own sin; Hos 12:8 — prosperity impairs Ephraim's moral self-evaluation. The record exceeds the person's own moral evaluation capacity — God's assessment of the record is more accurate than the person's self-assessment (Amo 5:12 — "I know how many are your transgressions"). The characteristic thus reveals the inherent limitation of self-directed moral evaluation.

**[CHAR-14]** E — Forgiveness received *corrects and deepens* moral evaluation. The woman of Luk 7:47 whose sins were many and who loved much had a more accurate moral self-evaluation (she recognised the many sins) than the Pharisee who loved little (implicitly evaluating himself as needing little forgiveness). The received forgiveness deepens moral evaluation by confirming what the seeker's moral evaluation recognised: that the sin-record was real, was many, and required this specific act of forgiving grace.

**[CHAR-15]** E — The generational pattern *impairs* moral evaluation in the active sinning phase and *enables* it only under pressure of consequences. Psa 78:32 — "they still sinned; despite his wonders, they did not believe" — the moral evaluation faculty fails to correctly identify the significance of the wonders for the community's moral orientation. The moral evaluation faculty is only correctly engaged when the outer consequences are undeniable (1Ki 8:47 — in captivity; Jer 8:14 — facing doom). The generational pattern delays and distorts correct moral evaluation until catastrophe forces it.

**[CHAR-16]** E — The sinner-identity *distorts* moral evaluation in the observer. Joh 9:24 — the Pharisees' wrong verdict on Jesus; Luk 13:2 — the wrong inference about Galilean sinners and their suffering. The self-righteous person's moral evaluation of others as sinners is systematically unreliable (Jesus corrects it; Joh 9:25 — honest uncertainty is more truthful than false certainty). The sinner's self-evaluation, when conscience-engaged, is more accurate (Luk 5:8; Luk 18:13; 1Ti 1:15).

**[CHAR-17]** E — The guilt-state *clarifies moral evaluation* when conscience operates correctly and *distorts* it when suppressed. Gen 42:21 — the brothers' guilt-state sharpens their moral evaluation of past conduct; they now correctly assess what they did as guilty. Eze 9:9 — "they say, 'The Lord does not see'" — the community's suppressed guilt produces an inverted moral evaluation: they misassess God's awareness and therefore their accountability. The guilt-state's clarifying effect on moral evaluation is its productive mode; its distorting effect (when guilt is suppressed) is its destructive mode.

**[CHAR-18]** E — Iniquity *distorts* the self-directed moral evaluation faculty. Psa 36:2 — "he flatters himself in his own eyes that his iniquity cannot be found out and hated" — the wicked person's self-directed moral evaluation cannot accurately assess the iniquity. Hos 12:8 — "they cannot find in me iniquity" — the moral evaluation of self is systematically skewed by wealth and pride. Conversely, the other-directed moral evaluation (Jer 14:7 — "our iniquities testify against us") is more accurate: the prophetic tradition's evaluation of the community's iniquity is correct. Iniquity impairs self-evaluation; it does not impair accurate evaluation by conscience or prophetic witness.

**[CHAR-19]** E — Sustained transgression *inverts* the moral evaluation faculty. Pro 28:24 — the moral evaluation faculty is used to deny transgression rather than recognise it; Jer 2:29 — the evaluating faculty produces self-justification ("why do you contend with me?") rather than self-recognition. The sustained transgressor's moral evaluation is not eliminated but redirected: it becomes skilled at moral rationalisation in the self-direction. The remedy restores accurate self-evaluation: Psa 51:3 — "I know my transgressions" — the conscience-engaged penitent's accurate moral self-assessment.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Unintentional sinning operates through the *bypassing* of moral evaluation at the act-moment — not because the faculty is impaired but because it lacks input. The moral evaluation faculty requires the morally relevant facts to function; without them, it cannot assess the act as prohibited. The realisation phase shows the faculty operating correctly once the information is available: it correctly identifies the act as sin and drives the confession response (Lev 5:5; Num 22:34).

**[CHAR-20]** E — Faithlessness *distorts* self-directed moral evaluation while leaving other-directed evaluation intact. 2Ch 28:22 — Ahaz becoming more faithless under distress cannot accurately evaluate his own condition; 2Ch 26:16/18 — Uzziah overstepping priestly bounds until the priests challenge him — the self-directed moral evaluation was impaired by pride. Conversely: Psa 119:158 — "I look at the faithless with disgust" — the faithful person's moral evaluation of others' faithlessness is acute; Jer 3:11 — God's comparative moral evaluation is precise.

**[CHAR-21]** E — Perversion *inverts* the moral evaluation faculty. Isa 29:16 — the creature evaluating the potter as if the clay could assess the maker — the most extreme moral-evaluation inversion: the creature's evaluative faculty is so perverted it assesses the creator incorrectly. Pro 19:3 — "his heart rages against the Lord" after his own folly ruins his way — the moral evaluation faculty wrongly assigns blame outward to God rather than inward to the self. Pro 2:14 — "delight in the perverseness of evil" — the evaluative faculty assesses perversity as delightful rather than shameful.

**[CHAR-22]** E — Injustice *inverts* the self-directed moral evaluation faculty while the God-centred moral evaluation remains intact in others. Zep 3:5 — "the unjust knows no shame" — self-directed moral evaluation eliminated; Pro 29:27 — "an unjust man is an abomination to the righteous" — the righteous person's moral evaluation of the unjust is acute. The unjust person cannot accurately evaluate their own injustice (shame absent) while the righteous observer evaluates it precisely (abomination).

**[CHAR-3]** E — Genuine confession *deepens* moral evaluation: the act of naming sin precisely requires and exercises the moral evaluation faculty. The more specific and layered the confession, the more deeply moral evaluation has operated. Num 12:11 — "done foolishly" adds a characterological dimension to the evaluation; Mat 27:4 — "betrayed innocent blood" adds a moral-victim dimension. These are not mere formulas but precise moral evaluations applied to specific acts. Hollow confession (Deu 1:41) shows moral evaluation present but truncated — the evaluation does not extend to assessing the next proposed action ("we will go up and fight") against the same standard.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Conscience suppression *impairs* moral evaluation specifically in its self-directed application. The moral evaluation faculty produces inaccurate verdicts when turned on the self: "I am innocent" (Jer 2:35 — false verdict), "things are fine because I am prospering" (Ecc 8:12 — false verdict). The faculty continues to operate but its outputs about the self are corrupted by the absence of accurate God-knowledge (1Cor 15:34) and the absence of the fear of God (Ecc 8:12) that would calibrate the evaluation correctly.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Refusal to repent *distorts* moral evaluation through minimisation (1Ki 16:31) and *bypasses* it in the deliberate-sinning mode (Heb 10:26 — the evaluation is correct but the will overrides it). Sustained refusal may impair moral evaluation by habituating the person to the minimisation assessment until it becomes the default cognitive framework, making accurate evaluation progressively harder.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Habitual defection *distorts* moral evaluation within the person: the self-reinforcing structure of Hos 8:11 (altars for sinning producing more sinning) implies a moral evaluation that finds the altars acceptable or even desirable — the sinning course has been normalised such that the moral evaluation faculty no longer registers it as problematic. Exo 9:34's Pharaoh — who sinned yet again once the plague ceased — reveals a moral evaluation that assessed the absence of immediate pressure as permission to resume sinning; the moral evaluation is responding to external consequence rather than to moral truth.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Contagious sin *distorts* the moral evaluation faculty by recalibrating the community's moral reference baseline from God's standard to the leader's transmitted sinning course. When the leader's authority-transmitted sinning becomes the operative norm, the community's moral evaluation assesses their own conduct against that norm: 1Ki 14:22 — they surpass even their fathers' sin, but their moral evaluation does not register this as extraordinary departure because the fathers' sin is already the operative baseline. The distortion accumulates generationally.

**[CHAR-8]** S — The corpus does not evidence how political revolt affects the moral evaluation faculty of the revolting parties. The moral evaluation is supplied by the narrator (theological framing) rather than attributed to the inner moral assessment of those involved in the revolt.

**[CHAR-9]** E — Sinful speech *expresses and deepens* impaired moral evaluation. The distorted moral-evaluation outputs of the corrupted heart (false verdicts — Mat 15:19 "evil thoughts") find their completed form in slanderous or blasphemous speech. Once articulated, the false moral verdict consolidates in the speaker's self-understanding and is more difficult to retract. Mar 14:64 — "they all condemned him as deserving death" — the blasphemy-verdict once spoken becomes the ground of action; the moral evaluation is hardened by its verbal articulation.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The characteristic inverts moral evaluation rather than simply impairing it. The inversion is active and sustained: the wicked person's moral compass has not disappeared but has been rotated so that what is perverse is known and chosen (Pro 10:32), what is unjust is rewarded (Isa 5:23), and what is good is despised (Psa 10:3 — "renounces the Lord"). This inversion is itself a form of deep impairment — the faculty is present but systematically misdirected. It also bypasses the corrective function of moral evaluation: the wicked person's moral assessment does not serve as a corrective to their conduct because the assessment itself is corrupted.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The characteristic inverts moral evaluation rather than simply eliminating it. The constitutionally evil person evaluates — they make moral assessments — but the evaluations are systematically wrong because the constitutional condition has skewed the standard. Mat 22:18 (vc=14408 — VCG-05): Jesus perceives their "malice" (ponēria) as a calculated entrapment — they evaluate their entrapment scheme as cunning and justified (self-assessed as moral victory). 1Pe 2:16 (vc=14370 — VCG-05): evil as the corrupt aim that freedom can serve — they evaluate freedom as a legitimate cover for evil. The moral evaluation faculty is present, active, and systematically inverted by the constitutional condition.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The characteristic perverts the moral evaluation faculty rather than eliminating it. Pro 17:15 (vc=1690 — VCG-01): perverted judgment — the evaluative faculty is operative but systematically inverted. Luk 16:15 (vc=21 — VCG-02): "you justify yourselves before men" — the moral evaluation faculty is actively deployed in self-justification rather than honest assessment. Pro 26:25 (vc=1694 — VCG-02): seven abominations hidden beneath gracious speech — the person evaluates their own inner state and constructs a concealing performance, showing they know their inner evaluation is negative (hence the concealment). The moral evaluation faculty is present, operating, but systematically misdirected — assessing others wrong and oneself with self-justifying bias.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The characteristic impairs the moral evaluation faculty by reducing its capacity to assess the gravity of idolatrous acts. Eze 8:17 (vc=65980 — VCG-05): abomination treated as trivial — the evaluative severity-assessment is impaired. The characteristic bypasses the faculty in the sense that the person proceeds with idolatrous acts without the evaluative check that would declare them abominable. This is connected to the cognitive impairment of the gravity-assessment function (T3.2.2). The moral evaluation faculty has not disappeared — the person still evaluates (Deu 13:14 — VCG-02: the community is expected to evaluate carefully when reports of apostasy arise) — but the faculty no longer accurately assesses the idolatrous acts as abominable to God.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The characteristic impairs and inverts the moral evaluation faculty. Psa 14:4 (VCG-03): moral knowledge absent — the faculty is impaired. Pro 30:20 (VCG-04): moral wrong evaluated as not-wrong — the faculty is inverted. Isa 59:4 (VCG-02): courts subverted — the institutional moral evaluation is bypassed by the scheming of those in power. The characteristic does not eliminate the capacity for moral assessment — Pro 30:20 shows the person still evaluating and rendering a verdict; it inverts the verdicts that the faculty produces. This is not cognitive impairment but moral-evaluative inversion.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The characteristic inverts and perverts the moral evaluation faculty. Rom 14:16 (VCG-02): calling good things evil — the faculty is operational but producing inverted outputs. Joh 18:30 (VCG-03): the innocent named as evildoer — systematic moral inversion. Jude 10 (vc=14355 — VCG-01): "blaspheme all that they do not understand" — here the moral evaluation faculty is not just inverted but bypassed: contempt substitutes for moral assessment rather than corrupting it. The moral evaluation faculty is thus engaged differently by VCG: VCG-01 bypasses it (contempt replaces assessment); VCG-02/03 invert it (produce false verdicts naming evil as good or good as evil).

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster reveals that M10b characteristics corrupt moral evaluation through two modes: (a) bypass (contempt substituting for assessment — Char 6 Jude 10), and (b) inversion (the faculty producing systematically false moral verdicts — Chars 3, 5, 6). The cluster does not impair the moral evaluation faculty's operational capacity (the person still evaluates) but corrupts the faculty's accuracy and orientation — making it produce verdicts that justify the evil rather than convicting it.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The characteristic deepens moral evaluation in the direction of categorical precision. Lev 10:10 and 11:47 (M10c-B-VCG-01) name the cultivation of clean/unclean discernment as the purpose of the purity laws — this is a systematic deepening of the moral evaluation faculty through repeated categorical engagement. The purity system trains the person to make finer and finer moral-ritual assessments. The NT revision (Act 10:28, M10c-B-VCG-05) shows this same faculty requiring revision at a higher level: God's word requires that the moral evaluation framework (who is clean/unclean) be revised to include what had been categorically excluded.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The characteristic impairs moral evaluation in its advanced form — Tit 1:15 (VCG-03 reference): "to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure; both their minds and their consciences are defiled" — the standard-setting faculty (mind) and the response-faculty (conscience) are both compromised, making moral evaluation unreliable. The person cannot correctly assess the moral character of their own condition or of the things they engage with. However, the characteristic does not simply eliminate moral evaluation: Isa 6:5 shows it still functioning at the point of encounter with holiness — the prophet's evaluation of himself as unclean remains correct. The characteristic impairs ongoing self-evaluation but not the acute recognition-event triggered by direct encounter with holiness.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The characteristic impairs moral evaluation at the institutional and personal level. Eze 22:26 (VCG-05): the collapse of priestly moral evaluation is both a symptom and a cause of the corporate defilement — the institution meant to maintain moral evaluation standards has failed. Jer 2:23 (VCG-02): the community's self-evaluation is distorted by self-deception. The characteristic also enables a future restored moral evaluation: Eze 44:23 (VCG-05) — the new priestly order will teach the people to distinguish correctly. The characteristic impairs and then restores moral evaluation as part of its eschatological trajectory.
**[CHAR-4]** S — Not evidenced within the 21-verse corpus for the person's own moral evaluation faculty.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Characteristic 1 deepens moral evaluation through categorical formation (the purity system as moral-evaluation curriculum). Characteristic 2 both preserves and impairs: the crisis-recognition capacity remains even in the advanced state (Isa 6:5 — triggered by encounter with holiness) but ongoing ambient moral self-evaluation is progressively compromised (Tit 1:15 reference — "nothing is pure to the defiled"). Characteristic 3 impairs moral evaluation at the institutional level (Eze 22:26 — priestly failure propagates the defilement by removing the institutional moral-evaluation faculty) and at the community level (Jer 2:23 — self-deceptive denial), while promising its restoration (Eze 44:23 — new priestly vocation of teaching moral evaluation). Characteristic 4 bypasses moral evaluation entirely.

questions.question_text: Across the verses, what does the pattern of engagement and non-engagement with moral evaluation indicate about the characteristic's nature?

findings.session_b_note:
The moral evaluation engagement pattern reveals that forgiveness is not morally neutral — it is morally serious at every point:

- It presupposes a moral order that has been violated (the legitimate claim)
- It operates through the recognition of moral debt (scale of sin, scale of forgiveness received)
- It generates moral clarity about the self's own relational position (Mat 18 parable)
- It demands moral consistency between received and given (the structural logic of Mat 6:14-15; Mat 18:35)

Forgiveness does not dissolve the moral standard — it operates *within* it and *through* it. The act of forgiving does not say "the wrong didn't matter" but "the wrong mattered, the claim is legitimate, and I am releasing it." This moral seriousness is what distinguishes forgiveness from indifference, tolerance, or minimisation of wrong.

findings.session_b_note:
The pattern reveals a complex bidirectional relationship: compassion is both subject to moral evaluation (it can be assessed as appropriate or inappropriate in context) and itself a moral evaluative standard (the criterion against which other practices and persons are assessed). This is not a contradiction — it is the mark of a morally mature characteristic.

Compassion operates within the moral order (it can be rightly suppressed by justice) while simultaneously providing the inner standard by which the moral order's authenticity is tested (chesed as the criterion of genuine covenant relationship). This places compassion at the centre of the programme's moral anthropology: not above the moral order (exempt from evaluation) and not below it (merely a feeling to be assessed) but within and constitutive of it — the characteristic whose presence or absence is the most direct indicator of authentic moral life.

findings.session_b_note: The pattern reveals that contrition is foundationally a moral-evaluative condition — it cannot exist without the moral evaluation faculty having been genuinely engaged. Contrition is the affective-constitutive response to accurate moral self-knowledge. This is why it is the precondition for genuine repentance: repentance requires an accurate assessment of what needs to change; contrition is the inner-being state that arises from that assessment having been genuinely made.

findings.session_b_note: The pattern reveals that moral evaluation is an essential pre-condition for righteous fellowship: the person must first evaluate the moral character of fellowship partners before entering genuine righteous fellowship. Fellowship that bypasses moral evaluation risks becoming complicit (Mat 23:30, finding 062-SD003). The characteristic requires moral evaluation at the entry-point; it does not bypass it at the beginning, though sustained wrong fellowship may progressively diminish it.

findings.session_b_note: The moral evaluation engagement reveals that goodness is inherently normative — it carries a standard against which everything is assessed. The programme's registry is named "goodness" but its data is full of moral verdicts, comparative rankings, and assessments. This confirms that goodness and the moral evaluation faculty are structurally co-dependent: genuine goodness calibrates moral evaluation (goodness is the standard); moral evaluation expresses goodness (the good person judges rightly). The corruption of goodness corrupts moral evaluation — the most severe distortion is not the absence of evaluation but its inversion. This reveals that goodness is not just a positive quality but a normative anchor for the entire moral evaluation architecture of the inner being. (OBS-067-OBS-021, OBS-067-OBS-027, OBS-067-OBS-049)

findings.finding_value: T3 confirmed that goodness is fundamentally integrating — it engages and aligns every faculty (Q&A-095). T6 confirmed that goodness is centrally connected across the programme's characteristic landscape — broad co-occurrence, shared anchors at the highest-density synthesis nodes, root-vocabulary sharing across three families. These two findings are structurally related: a characteristic that is internally integrating (T3) is also externally connecting (T6). The Mic 6:8 anchor (T6.6 — shared with 6 registries) integrates justice, kindness, love, humility, compassion, and will in a single verse — this is the structural expression of goodness's integrating faculty-engagement. Gal 5:22 (shared with 5 registries) integrates Spirit-fruit characteristics in a cluster — the same integrating logic. The characteristic that most fully integrates the inner faculties (T3) is also the characteristic most structurally connected to adjacent characteristics (T6). Integration within produces connection without.

findings.session_b_note: The moral evaluation pattern reveals love as the moral faculty's primary standard-source. The person calibrated by love-of-God sees evil as evil and good as good (Psa 97:10) — the love-orientation determines the correctness of the moral evaluation. This means moral failure is often misdiagnosed: what looks like impaired moral faculty may be a disordered love-faculty — the person who evaluates wrongly does so because they love wrongly (Luk 16:14 — money-love produces moral mockery). The pattern implies that moral formation cannot proceed without love-formation: sharpening the moral faculty without reordering the love-faculty produces moralists who identify evil correctly but love wrongly. The data's architecture places love prior to moral evaluation: love → moral evaluation → right action, not moral evaluation → motivation → action. Love calibrates the evaluator before the evaluation occurs.

Mercy is not moral blindness but moral overflow — it sees the wrongdoing clearly (hence the need for atonement, not the denial of it) and then exceeds strict accountability. OBS-111-070, OBS-111-036.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-003: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion re…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion responds, it does not originate or create. It is the most responsive of the faculties-engaging characteristics. Second, affect and moral action are structurally unified in compassion — not sequentially related but simultaneous. Affect is the mechanism of movement (splanchnizō is both the felt inner event and the cause of the action), not a precursor or accompaniment. This is unique among the characteristics reviewed: in most other registries, affect and volition are distinguishable stages; in compassion, the felt movement is already the morally motivated action beginning. A third distinctive finding: compassion converts moral knowledge into motivated action — it is the motivational ground of conscientiousness, not a product of it. The conscience faculty engagement reveals compassion as conscience-healing: it addresses the pitiable condition that conscience perceives as a moral claim, resolving the tension between moral knowledge and moral incapacity. The three relational modes (building/sustaining — chesed; restoring/repairing — splanchnizō; extending across difference — Good Samaritan) are a new finding not in the instruction typology.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-003: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked …
findings.finding_value: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I but the grace of God that is with me." Agency is not displaced but constituted by grace. This relationship holds in paradox that the T3.6 prompt options (enable/deepen/bypass/impair) cannot accommodate — a prompt design limitation noted for catalogue revision. Second, grace produces moral clarity (T3.8 — sharpens moral evaluation rather than bypassing it): the person who recognises grace has made a precise moral evaluation (they know they received what they did not deserve). Third, grace and conscience are mutually necessary: grace is the condition within which conscience can operate fully without destroying the person; conscience without grace produces condemnation; grace without conscience produces presumption (T3.9). Fourth, grace is the primary relational faculty developer in the registry's evidence — it reaches every relational register (vertical access, horizontal forgiving, speech-grace) and enables each one. Creativity (T3.5) is the one genuinely silent faculty — not an impairment but a non-engagement: grace receives and constitutes, it does not create.

findings.session_b_note: The pattern reveals that covenant is intrinsically moral — it cannot be separated from moral evaluation because its structure embeds evaluation within it. The covenant oath (with its curse for breach — OBS-034-007) is not merely a relational bond but a morally evaluative structure: the person under covenant is always already under moral assessment relative to the covenant's terms. This means covenant is not a merely relational or emotional reality but a morally accountable one — being in covenant means being accountable to a standard. The new covenant's internalisation of the standard (law on the heart — Heb 8:10) means the moral evaluation faculty itself is transformed: the person evaluates from within a renewed inner standard rather than against an external one. The pattern confirms that the Moral Character dimension (05) is correctly assigned to multiple covenant groups — covenant-keeping is constitutively a moral-character reality.

findings.finding_value:
The wealth domain is one of Scripture's primary testing grounds for the moral evaluation faculty. M46-A and M46-B name the distortions: self-evaluated as rich but actually poor (M46-A); others evaluated by material condition rather than by character (M46-B). M46-C and M46-D name the right exercise of moral evaluation in the wealth domain. The cluster confirms that wealth systematically challenges the person's capacity for accurate moral evaluation — particularly self-evaluation.

[Cluster-level addition — Phase 9 cross-sub-group review] The moral evaluation faculty is systematically challenged across all four sub-groups: M46-A shows catastrophic failure of moral self-evaluation (Rev 3:17 — not realising their actual condition; Hos 12:8 — declaring innocence through self-assessed wealth); M46-B shows moral evaluation of persons by wrong criteria (Jam 2:2-4 — evaluating by material condition rather than character); M46-C provides the right framework for moral evaluation in the wealth domain (Pro 15:6; Pro 28:6 — character as the criterion); M46-D shows the highest exercise of moral evaluation in the domain (Heb 11:26 — Moses's reckoning of reproach as greater wealth than Egypt's treasures). The wealth domain is one of Scripture's primary proving grounds for the moral evaluation faculty. Every sub-group shows a distinct mode of engagement with moral evaluation — and the cluster as a whole traces the faculty's distortion (M46-A, M46-B) to its right exercise (M46-C, M46-D) to its highest Christological expression (M46-D, 2Cor 8:9; Heb 11:26).
