Psa 36:2: the wicked flatters himself that his iniquity cannot "be found out and hated" — the conscience (the faculty that would find out and hate iniquity) is suppressed or evaded. Pro 5:12: "how I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof!" — hatred of discipline is a suppression of the conscience's external channel. In the righteous register: the person who hates evil (group 550-NEW-02) has a functioning conscience that produces sustained opposition to what violates moral truth.

Group 172-002 (contempt of reproof) shows conscience's relationship to contempt most clearly. Pro 5:12: "my heart despised reproof" — the contempt of reproof is the contempt of the mechanism through which conscience operates. Reproof is conscience made external; despising reproof is the inner act of closing the conscience's external channel. The characteristic attacks the conscience's access to the person.

Abhorrence is what a functioning conscience feels in the presence of moral violation. Righteous abhorrence (group 252-001) is the conscience's deepest response to what is genuinely repugnant. Inverted abhorrence (group 252-002) is the sign of a conscience that has been comprehensively corrupted — it now recoils from the right thing and welcomes the wrong.

The conscience's restraining function is what cruelty has removed. Pro 12:10: "the mercy of the wicked is cruel" — the conscience's alarm signal is not operative in restraining the person's conduct. Lam 4:3: the comparison with jackals (who nurse their young) shows that even the animal nurturing instinct is present where the cruel person's conscience has been silenced.

Reproach and conscience interact in two directions. When reproach is deserved (group 322-002): Jer 31:19 — "I was ashamed, and I was confounded, because I bore the disgrace of my youth" — the conscience confirms the reproach as appropriate, producing shame and genuine penitence. When reproach is undeserved (group 322-001): the conscience is what enables the person to know the reproach is unjust and to appeal against it to God.

1Pe 5:8's "be sober-minded" includes conscience-awareness — the adversary relationship demands that the person maintain moral clarity about what they are facing and how to respond. The conscience keeps the person's response within the bounds of what is appropriate.

Malice represents the conscience's most complete corruption — the faculty now rejoices at what should produce sorrow and finds pleasure in what should produce moral recoil. The conscience has not merely been suppressed (as in M06-D) but has been inverted to celebrate what it was made to condemn.

Conscience is the distinctive faculty of M05-D. No other sub-group evidences good conscience as explicitly or consistently. **[A1 — God Righteousness]** Yes — "when Paul reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment, Felix was alarmed" (Act 24:25, VSG M26-A1-006). The encounter with the standard of divine righteousness activated Felix's conscience — alarm is the conscience's response to the recognition that one falls short of the standard. God's righteousness invades the conscience of those who hear it.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Yes — "For our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God, and supremely so toward you" (implied in A2 through the conscience's testimony to righteous behavior). More directly: the righteous person's conscience provides testimony to their righteousness — and the absence of guilt in the conscience is itself a marker of righteous standing (1Cor 4:4, in the unrouted group: "I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted" — the conscience's clearance is not the final word, but it is a real signal).

**[C — Justification]** Yes — the freedom from condemnation (4846-002) is a conscience-state as well as a judicial state. "Heb 9:14" (adjacent to the 1099-001 group in C): "how much more will the blood of Christ... purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God." The justified conscience is a purified conscience — justification reaches the conscience directly.

**[E — Condemnation]** Yes — and centrally. Autokatakritos (self-condemned, Tit 3:11, VSG 4848-001) is the conscience turned against the self: the person whose own inner witness pronounces them guilty. 1Cor 4:4 (unrouted group): "I am not aware of anything against myself" — the conscience as the instrument of self-assessment. The E-sub-group is where conscience operates most explicitly in its judicial mode.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** Yes — the instruction "count yourselves dead to sin" (Rom 6:11) is addressed to the conscience-moral complex: the person who has received justification is told to reckon their conscience in accordance with the declared reality. The reckoning faculty directly engages and reorients the conscience.

**[G — Structural Opposites]** Yes — the hard and impenitent heart (Rom 2:5) names a conscience that has been suppressed or silenced. The wicked person whose conscience has ceased to function is described by Paul as one who "stores up wrath" — the suppression of conscience does not eliminate the judicial reality; it only delays its encounter.

**[CLUSTER — T3.9]** E. Conscience is a primary faculty engaged throughout M26. The key conscience-engagements: (1) alarm at the divine standard (A1: Felix); (2) testimony of righteous behavior to the self (A2); (3) purification through justification (C); (4) self-condemnation as conscience turning against the self (E: autokatakritos); (5) reorientation of conscience through reckoning (F); (6) suppression and hardening of conscience in wickedness (G). The session log finding (confirmed here) that conscience is the primary faculty for the M26-E sub-group is fully supported.

---

**Cross-cluster finding 4 — Conscience as primary faculty for the judicial dimension**
The conscience (T3.9) is the inner faculty most specifically engaged by the cluster's judicial dimension (E: condemnation; C: justification). The alarm of Felix at the standard of God's righteousness (A1-006), the self-condemnation of the autokatakritos (E: Tit 3:11), and the purification of the conscience through Christ (C-adjacent: Heb 9:14) all engage the conscience as the primary judicial faculty of the inner life. The reckoning faculty (F) operates in the mind as the cognitive-deliberative mode; the conscience operates as the inner judicial witness and registrar. The two faculties work together but occupy distinct roles.

DŌRON SUPPLEMENTARY (Phase 10, 2026-05-14):

Heb 9:9 (6837-004): "gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the conscience of the worshipper." This is the definitive dōron-conscience text within M39-A: the grace-vocabulary's external form (gift/dōron) is explicitly named as insufficient to address the conscience. Grace in its fullest form (charis — Eph 2:8) is what the conscience requires; external gift-offerings cannot deliver it.

findings.finding_value: M01-A engages conscience through fear's role as interior moral restraint: Lev 19:14 (fear of God operating as conscience in situations of power over the vulnerable — an interior witness that prevents exploitation); Neh 5:9; 5:15 (fear of God operating as Nehemiah's interior restraint against the abuse of authority — functioning as conscience before any external witness speaks). The 2Cor 5:11 material (M01-A-VCG-04: "knowing the fear of the Lord shapes the will toward persuasion of others — a motivating inner awareness of divine accountability that **can be known by conscience**") explicitly names conscience alongside fear.

M01-B engages conscience through the social-fear corpus: 1Sa 15:24 (Saul confesses that social fear displaced his conscience — the fear of people overrode the fear of God that should have governed); 2Sa 1:14 (David's rebuke frames the absence of fear as a moral failure — "the messenger lacked the reverential dread that should have prevented him from touching God's anointed, exposing a void in **his inner conscience**").

M01-F-VCG-04 engages conscience through anticipatory guilt: Act 24:25 (Felix became alarmed as Paul reasoned about righteousness, self-control, and coming judgment — "moral and eschatological argument penetrated his inner being and produced a **frightened, avoidant response**" — conscience stirred by fear of judgment producing avoidance rather than repentance). Job 15:21 (M01-B-VCG-05: "the wicked man hears dreadful sounds in his ears even in prosperity — dread as an **internal auditory experience haunting the conscience** and anticipating destruction").

The conscience is engaged across M01 in three modes: (1) **activated** by reverential fear of God (M01-A: fear as interior moral witness); (2) **suppressed** by social fear displacing it (M01-B-VCG-04: crowd-fear overriding conscience); (3) **haunted** by anticipatory judgment-dread (M01-F: the conscience as the site of anticipated divine judgment).

Yes. Gen 34:7 (M02-B-VCG-02): "the sons of Jacob are incensed because Shechem's act violated a moral order ('such a thing must not be done') — meaning their anger is conscience-driven, arising from outrage at an objective wrong done to their family." The conscience perceives the violation of the moral order and anger is the response. Neh 5:6 (M02-B-VCG-04): Nehemiah's anger at oppression is explicitly a conscience-response to injustice among his people.

2Cor 7:11 (M02-C-VCG-02): indignation produced by godly grief represents the conscience operating accurately — the person has genuinely reckoned with their wrongdoing and the indignation is the conscience's verdict on the wrong done.

Yes, prominently. Conscience is evidenced as both a trigger and a product of grief in M03. Eze 9:4 (M03-E-VCG-01): grief arising from conscience's response to witnessed wickedness — God marks those whose inner sighing expresses genuine conscience-driven grief. Joh 21:17 (M03-C-VCG-01): Peter's grief arises from conscience's recognition of his past failure. 2Pe 2:8 (M03-BOUNDARY): Lot's soul tormented day after day by witnessing lawless deeds — conscience-driven anguish.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Partially. Psa 51:8 ("let the bones that you have broken rejoice") is the most direct conscience-connection: the broken bones are the bodily image of a conscience-struck person (Psa 51 is David's penitential psalm); the asked-for restoration of exultation in the broken bones presupposes that conscience has done its work (conviction, confession) and exultation is the state that follows restoration. The characteristic engages conscience in the sequence: conviction → confession → restored exultation, not in the exultation itself.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, in a specific sequence. Psa 51:8, 12 — David's loss of joy is the direct consequence of his sin, and his restoration of joy is sought after genuine repentance (Psa 51:17 — the broken and contrite heart). The sequence is: conscience convicts → joy is lost (Psa 51:8) → repentance → restoration of joy (Psa 51:12). Ecc 8:15's commendation of joy "for God has already approved what you do" implies that conscience clearance is a precondition for genuine, untroubled joy. Pro 29:6 ("a righteous man sings and rejoices") implies that the righteous man's freedom from the snare of sin enables joy.

**[CHAR-7]** S — The M04-E-VCG-02 and M04-F corpus does not show Suffering-Joy engaging the conscience (the acute witness of sin, guilt, and conviction) directly. Act 16:34 (the jailer came to faith after apparent conviction — the surrounding narrative implies prior conscience-work, but the verse itself focuses on the rejoicing that follows). The characteristic's relationship with conscience is indirect and not evidenced in the primary corpus.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. Eze 36:31 — "your deeds that were not good, and you will loathe yourselves" — the evaluative faculty turned inward in conviction: the recognition that one's own past deeds were not-good produces self-loathing; this is the moral conscience engaging through the Gladness-evaluation faculty. Pro 20:23 — "false scales are not good" — the moral conscience is engaged through the evaluative standard. 1Sa 26:16 — "this thing you have done is not good" — conscience speaks through the not-good verdict.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Partially: (1) **M04-H-VCG-04's negated Delight** as divine condemnation — Heb 10:38 ("my soul has no pleasure in him") is the divine-conscience-equivalent: God's withholding of delight functions as his verdict on the person who shrinks back; (2) **1Cor 10:5** ("with most of them God was not pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness") — God's displeasure as the conscience-verdict of history; (3) **Job 6:10** (sa.lad in M04-G-VCG-01 — "I would even exult in pain unsparing, for I have not denied the words of the Holy One") — Job's clear conscience expressed as a form of inner exultation even in pain; fidelity to God's word sustains the inner person against conscience-guilt; (4) **Psa 51:6** ("you delight in truth in the inward being") — God's delight in inner truth is the positive conscience-standard; where it is met, Delight follows; where it is absent, God's delight is withheld.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Partially: (1) **Pro 15:26** — "thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to the Lord, but gracious words are pure" — the contrast between wicked thoughts (conscience-bad) and gracious words (conscience-pure) shows that Pleasure in speech is conscience-indexed; genuinely pleasant speech is also morally pure; (2) **Ni.cho.ach withheld** (Lev 26:31) — God's non-reception of the unfaithful's aromas implies the conscience of the worshiper should recognise that their worship has failed the covenant standard; the absent ni.cho.ach is an implicit conscience-signal; (3) **Job 20:18** (the wicked gets no enjoyment) — the blocked Pleasure of the wicked is itself a conscience-indicator: natural Pleasure is denied as a consequence of moral failure.

**[CHAR-6]** S — The M04-I corpus does not directly evidence Wonder engaging the conscience (the acute inner witness of sin, guilt, and conviction). Job 42:3's "things too wonderful for me" comes after Job's confrontation with God in the whirlwind; the conscience may have been engaged prior to Wonder in that sequence, but Wonder itself is the response to the incomprehensible divine display rather than the conscience's direct engagement.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Conscience engagement is partial and indirect across most of the seven: (1) **Mediated conscience engagement**: Joy (Char 2) — Psa 51:8, 12 shows Joy's absence as a diagnostic of sin; restoration of Joy follows conscience's work (conviction → confession → restoration of joy); (2) **Evaluative conscience**: Gladness (Char 3) — Eze 36:31 (loathing of one's own "not good" deeds) shows the Gladness-evaluation faculty producing conscience-like self-assessment; (3) **Implicit conscience-signal**: Pleasure (Char 5) — the withheld ni.cho.ach (Lev 26:31) is an implicit conscience-signal about covenant failure; Delight (Char 4) — God's "soul has no pleasure in him" (Heb 10:38) functions as a conscience-verdict; (4) **Post-conscience state**: Exultation (Char 1) — exultation is the state that follows conscience's completed work (Psa 51:8's restored rejoicing of broken bones); (5) **Silent**: Wonder (Char 6) and Suffering-Joy (Char 7) do not directly engage the conscience in the corpus.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, and this is CHAR-1's most distinctive inner-faculty relationship. Conscience is the faculty that registers guilt, moral failure, and deviation from the right — and shame is what the conscience *feels* when it makes those registrations. The M07-B-VCG-04 material (Jer 6:15; 8:12; 3:3) is entirely about the conscience's relation to shame: the loss of the capacity for shame = the death of the conscience. The M07-C-VCG-01 material (Ezr 9:6; 2Ch 30:15; Jer 31:19; Eze 43:10-11) shows the conscience receiving the shame signal and activating corrective response. The M07-B-VCG-05 corrective-shame passages (1Cor 6:5; 15:34) explicitly invoke shame to activate the conscience. Conscience and shame are functionally fused in the CHAR-1 evidence.

**[CHAR-2]** E — CHAR-2 may activate conscience as a secondary effect when the humiliated person recognises the moral cause (VCG-03: those who strive against God's servant are put to shame and their aggression's futility is recognised). But CHAR-2 primarily bypasses conscience as the receiving faculty — the humiliation arrives regardless of what the conscience says. The moral-corrective function of VCG-03 is delivered from outside (divine act) rather than through the conscience from within.

---

**[CHAR-3]** S — The 15-verse corpus does not directly evidence CHAR-3 engaging or impairing the conscience specifically. The judge's self-acknowledged absence of regard (Luk 18:4) is the closest — he is conscious of his lack of respect. Silent on conscience as the specific receptive faculty.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4 is the conscience's primary mode of shame-recognitive operation. 2Cor 4:2 — "commend ourselves to everyone's conscience in the sight of God" — names the conscience as both CHAR-4's location and its relational field. VCG-03 shows the conscience inverted. The conscience is CHAR-4's defining constitutional location.

---

**[CHAR-5]** S — The 24-verse CHAR-5 corpus does not directly evidence the conscience as the specific receptive faculty for CHAR-5. The contempt-er's conscience is implicated (the self-righteous person of Luk 18:9 has a malfunctioning conscience-conscience relationship), but the conscience as the faculty specifically engaged by CHAR-5 in its received form is not directly evidenced. Silent.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — Conscience is CHAR-6's primary inner faculty: the clean conscience is what innocence produces and what guilt-shame's absence confirms. The absence of the guilty conscience is the inner condition of CHAR-6. The loss of innocence-capacity (Hos 8:5) is simultaneously the loss of the conscience's capacity for guilt-recognition (the conscience that can no longer recognise its own moral failure cannot attain innocence). CHAR-6 and the conscience are structurally linked: functional conscience + no deliberate wrongdoing = CHAR-6's inner condition.

---

**[CLUSTER]** E — Conscience is the cluster's most important inner faculty, not because it appears most frequently as the explicit constitutional location but because its condition determines the outcome of every characteristic. The cluster-level conscience-thesis: (1) Functioning conscience → appropriate shame-reception (corrective Char 1 M07-C), accurate identification of the shameful (Char 4), maintained innocence (Char 6). (2) Seared conscience → shame-incapacity (Char 1 M07-B's refusal — Jer 6:15), moral blindness, loss of innocence-capacity. (3) Inverted conscience → glorying in shame (Char 4's VCG-03 — Phili 3:19). These three conscience-states correspond to three M07 outcome trajectories: the corrected person, the morally blind person, and the morally inverted person. The cluster's most significant pastoral and anthropological finding: the conscience is the single internal faculty through which the entire shame-field's outcomes are determined. Its health, corruption, or loss is the cluster's primary diagnostic indicator.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence bears on conscience primarily through its conspicuous absence in the proud person's narrative. 2Ch 26:16 (vc=34044, M08-A1-VCG-01): "when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction. For he was unfaithful to the Lord his God" — the progressive pride-growth shows no evidenced conscience-resistance before the catastrophic act of entering the temple. Jer 49:16 (vc=34054, M08-A1-VCG-03): "the horror you inspire has deceived you" — the proud person is deceived by their own state, not convicted by it; conscience would produce conviction, but deception is what CHAR-1 generates instead. Dan 4:37 (vc=34094, M08-A4-VCG-04): pride is "something one walks in — a habitual inner posture" — the habituation language implies that conscience has not been exercising its acute witness-function; the habitual gait of pride does not produce the inner disturbance of conscience.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The evidence suggests CHAR-2 bypasses conscience. The repeated presumption in Neh 9:16 (vc=34120, M08-B-VCG-01) and Neh 9:29 (vc=34126) — "even after warnings, they acted presumptuously again" — evidences a community pattern in which conscience does not generate self-correction even after repeated corrective intervention from God. Psa 119:69 (vc=34100): "the insolent smear me with lies" — the active, calculating deception implies an inner person whose conscience-function has been overridden by the will's self-justifying momentum.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes — conscience is uniquely central to CHAR-3's examined form. 2Cor 1:12 (vc=33912, M08-C-VCG-02): "the testimony of our conscience" as the ground of Paul's boasting — conscience's affirmative testimony grounds legitimate self-commendation. This is the most direct engagement with conscience evidenced in M08's §3 corpora: conscience functions as the positive ground for examined boasting. For VCG-01: conscience is bypassed — the self-directed boaster claims what conscience would not confirm (Rom 2:23: breaking the law one boasts in).

**[CHAR-4]** E — Indirectly. 1Ti 6:4 (vc=33925, M08-D-VCG-02): conceit paired with "understanding nothing" and "unhealthy craving for controversy" — the conscience, which would generate discomfort at the controversy-craving and the epistemic blindness, appears to be inactive. 1Ti 3:6 (vc=33924, M08-D-VCG-02): the person who falls into the devil's condemnation has not registered the inner warning that conscience should provide. CHAR-4's epistemic blindness ("understanding nothing") is the broadest possible description of conscience failure.

**[CHAR-5]** S — The verse evidence in §3.D is largely silent on direct conscience engagement for CHAR-5. The moral failures that CHAR-5 produces (Eze 16:49; Hab 2:9) imply conscience bypass, but no verse explicitly names conscience-resistance or conscience-bypass in relation to CHAR-5 specifically.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All five characteristics engage the conscience, but with different modes of engagement. CHAR-1, CHAR-2, CHAR-4, and CHAR-5 bypass conscience — the characteristics operate without or against the corrective inner witness. CHAR-3 uniquely engages conscience positively: 2Cor 1:12 (M08-C-VCG-02) names the testimony of conscience as the ground of Paul's legitimate examined boasting. The cluster-synthesis: conscience is universally bypassed by four M08 characteristics, but uniquely engaged and positively deployed by CHAR-3's examined discourse. This makes CHAR-3's VCG-02 register the only space within M08 where the conscience functions correctively rather than being bypassed.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, explicitly and distinctively. Phili2:12 — sustained obedience rooted in "fear of God rather than social pressure" — the conscience functions as the internal sustainer when external accountability is removed. The conscience provides the inner verdict that the submission is right and maintains it without external reinforcement. Col3:22 — "fearing the Lord" — the theological-moral orientation of the conscience toward God's authority. Eph6:1 — "for this is right" — the conscience's verdict of moral rightness as the ground of the obedience command.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, directly. Contrition is the acute inner state that a functioning conscience produces when it genuinely registers the moral weight of the person's failure before God. The brokenhearted and crushed in spirit (Psa34:18) are those whose conscience has genuinely registered the gravity of their condition — the breaking is the conscience's accurate witness becoming felt reality rather than merely acknowledged proposition. Isa57:15 — the contrite in spirit as those whom God revives — confirms that the contrite state is the fruit of a genuinely functioning conscience rather than its distortion.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The conscience is engaged through the self-assessment of shared weakness (Heb5:2). Genuine conscience function — the inner witness of one's own moral condition — is what enables the high priest to know that "he himself is beset with weakness." This self-knowledge through conscience function is the enabling ground of metriopatheō. The person whose conscience is suppressed or non-functioning cannot access the self-awareness of shared weakness that enables gentleness.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Semnotēs engages the conscience through its pairing with integrity (Tit2:7) — integrity names the moral-incorruptibility that genuine conscience function produces. The person of genuine semnotēs is one whose settled moral gravity is consistent with genuine conscience function — the dignity is not a social mask over a privately-compromised conscience but the outward expression of genuine inner moral seriousness. 1Ti3:4's "all dignity" implies a comprehensiveness that would not be possible with an internally-compromised conscience.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Psa51:12 directly evidences conscience-engagement. The psalm is the archetypal conscience-awakened penitential prayer — Psa51:1–11 is the extended conscience-response to David's moral failure. The request for a willing spirit (Psa51:12) comes after the conscience has fully registered the failure and its consequences. The characteristic in its VCG-02 register is thus post-conscience: it is what is sought after the conscience has done its full work of conviction and the person is ready for the spirit's renewal.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Conscience engagement is clearly present. Lev26:41 — the "uncircumcised heart" that must be humbled is a conscience-adjacent term: the uncircumcised heart is the inner faculty that has not been penetrated by the moral reality of one's situation; humbling involves that penetration. The ka.na corpus evidences humbling consistently following divine address that awakens the conscience: 2Ki22:19 (hearing God's words against the place and its inhabitants — the conscience registers the personal claim of universal judgment); 2Ch33:12 (Manasseh in distress — acute awareness of his sin's consequences); 2Ch33:23 (Amon's increasing guilt as the correlate of not humbling — conscience function impaired by persistent non-humbling). Conscience in this corpus functions as the inner witness that sin and failure are genuinely one's own and require a response.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All six characteristics engage the conscience, and the conscience's function across the cluster maps the cluster's constitutionally deepening engagement. CHAR-1: the conscience registers divine address and the humbling responds to it; heart-hardness (Lev26:41) is conscience impaired. CHAR-2: the conscience is M09-C's most distinctive secondary constitutional location — it sustains submission when external accountability is removed (Phili2:12); genuine submission is distinguished from eye-service by conscience function. CHAR-3: contrition is the most direct evidence of genuine conscience function — the crushed spirit is the sign that the conscience's witness has genuinely registered. CHAR-4: the characteristic presupposes and confirms genuine conscience self-awareness (shared weakness — Heb5:2). CHAR-5: paired with integrity (Tit2:7) — dignity confirms that the conscience is functioning genuinely rather than being masked by performed gravitas. CHAR-6: the willing spirit flows from a conscience in good standing with God (VCG-01); the disruption of Psa51:12 is explicitly post-conscience-crisis. Cluster-level: conscience is a universal secondary faculty across all six M09 characteristics. The cluster's most important conscience-finding is the diagnostic use of CHAR-3 — genuine contrition is the most reliable indicator of conscience health in the cluster; its absence (hardening) is the most reliable indicator of conscience dysfunction.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — Conscience is engaged throughout the corpus. Pre-act: Gen 39:9 — conscience names the potential act as "great wickedness" before commission; Psa 4:4 — pondering as conscience-activating practice. Post-act: Gen 42:22 — Reuben's retrospective conscience: "Did I not tell you not to sin against the boy? But you did not listen. So now there comes a reckoning for his blood." Lev 4:23 — the sin "made known" to the offender is a conscience-event. 1Jo 1:10 — denying sinfulness is a conscience-suppression act ("we make him a liar, and his word is not in us").

**[CHAR-10]** E — The conscience is engaged primarily through enticement. Jam 1:14 — the conscience's natural resistance to sin is the implicit faculty that enticement must bypass: the "luring" (Jam 1:14) implies that something in the person recognises the sinfulness (the lure is required precisely because direct approach would trigger conscience resistance). 2Pe 2:14's "insatiable for sin" — the insatiability implies a conscience that has been progressively numbed; if the conscience were fully active, the sinful appetite would be constrained.

**[CHAR-11]** E — The conscience is engaged through the condition's relationship to moral recognition and guilt. Joh 9:41 — "your guilt remains" — the conscience's verdict of guilt persists in those who claim to see but remain in the condition; conscience is the faculty whose verdict the condition overrides through self-deception. Rom 4:8 — "the Lord will not count his sin" — the blessed condition of non-counting is what the conscience needs: the conscience knows the condition's reality (it generates guilt) but the divine non-counting addresses what the conscience has registered. Act 22:16 — "wash away your sins, calling on his name" — the washing is what the conscience requires for purification.

**[CHAR-12]** E — The conscience is engaged through its *suppression* in the enslaved condition. Eph 4:26 — "be angry and do not sin" — the command implies that the conscience should resist the slide from anger into sin; if sin's enslaving power operates unchecked, the conscience's resistance capacity is progressively diminished. 1Jo 5:16 — "sin that leads to death" — the most severe form of enslavement suggests a conscience that has been so thoroughly suppressed that it no longer generates the signal that enables the intercessory remedy; the enslaving power has silenced the conscience's mediating function.

**[CHAR-13]** E — The conscience is the primary mediating faculty between the objective divine record and the person's subjective awareness of it. Num 5:6 — "that person realizes his guilt" — conscience is the realisation-faculty that makes the objective record subjectively accessible; Lev 4:23 — "the sin which he has committed is made known to him" — the making-known is what conscience does when functioning. Psa 51:3 — "my sin is ever before me" — the conscience's persistent presentation of the record to the person's awareness is its characteristic operation.

**[CHAR-14]** E — The conscience is the faculty that makes seeking possible. Lev 4:14 — "when the sin which they have committed becomes known" — the conscience registers the committed sin as the prerequisite for seeking. Lev 23:27 — "you shall afflict yourselves" — the self-affliction is the conscience's response made into a required posture; the Day of Atonement is structured around the conscience's collective engagement with the community's sin. Lev 10:19 — Aaron's question about whether his grief-stricken state would make the sin-offering unacceptable to God — the conscience is what registers the potential incongruity between inner state and ritual act.

**[CHAR-15]** E — Yes — the corporate confession engages the conscience. 1Ki 8:47 — "saying, 'We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly'" — the confession is the conscience's collective recognition and naming of the sinning-condition; the specificity of "perversely and wickedly" suggests a conscience that has registered the nature of the failure. Jer 8:14 — "because we have sinned against the Lord" — the corporate conscience identifies the moral cause of the doom.

**[CHAR-16]** E — The conscience is the primary faculty for self-recognition of the sinner-identity. Luk 5:8 — Peter's spontaneous recognition "I am a sinful man, O Lord" — the conscience operates unbidden in the presence of holiness; Luk 18:13 — the tax collector's penitential plea "be merciful to me, a sinner" — the conscience's verdict drives the physical self-abasement; 1Ti 1:15 — Paul's "of whom I am the foremost" — the apostolic conscience's honest accounting of its own worst condition.

**[CHAR-17]** E — The conscience is the defining faculty of CHAR-17. The definition identifies the characteristic as "the conscience's recognition of moral liability before God." Every instance of guilt-realisation in the corpus (Lev 4:13/22/27; 5:2/3/4/5; Num 5:6; Hos 5:15 — "until they acknowledge their guilt") is a conscience event. 1Sa 25:31 — pu.qah — "pangs of conscience" — the single Hebrew term that directly names the conscience's affective-somatic experience of guilt. Conscience IS the characteristic's primary inner faculty; guilt-as-inner-state is conscience in its guilt-awareness mode.

**[CHAR-18]** E — Conscience is engaged as a secondary responder (unlike CHAR-17 where it is primary). 2Sa 24:10 — "David's heart struck him after he had numbered the people. And David said to the Lord, 'I have sinned greatly'" — the conscience activates spontaneously in response to recognised iniquity; Psa 38:18 — "I confess my iniquity; I am sorry for my sin" — conscience produces confession and sorrow; Lev 26:40/41 — confession requires the humbled heart that presupposes conscience-engagement.

**[CHAR-19]** E — Yes — conscience is engaged as the interior monitor that transgression progressively suppresses. Psa 36:1 — "transgression speaks to the wicked deep in his heart; there is no fear of God before his eyes" — the transgression has displaced the God-fear that is conscience's marker; Pro 28:13 — "whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper" — the concealment is an active conscience-suppression act. Psa 51:3 — "I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me" — the engaged conscience produces the constant inner awareness that precedes repentance.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes — but in its *retrospective* mode. Lev 5:5 ("when he realizes his guilt... and confesses") — the conscience engages upon realisation of guilt: it processes the moral reality of the past act once the relevant information is available. Num 22:34 — Balaam's conscience fires immediately when the angel discloses the truth: "I have sinned, for I did not know." The conscience is activated by the information-event, not by the act itself (which occurred below conscience's awareness horizon).

**[CHAR-20]** E — Yes — conscience is centrally engaged. Ezr 9:4 — "all who trembled at the words of the God of Israel... gathered around me while I sat appalled" — the conscience-engaged community trembles; Ezr 10:6 — Ezra "mourning over the faithlessness of the exiles" — the conscience's grief-response to faithlessness; Lev 26:40 — "if they confess their iniquity and... treachery" — the confession is a conscience-act; Psa 73:15 — "if I had said, 'I will speak thus,' I would have betrayed the generation of your children" — the conscience's deliberative checking of potential faithlessness-through-speech.

**[CHAR-21]** E — Yes — through the confession-producing and the conscience-bypassing dimensions. (1) *Confession-producing conscience*: Job 33:27 — "I sinned and perverted what was right" — the conscience produces the confession of perversity; Dan 9:5 — "we have sinned and done wrong" — communal conscience-confession; 1Ki 8:47 — "we have acted perversely" — the conscience-acknowledgment; (2) *Conscience-bypassing*: Pro 2:14 — "delight in the perverseness of evil" — the conscience has been bypassed to the point that perversity produces delight rather than shame; 2Pe 2:12 — "irrational animals... blaspheming" — the conscience is not operational in the animal-instinctual mode.

**[CHAR-22]** E — Yes — through the shame-diagnostic and the confession passages. (1) *Conscience absent in the unjust*: Zep 3:5 — "the unjust knows no shame" — the conscience's shame-function is inoperative; (2) *Conscience operational in the just*: Job 34:32 — "if I have done iniquity, I will do it no more" — the conscience-driven commitment to cease; Job 6:29 — "let no injustice be done" — the conscience's appeal against unjust treatment; (3) *Conscience seeking vindication*: Psa 7:3 — "if there is wrong in my hands" — the conscience's honest self-examination.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Conscience is the *primary* faculty engaged in confession — this is the brief's definition: "conscience in confessional mode." 2Sa 24:10 — "David's heart struck him" — the conscience (heart in its moral-witness function) is the initiating faculty. Shimei's confession — "your servant knows that I have sinned" (2Sa 19:20) — is grounded explicitly in the conscience's knowledge. Judas's confession — "I have sinned by betraying innocent blood" (Mat 27:4) — names what the conscience has identified: the specific moral wrong of betraying an innocent person. Confession is conscience externalised through speech.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Conscience is the *defining faculty* of this characteristic — it is what is suppressed. The characteristic is conscience in its malfunctioning mode: (1) Absent: Jer 16:10 — no conscience signal fires (the people genuinely do not know their sin); (2) Denied: Jer 2:35 — conscience's potential signal is overridden by the active denial; (3) Numbed: Ecc 8:12; 1Cor 15:34 — habituated sinning and spiritual stupor produce progressively numbed conscience. Tit 3:11 — "self-condemned" — the conscience is operating implicitly (producing a self-condemnation verdict) but its output is not consciously received or acknowledged.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The conscience is engaged in refusal to repent through its *presence but ineffectiveness* — unlike CHAR-4 (where conscience is absent or suppressed), CHAR-5 presupposes a conscience that has registered the call to turn but whose signal the will is refusing. Heb 10:26 — "after receiving the knowledge of the truth" — implies that the truth has been known (conscience-accessible) but the sinning continues deliberately. Neh 9:29 — "you warned them" — the warnings reach the community, and the community's refusal to respond is a conscience-override: the warning is received (conscience-signal delivered) but the will stiffens against it. The conscience in CHAR-5 is not absent but overridden.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The conscience is engaged in habitual defection through its *progressive numbing*. 1Sa 2:25 — "they would not listen to the voice of their father" — the father's voice (representing the corrective moral input that conscience should supply from within) is refused; when the external conscience-surrogate is consistently refused, the internal conscience is presumably equally unavailable. Exo 9:34 — "sinned yet again and hardened his heart" — the hardening that enables repeated sinning is the progressive numbing of the conscience's signal: each sinning-and-hardening cycle reduces the conscience's corrective capacity.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The conscience is engaged in the community through its *gradual numbing* as the transmitted sinning becomes normalised. Exo 23:33's snare imagery implies that by the time the community perceives what has happened (the snare closing), the conscience has already been bypassed. The progressive character of the transmission (1Ki 22:52 — three generations; 2Ki 21:11 — Manasseh's sustained transmission) shows a conscience that is being gradually habituated to the sinning direction until it no longer registers the sinning course as deviant. For the leader: 1Ki 16:19 — "doing evil in the sight of the Lord" — the narrator's moral evaluation stands against the leader's apparent lack of conscience-registration about their own sinning.

**[CHAR-8]** S — The 9-verse corpus contains no conscience vocabulary in connection with political revolt. The characteristic is described through political-action language without any named conscience-response in the revolting parties.

**[CHAR-9]** E — The conscience is engaged through its *suppression* in sinful speech's operation. 1Ti 1:13 — Paul's former blasphemy was from "ignorant unbelief" — the conscience was not functioning to register the moral weight of the blasphemous speech (the ignorance prevented it). The practitioner of sustained slander (1Ti 6:4 — "unhealthy craving") has a conscience that does not effectively resist the slanderous output. VCG-03's beast represents the extreme: the conscience is entirely absent or overridden — the creature's total constitution is blasphemous without any conscience-resistance.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. Conscience engagement is central to this characteristic. The primary evidence is Psa 36:1 (VCG-02): "transgression speaks to the wicked deep in his heart; there is no fear of God before his eyes" — the inner voice of transgression has displaced the voice of conscience (God-fear). This is the characteristic's definitive conscience-engagement pattern: the conscience has been replaced by an internal governance structure that speaks for wickedness rather than against it. Pro 10:24 (VCG-06): "what the wicked dreads will come upon him" — the inner dread is a conscience-residue that the wicked person cannot fully suppress; the conscience retains enough function to produce dread of the consequences the wicked person knows are coming. Job 34:18 (VCG-10): "who says to a king 'worthless one' and to nobles 'wicked man'" — divine authority applies the conscience-verdict to nobles regardless of social rank.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes. The conscience is centrally engaged. Heb 10:22 (vc=14426 — VCG-06) is the primary conscience evidence: "hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience" — the conscience is named as the specific faculty that has been constitutionally corrupted ("evil conscience") and that blocks approach to God. Act 8:22 (vc=14361 — VCG-05): "the intent of your heart may be forgiven you" — the heart's intent is addressed by repentance and prayer, implying a conscience-level reckoning with the constitutional evil. Rom 1:18 (vc=14336 — VCG-05): "suppress the truth" — suppression is the conscience's relationship to the truth it knows; the constitutional evil generates the suppressive act that prevents conscience from functioning.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. The conscience is the central and most extensively evidenced faculty in this characteristic — VCG-04 (11 verses) is entirely devoted to the conscience's relationship with abomination. The conscience engages the characteristic across three states: (1) wholly silenced — Jer 6:15 (vc=1680 — VCG-04) and Jer 8:12 (vc=1696 — VCG-04): "not at all ashamed; they did not know how to blush" — complete conscience-silencing with no shame or blushing; (2) awakened and grieving — Eze 9:4 (vc=1698 — VCG-04): those who sigh and groan over others' abominations — a conscience responding with grief; (3) restored to full function — Eze 36:31 (vc=1681 — VCG-04): memory restored producing self-loathing; Eze 44:13 (vc=66003 — VCG-04): bearing shame permanently. The conscience is the defining inner faculty through which abomination is registered, shamed, or ignored.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes. The conscience is engaged primarily through its deadening and eventual reactivation. Eze 6:9 (vc=1697 — VCG-05): survivors "will be loathsome in their own sight for the evils they have committed, for all their abominations" — the post-judgment conscience generates self-loathing; this implies that during the period of abomination the conscience was suppressed. Eze 8:17 (vc=65980 — VCG-05): treating abomination as a light matter shows a conscience that no longer registers the gravity of idolatrous acts. Deu 27:15 (vc=65937 — VCG-02 — from CHAR-3's corpus but structurally parallel): the idol set up "in secret" implies a conscience that knows the act is wrong while the will proceeds — conscience still active but overridden.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes. The conscience is engaged through progressive deadening. Pro 30:20 (vc=38222 — VCG-04): "I have done no wrong" — the conscience that should register wrongdoing produces nothing; it has been entirely silenced through sustained iniquity. Psa 36:4 (vc=38235 — VCG-02): "he does not reject evil" — the failure to reject evil implies that the conscience no longer produces the rejection-impulse that would arrest the scheming. Psa 66:18 (vc=38182 — VCG-04): "if I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened" — the psalmist's awareness that cherished iniquity forecloses divine hearing shows a conscience still functional (warning against this state), while the person who has actually reached that state (Pro 30:20 — VCG-04) has a silenced conscience.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes. The conscience is engaged primarily through its foreclosure in VCG-01. Rev 16:9 (vc=14352 — VCG-01): "they did not repent" — the conscience's convicting function that should produce repentance has been entirely suppressed; the characteristic has silenced the conscience-induced impulse toward repentance. Rev 16:11 (vc=14350 — VCG-01): "they did not repent of their deeds" — the deeds-conscience link is specifically severed: consciousness of deeds does not produce conscience-engagement with them. For VCG-03: 1Pe 3:16 (vc=14380 — VCG-03): "having a good conscience, so that when you are slandered, those who revile your good behavior in Christ may be put to shame" — the good conscience of the falsely accused is specifically named as the counter-characteristic; its presence exposes the false accusers' lack of conscience-grounded behavior.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The conscience is the cluster's most universally and deeply evidenced inner faculty — all six characteristics engage with conscience, primarily through its suppression. Char 3's VCG-04 (11V conscience corpus — Jer 6:15/8:12 no shame/blush; Eze 9:4 grieving; Eze 36:31 self-loathing restored) provides the richest conscience evidence across the entire M10b cluster. Char 6 (Rev 16:9/11 — "they did not repent" as conscience-silencing under maximum pressure) shows the most extreme conscience-suppression. Char 5 (Pro 30:20 — "I have done no wrong" — conscience co-opted to produce false self-exculpation) shows the most active conscience-corruption. Chars 1 (Psa 36:1 — no fear of God), 2 (Heb 10:22 — sprinkling of conscience required for approach), and 4 (Eze 8:17 — abomination treated as trivial) all show conscience in failed states.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, prominently. The most direct evidence is Lev 5:2-3 (M10c-A-VCG-01): defilement can be hidden from the person, but "when he comes to know it and realises his guilt" — the conscience awakens as the first inner response to recognition of the incurred condition. The guilt here is the conscience's naming of the defilement as a real condition that must be addressed. The Num 19:13 (M10c-A-VCG-07) formulation — "his uncleanness is still on him" — shows the conscience's awareness of an unresolved condition as a persisting reality. Act 10:14 (M10c-B-VCG-05) — Peter's conscience-level conviction that resists the divine vision — shows the conscience formed by the categorical system as itself a highly active inner witness operating at the boundary of the permitted and forbidden.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, centrally. The conscience is the primary inner faculty engaged by Characteristic 2. 1Cor 8:7 (VCG-03): "their conscience, being weak, is defiled" — the conscience is both the faculty that is susceptible to defilement and the locus of the defilement-state in this verse. The defilement originates in the conscience itself (acting against conviction), not in an external contact. Tit 1:15 (VCG-03 reference): "their consciences are defiled" — advanced defilement has penetrated the conscience as a faculty, compromising its witness function. Isa 6:5 (VCG-01): the prophet's conscience functions correctly at the moment of divine encounter — "woe is me! For I am a man of unclean lips" — the conscience names the condition accurately.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, at three evidenced points. (1) Prophetic confrontation of corporate conscience: Jer 2:23 (VCG-02) — the prophetic challenge ("how can you say, 'I am not unclean'?") is a direct confrontation of the community's corporate conscience, naming the gap between self-justifying claim and actual condition. (2) Individual conscience of maintained purity: Eze 4:14 (VCG-05) — "I have never defiled myself" — the prophet's conscience is active in defending his lifelong maintained purity; the conscience here functions as the inner witness of sustained integrity. (3) Corporate future conscience: Eze 20:43 (VCG-02) — the community will "loathe yourselves" — the future self-loathing is the eschatological activation of corporate conscience: a collective inner witness of guilt over the corporate defilement-state.

**[CHAR-4]** S — The 21-verse corpus does not evidence engagement with the person's conscience. The conscience — as the inner witness of sin, guilt, and conviction — is not named as active or suppressed in any of the 21 verses. The condition is not about guilt or conviction but about domination by an external spiritual force.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster reveals a 3 E : 1 S conscience-engagement pattern — Characteristics 1, 2, and 3 engage conscience; Characteristic 4 does not. Characteristic 1 engages conscience as the primary immediate-response faculty (Lev 5:2-3 — "he comes to know it and realises his guilt"; Act 10:14 — Peter's categorical conviction as deeply formed conscience). Characteristic 2 engages conscience as the primary locus of defilement (1Cor 8:7 — "conscience is defiled") and as the progressive casualty of sustained defilement (Eph 4:19 — callousness as conscience-suppression). Characteristic 3 engages conscience at the corporate level through prophetic confrontation (Jer 2:23 — prophetic challenge to corporate conscience's denial) and as the future instrument of repentance (Eze 20:43 — the corporate conscience's eventual self-loathing). Characteristic 4 bypasses conscience entirely — the condition is not guilt-based but domination-based.

findings.session_b_note:
**Resolves what conscience has registered:** Received forgiveness resolves the conscience-charge — the guilt held by conscience is cancelled. 1Jo 1:9 — cleansed from all unrighteousness — implies a clean conscience as the outcome of received forgiveness.

**Sharpens conscience (in the context of Mat 18):** The parable sharpens the conscience of the withholder by making the moral incongruence of their position visible. Received forgiveness, properly received, makes conscience more acute about the obligation to extend forgiveness.

**May be bypassed if forgiveness is received superficially:** F-002 names the misuse — verbal/legal forgiveness without heart-level release. A person who receives forgiveness at the outer level without inner reception may bypass the conscience-level resolution — the charge is formally cancelled but not inwardly resolved.

*New finding:* The relationship between forgiveness and conscience has two distinct modes: (1) received forgiveness that reaches the conscience-level resolves the guilt-charge and produces inner peace; (2) received forgiveness that does not reach the conscience-level leaves the inner dis-ease unresolved. This distinction parallels the heart-level distinction of Mat 18:35 (from the heart vs. merely formal) and extends it to the conscience faculty specifically.

findings.session_b_note:
Deepens and enables. SD026 (Zec 12:10): the spirit of grace produces mourning — conscience at its deepest: not merely moral verdict but grief at the relational and personal cost. Grace enables the conscience to feel fully without destroying the person — because what the conscience reveals is held within the grace simultaneously given. Grace makes safe space for conscience to do its fullest work.

*New finding as a T3-level statement: grace as the condition within which conscience can operate fully without destroying the person is not previously stated in these terms.*

findings.session_b_note:
**Compassion may enable conscience indirectly:** The recognition of one's own pitiable condition (eleeinos — Rev 3:17) requires a form of inner-witness function that is conscience-adjacent — the capacity to see one's own true moral and spiritual state. Where compassion creates the inner environment for honest self-perception, it may enable the conscience to function more accurately. The self-deceived Laodiceans' failure of conscience is linked to their failure of compassion-reception.

**Compassion as the ground of moral return (Joel 2:13):** "Rend your hearts... for he is gracious and merciful (rachum ve-channum)." The divine compassion-character is the reason given for the inner act of moral rending. Compassion here enables the conscience to act: knowing that God is compassionate makes it possible to face and act on conscience's witness. Without the certainty of divine compassion, conscience might produce paralysis rather than return.

**What is missing (P):** Whether compassion heals or restores damaged or silenced conscience is not addressed. This is a gap for Session D, potentially intersecting with the forgiveness registry (R064).

findings.session_b_note:
Contrition **validates and honours** the conscience — it gives the conscience's witness its appropriate weight in the inner being. The contrite person does not suppress, argue against, or minimise what their conscience witnesses; they receive it and allow it to reach spirit and heart level. In this sense, contrition enables the conscience to do its full work: to convict not merely at the surface level of social shame but at the level of genuine inner-being transformation.

The hardened posture (Jer 44:10) implies conscience-suppression: the people have not responded to the repeated confrontations with their condition. The absence of contrition may actively impair conscience by teaching the inner being to resist its witness. Contrition, by contrast, is the inner-being posture that permits conscience to reach its full constitutional depth.

*New finding: contrition and conscience are mutually enabling — conscience provides the content of contrition; contrition enables conscience to do its full work by receiving its witness without resistance.*

findings.session_b_note:
**Enabling/Deepening conscience:** Righteous companionship (fear-of-God community) provides a relational context that supports and deepens conscience — being among those who evaluate morally by God's standards reinforces the person's own conscience. The divine-witness function (Mal 2:14) externalises conscience, confronting what has been suppressed internally.

**Purifying conscience:** Pro 20:30 — disciplinary fellowship-wounding reaches the innermost parts for cleansing. This is an enabling function: conscience is not merely confronted but purified by the wounding mechanism.

**Impairing/Suppressing conscience:** Mat 23:30 — the Pharisees' conscience is functioning in suppressed mode: they construct a hypothetical self-defence that avoids registration of their actual moral culpability. Wrong fellowship (in this case, inherited moral alignment with the blood-guilty) impairs conscience by providing a relational framework that normalises what should be registered as wrong.

**New finding:** Fellowship's relationship with conscience is bidirectional: righteous fellowship deepens and purifies conscience; wrong fellowship suppresses and impairs it. The mechanism in both directions operates through the relational bond — what the person is joined to determines whether conscience is activated or anesthetised.

findings.session_b_note: Goodness enables and deepens conscience — specifically through the not-goodness register. The recognition of not-goodness (884-006 and Eze 36:31) is a conscience operation enabled by the standard of the good: only a person who has access to the standard of genuine goodness can accurately recognise their own not-goodness and respond with appropriate conviction. The distortion form (Mal 2:17 / Jer 44:17) shows conscience impaired: when goodness is redefined, the conscience's witness becomes unreliable — it applies the wrong standard and produces false moral comfort. Conversely, disordered love may **impair** conscience: the money-lover (Luk 16:14, OBS-103-136) who ridicules Jesus' teaching has a conscience whose sensitivity to error is dulled by the competing love-object. findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-111-003: Reading T3 as a whole reveals mercy as a faculty-activating characteristic — it does not primarily engage one or two faculties but activates the inner-being faculty system comprehensively. The pattern…
findings.finding_value: Reading T3 as a whole reveals mercy as a faculty-activating characteristic — it does not primarily engage one or two faculties but activates the inner-being faculty system comprehensively. The pattern: mercy enables perception (face-access), opens cognition in both directions (upward to divine knowledge; downward to self-knowledge), creates an asymmetric memory structure (divine forgetting / human remembering), engages affect as its native register, expands volition (received mercy increases mercy-capacity), demands agency, reframes moral evaluation (mercy as higher-order moral evaluation), presupposes and deepens conscience, enables conscientiousness, and constitutes relational capacity. The single faculty not evidenced is creativity (T3.5.2 — S status). Reading T3 together: mercy is characterised by faculty-comprehensiveness; its absence (mercilessness in Rom 1:31) appears alongside affective incapacity (*astorgos*) and other faculty-failures — confirming that mercy's presence is correlated with full faculty activation and its absence with faculty contraction.

findings.finding_value: T2 maps mercy's constitutional locations (soul, mind, heart, body, spirit-soul interface) and T3 maps its faculty engagements. Reading together: the constitutional locations and the faculty engagements are co-extensive. Soul-level location (T2) corresponds to conscience and moral evaluation faculty engagement (T3) — the soul is where guilt resides and where conscience/moral evaluation operate. Mind-level location (T2, memory-erasure) corresponds to memory faculty engagement (T3, asymmetric memory structure). Heart/splanchna location (T2) corresponds to affect faculty (T3). The receiving-before-generating origin (T2) corresponds to relational capacity as foundational enabler (T3.11). T2 and T3 together: constitutional location and faculty engagement are two descriptions of the same inner-being reality — where mercy operates constitutionally (T2) is where it activates faculties (T3).

Reading T3 and T5 together: the faculty deepening identified in T3 (conscience deepened, volition expanded, relational capacity constituted) is the mechanism through which T5's formative arc operates. Mercy forms character (T5) by deepening and expanding the inner faculties (T3) — the formation is not abstract but faculty-specific. findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-003: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion re…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion responds, it does not originate or create. It is the most responsive of the faculties-engaging characteristics. Second, affect and moral action are structurally unified in compassion — not sequentially related but simultaneous. Affect is the mechanism of movement (splanchnizō is both the felt inner event and the cause of the action), not a precursor or accompaniment. This is unique among the characteristics reviewed: in most other registries, affect and volition are distinguishable stages; in compassion, the felt movement is already the morally motivated action beginning. A third distinctive finding: compassion converts moral knowledge into motivated action — it is the motivational ground of conscientiousness, not a product of it. The conscience faculty engagement reveals compassion as conscience-healing: it addresses the pitiable condition that conscience perceives as a moral claim, resolving the tension between moral knowledge and moral incapacity. The three relational modes (building/sustaining — chesed; restoring/repairing — splanchnizō; extending across difference — Good Samaritan) are a new finding not in the instruction typology.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-003: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked …
findings.finding_value: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I but the grace of God that is with me." Agency is not displaced but constituted by grace. This relationship holds in paradox that the T3.6 prompt options (enable/deepen/bypass/impair) cannot accommodate — a prompt design limitation noted for catalogue revision. Second, grace produces moral clarity (T3.8 — sharpens moral evaluation rather than bypassing it): the person who recognises grace has made a precise moral evaluation (they know they received what they did not deserve). Third, grace and conscience are mutually necessary: grace is the condition within which conscience can operate fully without destroying the person; conscience without grace produces condemnation; grace without conscience produces presumption (T3.9). Fourth, grace is the primary relational faculty developer in the registry's evidence — it reaches every relational register (vertical access, horizontal forgiving, speech-grace) and enables each one. Creativity (T3.5) is the one genuinely silent faculty — not an impairment but a non-engagement: grace receives and constitutes, it does not create.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-009: T1's immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response) is the affective-volitional expression of T3's faculty engagement at the moment grace arrives. T3…
findings.finding_value: T1's immediate response pattern (fear → mourning → prostration as the creaturely recognition response) is the affective-volitional expression of T3's faculty engagement at the moment grace arrives. T3.4 (affect is the first named faculty engaged by grace) and T3.6 (the agency-constituting paradox of 1Cor 15:10) together explain why T1.5 finds the creaturely recognition response before positive states settle: grace first produces the affective recognition (fear, mourning) before constituting the agency through which the person responds (prostration as the body enacting the inner posture that grace has produced). T1's finding that grace requires creaturely recognition to complete its operation (T1.7) is T3.1's finding at the faculty level: grace requires and enables perception simultaneously.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-014: T2's constitutional movement (spirit reception → soul standing → capacity → character expression) maps onto T3's faculty engagement sequence. The spirit-reception stage (T2.1) corresponds to T3.1 (per…
findings.finding_value: T2's constitutional movement (spirit reception → soul standing → capacity → character expression) maps onto T3's faculty engagement sequence. The spirit-reception stage (T2.1) corresponds to T3.1 (perception — grace enabling the inner sight and hearing that receives it). The soul-standing stage (T2.2) corresponds to T3.9 (conscience — grace as the condition within which conscience can operate without destruction) and T3.8 (moral evaluation — the standing produces the clarity of moral self-assessment). The capacity-gifting stage (T2.1 — spirit level) corresponds to T3.7 (agency — capacity given constitutes agency for the task). The character-expression stage (T2.7 — outward through body-soul) corresponds to T3.10 (conscientiousness — the integrated moral-action expression of received grace-character). T2 maps the constitutional space; T3 maps the faculties active at each spatial level; the two tiers describe the same movement from orthogonal perspectives.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-020: T3's faculty findings are the synchronic expression of T5's diachronic formation arc. The creaturely recognition response (T5.2 — fear → mourning → prostration as the consistent transitional state in …
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty findings are the synchronic expression of T5's diachronic formation arc. The creaturely recognition response (T5.2 — fear → mourning → prostration as the consistent transitional state in all grace-sequences) is the affective-faculty event (T3.4) at the moment of grace-arrival, which then constitutes the volitional-faculty alignment (T3.6 — the agency-constituting paradox) that enables the conscientious expression (T3.10). T5's formation arc (sustained work producing character-quality) is the longitudinal development of T3.9's finding (conscience operating fully within grace) into T3.10's finding (conscientiousness as the integrated moral character that grace constitutes over time). The person who has been formed by grace through the T5 formation arc is the person in whom T3's faculty engagements have been progressively deepened and integrated.

findings.session_b_note: Covenant deepens and clarifies conscience — it does not bypass or impair it. (1) Deepening: covenant gives conscience a specific and weighty object — the person under covenant is not merely subject to a vague moral awareness but to conscience-testimony regarding specific covenantal obligations. The covenant's clarity (written law, specific obligations, sworn terms) makes conscience's work more precise. (2) The new covenant deepens conscience further by internalising the standard — law written on the heart (Heb 8:10) means conscience operates from within the person's own renewed moral constitution, not merely against an external standard. (3) The guilt co-occurrence data (OBS-034-031) confirms that covenant contexts regularly produce the conscience-awareness of failure — the covenant is the framework within which guilt is named and experienced. (4) The Hebrews argument (Heb 9:9; 10:1-2 context, though outside the verse set) implies that the old covenant's sacrificial system could not fully clear the conscience — the new covenant's superior blood does. This trajectory — old covenant engaging but not fully clearing conscience; new covenant engaging and clearing it — is implied by the data without being directly stated in the programme's verse set.

findings.session_b_note: Three conscience-patterns: (1) Suppressed conscience impairs peace (the primary direction): Psa 32:3 — suppressed conscience → bones wasting, no peace; the relationship is causal — withheld confession prevents peace; (2) Exercised conscience enables peace: Psa 32:5 — acknowledged sin → forgiveness → relief; the confession that exercises conscience leads to peace as its outcome; (3) False peace bypasses conscience: Deu 29:19 — the stubborn heart generates false peace by bypassing the conscience's witness; this is the bypass pattern — false shalom is what remains when conscience is overridden. The conscience is thus both the gateway to peace (through confession) and the faculty whose suppression most directly destroys peace (Psa 32:3). No other inner faculty has this bidirectional gateway function as clearly documented in the data.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-117-003: T3 identifies conscience as peace's primary gateway faculty — the inner faculty whose state most directly determines whether genuine peace is constitutionally accessible. Three conscience-patterns: su…
findings.finding_value: T3 identifies conscience as peace's primary gateway faculty — the inner faculty whose state most directly determines whether genuine peace is constitutionally accessible. Three conscience-patterns: suppressed conscience destroys peace somatically (Psa 32:3 — bones wasting); exercised conscience restores peace through confession (Psa 32:5); bypassed conscience produces false peace (Deu 29:19). No other inner faculty has this bidirectional gateway function as clearly documented. The moral evaluation faculty (T3.8) confirms: authentic peace enables right moral judgment; false peace corrupts it. The practical implication: the route back from peacelessness is through conscience-exercise (confession, acknowledgment, remembering God's faithfulness), not through direct emotional management.

findings.session_b_note: The Spirit-giving (Neh 9:20) and prophetic warning (Neh 9:30) in the endowing and covenantal modes can be read as conscience-forming and conscience-engaging: God's Spirit and prophets address the inner moral witness. The refusal to give ear to prophetic warning represents a suppression of conscience-input that leads to judicial giving-over. In this sense the characteristic (Spirit-giving, warning-giving) enables conscience, and its rejection impairs it. The eschatological giving that produces "oaks of righteousness" (Isa 61:3) would imply a restored moral inner life including conscience. Gap: these are inferences from the data, not direct statements. The data is richer on moral evaluation (T3.8) than on conscience specifically.

M46-A is the sub-group that most clearly shows what an impaired conscience looks like in the wealth domain.
