findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-099-003: T3 reveals that kindness engages a remarkably wide range of inner faculties — nine of eleven are evidenced with at least partial engagement. The two genuine absences (imagination and creativity) are s…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals that kindness engages a remarkably wide range of inner faculties — nine of eleven are evidenced with at least partial engagement. The two genuine absences (imagination and creativity) are structurally coherent: kindness is relational and loyally directed, not generative. The most significant faculty engagements are: (a) volition — kindness is chosen, not merely felt; the "put on" and "love kindness" language makes this constitutive; (b) agency — chrēsteuomai names love actively exercising kindness — kindness is enacted, not passive; (c) relational capacity — kindness constitutes relationships in their quality, not merely accompanies them; (d) conscientiousness — the chasid represents the full integration of moral awareness, will, and action in consistent reliable pattern; (e) taste as the primary perceptive mode — "tasted that the Lord is good" establishes that kindness is encountered experientially before it is understood conceptually. The pattern across all engaged faculties: kindness integrates the whole inner person — it does not operate as a single-faculty characteristic but as a whole-person orientation. T3's most significant intra-tier finding: kindness is a multi-faculty characteristic whose breadth of engagement reflects its status as a constitutive relational orientation rather than a single affective or volitional act.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-099-009: T1's finding that kindness is primarily a disposition (not merely an act) is confirmed and deepened by T3's faculty analysis. The disposition identified in T1 requires the full engagement of multiple …
findings.finding_value: T1's finding that kindness is primarily a disposition (not merely an act) is confirmed and deepened by T3's faculty analysis. The disposition identified in T1 requires the full engagement of multiple faculties — volition (it is chosen), agency (it is enacted), conscientiousness (moral awareness + will + action integrated), and relational capacity (it constitutes relationship quality) — which together explain why it is dispositional rather than episodic: a characteristic that engages this many faculties simultaneously is, by its nature, a settled whole-person orientation rather than a single-faculty response. T1's three-mode finding (disposition / deliberate act / Spirit formation) is reflected in T3's faculty pattern: the dispositional mode engages conscientiousness and relational capacity; the deliberate act mode engages volition and agency; the Spirit-formation mode produces the integrated faculty engagement over time. The counterfeit (chrēstologia — T1.4.3 / Q&A-024) maps onto T3's faculty analysis as the pathology of the speech-mode: it engages the communicative faculty while bypassing genuine moral evaluation and conscientiousness — presence of outward form without inner faculty integration.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-099-014: T2's finding that kindness is located in the heart and moves outward through a constitutional trajectory (Spirit → heart → disposition → acts) connects structurally with T3's finding that kindness eng…
findings.finding_value: T2's finding that kindness is located in the heart and moves outward through a constitutional trajectory (Spirit → heart → disposition → acts) connects structurally with T3's finding that kindness engages the heart's integrating faculties — volition, agency, conscientiousness, moral evaluation, relational capacity, and conscience. The heart in T2 is not merely a location label but the integrating site where all these faculties converge (T2.3.2 — Q&A-045). The constitutional movement pattern in T2 (downward-outward from Spirit to acts) is powered by the multi-faculty engagement that T3 documents: the Spirit-formation produces the heart-level disposition, but the heart exercises volition (choosing to be kind), agency (enacting kindness), and conscientiousness (sustaining kindness reliably over time) to move the disposition into action. The T3 finding that kindness engages taste as the primary perceptive faculty (1Pet 2:3 — "tasted that the Lord is good") is the perceptive entry point for the T2 constitutional movement: the person first tastes divine kindness, then the Spirit forms it in the heart, then the heart's faculties exercise it outward. The two tiers together describe a complete inner-to-outer movement with both location (T2) and mechanism (T3) identified.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-099-019: T3's faculty analysis and T4's relational interface analysis are structurally interdependent in a specific way: the faculties that kindness most strongly engages (volition, agency, relational capacity…
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty analysis and T4's relational interface analysis are structurally interdependent in a specific way: the faculties that kindness most strongly engages (volition, agency, relational capacity, conscientiousness) are precisely the faculties required for the T4 relational circuit to operate. Relational capacity (T3.11) is what makes the T4 interfaces possible at all — the person must have the constitutional equipment for genuine connection before kindness can flow in any direction. Agency (T3.7) is what makes the T4 giving direction concrete — not passive benevolence but enacted care. Conscientiousness (T3.10) is what makes the T4 circuit sustainable across time — the chasid who reliably keeps covenant. The T4 communal interface (Moses's intercession; the chasidim assembly) requires an intercessory capacity (T3 — memory + relational capacity) that knows how to appeal on behalf of others. The two tiers together describe a portrait of the whole inner person oriented outward: T3 names the inner equipment and T4 names the relational directions in which that equipment is deployed.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-099-021: T3's finding that kindness engages volition, agency, and conscientiousness as an integrated whole maps onto T6's causal network in a specific way: it is precisely these three faculties operating toget…
findings.finding_value: T3's finding that kindness engages volition, agency, and conscientiousness as an integrated whole maps onto T6's causal network in a specific way: it is precisely these three faculties operating together that make the T6 causal chain function. The T6 finding that received human kindness causes its reproduction (2Sa 10:2 — "as his father dealt loyally with me, so I will deal loyally") requires all three: the cognition (knowing what was done), the moral evaluation (recognising the obligation), and the agency (acting on it). The T6 co-occurrence finding that kindness clusters with faithfulness, patience, and humility maps onto T3's multi-faculty profile: faithfulness requires conscientiousness; patience requires impulse-control at the volitional level; humility requires conscience and moral evaluation. The T3 finding that imagination and creativity are absent connects with T6's finding that kindness is a central node in a relational-moral web — it is constitutively oriented toward the actual other, not toward the imagined or created.

findings.session_b_note: Yes — centrally. Peace is among the most relationally engaged characteristics in the programme. Evidence spans multiple dimensions: (1) Friendship bond (H7965J, 2510-001) — shalom as the inner relational bond of loyalty and heart-union (1Ch 12:17); (2) Greeting-blessing (H7965K, 2511-001) — the invocation of peace as the act of goodwill toward another; (3) Covenant peace (2508-002) — the relational condition between God and his people; (4) Peacemaking (G1517, Jam 3:18) — the capacity to make peace between parties; (5) G1514 eirēneuō — actively being at peace with all (Rom 12:18); (6) Eph 2:14-16 — Christ making peace between Jew and Gentile, creating one body. The relational dimension of peace is not peripheral but constitutive — the peace vocabulary is inherently directed toward-another.

The relational dimension of peace is not peripheral but constitutive — the peace vocabulary is inherently directed toward-another.

findings.finding_value: T3 maps inner faculty engagement; T4 maps relational directions. The synthesis: the relational capacity (T3.11) and the relational interfaces (T4) describe the same reality from different angles — the inner equipment (T3.11) and its external directions (T4). The conscience (T3.9 — gateway faculty for peace) connects directly to T4.2 (human to God): the human's movement toward God in confession (T4.2) is precisely the conscience-exercise that opens the peace-channel (T3.9). The volitional faculty (T3.6) connects to T4.3 (giving): genuine extension of peace requires authentic inner orientation (T4.3.2) — which is exactly the T3.6 finding that the giving of peace is a volitional act flowing from identity (Psa 120:7). Inner faculty and relational direction are structurally interconnected throughout.

The faculty map and the lexical-literary analysis describe the same biblical reality through different analytical lenses.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-060-003: T3 as a whole reveals that this characteristic engages virtually every inner faculty in the programme's 11-faculty model — the only consistent gap is creativity (T3.5, S across three prompts). The pat…
findings.finding_value: T3 as a whole reveals that this characteristic engages virtually every inner faculty in the programme's 11-faculty model — the only consistent gap is creativity (T3.5, S across three prompts). The pattern of engagement is not uniform: perception is engaged as precondition (God hears before giving); cognition is constituted (wisdom is given, not generated); memory is deepened (the narrative-temporal dimension of covenantal giving); affect is the source of giving (compassion, anger) and the target of transformation (mourning→gladness); volition is called forth and elevated (genuine giving cannot be coerced); agency is the bridge between disposition and act; moral evaluation both produces and is produced by the characteristic; conscience is engaged indirectly through Spirit-forming and prophetic warning; conscientiousness at the human apex is the full integration of all three (moral awareness, will, act). Relational capacity is intrinsic — every mode is two-party. What T3 reveals as a whole: faithfulness-as-giving is not a faculty-specific characteristic but a whole-person characteristic — it recruits and integrates all active faculties into a unified inner-being act. The creativity silence is the only dimension where the data cannot confirm engagement.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-002: The disposition-in-action definition (T1) requires the full inner faculty set to be operational (T3). The triadic architecture (source → act → object) maps directly onto faculty engagement: the source…
findings.finding_value: The disposition-in-action definition (T1) requires the full inner faculty set to be operational (T3). The triadic architecture (source → act → object) maps directly onto faculty engagement: the source requires affect (compassion/anger motivating), volition (choosing to give), and moral evaluation (assessing rightness); the act requires agency (initiating the transfer); the object requires relational capacity (attending to the other's condition). No individual faculty is the characteristic — but the characteristic integrates all of them in a coordinated whole. What this pair reveals: the definition of faithfulness-as-giving is not an abstract proposition but a faculty-integration event. The characteristic exists only when the full inner-being architecture — affective, volitional, agentive, relational — is engaged together. This is why the apex instance (Job 1:21, Isa 50:6) represents the highest form: all faculties operating in unified inner-being act.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-007: The constitutional locations (T2 — spirit, heart, soul, hidden inner parts, body) and the inner faculties (T3 — perception, cognition, memory, affect, volition, agency, moral evaluation, relational ca…
findings.finding_value: The constitutional locations (T2 — spirit, heart, soul, hidden inner parts, body) and the inner faculties (T3 — perception, cognition, memory, affect, volition, agency, moral evaluation, relational capacity) are not independent — they occupy the same inner-being territory from two different analytical perspectives. T2 asks where; T3 asks which faculty. Reading them together reveals: the heart (leb, T2.3) is the location of affect-volition integration (T3.4, T3.6) — where compassion (affect) determines giving (volitional act). The hidden inner parts (tukhoth, T2.5) are the constitutional home of the cognitive-formative faculty (T3.2 — the wisdom that is given there). The body (T2.6-7) is the somatic site of agentive expression (T3.7 — agency expresses through the body). The spirit (ruach, T2.1) is both the object of constitutive giving and the faculty whose depletion the eschatological giving addresses — connecting to the agency and relational capacity faculties that cannot operate from a faint spirit. What this pair reveals: constitutional location and faculty engagement are two descriptions of the same inner-being event. The characteristic is located constitutionally precisely where the relevant faculties operate.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-012: The faculty engagement pattern (T3 — perception, affect, volition, relational capacity all engaged) and the relational interface structure (T4 — God-to-human, human-to-God) reveal a faculty-interface …
findings.finding_value: The faculty engagement pattern (T3 — perception, affect, volition, relational capacity all engaged) and the relational interface structure (T4 — God-to-human, human-to-God) reveal a faculty-interface correspondence. In the God-to-human direction: divine hearing (T3.1 — perception) precedes compassionate giving (T4.1 — responsive basis); divine affect (T3.4 — rahamim, leb) determines the direction of giving (T4.1 — basis of extension); divine relational capacity (T3.11) is the prior orientation that makes the giving possible. In the human-to-God direction: human perception (Q2 — recognising divine sovereignty), human affect (blessing under loss), human volition (choosing to give glory), and human relational capacity (genuine correspondence) are all required for the giving to be genuine (T4.2 — inner posture). What this pair reveals: the relational interfaces are not external channels through which giving flows; they are relational events in which the inner faculties of both parties are engaged simultaneously and correspondingly. The correspondence is not mechanical but genuinely personal.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-014: The full-person faculty integration (T3 — all major faculties engaged) and the producing/produced-by structural position (T6) reveal that the characteristic's hub position is sustained by its faculty-…
findings.finding_value: The full-person faculty integration (T3 — all major faculties engaged) and the producing/produced-by structural position (T6) reveal that the characteristic's hub position is sustained by its faculty-integration property. It produces worship (R121, R176) because worship is the proper faculty response to received giving (T3 — perception of divine giving → affect of gratitude → volition of blessing → relational act of worship). It is produced by love (R103) and trust (R059) because love and trust are the inner-being sources from which the giving proceeds (T3 — affect motivates, volition commits, agency enacts). The causal sequences (T6.2) are faculty sequences in disguise: each sequential step is a faculty transition (suffering perceived → compassion moved → giving enacted). What this pair reveals: the structural network of this characteristic in the inner-being landscape is held together by faculty transitions. The characteristic is a hub because it is where multiple faculty-driven causal sequences converge and produce giving as their common expression.

Most comprehensively affected faculty. Gen 37:4: "they hated him and could not speak peacefully to him" — the direct consequence of hatred is the loss of peaceful speech, which is the basic instrument of relational connection. Pro 15:17: "a fattened ox and hatred with it" — the presence of hatred in a household makes even abundance miserable. The relational capacity, when organised by hatred, is not destroyed but inverted — the capacity for connection remains but is directed against rather than toward the other.

Contempt closes the relational capacity toward the despised object entirely. Isa 1:4: "they have despised the Holy One of Israel, they are utterly estranged" — contempt produces total estrangement. Unlike hatred which organises the relational capacity against the hated person, contempt removes the person from the relational field altogether — they are beneath regard, which means beneath relational engagement.

Abhorrence destroys the relational capacity toward the object completely through social abandonment. Job 19:19: "all my intimate friends abhor me, and those whom I loved have turned against me." Job 30:10: "they keep aloof from me; they do not hesitate to spit at the sight of me." This is more total than hatred (which at least maintains the hostile relational connection) and more total than contempt (which dismisses but does not necessarily avoid all contact). Abhorrence produces complete relational withdrawal.

Cruelty destroys the relational capacity in a specific way: it removes the person from the relational register of mercy and care, replacing it with domination and destruction. Lam 4:3: the daughter of the people has become "like the ostriches in the wilderness" — the nurturing relational capacity has been removed. The relational capacity remains in a functional sense (the cruel person relates to others) but has been stripped of the qualities that make relation genuinely human.

Reproach assaults the relational capacity from the outside: Psa 31:11: "those who see me in the street flee from me" — the social isolation reproach produces is total. But the relational capacity toward God intensifies: the extensive appeal literature of M06-E (Psa 69:13, Jer 15:15, Joel 2:17, Lam 5:1) shows the relational capacity toward God intensifying as the relational capacity toward other humans is stripped. The characteristic strips horizontal relationships and drives the person toward the vertical relationship.

The adversary relationship reorganises the relational capacity — the person in the adversary relationship turns their relational capacity toward God (appeal) and away from the adversary (opposition). The adversary relationship is itself a relational structure that generates the appeal-posture as the primary relational response.

Malice destroys the relational capacity toward the object of malice completely — the other exists only as the occasion for pleasure in their suffering. The relational capacity has been perverted into its opposite: what was made for genuine connection now orients toward the other's destruction with joy.

Yes — constitutively. Love is the relational characteristic par excellence: it is constituted by directed attachment toward another person. The great commandment (Mat 22:37 — Group 1542) names love toward God and neighbour as the two primary relational orientations of the person.

Yes — compassion is constitutively relational: triggered by the perceptive encounter with another's suffering, it produces action toward the sufferer. The directional asymmetry (compassion flows from greater to lesser; human never shows compassion toward God — Group 1596 analysis) confirms its relational structure.

Yes — mercy is inherently relational in its judicial frame: it always involves the greater (authority) and the lesser (guilty/helpless) in a defined relational position. Mat 5:7 (Group 1631): "the merciful shall receive mercy" — the reciprocal relational structure.

Yes — kindness (chrēstotēs) is explicitly relational: "he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil" (Luk 6:35 — Group 1469) — the relational reach extends to enemies. Goodness builds relational capacity (Rom 15:14 — Group 1097: "full of goodness, able to instruct one another").

Yes — gentleness is the most relationally-defined characteristic in its operational structure: it exists only as the quality of engagement with another person. Every major evidencing is relational in context (restoration, correction, defence, endurance, courtesy).

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** Yes — God's righteousness is the basis of covenant relationship: "I will be their God, in faithfulness and in righteousness" (Zec 8:8, VSG M26-A1-003). Righteousness is constitutive of the divine-human covenant — it defines how God relates. The appeal to God's righteousness (A1-004: "in your righteousness deliver me") is a relational act — it engages God through his character as the basis of appeal.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Yes — M26-A2-012 (righteousness extending outward to others) is entirely relational: guiding the neighbor (Pro 12:26), caring for the animals (Pro 12:10), doing justice and delivering from the oppressor (Jer 22:3), treating workers fairly (Mat 20:4), flowing as an ever-flowing stream (Amo 5:24). Righteousness in A2 is constitutively other-directed — it reaches out in relationship.

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** Yes — uprightness is expressed in truthful speech toward others and in the refusal to participate in systems of oppression (Isa 33:15). Uprightness is a relational quality — it determines how the person relates to others through honesty, truth-telling, and the refusal of corrupt relational practices (bribery, deceit).

**[C — Justification]** Yes — justification is fundamentally a relational act: it changes the person's standing before God. "Being justified by his grace we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life" (Tit 3:7) — the relational category of heir-status follows justification. The justified person stands in a new relational position before God.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** Yes — D is relational throughout: the wrong done is relational (one person wronging another), the cry for justice is relational (addressed to God), the commission is relational (the avenger serves the wronged on behalf of God). D engages relational capacity in all three of its relational dimensions.

**[E — Condemnation]** Yes — condemnation is a relational verdict: the judge and the condemned are in a specific relational position. The freedom from condemnation (Joh 8:10–11) is relational healing: Jesus' declaration ("neither do I condemn you") restores the woman to a relationship no longer defined by guilt-verdict.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** Yes — the reckoning faculty engages relational capacity indirectly: the person who reckons correctly ("count yourselves dead to sin, alive to God") reorients their relational standing — they now relate to God as one who is alive to him, not dead in sin. The reckoning act reframes the relational position.

**[G — Structural Opposites]** Yes — wickedness distorts relational capacity: it oppresses (Jer 22:3), exploits (Jer 22:13), persecutes (M26-A2-016: plotting against the righteous), and falsifies judicial relationships (Pro 17:15: justifying the wicked and condemning the righteous). Wickedness is relationally destructive.

**[CLUSTER]** E. Righteousness enables, deepens, and extends relational capacity — it enables right relationship with God (C: justified standing), other persons (A2-012: outward-flowing righteousness), and the community (A2-015: preservative presence). Wickedness impairs and destroys relational capacity at every level. The cluster portrait is of a characteristic that is constitutively relational in all its modes.

findings.finding_value: M01-A engages the relational capacity directly and pervasively. Reverential fear of God is the ground of human-human relationships throughout M01-A: Lev 19:14 (fear governing treatment of vulnerable others — relational ethics rooted in divine fear); Lev 25:17; 36; 43 (fear governing economic relationships and power-over-servant relationships); Gen 42:18 (Joseph's fear of God governing his treatment of his brothers — "an inner moral orientation that governs his treatment of others and gives him a reason not to exploit his power"). Fear of God governs relational conduct toward others precisely where human oversight is absent.

Psa 25:14 (anchor: "the fear of God positions a person for intimate **covenant relationship** with the Lord — those whose inner life is marked by this reverence receive God's **friendship** and knowledge of his covenant") is the most explicit human-divine relational statement. Fear enables genuine relationship with God.

M01-B's social fear (B-VCG-04) engages the relational capacity by distorting it: fear of social consequences governs relational behavior (Joh 9:22: parents' fear of the Jews governing their speech and deflecting questions to their son; Joh 19:38: Joseph's discipleship hidden because fear of the Jews governed his public behavior). (1) *Vertical relational damage*: Eze 39:23 — "they dealt so treacherously with me that I hid my face from them" — the divine-face-hiding is the ultimate relational consequence; 1Ch 10:13 — "Saul died for his breach of faith... he broke faith with the Lord" — death as the relational severance endpoint; (2) *Horizontal relational damage*: Lam 1:2 — "all her friends have dealt treacherously with her; they have become her enemies" — friends converted to enemies; Jer 12:6 — family members planning destruction behind friendly words; (3) *Marriage-covenant relational damage*: Mal 2:14 — "been faithless to the wife of your youth, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant" — the most intimate human bond broken.

**[CHAR-21]** E — Yes — through the discord-sowing and the creator-creature-inversion dimensions. (1) *Discord-sowing*: Pro 6:14 — "continually sowing discord" — perversity actively fractures relational bonds; Pro 16:28 — "a dishonest man spreads strife, and a whisperer separates close friends" — the perverse person's relational impact is strife and friendship-separation; (2) *Creator-creature relational inversion*: Isa 29:16 — the creature denying the creator — the fundamental God-human relationship is inverted; (3) *Covenant-forgetting*: Jer 3:21 — "perverted their way; forgotten the Lord their God" — the God-relationship is broken by the perversion.

**[CHAR-22]** E — The relational capacity is constitutively engaged — injustice is always done *toward* persons. (1) *Against persons directly*: Job 6:29 — "let no injustice be done" to Job — the relational victim-dimension; Psa 43:1 — "from the deceitful and unjust man deliver me" — the unjust as relational predator; (2) *Against social-relational structures*: Lev 19:15 — "you shall do no injustice in court" — the judicial relationship; Mic 3:10 — "build Zion with blood" — the civic-relational structure corrupted; (3) *Against the God-relationship*: Jer 2:5 — "what wrong did your fathers find in me that they went far from me?" — the relationship with God as the relational frame against which injustice operates.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. Confession is constitutively relational: it is always addressed to a relational other. VCG-01's individual confessions are predominantly God-directed ("against the Lord," "against you" — Dan 9:11; Luk 15:21). VCG-02's corporate confessions are community-enacted before God ("we have sinned against you" — Judg 10:10; 1Sa 7:6). Person-directed confessions appear: Exo 10:16 (against "the Lord your God, and against you" — both God and Moses), 2Sa 19:20 (Shimei to the king). Mat 27:4 (Judas to the priests). The relational capacity is engaged by the very directional structure of confession: it requires a recipient, and the choice of recipient (God vs person vs community) shapes what the confession is.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Relational capacity is engaged through its *vertical impairment*. Jer 2:35 — the false claim "I am innocent; surely his anger has turned from me" — the person believes they are in a good standing with God that does not actually exist. The relational capacity has been used to construct a false relational self-understanding: the person thinks they have a relationship with God that is untroubled, when in fact God has declared judgment. The false relational positioning is the consequence of conscience suppression operating on the vertical God-human relationship.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The relational capacity is engaged through its *persistent impairment*. The Kings who "did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam" maintained a damaged relationship with God across their reigns — the relationship was not ended by the refusal but was persistently maintained in a state of non-restoration. Neh 9:29 — "you warned them in order to turn them back to your law" — God's initiative was relational (turning them back toward himself through his law), but the refusal sustained the relational distance. Heb 10:26 — "there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins" — the foreclosure of the sacrifice is also a relational foreclosure: the mechanism by which the relational breach could be addressed is closed off.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The relational capacity is engaged through its *fundamental misdirection*. 2Ki 17:7 — "sinned against the Lord their God... and had feared other gods" — the relational capacity has been transferred: the reverence, allegiance, and relational commitment that belongs to the covenant Lord has been directed toward other gods. The relational capacity remains fully operative (they are in relationship — fearing, worshipping, serving) but its objects are wrong. 1Jo 3:6 — "no one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him" — the knowing of Christ is a relational-epistemic condition; its absence in the habitual sinner shows the relational capacity for God-knowledge is not operative.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The relational capacity is the *medium* of contagious sin: the authority relationship between leader and community is the channel through which the sinning direction is transmitted. The relational capacity is constitutively engaged in the characteristic: without the leader-community relational bond (the authority relationship), there is no transmission mechanism. 1Ki 16:2 — "I exalted you... leader over my people Israel" — the relational structure (leader over people) is named as the framework within which the sinning transmission occurs.

**[CHAR-8]** E — The relational capacity is the *medium* of political revolt: revolt requires a pre-existing governing relationship to break. 2Ki 1:1 — "Moab rebelled against Israel" — the suzerain-vassal relationship (Moab under Israel's authority) is the relational context within which revolt occurs. 1Ki 12:19 — "Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David" — the Davidic-covenantal governing relationship is the relational context. Political revolt is a relational act — it can only occur within and against a pre-existing relational structure of governing authority.

**[CHAR-9]** E — The relational capacity is constitutively engaged: sinful speech is always directed at a relational target. Mat 15:19 — slander is directed at persons (relational-horizontal). Rev 13:6 — "blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name and his dwelling" — directed at God (relational-vertical). Eph 4:31 — slander is listed among dispositions that damage the community's relational fabric. The characteristic cannot exist without a relational target; it is constitutively a relational-destructive act.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. Relational capacity is severely engaged and distorted. The characteristic manifests primarily as relational predation and deception: Psa 28:3 (VCG-08) — "speak peace with their neighbors while evil is in their hearts" — the relational surface is deceptive; Psa 37:12 — "gnashes his teeth at him" — relational hostility is the authentic posture beneath the surface; Pro 12:6 — "the words of the wicked lie in wait for blood" — speech as a relational weapon. The relational distortion extends to the divine-human relationship: Psa 15:29 — "the Lord is far from the wicked" — the vertical relational capacity is foreclosed; Pro 15:8 (VCG-09) — the wicked person's religious approach (sacrifice) is repugnant to God — the relational approach mechanism is corrupted. The community-wide relational consequence is documented at Pro 11:11 (city overthrown by wicked speech) and Hab 1:4 (justice perverted).

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes. Relational capacity is damaged and redirected by the characteristic. 3Jo 10 (vc=14454 — VCG-04) is the most concentrated evidence: Diotrephes's domineering malice involves refusal to welcome, obstruction of others, and expulsion from the church — the characteristic has converted the relational faculty into an instrument of control and harm. 2Jo 11 (vc=14453 — VCG-04): association with the wicked person communicates their wickedness — the relational capacity becomes a vector for the characteristic's spread. Eph 4:31 (vc=14365 — VCG-05): the cluster of relational vices (bitterness, wrath, anger, clamor, slander, malice) all emerging from the constitutional kakia — the relational sphere is the primary location where the characteristic's damage is expressed. 2Th 3:2 (vc=14450 — VCG-06): faithlessness grounds depravity — the relational-covenantal dimension (faith) is the ground the characteristic has corrupted.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. Relational capacity is extensively engaged. Pro 3:32 (vc=1686 — VCG-02): the devious person is excluded from divine confidence — the relational capacity for intimacy with God is foreclosed by the abominable inner character. Pro 29:27 (vc=65959 — VCG-01): "an unjust man is an abomination to the righteous" — the relational incompatibility between the abominable and the upright operates at the human-horizontal level; they are mutually repulsive. Mal 2:11 (vc=66004 — VCG-04): faithless mixed devotion — covenant betrayal as abomination — shows the covenantal relational bond shattered by abominable inner choice. Eze 44:13 (vc=66003 — VCG-04): those who committed abominations are barred from sacred service — their relational access to the holy is permanently curtailed.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes. Relational capacity is perverted and damaged. Deu 32:16 (vc=65938 — VCG-02): "they stirred him to jealousy with strange gods; with abominations they provoked him to anger" — the covenant relationship with God is the primary relational domain damaged. Eze 5:11 (vc=65969 — VCG-05): "I will withdraw" — the divine-human relational capacity is severed by idolatrous abomination. Mal 2:11 parallel structure (from CHAR-3 corpus but applicable): faithless devotion as a covenant-betrayal. Eze 6:9 (vc=1697 — VCG-05): "their whoring heart that has departed from me" — the relational language of marriage-covenant is used: idolatrous abomination is experienced as relational infidelity, a whoring away from God.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes. The relational capacity is comprehensively damaged and weaponised. Psa 28:3 (vc=38232 — VCG-03): "workers of evil, who speak peace with their neighbors while evil is in their hearts" — the relational capacity for authentic connection is replaced by deceptive surface-relational performance; the neighbor relationship is instrumentalised as cover for inner evil. Psa 14:4 (vc=38229 — VCG-03): "evildoers who eat up my people" — the relational capacity for care is inverted into predatory consumption. Psa 55:3 (vc=38188 — VCG-01): enemies "drop trouble upon me, and in anger they bear a grudge" — sustained grudge as the relational posture of sustained iniquity against others.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes. The relational capacity is comprehensively damaged or weaponised. For the God-human relationship (VCG-01): Rev 16:9/11/21 (VCG-01) — the divine-human relationship is the direct target of the cursing; the characteristic severs the person from any genuine movement toward God by converting encounter with God (even judgment) into an occasion for increased relational hostility. For the human-human relationship (VCG-02/03): 1Cor 4:13 (vc=14351 — VCG-02): slander reduces the slandered to "the scum of the world, the refuse of all things" — the relational capacity for honest mutual regard is destroyed through defamation; 1Pe 2:12 (vc=14377 — VCG-03): false accusation as evildoers — the relational capacity for accurate communal recognition of the person is perverted into false hostile identification.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All six characteristics comprehensively damage relational capacity, confirming that M10b inner evil is inherently anti-relational. The divine-human relational impact is documented in every characteristic: Char 1 (cannot stand in divine presence — Psa 5:4), Char 2 (alienated from the life of God — Eph 4:18), Char 3 (excluded from divine confidence — Pro 3:32), Char 4 (divine presence withdraws — Eze 5:11), Char 5 (divine ear closed — Psa 66:18), Char 6 (divine glory withheld — Rev 16:9). The human-human relational impact: Char 5 (evildoers eating up the people — Psa 14:4), Char 6 (false accusation as hostile relational weapon — 1Pe 2:12), Chars 1 and 3 (mutual abomination of wicked and righteous — Pro 29:27). The cluster reveals that M10b characteristics damage both vertical (divine-human) and horizontal (human-human) relational capacity.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, substantially. The characteristic structures relational capacity in both its impairment and its positive expression. Impairment: the defilement-state severs or restricts relational participation — the person with skin disease dwells alone outside the camp (Lev 13:46, M10c-B-VCG-03); defiling persons are sent out of the camp (Num 5:2, M10c-A-VCG-07); corpse-contact defilement bars the person from communal worship (Num 9:6, M10c-A-VCG-07). The characteristic structurally limits the relational scope of the defiled person within the covenant community. Positive expression: the duty not to transmit one's defilement state (Lev 15:11, M10c-A-VCG-06 — washing hands before contact) and the public self-declaration (Lev 13:45, M10c-B-VCG-03) are relational acts that protect others. The 1Cor 7:14 (M10c-B-VCG-05) covenantal-status use shows the characteristic's relational scope extending to family relationships — the believing spouse's holiness affects the unbelieving spouse and children.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes. The characteristic operates in the relational domain in several ways. Eph 5:5 (VCG-04): the impure person "has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God" — the characteristic severs the relational capacity toward God at its most fundamental level (covenantal inheritance). 2Cor 6:17 (VCG-03): "go out from their midst, and be separate from them... then I will welcome you" — the unclean condition blocks divine welcome; separation from the defiling environment is the condition for divine relational restoration. Mat 23:27 (VCG-04): the hypocrites' inner defilement is masked from human relational perception — they appear relationally acceptable to others while their inner condition makes them morally inaccessible. The characteristic thus operates both vertically (God-human relational barrier) and horizontally (human-human relational deception).

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, as its primary domain. The characteristic is constitutively relational — it arises from the betrayal of covenantal relationships (VCG-01: sexual betrayal of marriage and family covenant), desecrates the community's relationship with its sacred environment (VCG-03/04), and severs the covenantal relationship with God (Eze 5:11 — divine withdrawal; Eze 20:31 — God refuses to be inquired of). Num 5:27-28 (VCG-01) shows the most direct relational engagement: the ordeal law is the mechanism for adjudicating whether the covenantal marital relationship has been violated; the defilement-state is the objective marker of that relational betrayal.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes, as its primary social consequence. The characteristic severs the person's relational capacity: Mar 5:2 (VCG-01) — "utterly cut off from clean, communal life"; Mar 9:25 (VCG-01) — hearing suppressed (cannot receive others' speech); Mar 1:23 (VCG-01) — the synagogue community is disrupted. Relational severance is comprehensive: the person cannot maintain normal social bonds (Mar 5:2), cannot engage in family life (Luk 9:42 — the boy must be "given back to his father"), and cannot participate in worship (Mar 1:23).

**[CLUSTER]** E — All four characteristics engage the relational capacity, confirming the M10c cluster as constitutively relational — every register of defilement disrupts the person's relational existence. Characteristic 1 structures relational capacity through impairment (exclusion from community and worship — Lev 13:46, Num 9:7) and through relational responsibility (duty not to transmit — Lev 15:11; 1Cor 7:14 — the believing spouse's holiness affecting the family). Characteristic 2 impairs relational capacity vertically (Eph 5:5 — no inheritance in the kingdom) and corrupts it horizontally (Mat 23:27 — concealment of inner defilement behind acceptable exterior). Characteristic 3 damages relational capacity at every level comprehensively: covenantal marital bonds (Num 5 ordeal), corporate-divine covenant (Eze 20:31 — God refusing inquiry), community-land bond (Mic 2:10), community-sanctuary bond (Eze 5:11), community-nations bond (Lam 1:17/4:15). Characteristic 4 severs communal belonging as its primary social consequence (Mar 5:2 — "utterly cut off from clean, communal life"; Mar 9:25 — hearing suppressed, preventing reception of others' speech).

findings.session_b_note:
**Enables relational capacity:** F-003 — vertical reception enables horizontal extension. The person who has received divine forgiveness has an expanded relational capacity — they can now extend to others what they have received. OBS-064-029: the love-orientation produced by received forgiveness is itself a relational capacity — a genuine disposition toward others.

**Restores relational capacity:** F-008 — forgiveness makes possible "a relationship that would otherwise be closed or broken." Guilt and grievance close relational capacity; forgiveness reopens it. The relational capacity is not created ex nihilo but restored to function.

**Impairs relational capacity (when withheld):** OBS-064-001 — "the absence of forgiveness poisons the inner life of the withholder." The poisoning is, among other things, a relational impairment — the withholder's relational capacity is constrained by the retained grievance, both in the specific relationship (the offender) and potentially more broadly (the inner life generally).

findings.session_b_note:
**Compassion expands relational capacity beyond natural boundaries:** The Good Samaritan pattern is the clearest evidence: compassion extends relational capacity to those outside the natural in-group (the wounded Jew, the stranger). Mark 1:41 — compassion toward the leper — crosses the ritual-impurity boundary. The compassion-characteristic enables the person to relate genuinely across boundaries that would otherwise exclude.

**Compassion deepens relational capacity through solidarity:** Sumpaschō (1 Cor 12:26 — "if one member suffers, all suffer together") names the deepest form of relational connection within the community: a genuine constitutional solidarity in which the suffering of one is felt by all. Compassion deepens relational capacity to the point where the boundary between self and other becomes permeable at the affective level — the other's suffering becomes one's own inner experience.

**Compassion does not bypass relational capacity:** The data shows no evidence of compassion operating in isolation from genuine relational engagement. Even the metriopatheō (moderated compassion) of Heb 5:2 is a form of deepened relational engagement — not a distancing strategy but a calibrated presence. Compassion is never described as operating at a distance or substituting for genuine relational contact.

**The eusplanchnos (tender heart) as the relational pre-condition:** The tender heart of 1 Pet 3:8 names the inner quality that makes genuine relational capacity possible. Without this constitutional openness, compassion cannot arise and relational capacity remains closed or defended. The tender heart is the relational pre-condition that compassion both requires and, over time, deepens.

findings.session_b_note:
Contrition **restores and deepens** relational capacity in the vertical direction. The contrite posture is the one that draws divine nearness (Psa 34:18), divine dwelling (Isa 57:15), and divine attention (Isa 66:2) — the relational connection between God and the human person is re-established or deepened through the contrite condition. The hardened posture (Jer 44:10) corresponds to relational distance from God.

In the horizontal direction, the data is insufficient to determine whether contrition deepens or restores relational capacity toward other humans. The corporate instance (Psa 44:19) involves shared suffering rather than relational reconnection between individuals. The Psa 51 context (sins against Bathsheba/Uriah implicit) does not include verses that address horizontal relational restoration.

*New finding: contrition specifically restores and deepens vertical relational capacity — the God-human connection is the primary relational dimension engaged. Horizontal relational impact is a gap.*

findings.session_b_note:
**Enabling and deepening:** Righteous fellowship (group 873-001, 873-002, 7566-001) actively deepens the person's relational capacity — being in genuine fellowship with God and with others expands the person's constitutional capacity for genuine connection. The horizontal is grounded in and deepened by the vertical (1Jo 1:3: *our fellowship is with the Father and his Son*).

**Impairing:** Idolatrous joining (Hos 4:17), wrong-fellowship moral alignment (Isa 1:23), and covenantal faithlessness (Mal 2:14) all impair relational capacity — the joining capacity is engaged but misdirected or broken, leaving the relational faculty damaged rather than deepened.

**New finding:** The instruction notes (Section 9, T3.11) that a productive distinction exists between characteristics that *build/sustain* relational connection and those that *restore/repair* it. Fellowship falls into both categories: righteous fellowship builds and sustains relational capacity (Psa 119:63, 873-001, 873-002), while the wound-fellowship vocabulary (Pro 20:30, Isa 53:5) and the proclamatory-fellowship chain (1Jo 1:3) carry a restorative dimension — fellowship is the instrument through which broken relational states (separation, corruption, idolatrous bondage) are restored to genuine participation.

findings.session_b_note: Goodness enables and deepens relational capacity. The Spirit-produced chrēstotēs (886-002) is itself a relational capacity — it is the inner disposition enabling generous engagement toward others. Rom 15:14's "able to instruct one another" names a relational capacity (mutual edification) produced by goodness. The giving of goodness toward others (Col 3:12 — put on kindness; Mic 6:8 — love kindness and do justice) requires and develops relational capacity. Goodness in its distorted or absent form impairs relational capacity: Rom 3:12 names the unregenerate condition as one of total goodness-absence — which implies relational incapacity for genuine goodness toward others. The Haman instance (Est 5:9) shows how goodness-without-root produces a fragile inner state that makes genuine relational goodness toward others unstable. (OBS-067-OBS-017, OBS-067-OBS-039, OBS-067-OBS-046)

findings.session_b_note: Love **enables, deepens, and restores** relational capacity — it is the primary characteristic that constitutes and sustains the relational faculty. Enabling: Joh 13:34 (OBS-103-145) — love constitutes the new relational community from scratch; the love-commandment creates a relational structure that did not exist before it. Deepening: Joh 15:15 (OBS-103-052) — love deepens the disciple relationship from servant-level to friend-level through knowledge-disclosure; love's deepening of the bond changes its constitutional character. Restoring: Luk 15:20 (OBS-103-057) — the father's love restores the broken son-relationship through compassion and embrace. Joh 21:17 (OBS-103-153) — Jesus' love restores Peter's relational capacity after denial. Disordered love impairs relational capacity: love-of-self (filautos — OBS-103-137) produces the self-enclosed orientation that cannot genuinely connect to another.

findings.session_b_note: Mercy enables and constitutes relational capacity in several distinct ways: (1) Mercy enables face-to-face access (Gen 32:20 — the appeasement-mercy enables Jacob to see Esau's face). (2) Mercy constitutes community (1Pe 2:10 — mercy reception constitutes "God's people"). (3) Heb 2:17 (OBS-111-033) — Christ's mercy-capacity was enabled by incarnational solidarity; mercy-capacity requires experiential solidarity. *New finding: mercy is the foundational enabler of relational capacity — it creates the conditions under which genuine face-to-face encounter, community membership, and compassionate extension are possible.* OBS-111-033, OBS-111-040, OBS-111-053.

findings.finding_value: Reading T3 as a whole reveals mercy as a faculty-activating characteristic — it does not primarily engage one or two faculties but activates the inner-being faculty system comprehensively. The pattern: mercy enables perception (face-access), opens cognition in both directions (upward to divine knowledge; downward to self-knowledge), creates an asymmetric memory structure (divine forgetting / human remembering), engages affect as its native register, expands volition (received mercy increases mercy-capacity), demands agency, reframes moral evaluation (mercy as higher-order moral evaluation), presupposes and deepens conscience, enables conscientiousness, and constitutes relational capacity. The single faculty not evidenced is creativity (T3.5.2 — S status). Reading T3 together: mercy is characterised by faculty-comprehensiveness; its absence (mercilessness in Rom 1:31) appears alongside affective incapacity (*astorgos*) and other faculty-failures — confirming that mercy's presence is correlated with full faculty activation and its absence with faculty contraction.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-009: T1 identifies the enabling conditions for mercy-reception (guilt-awareness, humility, persistence, soul-affliction) and T3 maps mercy's faculty engagements. Reading T1 and T3 together: the enabling co…
findings.finding_value: T1 identifies the enabling conditions for mercy-reception (guilt-awareness, humility, persistence, soul-affliction) and T3 maps mercy's faculty engagements. Reading T1 and T3 together: the enabling conditions for mercy-reception (T1) are precisely the conditions that require the full faculty activation identified in T3. Guilt-awareness requires conscience (T3.9) and moral evaluation (T3.8); humility requires affect (T3.4) and embodied posture; persistence requires volition (T3.6) and agency (T3.7); soul-affliction requires affect (T3.4) and relational capacity (T3.11). T1's enabling conditions are T3's faculty activation in a single moment — mercy-reception requires the whole inner faculty system to be engaged.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-014: T2 maps mercy's constitutional locations (soul, mind, heart, body, spirit-soul interface) and T3 maps its faculty engagements. Reading together: the constitutional locations and the faculty engagement…
findings.finding_value: T2 maps mercy's constitutional locations (soul, mind, heart, body, spirit-soul interface) and T3 maps its faculty engagements. Reading together: the constitutional locations and the faculty engagements are co-extensive. Soul-level location (T2) corresponds to conscience and moral evaluation faculty engagement (T3) — the soul is where guilt resides and where conscience/moral evaluation operate. Mind-level location (T2, memory-erasure) corresponds to memory faculty engagement (T3, asymmetric memory structure). Heart/splanchna location (T2) corresponds to affect faculty (T3). The receiving-before-generating origin (T2) corresponds to relational capacity as foundational enabler (T3.11). T2 and T3 together: constitutional location and faculty engagement are two descriptions of the same inner-being reality — where mercy operates constitutionally (T2) is where it activates faculties (T3).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-019: T3 shows mercy activating the full faculty system (perception, cognition, memory, affect, volition, agency, moral evaluation, conscience, conscientiousness, relational capacity) and T4 shows mercy ope…
findings.finding_value: T3 shows mercy activating the full faculty system (perception, cognition, memory, affect, volition, agency, moral evaluation, conscience, conscientiousness, relational capacity) and T4 shows mercy operating across three relational directions (God→human, human→God, human→human). Reading together: the faculty activations in T3 are the inner capacities that each T4 relational direction requires. God→human mercy (T4.1) engages mercy's receptive faculty complex — conscience, moral evaluation, affect, memory (asymmetric structure). Human→God mercy (T4.2 — mercy-seeking) engages volition, agency, affect, conscience, and perception (face-toward-God). Human→human mercy (T4.3) engages moral evaluation, agency, volition, and relational capacity. The three relational directions of T4 are served by the specific faculty subsets activated in T3.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-021: T3 shows mercy as a faculty-comprehensive characteristic and T6 shows mercy as a structurally integrative hub characteristic. Reading together: the faculty-comprehensiveness (T3) is what enables the s…
findings.finding_value: T3 shows mercy as a faculty-comprehensive characteristic and T6 shows mercy as a structurally integrative hub characteristic. Reading together: the faculty-comprehensiveness (T3) is what enables the structural hub position (T6). A characteristic that activates all (or nearly all) inner faculties is positioned to connect to the widest range of adjacent characteristics — which is exactly what T6's co-occurrence and cross-registry data shows. Mercy's structural hub position in T6 is the cross-registry expression of its faculty-comprehensiveness in T3. The one missing faculty (creativity, T3.5.2 — S) corresponds to the one connection not evidenced in T6 — creative production is not a named output of mercy in the cross-registry data.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-030-003: Reading T3 as a whole reveals that contrition engages virtually every inner faculty — with one exception (creativity, T3.5 — data silent). The pattern across the engaged faculties is consistent: contr…
findings.finding_value: Reading T3 as a whole reveals that contrition engages virtually every inner faculty — with one exception (creativity, T3.5 — data silent). The pattern across the engaged faculties is consistent: contrition deepens and opens rather than impairs or bypasses. It deepens perception (opens to divine address), deepens cognition (enables accurate self-knowledge), deepens affect (makes grief and longing both fuller), redirects volition (from self-assertion to God-direction), converts agency (from self-directed to God-seeking), deepens moral evaluation (requires and enables accurate self-assessment), deepens conscience (allows conscience's verdict to reach the spirit/heart), deepens conscientiousness (grounds it in inner reality rather than performance), and enables relational capacity (specifically for divine nearness). The single thread running through all faculty engagements is: contrition removes self-protective barriers — it is the inner-being event in which every protective reflex is dissolved, leaving the person fully exposed and open. This is why it enables rather than impairs every faculty: openness is the condition in which all faculties function most truthfully.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-030-019: The faculty tier (T3) establishes that contrition opens every engaged faculty toward God (perception deepened for divine address, volition redirected toward God, agency converted to God-seeking, relat…
findings.finding_value: The faculty tier (T3) establishes that contrition opens every engaged faculty toward God (perception deepened for divine address, volition redirected toward God, agency converted to God-seeking, relational capacity enabled for divine nearness); the relational tier (T4) shows that the primary relational direction is indeed toward God. T3 and T4 are aligned: the faculty effects all point in the same direction that T4's relational analysis names as the primary direction. The faculties do not pull in multiple directions — they converge on the vertical relational axis. This convergence is analytically significant: it means contrition is constitutively God-directed at the faculty level, not merely structurally positioned toward God.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-003: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion re…
findings.finding_value: T3 reveals two structurally distinctive findings about compassion's faculty engagement. First, creativity is entirely silent (three S ratings) — the most informative absence in the tier: compassion responds, it does not originate or create. It is the most responsive of the faculties-engaging characteristics. Second, affect and moral action are structurally unified in compassion — not sequentially related but simultaneous. Affect is the mechanism of movement (splanchnizō is both the felt inner event and the cause of the action), not a precursor or accompaniment. This is unique among the characteristics reviewed: in most other registries, affect and volition are distinguishable stages; in compassion, the felt movement is already the morally motivated action beginning. A third distinctive finding: compassion converts moral knowledge into motivated action — it is the motivational ground of conscientiousness, not a product of it. The conscience faculty engagement reveals compassion as conscience-healing: it addresses the pitiable condition that conscience perceives as a moral claim, resolving the tension between moral knowledge and moral incapacity. The three relational modes (building/sustaining — chesed; restoring/repairing — splanchnizō; extending across difference — Good Samaritan) are a new finding not in the instruction typology.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-019: T3's perceptive-trigger finding (compassion is activated by sight — splanchnizō is perceptively dependent) and T4's scope-by-need finding (scope is determined by perceived need, not covenantal standin…
findings.finding_value: T3's perceptive-trigger finding (compassion is activated by sight — splanchnizō is perceptively dependent) and T4's scope-by-need finding (scope is determined by perceived need, not covenantal standing) are the same finding from two analytical perspectives. T3 names the faculty (perception) and its function (triggering compassion by seeing the pitiable condition); T4 names the relational consequence (scope defined by what is seen). The cross-boundary extension in T4 (Nineveh, Samaritan/Jew) is the relational expression of T3's merit-independence: compassion is perceptively dependent (it must see the need) but merit-independent (it does not assess the moral standing of the one seen). The three relational modes in T3.11 (building/sustaining, restoring/repairing, extending across difference) correspond precisely to T4's chesed/splanchnizō/cross-boundary structure.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-003: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked …
findings.finding_value: T3 produces four structurally significant findings about grace's faculty engagement. First, grace is agency-constituting rather than agency-replacing: 1Cor 15:10 holds in explicit paradox — "I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I but the grace of God that is with me." Agency is not displaced but constituted by grace. This relationship holds in paradox that the T3.6 prompt options (enable/deepen/bypass/impair) cannot accommodate — a prompt design limitation noted for catalogue revision. Second, grace produces moral clarity (T3.8 — sharpens moral evaluation rather than bypassing it): the person who recognises grace has made a precise moral evaluation (they know they received what they did not deserve). Third, grace and conscience are mutually necessary: grace is the condition within which conscience can operate fully without destroying the person; conscience without grace produces condemnation; grace without conscience produces presumption (T3.9). Fourth, grace is the primary relational faculty developer in the registry's evidence — it reaches every relational register (vertical access, horizontal forgiving, speech-grace) and enables each one. Creativity (T3.5) is the one genuinely silent faculty — not an impairment but a non-engagement: grace receives and constitutes, it does not create.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-019: T3's agency-constituting finding (grace constitutes rather than replaces agency — 1Cor 15:10) and T4's human-to-God direction (supplication as the human posture of appeal — requiring genuine human age…
findings.finding_value: T3's agency-constituting finding (grace constitutes rather than replaces agency — 1Cor 15:10) and T4's human-to-God direction (supplication as the human posture of appeal — requiring genuine human agency in the act of plea) are structurally aligned. The constituted agency (T3.7) is precisely the agency that supplication requires: the creature must genuinely appeal, not merely receive passively. T3's finding that grace and conscience are mutually necessary (T3.9) corresponds to T4's relational-access finding: grace transforms the threshold of human-to-God approach (prosagōgē — SD035) from impassable to open, which is the relational expression of T3.9's constitutional finding that grace creates the condition within which conscience can operate fully without destruction. T3 names the inner-being event; T4 names the relational consequence of the same event.

findings.session_b_note: Covenant fundamentally enables and sustains relational capacity — it is the structure that makes sustained, reliable, deepening connection possible. Without covenant, relational connection is vulnerable to dissolution — it has no formal structure to hold it across time and circumstances. With covenant, relational capacity is both protected (the formal bond) and cultivated (the sustained engagement within the bond produces deeper knowing and love). The new covenant specifically deepens relational capacity between God and human: "they shall all know me" (Jer 31:34 — OBS-034-040) names an intimate personal knowing across all persons within the covenant — the relational capacity for knowing God is democratised and deepened simultaneously. Covenant breach impairs relational capacity — the divorce metaphor (OBS-034-043) and covenantal exclusion (OBS-034-060) show that broken or absent covenant produces relational rupture and desolation.

findings.session_b_note: Kindness is one of the primary characteristics that builds and sustains relational connection — it constitutes relationships in their quality, not merely accompanies them. Chesed is the inner substance of covenant relationship [XREG: H2617A, OBS-099-083]. The im.ma.di groups frame kindness as the quality making relational presence real rather than nominal [OBS-099-065–071]. 1Sa 20:14 — request for relational faithfulness to be maintained into the future [OBS-099-070]. The chasid's relational quality is his defining identity before God and others [XREG: H2623, OBS-099-094]. The person without kindness has relationships in form but not in substance.

findings.session_b_note: Authentic peace deeply enables and deepens relational capacity. Evidence: (1) 1Ch 12:17 — the sha.lom-friendship produces heart-union; (2) Eph 2:14-16 — Christ's peace breaks down the "dividing wall of hostility" and creates one body from two peoples — peace is the engine of the most dramatic relational restoration in the NT; (3) Jer 29:7 — seeking the welfare of the exile city requires expanding relational capacity to include the former enemy's community; (4) 1Sa 25:6 (2511-001) — the greeting-blessing as an act of relational goodwill. Conversely: peacelessness impairs relational capacity — Gen 37:4 ("they hated him and could not speak peacefully to him") — the absence of sha.lom-orientation makes genuine relational connection impossible; Jer 20:10 (anshei sha.lom who betray) — false sha.lom destroys relational capacity through betrayal. The instruction note for T3.11 distinguishes characteristics that build/sustain connection from those that restore/repair it — this registry does both: shalom builds connection (friendship, greeting, covenant) and restores broken connection (Eph 2:14).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-117-012: T3 maps inner faculty engagement; T4 maps relational directions. The synthesis: the relational capacity (T3.11) and the relational interfaces (T4) describe the same reality from different angles — the…
findings.finding_value: T3 maps inner faculty engagement; T4 maps relational directions. The synthesis: the relational capacity (T3.11) and the relational interfaces (T4) describe the same reality from different angles — the inner equipment (T3.11) and its external directions (T4). The conscience (T3.9 — gateway faculty for peace) connects directly to T4.2 (human to God): the human's movement toward God in confession (T4.2) is precisely the conscience-exercise that opens the peace-channel (T3.9). The volitional faculty (T3.6) connects to T4.3 (giving): genuine extension of peace requires authentic inner orientation (T4.3.2) — which is exactly the T3.6 finding that the giving of peace is a volitional act flowing from identity (Psa 120:7). Inner faculty and relational direction are structurally interconnected throughout.

findings.session_b_note: The characteristic enables and restores relational capacity. The eschatological giving (Hos 2:15, OBS-060-050) directly restores relational responsiveness: "she shall answer" — the restored capacity to respond to God is the measure of the transformation. Relational capacity was lost (Israel had abandoned God); the eschatological giving restores it. The Spirit-giving (Neh 9:20) enables the formative capacity that undergirds relational wisdom. The covenantal giving (872-001) sustains the relational framework within which genuine connection is possible: the covenant is the relational structure that God's giving establishes and maintains. The characteristic does not impair relational capacity in any evidenced instance; where the relational correspondence breaks (glory withheld from God), the impairment is on the human side, not produced by the characteristic itself.

Relational capacity is the most universally and centrally engaged faculty across all seven sub-groups — equal in universality with volition and agency. This is the primary cluster-level faculty finding: M05's characteristics all constitute, enable, or express the relational capacity of the inner person. The cluster as a whole is the relational-capacity cluster — its characteristics are the inner equipment for genuine engagement with God and with other human persons. The variations between sub-groups are in the mode of relational engagement: love as directed attachment; compassion as responsive inner movement; mercy as authority-toward-helplessness; goodness as moral-generative expression; gentleness as non-coercive mode; comfort as grief-directed relief; fellowship as shared participation.
VCG05 (shared orientation): relational harmony as a mode of wisdom expression.

findings.finding_value: Ordered character-wealth and the inner life beyond material circumstance enable and expand relational capacity. M46-C recognises the relational equality before God that wealth does not create or destroy. M46-D actively extends relational capacity through giving, releasing, and the Christological pattern of self-impoverishment for others' enrichment.

findings.finding_value: M01-A **enables and deepens** relational capacity. Fear of God is the ground of trustworthy, just, and generous relational conduct (Exo 18:21: fear of God as an inner moral quality qualifying men for leadership paired with trustworthiness; Act 10:2: Cornelius's fear of God expressing outwardly in "generous almsgiving and continual prayer"). Fear of God produces the inner orientation from which genuine other-regard flows.

Social fear **impairs** relational capacity by substituting crowd-fear for genuine other-care: Gal 2:12 (Peter's withdrawal damaging the relational community); Joh 9:22 (parents' fear-governed deflection damaging their son's witness). Social fear produces relational withdrawal, inauthenticity, and betrayal.

Dismay **impairs** relational capacity: Psa 31:11 (M01-B-VCG-04: "the psalmist has become an object of dread to his acquaintances — his suffering causes those who know him to recoil in alarm, so that dread **operates as a social and relational rupture**"). Dismay drives others away and disrupts relationship.

Ordered fear (M01-A) enables relational depth; social fear (M01-B-VCG-04) impairs relational authenticity; dismay (M01-D) ruptures relational bonds; pastoral anxiety (M01-F-VCG-05) flows from and expresses genuine relational care. The cluster's relational picture is complex and differentiated.

Disordered anger impairs relational capacity: M02-F-VCG-01 corpus shows quarreling as a form of relational destruction (1Cor 1:11 — divisive inner conflict in community relationships; Gal 5:20 — hostile conflict as a work of the flesh). Est 3:5 (M02-B-VCG-03): Haman's rage taking possession of him locks his entire relational focus on one object (Mordecai's destruction) — relational capacity narrows to a single destructive aim.

1Cor 13:5 (M02-D-VCG-03): love's refusal to be provoked shows that the mature relational capacity governs and moderates the anger-response. The development of relational capacity (toward love's pattern) deepens the ability to receive provocation without anger. Inversely, anger's governance deepens relational capacity.

Grief deepens relational capacity: commanded weeping-with (Rom 12:15 — M03-A-VCG-05) shows that entering into another's grief expands relational capacity by extending empathic solidarity. The Corinthians' mourning becoming a sign of repentance and relational restoration (2Cor 7:7 — M03-B-VCG-04) shows grief restoring damaged relational bonds. Grief can also signal the depth of relational capacity — the depth of David's grief for Absalom (2Sa 18:33 — M03-A-VCG-01) reveals the depth of his relational bond. Where grief is absent in contexts requiring it, relational capacity may be impaired (1Cor 5:2 — M03-B-VCG-04; Amo 6:6 — BOUNDARY).
